en: Preface to the *Commentary on the Essentials of the Amitābha Sūtra*:
To speak briefly, the essential heart-essence of all Buddhas is the wondrous gateway of the Pure Land and its inconceivable realm.

It is likewise the secret marrow of the Dharma-treasury and the compass for Bodhisattvas. Indeed, it is because sentient beings are deluded and turn their backs upon their inherently existing homeland.
This is the place of peace and bliss. Therefore, our Śākyamuni, the Greatly Compassionate and Benevolent Honored One, could not bear to look on with indifference;

he employed the four minds and laid bare his very heart and liver. Taking this Dharma of the directly realized Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment, he pointed it out directly to people, like bestowing a *maṇi* jewel upon a destitute son, or like granting a *gāthā* to one suffering from a grave illness. He cuts across birth and death abruptly and with urgency.
Rescuing the deluded masses, from time immemorial, the benefit obtained has been exceptionally profound;

those who attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss are as numerous as the dust motes of the great trichiliocosm, making it difficult even to mention the number of those transformed and sent there. Although the ocean-treasury of the scriptures is vast and boundless, for forty-nine years no other special teaching was revealed.
Thus, it can be seen that the single sutra of Amitābha is the light within the darkness of the nine realms.
The Lamp Torch: A Great Bridge to the Other Shore. Since the Dharma stream first shook the East, the Lotus School was first established by Master Huiyuan during the Jin dynasty.

From the time of its founding until the flourishing propagation and extensive commentaries of the various Patriarchs of the Pure Land tradition, they have appeared like the wind throughout successive generations;

their ranks stand in solemn array, too numerous to be fully enumerated. At the end of the Ming dynasty, the Elder of Lingfeng suddenly appeared in this turbid world, becoming especially a beacon of light.
A single blue lotus emerges from his dwelling; amidst the paths of the lost, he reveals the mass of Great Wisdom.

Like the sun filling the nine heavens, it puts to rest the visions of the blind-born and the one-eyed, leaving no darkness unbroken. He prunes away redundant texts to compose this Essential Commentary, like using a wedge to remove a wedge.
That nothing remains unincorporated—how could this not be the work of a master craftsman of sublime capability? Why, then, is the title now being transcribed?

It is because this is the work of Dharma Master Liang of Zifu Jingye Temple; he deeply laments that those who have recently entered the path possess meager wisdom and shallow insight, that their learning is inferior and their understanding sparse, making it difficult for them to penetrate the essential heart-teachings of the Elder Ouyi. Fearing that the ignorant and deluded might sink into oblivion...

It falls away from all heterodox views. While clinging to principle and neglecting phenomena, [the Buddha] specifically employed skillful means and non-active wondrous wisdom to add flowers upon brocade, guiding the deluded and revealing the level path.
This *Jiaolu* (Excerpts on the Path of Awakening) clarifies the profound meaning;

it explains both nature and cultivation, and its excellent integration is truly marvelous. These sincere words from the Golden Mouth accord with the teachings of the Patriarchs; thus, my purpose is fulfilled.

In my leisure time from sitting meditation, I have compiled these writings into a volume. My friend requested that I provide a preface; yet, considering my own lack of ability, I am ashamed of my own emptiness.
With a mouth that is stammering and a tongue that is dull, how could I dare to wield an axe at the gate of Ban? However, as the matter could not be avoided, I have forced myself to summon my courage.
Reflecting deeply upon it, I felt that one cannot discard the Dharma because of a person’s limitations. Thus, I respectfully request the aid of the brush (Mao Ying) and paper (Chu Xian).
Born, he eavesdropped on their conversation to provide supportive words.
I look up with hope that you, O noble and wise one, will circulate this commentary, so that the single-blooded heart of Master Liang may not be obscured.

Furthermore, I pray that each person may swiftly reach the profound palace beyond the mundane shell, personally arrive at the divine abode of peaceful wisdom, and securely undergo transformation in the Lotus Land.
This is the preface. Written with reverent care on the twenty-first day of the first month of summer in the thirtieth year of the Daoguang era,
by the practitioner of Pure Land, Liàn-cūn, at the Red Lotus Mountain (Hóngluó-shān) Ēyǒu Hermitage,
who washed his hands in devotion before recording this.
I have thus received this preface to the *Commentary on the Essentials of Amitābha*. Indeed, this single work possesses great efficacy within the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land.

Every word reveals the ultimate truth; every phrase is sincere and authentic. When manifesting principle, it penetrates both essence and phenomena, so that the two eyes of wisdom are perfectly clear. When discussing phenomena...
I bare my heart and gall; my liver and intestines are utterly rent asunder. I shatter the false delusions of the shadowy conditions and expand upon the "mind-only" nature of the four lands.
I sweep away the biased calculations of the provisional and the Hinayana, clarifying the single essence of the three bodies. Thus, actual reality is none other than the ultimate principle of truth.
Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra cannot transcend its threshold. When one illuminates inherent evil, it is seen as the total embodiment of inherent goodness;
even parrots and mynas reach this domain. Thus, the wondrousness of the inconceivable is pointed out entirely within the ten evil deeds;
the rare and most difficult-to-attain principle is fully manifested amidst the five turbidities. Therefore it is said: "One utterance of Amitābha Buddha."
This is the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi attained by our original teacher Śākyamuni in this world of five turbidities;
he now bestows the entirety of this realized fruit upon sentient beings in this defiled and evil age.
This is the sphere of practice of all Buddhas, which only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully exhaust; it cannot be believed or understood through the self-power of the nine realms.
Ah! Were it not for the true Buddha-eye, how could one see this? How could one speak this?

Since there exists such a wondrous sutra, there must necessarily be such a wondrous interpretation. It truly serves as a great bridge across the ocean of suffering. (I), however, am by nature dull and ignorant;
although I have lectured on this commentary more than ten times, despite exhausting my spirit and concentrating my thoughts, I forget it as soon as the lecture concludes. Therefore—
In the year of Jihai (1899), I entered the summer retreat at Baotong Temple in Wuchang. Together with two or three fellow practitioners of the Lotus School, I expounded this commentary.

As I explained it, I recorded it; subsequently, these notes were gradually compiled into volumes. I do not dare claim that this is for the sake of propagating the Dharma or benefiting sentient beings;

rather, it is truly for my own convenience as a dull-witted person. Thus, it is called the *Biànméng Chāo* (Notes for My Own Convenience). May those who read this book not mistake it for a formal commentary. I pray you.
Deeply admiring [this work], the student Lian wrote this preface at the Red Swallow Patriarchal Hall.
*An Essential Explanation of the Buddha’s Shorter Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, with an abridgment in two volumes,
Volume One, composed by the Red Swallow Bhikṣu Dama.
Compiled by the Zifu Śramaṇa Dalin. △ Explanation of this Commentary.
The main section is divided into three parts: first, the introduction to the meaning; second, the explanation of the sūtra; third, the concluding remarks.
Within the first part, there are four sections: first, the title; second, the translators; third, the author of the commentary; fourth, the formal introduction. Regarding the title: [End of fragment]

II. First, the title of the sutra; second, the title of the commentary. The title of the sutra is further divided into three parts: first, clarifying the general and specific titles; second, clarifying the establishment of the title; third, the formal explanation of the title.

The first part [clarifying the general and specific titles] is further divided into five sections: first, regarding the entire dispensation; second, regarding a single gate; third, regarding a single sutra;
fourth, regarding a single title; fifth, regarding a single character. △ Now, the first section.
[Commentary]: All sutras possess both general and specific names. Regarding the three aspects of teaching, practice, and principle, each may be discussed in terms of the general and the specific.
Now, the Buddha speaks of the five characters of Amitābha; because their name differs from that of other scriptures, the teaching is distinct. Yet they are equally called "sutras."

Therefore, the teachings are universal; because practices arise based on the teachings, they differ according to those practices, and thus practices are distinct. Yet, as all paths lead back to the same serene light, practices are also universal.
Although the principle is nameless, the principle is named by means of the gates; the principle conforms to the gates, and through the four teachings and sixteen gates, one enters the principle.
Thus, while the principle is distinct [in its manifestations], the gates conform to the principle: the principle entered through a single gate is the very same principle entered through all gates.

Regarding Principle (*li*): it is the principle entered through all gates, which is precisely the principle of a single gate; therefore, the principle is universal. This is explained in terms of the entirety of the teaching (*eka-saṃsāra*).
Next, regarding the perspective of a single gate: this refers to the single gate of the Pure Land. Since the three Pure Land sutras are all extant in the world, their teachings are distinct.
Yet, because they are all equally titled "Sutras of Amitābha," their teachings are universal. Taking the invocation of the name and meditative visualization as the practice.
Because they are not the same, the practices are distinct; because they are equally termed "pure karma," the practices are common. Because the four lands are solely mind, the principle is distinct;
because the four lands are solely mind, the principle is common. This is according to one gate. △ Third, regarding one sutra:
from "Thus have I heard" to "having paid homage, they departed," the three divisions of introduction, main body, and dissemination are different; therefore, the teachings are distinct.

Because the beginning, middle, and end constitute a single goodness as a whole, the teaching is universal (*sāmānya*). Because faith, aspiration, and practice differ from one another, the practices are distinct (*viśeṣa*).
Because they all return to the Pure Land, the practices are universal. Because the Land of Ultimate Bliss horizontally encompasses the four lands (*catur-bhūmi*), the principles are distinct.

Because the four lands are identical within the single Land of Ultimate Bliss, the principles are universal. This is based on a single sutra. △ Fourth, regarding a single title: the universal and the particular... two... [text fragment].

Because they are distinct names, the teachings are distinct. Because they are combined into a single title, the teachings are common. Because they consist of the speaker and the spoken, the practices are distinct.

Because they are both the same Buddha, the practices are common. Because they are Śākyamuni and Amitābha, the principles are distinct. Because they are one and the same Dharmakāya, the principles are common.
This is based on the single title. △ Fifth, regarding a single character: because they are Chinese and Sanskrit, the teachings are distinct. They are the same...
"Reversing [the order] constitutes awakening; therefore, the teaching is universal (*sāmānya*). Because one awakens oneself and awakens others, the practice is distinct (*viśeṣa*).

Because awakening is fulfilled, the practice is universal. Because they are identical yet always six, the principle is distinct. Because they are six yet always identical, the principle is universal. This concludes the clarification of the universal and the distinct.

△ Second, explaining the establishment of the title: Although all sutras have immeasurable individual names, they do not exceed the three categories of person (*pudgala*), dharma, and metaphor (*upamā*).
These three have seven distinct ways of establishing a title: single, compound, and complete. Regarding the single category, there are single persons, single dharmas, and single metaphors.
A single person refers to cases where both the speaker and the subject spoken of are [the same], as in this sutra...
Regarding "person": the Buddha is the ultimate person. Within this, there is neither dharma nor metaphor; therefore, it is called the "single person. Regarding the "single dharma":
as in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, and others, there is neither person nor metaphor; therefore, it is called the "single dharma. Regarding the "single metaphor":
as in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, the *Ratnavyuha Sūtra*, and others, there is neither person nor dharma; therefore—
It is said: "Single metaphors" and "the threefold compound" are as follows: the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (The Lotus Sutra) is titled by means of both dharma and metaphor;
the *Tathāgata-siṃhanāda-sūtra* is titled by means of a person and a metaphor; the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and others are titled by means of a person and a dharma.
As for "complete [titles]," the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra* and others are...
The title is established by the complete presence of the person (*pudgala*), the dharma, and the analogy.

This concludes the clarification of the title. △ Third, the formal explanation of the title, which has two parts: first, the explanation of the specific names; second, the explanation of the general name. The first part [the explanation of the specific names] further has two sections: first, the individual explanation; second, the collective explanation.

The first [individual explanation] further has three sections: first, the explanation of the character "Buddha" (*buddha*); second, the explanation of the character "Expound" (*śāsana*); third, the explanation of...
Amitābha. The first section further has three parts: first, clarifying the two names—the general and the specific; second, clarifying the single and multiple aspects of the three bodies;

third, clarifying the six stages of realization regarding nature and cultivation. The first part [of the first section] further has two sub-sections: first, clarifying the general name; second, clarifying the specific name. Regarding the "two names—the general and the specific":
all Buddhas possess both general and specific names. As for the general, there are ten types of general...

Regarding the titles: specifically, they are Śākyamuni and Amitābha; generally, they manifest the ultimate fruit-virtue, while specifically they manifest the appearance according to the capacity of sentient beings.

Now, first we clarify the general titles, which are further divided into three parts: first, the explanation of the ten titles; second, the explanation of the Chinese and Sanskrit names; third, the general brief explanation. △ Now, for the first part:
as for the "ten titles," "Tathāgata" (Thus-Come One) is a title signifying that he follows and conforms to the traces of his predecessors. "Arhat" (Worthy One) is... [text continues]

"Arhat" (Worthy of Offerings) is the title for one who is fit to be a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). "Samyaksaṃbuddha" (Perfectly Awakened One) is the title for one who has fully known the *dharmadhātu*.

"Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna" (Endowed with Knowledge and Conduct) is the title for one whose fruit manifests the virtue of the cause. "Sugata" (Well-Gone) is the title for one who has excellently proceeded to *bodhi*. "Lokavid" (Knower of the World)."
"Attainer of the False and Penetrator of the True" is his title as one who reaches the ultimate; "Unsurpassed One" is his title for gathering and transforming beings through the Way;
"Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans" is his title for bestowing the Dharma according to their capacities; "Buddha" is his title for awakening and returning to the truth;
"World-Honored One" is his title for being uniquely honored within the three realms. Thus ends the clarification of the ten titles.
△ Second, explaining the Sanskrit and Chinese names: In the Sanskrit language, it is *Tathāgata*, also called *Tatāgata*.
This is translated as "Thus-Come One" (*Rúlái*). The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "He comes from nowhere, nor does he go anywhere; therefore he is named 'Thus-Come One'.
This is an explanation based on the *dharmakāya*. The *Dharmacakra-pravartana-śāstra* states: "The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is named 'Thus' (*tathā*)."
"Perfectly Awakened One" (*samyaksambuddha*) is translated as "Come" (*āgata*). This is explained in terms of the *saṃbhogakāya*. The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:

"Because one has come to achieve perfect awakening by riding upon the path of reality as it is, one is called the Tathāgata. This is explained in terms of the *nirmāṇakāya*. ○ In the Sanskrit language, *arhat*.

This is translated as "Worthy of Offerings" (*Arhat*), because they are worthy of receiving offerings from the ten realms. It is also translated as "Slayer of Thieves" (*Arahan*) and "Non-arising" (*Aluohan*).
The *Commentary on the Sutra of Contemplation* states: "In India, three names are closely related: *Arhā* is translated as 'Worthy of Offerings'; *Arhan* is translated as 'Non-arising';
*Aluhan* is translated as 'Slayer of Thieves'. In Sanskrit, it is called *Samyak-saṃbuddha*.

*Tathāgata*. This is translated as "Rightly and Universally Cognizant Awakening. It is called "Right" because the Dharma is without deviation; it is called "Universal" because wisdom is all-pervading;
it is called "Awakening" because one has emerged from the dream of birth and death. ○ In Sanskrit, this is *Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna*. This is translated as "Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the [three knowledges of] past lives, the divine eye, and the exhaustion of outflows are called...
Regarding the three knowledges (*vidyā*): although those of the three vehicles attain the three knowledges, they do not fulfill them; the Buddha fulfills them all. This is the distinction.
Because he is fully endowed with the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), he is called "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct" (*vidyācaraṇasampanna*).
○ In Sanskrit, he is called Sugata, which here means "Well-Gone. Alternatively, he is named Sugatu, which here means "Well-Departed. (From the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*).
It is said: "He has ascended to the foremost height and shall never return; therefore, he is called Sugata. [Sugata] is in Sanskrit *sugata*, which here means "Well-Gone.
He is called "Knower of the World" (*Lokavid*); in Sanskrit, *lokavid*. This refers to knowing two kinds of worlds: first, the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*);

second, the world of non-sentient things (*bhajanaloka*), as well as their true nature (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*). The *Bodhisattvabhūmi Sūtra* calls him "Knower of the World" (*Lokavid*). [Lokavid] is in Sanskrit...
"Anuttara" means "unsurpassed" (wúshàng). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Just as among all phenomena, nirvāṇa is unsurpassed;
so among the dharmas of sentient beings, the Buddha is unsurpassed. The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* calls him the "Unsurpassed One" (*anuttarapuruṣa*). The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says:
"Those who have something yet to be severed are called 'surpassable persons' (*sottarapuruṣa*); those who have nothing further to be severed are called 'unsurpassed persons' (*anuttarapuruṣa*)."
In Sanskrit, this is *puruṣadamyasārathi*. This means "the teacher who tames those men who are capable of being transformed.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Buddha, through great compassion and great wisdom, employs gentle and soft speech, harsh and urgent speech, and mixed speech, ensuring that beings do not lose the Way;
therefore, he is called the Teacher Who Tames. In Sanskrit, this is *śāstṛ*.
*Bhagavān*. This is translated as "Teacher of Gods and Humans. The *Mahā-śāstra* states:
"The Buddha demonstrates and guides what should be done and what should not be done, what is wholesome and what is unwholesome; people then practice according to his instructions. It further says:

Those to be delivered among beings of the other realms are few; those to be delivered among beings of the human and celestial realms are many. Therefore, he is called the Teacher of Gods and Humans (*śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*).
○ In Sanskrit, he is called *Buddha*; here it is translated as "The Awakened One" (*buddha*). This refers to awakening oneself, awakening others, and the fulfillment of awakening.

To realize that the nature is truly eternal and to understand that delusions are empty and false is called "awakening oneself. To employ unconditioned compassion (*nirālambana-karuṇā*) to deliver the realm of sentient beings is called "awakening [others]."
He has exhausted the source and reached the ultimate depth; with practice perfected and fruition complete, he is named "Perfectly Awakened" (*samyaksambuddha*).

In Sanskrit, he is called *lokajyestha*, which here means "World-Honored One. Possessing these nine titles above, he is revered by all beings; therefore, he is called the World-Honored One (*bhagavat*).
Because he is honored alike by those in heaven and those among men, the explanation of the Sanskrit and Chinese names is concluded.
△ Third, the general summary explanation: The *Fanyi mingyi ji* (Collection of Translated Names and Meanings) states: "That which is devoid of falsehood is called Tathāgata;

that which is a truly excellent field of merit is called Arhat; that which knows the dharma-realm is called Samyaksaṃbuddha; and that which possesses the three types of clear knowledge is called Vidyācaraṇa."
He has reached the goal; he does not return again, thus he is named "Well-Gone" (Sugata). He knows the realms of sentient beings, thus he is named "Knower of the World" (Lokavid).

He is without equal, thus he is named "Unsurpassed One" (Anuttara). He tames the minds of others, thus he is named "Tamer of Men" (Puruṣadamyasārathi). He serves as the eye for sentient beings, thus he is named "Teacher of Gods and Humans" (Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām).
He knows the three groups [of beings], thus he is named "Buddha. Possessing these ten virtues, he is named "World-Honored One" (Bhagavat). His wisdom is clear and penetrating.
The general titles are concluded.
△ Second, explaining the specific titles: although their names differ, their meanings are mutually interpenetrating. For example, Śākyamuni is translated as "Capable Benevolence" (Nengren);
how could there be a single Buddha who is not capable and benevolent? Amitābha is called "Immeasurable Life"; how could there be... [text ends]
It is not that [the Buddha] is not the Buddha or does not possess long life; rather, he establishes his teachings by adapting to the capacities of sentient beings and conforms to worldly conventions.
Here, we are specifically clarifying the Teacher who is able to preach: Śākyamuni Buddha. In Sanskrit, he is called Śākyamuni;

in this [language], it means "Able Benevolent One" (Nengren) and "Silent Stillness" (Jimo). "Able Benevolent One" is his clan name (*gotra*); "Silent Stillness" is his personal name (*nāmadheya*). "Able Benevolent One" is...
Regarding "clan" (gotra): the Buddha has five clans. First, Gautama; second, Ikṣvāku; third, Ādityavaṃśa;
fourth, Śākiya; and fifth, Śākya. Regarding the first, Gautama: it is also called Gotamī, which means "pure and virtuous.
The *Sūtra on the Twelve Wanderings* states that incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya*) ago, there was a Great Reed King (*Mahāmuñjaka-rāja*).
He renounced his status and left the household life, taking a Brahmin as his teacher; the teacher subsequently bestowed upon him the surname Kṣudra-Gautama.
Regarding the two lineages of Ikṣvāku, the *Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya* (or *Benxing jing*) states: King Mahāmūla attained the state of a royal ṛṣi and lived for an extremely long time.
When he grew old and could no longer walk, his disciples went out to seek food and drink, placing the ṛṣi in a basket and suspending it [from a tree].
Upon the branch of a tree, a hunter saw them from afar; thinking they were birds, he shot at them. Blood dripped onto the ground, from which two sugarcane stalks sprouted.
When the sun’s heat caused them to split open, one yielded a young boy and the other a young girl.

An astrologer established the name of the boy as Sujāta (Well-Born), immediately performed the consecration of his head, and named him King Ikṣvāku (Sugarcane King). The girl was named Bhadrā (Virtuous), who became his chief consort.

Regarding the "three clans of the Solar Lineage" (*sūryavaṃśa*): the *Benxing jing* (Sūtra on Past Deeds) states that they are also called the Solar Lineage because they emerged from sugarcane scorched by the sun.
Regarding the "four clans of the Śākya": King Ikṣvāku, having heard the slander of his secondary consort, banished the four crown princes to the north of the Snow Mountains.
There they established their own city and dwelt there; through their virtue, people flocked to them, and the father-king later felt regret.
He remembered them and sent a messenger to summon his four sons; however, they declined on account of their transgressions and did not return.
The father-king sighed and said, "My son Śākya [is named after] this clan. As for the five surnames, 'Śākyas' is the name of a grove. The *Buddhacarita-sūtra* states:
"Because he dwelt in the great forest of the Śākyas, he was called a Śākya. This establishes the surname based on the location.

Therefore, he is called Śākyamuni. Regarding the meaning of the name "Silent One" (Muni): the *Sūtra on Past Deeds* (*Pūrva-yoga-sūtra*) states that the members of the Śākya clan were by nature arrogant and talkative;
yet, upon seeing the Prince, they all became silent. The King said, "He should be named Muni.
This concludes the two names, both general and specific.

△ Second, clarifying the single and multiple aspects of the three bodies. Every Buddha is endowed with the three bodies, namely: the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
The Dharma-body is the essence of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*). The Reward-body is the perfection of initial enlightenment (*ādi-awakening*) wisdom.
The Transformation-body is the manifestation through compassionate response. The Dharma-body is named Vairocana; this means "pervading all places. The Reward-body...
The name *Vairocana* translates as "Pure and Full. The transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is named Śākyamuni, which translates as "Able Sage" or "Silent One.

Furthermore, each of the three bodies possesses both single and dual meanings. The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) in its single sense refers exclusively to the essence of reality that is primordially pure.
The Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) in its single sense refers exclusively to supreme merit and wisdom. The Transformation-body...
"Single" refers exclusively to the manifested response-body, like the moon in water. Regarding the "repetition" of the Dharma-body, there are two:
first, the Dharma-body of intrinsic purity, which is the original source-nature of sentient beings, the true and natural Buddha;
second, the wondrously ultimate Dharma-body free from defilement, which is the principle of the ultimate *dharmadhātu* realized by all Buddhas. Regarding the repetition of the Reward-body...
There are two types: first, the *saṃbhogakāya* for one’s own enjoyment, which is the ultimate fruit of the two virtues of wisdom and abandonment belonging to all Buddhas;

second, the *saṃbhogakāya* for the enjoyment of others, which refers to the marks and signs perceived by Bodhisattvas on the stages according to their mental capacity, wherein each and every mark and sign is without limit. Furthermore, there is the *nirmāṇakāya*.
First is the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body), which manifests the eight marks of enlightenment. Second is the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body), which suddenly appears where there was none.
Furthermore, the *nirmāṇakāya* is also called the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body), for it manifests in response to sentient beings, like the moon reflected in water.

Regarding the manifestation of the eight marks, there are again three types: first, the *viśiṣṭa-nirmāṇakāya* (superior response body), which is the aforementioned *parasaṃbhogakāya* (body of enjoyment for others). Second...

This refers to the body that manifests both inferior and superior forms. That which is perceived by the three vehicles of the Shared Teaching is "superior" because it is integrated into the Distinct and Complete Teachings;

however, it remains "inferior" because it still relies upon the consciousness of phenomena (*dharma-vijñāna*). Third is the inferior response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which is the body of a six-foot-old bhikṣu as seen in the Treasury Teaching (*Āgama*);
it relies solely on the consciousness of phenomena and does not realize the infinite principle of the ocean of marks. Therefore...

The name is "Inferior. Furthermore, there are two kinds of transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*): namely, the transformation body of the Buddha-realm and the transformation body that conforms to various types.
This concludes the section on the three bodies, both individually and collectively.
△ Third, regarding the six stages of identity between nature and cultivation: "Six" reveals the phenomenal characteristics of cause and effect; "identity" (*ji*) reveals the Buddha-nature.
Regarding the essence of this principle: because cultivation arises entirely from nature, it is called "six"; because cultivation is entirely contained within nature, it is called "immediate.
What are these six immediacies? First, immediate in principle; second, immediate by name; third, immediate in contemplative practice.
Fourth is the semblance stage (*sādharmya-īdṛśa*); fifth is the partial realization stage (*bhūmi-praveśa-īdṛśa*); sixth is the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-īdṛśa*).
Master Pūrṇaruci composed a verse on the six stages of Buddhahood, which says:

[Commentary] In movement and stillness, the principle is entirely present; In action and withdrawal, phenomena are utterly non-existent. Darkly one follows along with things; Profoundly one does not...

"Knowing the Return" (This verse concerns principle, which is precisely the Buddha. "The principle of movement and stillness is entirely [Buddha]" means that whether in motion or at rest, with respect to principle, it is entirely the Buddha-nature. "The phenomena of activity and concealment are utterly non-Buddha" refers to activity and concealment, which are movement and stillness;

because one does not realize that all phenomena are mind-only, the activities performed—whether moving or still—are entirely inconsistent with principle. "Darkly following things away" means that the substance of the Buddha-nature flows and transmigrates along with the six sense objects.)
"Vast and remote, they do not know where to return; they lack the power of awakening and illumination, and thus do not know how to return.
[Commentary] "Only now do I listen to the melody of non-arising; only now do I hear the song of immortality. Now I know that this very substance is it; I regret only my own wasted time.

(This verse praises the Buddha-nature as it is in its names. "Only now do I listen to the melody of non-arising; only now do I hear the song of immortality" refers to the realization of the principle of Buddha-nature. Buddha-nature is fundamentally neither born nor extinguished. Now I know...)

Regarding "realizing the essence as it is": the suffering that constitutes the present essence is itself the Dharmakāya; delusion is Prajñā; and karma is Vimukti. As for "turning instead to resent one's own wasted time": this refers to turning away from the principle within the state of practice (li ji wei zhong). It is an error to think that the concealment of practice and the exhaustion of phenomena are not [the truth].
[Commentary] "Moment by moment, one accords with the constant principle; thought after thought, one quiets the illusory dust.

One observes universally the nature of all phenomena; there is neither the false nor the true. (This verse refers to the stage of "Contemplation-Practice" [guanxing-ji], which is itself the Buddha. "Moment by moment, one accords with the constant principle" clarifies the efficacy of contemplative observation. The "constant principle" is the principle of the Dharmakāya, which is neither arising nor ceasing.

"Thought after thought, one quiets the illusory dust": the "illusory dust" refers to the delusions of the five stages of dwelling (wu-zhu-di-huo). This means that precisely when one accords with the constant principle, the delusions of the five stages are immediately stilled and do not arise. "One observes universally the nature of all phenomena" refers to the nature of phenomena regarding the two extremes. There is neither the false...)
"Neither true" means that it is the entirety of the Middle Way; therefore, it is said to be neither false nor true. [Commentary]:
Although the four abidings have already fallen away, the six sense objects are not yet entirely empty. There is still a film in the eye, and one sees red flowers in the void.

(This verse refers to the Buddha of Similarity. The "four abidings" refer to the two delusions of views and thoughts; views constitute one abiding, and thoughts constitute three abidings. "Already fallen away" means that the attachment to dharmas is severed later, while the attachment to self is severed first.)

That the six sense objects have not yet been emptied means that attachment to phenomena (dharmagrāha) has not yet been forgotten. Because of this attachment to phenomena, it is said that there is a film over the eye, causing one to see red flowers within the empty sky.

[Commentary]: "Suddenly the mind opens and awakens; all things are profoundly and transparently penetrated. Though the source is exhausted, it is not yet fully reached; one still sees the moon as dim and obscured. (Regarding "suddenly the mind opens and awakens":

by means of the wisdom of the Middle Way contemplation, one suddenly shatters one grade of ignorance. Regarding "all things are profoundly and transparently penetrated": the six sense-objects are empty. Regarding "the source is exhausted but not yet fully reached":
there are still forty-one grades of ignorance that have not been exhausted; therefore, it is said that "one still sees the moon as dim and obscured.")
[Commentary] That which was real from the beginning is now illusory; that which was illusory today is now entirely real.

It is simply a matter of returning to the nature as it was originally; not a single dharma is newly created. ("From the beginning" refers to the preceding five stages. "That which was real is illusory" means that the reality of the three virtues (triguṇa) is entirely constituted by the illusion of the three obstructions (trisaṃkleśa), like water turning into ice.

"Today" refers to the present stage of ultimate realization. "Illusion is entirely real" means that the illusion of the three obstructions is entirely constituted by the reality of the three virtues. "Simply returning to the nature as it was originally" means restoring the Buddha-nature (buddhadhātu) of its original state. "Not a single dharma is newly created" means that [it does not arise] from...)
[This means] obtaining water even outside of ice). [Commentary]:
These six are "identical" (ji) in meaning; they are all categorized within the four teachings, yet there are differences between the provisional and the real.

The first three teachings are provisional, while only the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) is real. In the Tripitaka Teaching (zangjiao), there is only "six" but not "identity," because the two truths do not interpenetrate (xiāngjí) therein.
Although in the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) the two truths are mutually identical, one cannot yet be "identical to the Buddha" because the Middle Way has not been realized.

Although the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao) speaks of the Middle Way, it does not establish the doctrine of the "six identities with the Buddha," for its Middle Way alone does not coincide with the two extremes.

Only in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is the meaning of the six identities with the Buddha complete; therefore, the doctrine of the six identities with the Buddha is judged solely according to the Perfect Teaching. Thus, they are identical...
The "Constant" (常) is sixfold, like the difference between ice and water. The "Six" and the "Constant" are identical, like the single essence of the nature of moisture.
This concludes the explanation of the character *Fo* (佛).

△ Second, the explanation of the character *Shuo* (說) is divided into two parts: first, clarifying that which cannot be spoken; second, clarifying that which can be spoken. Question: Regarding the *Lotus Sūtra*...

The Sūtra says: "The quiescent nature of all phenomena cannot be proclaimed in words. How, then, can it be explained? First, to clarify what is "inexpressible": if we summarize the four teachings: 1. **The Tripitaka Teaching**: It is said that the Dharma is profound and subtle, beyond the reach of words and letters; thus, it is inexpressible. 2. **The Shared Teaching**: It is said that the Dharma is empty and tranquil, transcending all conceptualization; thus, it is inexpressible. 3. **The Distinct Teaching**: It is said that the Dharma is inconceivable and ineffable, transcending the realm of thought; thus, it is inexpressible. 4. **The Perfect Teaching**: It is said that the Dharma is the Middle Way, free from all extremes of speech and silence; thus, it is inexpressible. There are thus four things that cannot be spoken of: namely, the arising of arising cannot be spoken of;

the arising of non-arising cannot be spoken of; the non-arising of arising cannot be spoken of; and the non-arising of non-arising cannot be spoken of. Why is it that the arising of arising cannot be spoken of?
"The arising of arising" refers to dharmas produced by causes and conditions. That which "cannot be spoken of" is the cause and condition itself.
Emptiness is where mental activity ceases and the path of language is cut off; therefore, it cannot be spoken of. This is the meaning of the Tripitaka (Āgama) teachings.
Why is it that "arising and non-arising" are ineffable? As for "arising and non-arising," it refers to the fact that while all phenomena do not arise, Prajñā arises.
This Prajñā does not arise from itself, nor does it arise from another, nor from both, nor without cause. Therefore, it is said:
"Arising and non-arising" are cut off from the path of language; therefore, they cannot be spoken of. This is the meaning of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*).
Regarding "the unarisen arising that cannot be spoken of": "the unarisen" is the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature), and "arising" is ignorance (*avidyā*).
The followers of the Two Vehicles realize the unarisen, yet they still undergo the arising of *dharmatā*; hence it is called "the unarisen arising. Whether it be *dharmatā* or ignorance...
It is clear that all [phenomena] are cut off from the path of language; therefore, they cannot be spoken of. This is the meaning of the Separate Teaching (pratyekabuddha-yāna).

Why is it that "non-arising non-arising" is unspeakable? Because it is attained through the cultivation of the Path. That is to say, both virtues—wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*)—are non-arising;
this is what is realized by the ultimate, supreme fruit. Since it is not even known by those in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), how could it be expressed in words?
This is the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). This has briefly clarified that which is "unspeakable. △ Second, clarifying that which is "speakable": The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Although all things are unspeakable, the ten links of dependent origination (*daśa-pratītyasamutpāda*) act as causes for birth, and thus can also be spoken of.

The ten links of dependent origination are the establishment of all phenomena (*dharmas*), ranging from the link of ignorance (*avidyā*) up to the link of existence (*bhava*). Thus they are established.
There are three meanings: namely, establishing sentient beings, establishing the conditions of their capacities, and establishing the vocal teachings.
These three mutually establish one another. If there were no sentient beings, there would be no conditions of capacity; if there were no conditions of capacity, there would be no vocal teachings;
and if there were no vocal teachings, there would likewise be no sentient beings. Regarding the establishment of sentient beings: there are two causes from the past and five fruits in the present.

They act as mutual causes and conditions, thereby establishing the conventional designation of a "sentient being" based upon the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Regarding the establishment of the causal conditions:

in the past, one may have cultivated either analytical practice (*vibhava-yoga*), essential practice (*svabhāva-yoga*), gradual practice (*anupūrva-yoga*), or sudden practice (*tatkṣaṇa-yoga*) as one's karma.
Moistened by ignorance (*avidyā*), this results in the fruit of the present five branches. Within this fruit of the aggregates, one further gives rise to the fundamental [afflictions].

Through habituation, there arises either the analytical practice of craving, grasping, and becoming; or the practice of craving for the essence, grasping, and becoming; or the gradual arising of craving, grasping, and becoming;
or the sudden arising of craving, grasping, and becoming. Because craving, grasping, and becoming thus arise, they serve as the conditions for the capacity [of the practitioner].

Regarding the establishment of the teachings through sound: because the arising of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) is analyzed, the Tripitaka teaching is evoked. This constitutes the "arising of arising" (*jāti-jāti*), which is inexpressible.
The ten links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) serve as the causes for this "arising of arising," and thus they can indeed be explained.

Explaining the Tripitaka teaching involves the doctrine of the arising of arising, as well as the wisdom, realization, severance, practice, stages, cause, and fruit. It takes the essence of the arising of craving, grasping, and becoming as its foundation.

Being moved by the Shared Teaching (Pāryāyika-yāna), this is called "the unutterable arising of non-arising. The ten links of dependent origination serve as the causes for this arising of non-arising, and thus may also be spoken of;
this explains the eight dharmas of the Shared Teaching. Because [afflictions] gradually arise from craving, grasping, and existence, one is moved by the Distinct Teaching (Vaibhūṣika-yāna).
This is called "the unutterable non-arising of arising. The ten links of dependent origination serve as...
It can also be said that non-arising gives rise to arising as its cause; this refers to the distinct teaching of the eight dharmas of non-arising giving rise to arising.
The sudden arousal of craving, grasping, and becoming brings about the Perfect Teaching; this is what is meant by the ineffable non-arising of non-arising.
It can also be said that the ten causal conditions (*daśa-pratyaya-dharma*) act as causes for the non-arising of non-arising.
This refers to the teaching of the eight dharmas of the non-arising of non-arising in the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*). These four [non-arisings] can be explained;
each possesses four gates, resulting in sixteen gates (4 × 4). Furthermore, each possesses the causal conditions of the four *siddhāntas*, totaling sixty-four *siddhāntas*. Moreover, there are...
The two practices of faith and dharma together comprise one hundred and twenty-eight *siddhāntas*, which are infinitely diverse when divided part by part.
This *Amitābha Sūtra* belongs to the Gate of Existence within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) and is the *paramārtha-siddhānta*; it fully encompasses the three lower *siddhāntas*.
It is the vocal teaching manifested in response to the karmic conditions and capacities of sentient beings. The explanation of the character "shi" (釋) is hereby concluded.
△ Third, the explanation of Amitābha. *Amitābha* is a Sanskrit term. According to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, it encompasses thirteen meanings:
namely, Immeasurable Life, Immeasurable Light, Boundless Light, Unobstructed Light, Unopposed Light, and so forth.

The thirteen names—Flame-Light King, Pure Light, Joyful Light, Wisdom Light, Uninterrupted Light, Inconceivable Light, Incomparable Light, and Light Surpassing the Sun and Moon—are merely designations;
they do not go beyond the meaning of "Light-Life" (*jōryū*). Therefore, this sutra refers only to "Light-Life.
"Light" signifies the nature of the mind extending horizontally throughout the ten directions. The ten directions are originally...
Because it is without limit, it is called "immeasurable" (*amita*). "Life-span" (*āyuṣ*) signifies the meaning of the nature of mind vertically exhausting the three periods of time.
Since these three periods have neither beginning nor end, it is called "immeasurable. Furthermore, within the horizontal there is the vertical, and within the vertical there is the horizontal;
as the horizontal and vertical mutually penetrate one another, they are inconceivable. Therefore, it is called "Immeasurable Amitābha," who has thoroughly realized the mind.
This is the source of the horizontal and vertical natures; therefore, it is called "Immeasurable Light and Life. The light and life of the three bodies are explained as in the commentary.
The individual explanations are concluded. △ Second, the combined explanation has two parts:

first, the combined explanation of the speaker; second, the combined explanation of what is spoken. The first part [the combined explanation of the speaker] further has two sections. First, clarifying what is...
Selection. Second, harmonizing with the three bodies. △ Now, for the first: regarding the phrase "spoken by the Buddha," there is a specific selection.
This is because there are four types of speakers in the sutras: namely, disciples, various sages, devas, and emanated persons. If these four were to speak...

The Tathāgata has certified this, and it may thus be called a sūtra. Since the beginning and end of this present sūtra both issue from the golden mouth [of the Buddha], it is said to be "spoken by the Buddha.
This concludes the clarification of what is excluded.
△ Second, reconciling the three bodies. Question: The Buddha possesses the three bodies. Now, when it is said that "the Buddha speaks," which body is it that speaks?

*Fanwang jing hezhu* (Combined Commentary on the Brahma Net Sutra) answers: Since the three bodies are neither identical nor different, it is inherently impossible to hold to the biased attachment of [specifying] which body preaches the Dharma.
However, because there are differences in the remedies [for specific afflictions], the teachings set forth in the various sutras differ.
The same. Some say that the retribution-body and transformation-bodies are not the true Buddha, nor are they the ones who preach the Dharma;

this is because they fear that people might cling to appearances and become deluded regarding the principle, and thus they point only to the fundamental awakening of the dharma-nature as the true Buddha.

Others say that the dharma-Buddha is the sacred realm of self-awakening, which is without words and without preaching; all instances of preaching the Dharma and manifesting ritual forms are merely the transformation-Buddhas.

This is because there is a fear that people might fall into the realm of conceptualization regarding the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). Therefore, it is only the transformation Buddha (nirmāṇakāya) that is shown to manifest the three wheels [of teaching, hearing, and practice].
In reality, however, it is the Dharma-body that preaches the Dharma and delivers sentient beings; yet it is not the Dharma-body alone, nor is it separate from the Dharma-body.

It is neither the reward body (saṃbhogakāya) nor the transformation body, yet it is not separate from either the reward or transformation bodies. If one grasps the meaning of the four *siddhāntas*, one will understand that the Dharma-body also preaches the Dharma.
It may be so. As it is said, "The reward and transformation bodies are not the speakers of the Dharma," it may also mean that only the reward and transformation bodies preach the Dharma.
As it is said, "The Dharma-body is without speech," it may also mean that the three bodies together preach the Dharma. As it is said, "The merit harmonizes with the Dharma-body;
it appears and goes everywhere," it may also mean that each of the three bodies preaches the Dharma. Dharma...
The *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha preaches the Dharma for bodhisattvas on the stages; the *sambhogakāya* Buddha preaches the Dharma for those prior to the stages, as well as for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
and the *hīna-nirmāṇakāya* Buddha preaches the Dharma for all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

It may also be said that the three bodies collectively have no verbal expression, just as it is said that not a single word was spoken during the forty-nine years [of Śākyamuni’s ministry]. If one does not understand this...

Regarding the causes and conditions of the *siddhānta*, to adhere to any single phrase [to the exclusion of others] is all termed slandering the Buddha. The first section, on the synthesis of the speaker, is concluded.
II. Synthesizing the Taught. Question: Since all three bodies are called Amitābha, which body is specifically being referred to here?
Answer: The Dharma-body of Quiescent Light refers to the Amitābha of the Perfect Teaching; the Retribution Buddha of True Reward refers to the Amitābha of the Separate Teaching;
the Exalted Response-body of Expedient Means refers to the Amitābha of the Shared Teaching; and the Inferior Response-body refers to the [Amitābha] of the Common Residence.
The Dharma-body Buddha can expound the Amitābha of all four teachings;
the Retribution-body Buddha can expound the Amitābha of three teachings—namely, the Tripitaka, Shared, and Distinct; and the Superior Response-body Buddha can expound the Amitābha of two teachings.
This refers to the Tripitaka and Shared [teachings]. An inferior response-body (hīna-nirmāṇakāya) can preach only one teaching, namely the Tripitaka.

Furthermore, when dwelling together under a tree, it must preach all four teachings because the faculties and dispositions of the audience are mixed. A response-body that combines the inferior and superior aspects preaches only three teachings, as those with the capacities for the Tripitaka teaching cannot perceive [the higher ones].
A superior response-body through skillful means (upāya) preaches only the Distinct and Complete teachings, causing them to see the Dharma.

Because it is the body [of the Buddha], because within the realm it cuts off all divisions, and because it is the true recompense for others' enjoyment, it is taught solely according to the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*), so as to cause all bodhisattvas to exhaust the source of ignorance.
The combined explanation is finished. The initial explanation of the distinct names is finished.
△ Second, explaining the general name: In Sanskrit it is called *sūtra*, or *sūdan*, or *sūtru*;
these are merely regional dialectal variations (*chūxià*) of that land, resulting in different translations here in this land. Some say it has no equivalent translation.

Some say there are translations [for these terms]. Tiantai explains this in three parts: first, clarifying that there are no translations; second, clarifying that there are translations; third, harmonizing both presence and absence of translation. △ Now, for the first:
regarding the absence of translation, the terminology of that region (India) is multifaceted and inclusive, whereas the terminology of this region (China) is simple and shallow.
One cannot translate a complex term with a simple one; thus, the original sound should be retained. Since it cannot be translated, [it remains as such].
It contains five meanings: first, the source of phenomena (dharmamūla), also called "birth"; second, subtle emergence; third, a gushing spring; fourth, a plumb line;
and fifth, a stringing of garlands. These five meanings alone cannot be translated [into Chinese]. Now, within each of these five, three aspects are established, resulting in fifteen meanings:
first, the source of the teaching-dharma; second, the source of the practice-dharma; and third, the source of the meaning-dharma.

I shall now explain this in detail. Regarding the term "the source of the Dharma" (*dharmamūla*): all things are ultimately ineffable; yet, through the four *siddhāntas* and the four conditions, there is verbal expression.

According to the *loka-siddhānta*, it is taught as the source of the teaching (*śāsana-mūla*). According to the *puruṣakāra-siddhānta* (for the sake of individuals and as an antidote), it is the source of practice (*pratipatti-mūla*).

According to the *paramārtha-siddhānta*, it is the source of meaning (*artha-mūla*). As for what is called the "source of the teaching": [The text continues with the definition of the source of the teaching.]
That which was spoken from the Golden Mouth has a single word as its root, from which immeasurable teachings branch out; therefore, the Buddha’s words are the root.
That the sūtras are the root of practice means they show people the dharma of non-contention, so that one may practice according to the instructions; thus, the sūtras are the root of practice.
That the sūtras are the root of meaning means that a single phrase investigates a single meaning, or a single phrase expresses [a specific significance].

The meanings are immeasurable; therefore, the Sūtra is the source of these meanings. To categorize these three types as "Dharma-gates": the source of the teaching is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*);
the source of practice is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); and the source of meaning is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) that perceives reality.

Since the meaning of "source of the Dharma" already contains many implications, it cannot be translated [into a single term]. ○ Second, regarding "slightly manifesting": the Buddha, by means of the four...
The *siddhānta* teachings employ skillful rhetoric that delights the minds of the multitude. Upon first hearing the *loka-siddhānta*, a slight understanding arises;

this refers to the "slight development" in terms of the teaching (*śāsana*). Upon first hearing the *pudgala-siddhānta* (the siddhānta for individuals), which provides remedies and counteracts, one generates goodness and destroys evil;

this is the "slight development" in terms of practice (*pratipatti*). Upon first hearing the *paramārtha-siddhānta*, one enters into principle; this is the "slight development" in terms of meaning (*artha*). These [three] are subsumed here.
Third, regarding the "Dharma-gates": in the Hinayana, these are the three gates of liberation; in the Mahayana, they are the secret treasury of the three virtues.
Third, regarding the "surging springs": the Buddha expounds the Dharma through the four *siddhāntas*. Its words and meanings are inexhaustible, and the flow of the Dharma is unceasing.
If one hears the *loka-siddhānta*, a single phrase explained can lead to the understanding of immeasurable phrases; this constitutes the "surge of teaching."

As for "spring": if one hears of the various remedial practices for sentient beings, giving rise to immeasurable modes of conduct and *dharma*-gates as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, this constitutes a spring of practice.
If one hears of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), its principle being like space and pervading all places, this constitutes a spring of meaning.

To bind these three together as dharma-gates: teaching is the unimpededness of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*); practice is the unimpededness of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*); and meaning is the unimpededness of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*).
Eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*) pervades all three. Regarding the "four carpenter's lines": the Buddha preaches the Dharma by means of the four *siddhāntas*.
First, the worldly standpoint (*lokasaṃvṛti*) carves away the false teachings of attachment and views; this serves as the line for teaching. If...
Hearing [the Dharma] serves as the counteractive for worldly beings; it causes one to distance oneself from unwholesome paths and enter the right path, acting as the guiding line for conduct.
If one hears the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it cuts through the near shore of craving and views, enabling one to reach the further shore, acting as the guiding line for the meaning.

To bind these three together as a gateway to the Dharma (*dharmamukha*): the teaching (*śāsana*) consists of right speech (*samyagvāc*), right action (*samyakkarmānta*), right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*), right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*), and right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*);
the meaning (*artha*) consists of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*). The fifth, "Binding the Garland" (*granthimālā*):

it binds the teaching, practice, and principle so that they do not fall apart, just like binding flowers into a garland. This is the "Worldly Perspectival Truth" (*lokasaṃvṛtisatya*) which binds the Buddha’s verbal teachings.

To serve as an antidote for people, there are the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the practices (*caryā*), and the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*). To bind these together as a dharma-gate constitutes the teaching on the fetters:
no error in speech; the practice of the fetters: no error in body; and the meaning of the fetters: no error in mind.
While it was formerly said that the *sūtra* contains five meanings, it now contains fifteen meanings. How could one possibly translate from Sanskrit using only Chinese? Furthermore, in this land...

The scriptures teach the constant Dharma. "Constant" means the sense of immutability; it cannot be altered or destroyed by celestial Māras or heterodox paths, and is thus called the constancy of the Name-and-Teaching (mingjiao).
It is truly authentic and without admixture, and nothing can surpass it, and is thus called the constancy of Practice (xing). It is profoundly still and unmoving.

There is absolutely no other interpretation; it is called the "Eternal Principle" (*li-chang*). Regarding the term *fa* (dharma), its meaning is "that which serves as a standard. This includes the standard of the teaching, the standard of practice, and the standard of principle.
Now, the direct translation of the term already contains these six meanings; how much more so when considering that the Sanskrit original is repetitive, making a single-word translation inadequate.

Regarding the "basis" (*yoni*), I shall now provide three explanations: namely, the basis of the teaching (*śāsana-yoni*), the basis of practice (*pratipatti-yoni*), and the basis of the principle (*artha-yoni*).
All sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras are called the "basis of the teaching" because they originate from the mind and speech of the Noble Ones (*ārya*).

All practices that accord with the truth, as well as similar practices, are designated as the "basis of practice" because they likewise originate from the mind and speech of the Noble Ones. Regarding all worldly...
Meaning (*artha*). The meaning of the supramundane, the meaning of skillful means (*upāya*), and the ultimate meaning all arise from the minds and mouths of the sages;

therefore, "meaning" is taken as the basis. Teaching arises from the *loka-saṃvṛti* (worldly) standpoint; practice arises from the standpoint of treating individuals according to their specific needs;

and meaning arises from the *paramārtha-saṃvṛti* (ultimate) standpoint. Second, it is translated as "conformity" (*kai*). This refers to conformity with conditions, conformity with phenomena, and conformity with principle. Regarding the world...

The "realm" (*dhātu*) explains the conditions for the seal; it serves as the seal of the activity that acts as an antidote for people. The "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*) explains the principle of the seal.

○ Third, the translation as "dharma-source" is as explained previously. ○ Fourth, the translation as "thread": the thread threads through and sustains the principles of teaching and practice, preventing them from falling into disorder.
Furthermore, the thread has the sense of being able to sew; that is, it sews the teaching, sews the practice, and sews the principle. Sewing the teaching...

The chapters and phrases are not disordered; one is thus capable of preaching the Dharma. As for the practice of sewing [the robe]: to follow the sutras is to practice correctly; to deviate from the sutras is to practice erroneously.
To sew according to worldly logic is that which is not sealed by the Truth (Dharma); it falls into the sixty-two types of erroneous views.
That which is sealed by the Truth is the convergence upon the single ultimate path. (5) This is the teaching of virtuous speech and also the teaching of virtuous conduct.

It is also the "excellent principle-teaching" (*suvyavasthāna-sūtra*), the "worldly well-spoken teaching" (*loka-prasiddha-sūtra*), the "teaching of virtuous conduct as an antidote for beings" (*pratipakṣa-kuśala-caryā-sūtra*), and the "ultimate truth excellent principle-teaching" (*paramārtha-suvyavasthāna-sūtra*). These are the five translations of the term *sūtra*.

△ Third, regarding the harmonization of existence and non-existence: if one says there is no translation [for the term], its name contains five meanings, and within each of these meanings, further meanings are contained.
These three meanings make its excellence even more apparent. If one were to provide translations for each term, every single translation would likewise possess these three meanings;
thus, the profound intent is further enhanced. Whether those [meanings] are present or absent, what contradiction or dispute could there be?

Interpreting it in this way, neither of the two schools suffers any loss, and there remains a rational basis for this. For now, I shall rely on a single name as the primary translation, yet I do not...

This would cause enmity between the two schools. Why? From antiquity to the present, the terms *śakra* and *brahmā* have been rendered as "flower" (*huā*), and all have been titled as "sūtras" (*jīng*).

If other translations were correct, why not change it to "cord-seal" (*xiànqì*)? Since this region [China] designates the works of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius as the "Five Classics" (*wǔjīng*), the term "sūtra" (*jīng*) was used to translate *sūtra*.
