△ Second, the explanation of the title of the *Shù* (Commentary) refers to the two characters *yàojiě* (Essential Explanation). *Yào* means "essential" or "crucial.

Although there are many essential points within the commentary, they are briefly summarized into three: first, the essence of the mind (*xīnyào*); second, the essence of the object (*jìngyào*); and third, [the essence of the practice].

This is the essential point of the Dharma-gate and the essential point of the mind. It involves both refutation and establishment. As for refutation, it refutes the deluded mind that is a reflection of conditions; as the text says:
"It is fundamentally not a mass of flesh, nor is it a reflection of conditions," and so forth. As for establishment, it establishes the true mind that is the reality of the object.

This is precisely the mind-nature of the Buddha in a single thought-moment. In the section "Discerning the Substance" within the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), regarding the "Phenomenal Aspects," it says:
"The essential core of the minds of all Buddhas. Later in the text, it states: "Exclusively elucidating the unsurpassed essential core of the mind.

The colophon says: "Is this not indeed the unsurpassed essential core of the mind? Within the "Essential Core of the Object" (*jingyao*), there is both refutation and establishment; first, the refutation:
This breaks through the deluded land of conditioned shadows; it addresses the habitual tendencies of accumulated delusion in the末法 (mofa) age.
Taking these deluded thoughts of conditioned shadows and calling them the "Pure Land of Mind-Only," one establishes the actual reality of the mind immediately.
This refers to the single phrase of the Buddha-name that is identical with the mind, as well as the four kinds of body and land of Mind-Only. As the subsequent text states: "First..."

All adornments are accomplished through the vows and practices of the Guide; they are manifested by the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), evoked by our own pure karma, and transformed by consciousness alone (*vijñaptimātra*).
The Buddha-mind and the sentient being’s mind act as mutual images and substances. How can one abandon this Pure Land to separately speak of a "Mind-Only Pure Land"?
One would surely fall into the derision of being like a rat claiming to be a bird or a crow claiming to be an eagle. Behold!
One who writes this must possess the eye of wisdom. This Dharma-gate is essential; it possesses both the phenomenal aspect (*shi*) and the principle aspect (*ri*).

As for the phenomenal aspect, it is the Pure Land of Horizontal Transcendence, which universally encompasses those of the three faculties. It is like the sky that covers all and the earth that supports all equally, surpassing all other Dharma-gates of vertical emergence.

As for the principle aspect, the mind and its objects are perfectly wondrous, naturally possessing the ten modes of contemplation (*jūjō kanpō*). One must clearly understand the essentials of the mind.

One gives rise to right faith. It is essential that clarity regarding the object [of practice] can inspire earnest vows; it is essential that clarity regarding the dharma-gate can establish actual practice.
These three dharmas are such that taking up one is to take up all three, and the entirety of the three is one.

The oneness and threeness are perfectly interfused and inconceivable. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "The mind capable of mindfulness is inconceivable, for it is itself the Buddha. This is the essence of the mind.
The Buddhas one contemplates are inconceivable, for they are identical with the mind; this is the essential point regarding the object.
Each single recitation is inconceivable; each of the hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions, and billions of recitations—every single sound—is inconceivable.
Because the mind and the Buddha are non-dual, this is the essential point of the Dharma-gate. Although the essentials are spoken of as three, they are one in their inconceivability;

it is thus a secret treasury and a numinous text, hence it is called the *Yaojie* (Essential Explanation). The title of the commentary is concluded. This concludes the first section, the heading, within the exposition of the meaning of the preface.
△ Second, the translators.
[Commentary] Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva.
[Sub-commentary] Regarding the "Tripiṭaka": first, the Sūtra Piṭaka, which is here called the "Scripture Piṭaka"; second, the Vinaya Piṭaka, or...
*Vinaya* is translated here as "extinction" (*nirodha*), or "skillful governance," or "discipline" (*vinaya*). The *Abhidharma-piṭaka* is also called *Abhidharma*;

it is translated as "Incomparable Dharma" (*anuttara-dharma*) and also rendered as "Treatise" (*śāstra*). One is called a "Dharma Master" (*dharmācārya*) because they take the teachings of the Three Piṭakas as their teacher, and because they have profound mastery of the Three Piṭakas and teach and transform humans and devas.
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there are five [types of Dharma Masters].

There are five kinds of Dharma Masters: first, those who receive and uphold [the teachings]; second, those who read; third, those who recite; fourth, those who explain and interpret; and fifth, those who transcribe the scriptures into scrolls.
Because this Master possessed these five virtues, he was called a Dharma Master. Kumārajīva’s full name should be Kumārajīva-śeṣa;
this is translated as "Child Longevity," meaning that although he was a child, he possessed the virtues of the aged. According to his biography, the Master...
When he entered the pass, it was precisely the fourth year of the Hongshi era of the Yao Qin dynasty, which was the first year of the Long’an era of Emperor An of the Eastern Jin.

His grandfather resided in India and had served as a minister to kings for generations. His father renounced his position and left the household life to travel for study until he reached the kingdom of Kucha.

When the king heard of his virtuous reputation, he gave him his daughter in marriage, and from her, Śrīmitra (Kumārajīva) was born. During the days that the Master remained in the womb, his mother’s [virtue] increased.
Huìbiàn left home at the age of seven. Following his mother to a temple, he saw the Buddha’s almsbowl and was filled with joy;

he then lifted it up to the crown of his head. Suddenly, he thought, "My body is small and lowly, yet this bowl is so large. How can I possibly lift it? His strength failed him, and it fell to the ground.

At that moment, he attained a sudden awakening to the truth that all phenomena are but mind. He recited a thousand verses daily. By the time he reached the age of nine, his eloquence had surpassed all others.
The heretics were all filled with shame and submitted. At the age of twelve, he encountered an arhat who marveled at him and said to his mother, "You must protect him;
when he reaches thirty-five years of age, he shall greatly propagate the Buddha-dharma and deliver immeasurable beings.

Furthermore, he studied the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) and the four Vedas (*caturveda*), and later studied the Mahāyāna, repeatedly defeating the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Throughout the distant and near lands, all...

This refers to his miraculous powers. After giving birth to Kumārajīva, his mother also left the household life; she was exceptionally intelligent among the nuns and had already realized the third fruit of the path.

Once Kumārajīva had received full ordination, his mother said to him, "The profound Vaipulya sūtras ought to be propagated in the capital of Qin. However, why would this not be detrimental to your own person?
Kumārajīva replied, "The practice of a Bodhisattva is to benefit others while forgetting one's own body. The Great Transformation must be carried out. [He then entered the fire pit.]
Huo Wuhen. In the ninth year of Fu Jian’s Jianyuan era, the Grand Astrologer reported: "A star of virtue has appeared in the western lands;
there must be a man of wisdom who will come to serve as a counselor. Fu Jian said, "I have heard that there is Kumārajīva in the Western Regions and Dao’an in Xiangyang—is this not the person?
Subsequently, he dispatched General Lü Guang to lead seventy thousand troops westward to campaign against Kucha.
At this time, he returned together with Kumārajīva. While on the road, Kumārajīva frequently spoke of various adaptive responses, all of which Lü Guang put into practice.
When Lü Guang heard that Yao Chang had killed Fu Jian and established his own rule over Xiliang, and later when Yao Xing succeeded to the throne, Lü Guang also died and was succeeded by Lü Long.
It was only after Yao Xing extinguished the Liang state that [Kumārajīva] entered the capital of Qin. The ruler of Qin treated him with great courtesy and invited him to enter the Ximing Pavilion.
The Emperor issued an edict to eight hundred śramaṇas, including Sengqie, to receive Kumārajīva’s instructions and collaborate on the definitive translation of various sūtras at Caotang Monastery.
Later, Vinaya Master Daoxuan once asked the celestial being Lu Xuanchang:

"Why is it that the sūtras and śāstras translated by Master Kumārajīva throughout his lifetime remain as fresh as ever to this day, and why do their practice and upholding continue to flourish? He replied: "It is because of the person who performed the translations."
He prioritized realization and attained the intent entrusted to him by the Buddha. Furthermore, from the time of Vipaśyin Buddha onward, he served as a master of scriptural translation.
It is also said that Kumārajīva’s rank was among the Three Sages (trividya-pudgala), and that Mañjuśrī directed and instructed him in the process of editing and determining the texts.

"Translation" (*yi*) means to render the Sanskrit (*fan*) into elegant Chinese (*hua*). According to the *Zhou Li*, the official who presided over the languages of the four quarters was called "Ji" (Guest) in the East.

In the south they were called *xiàng* (elephant); in the west, *dídi*; and in the north, *yì* (interpreter). When Dharmaratna and Kāśyapa Mātanga first arrived in the Han, the northern officials were already proficient in Western languages;
thus, although the scriptures had come from the West, they were termed "translated" (*yì*). Subsequent generations followed this precedent.
Therefore, it is still called a "translation. The section on the translator concludes.
△ Third, the Commentator.
[Explanation]: To the west, there was the śramaṇa Ouyi Zhixu, who provided this commentary.

[Commentary] "The Western Existence" (Sai-u) is an alternative appellation for the Great Master. It signifies that the two aspects of retribution—the environment and its inhabitants—truly exist in the West;
it does not merely discuss a partial principle while negating actual reality. There are further meanings, which should be examined in the Patriarch Xiyou’s *Jie* (Exegesis).
Fearing prolixity, they are not recorded here. As for "Śramaṇa," the Sanskrit term is sometimes rendered as "Sengmen"; the correct pronunciation is...
*Śramaṇa* is here translated as "merit" (*gōngláo*). This refers to the fact that one has achieved merit through the cultivation of the Path.
In the Western Regions, whether Buddhist or non-Buddhist, all who have left the household life are called *śramaṇas*; this is thus the general designation for those who have renounced the world.

In the language of Tang, it is explained according to its meaning as "diligent practice" (*śramaṇa*), because it refers to diligently practicing the path to *nirvāṇa*. The *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses* states:
"One who quiets the mind and reaches the fundamental source is therefore called a śramaṇa. Furthermore, there are four kinds of śramaṇas:
first, the śramaṇa who excels in the path, namely the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others; second, the śramaṇa who explains the path, namely those who proclaim the True Dharma.

The third refers to the "path-sustaining śramaṇa," namely those who cultivate wholesome qualities. The fourth refers to the "path-defiling śramaṇa," namely those who engage in various heterodox practices.
"Ōyì" (Lianchi) was the master’s dharma-name for Pure Practice. "Ō" (Lotus) signifies the two stages of Principle-Equivalence (*lī-jué*) and Name-Equivalence (*míng-zì-jué*).

"Lián" (Lotus) serves as a metaphor for the two stages of Contemplative Practice (*guān-xíng*) and Similarity (*xiāng-sì*). "Yì" (Benefit) signifies the two stages of Cultivation and Realization (*xiū-zhèng*). Thus, the name "Ōyì" encompasses the six stages of realization.

The flower symbolizes the stage of partial realization (*praveśa*), while the lotus symbolizes the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā*). Because the Master indicated that he resided within the stage of the mere name (*nāmamātra*), he was called "O-lü" (Wu).
As for "benefit" (*yi*), it refers to the benefits of the four *siddhāntas*, the explanation of which appears in the subsequent text.

The meaning is that in the mire of the present five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), one may only obtain the four benefits of the mere name; however, when the flowers bloom in a precious pond, one obtains the four [benefits] of the lotus pedestal.
...beneficial. Thus, he was styled Ouyi for the time being. As for Zhixu: "Zhi" (Wisdom) is likened to the sun rising in the east; this is the Master’s name.
According to the Master’s own biography, his secular surname was Zhong, his given name was Jiming, and he was also named Sheng, with the courtesy name Zhenzhi. His ancestors were from Bianliang.

The clan's original progenitor moved south of the Yangtze River and settled in Guru (Suzhou). His mother was of the Jin clan; because her father, Qi— (Note: The source text appears to be truncated at this point.)
Zhonggong recited the Great Compassion Mantra for ten years; he dreamed that a Bodhisattva brought him a son, who was subsequently born to him.

At seven years of age, he began eating vegetarian food. At twelve, he entered a private school and heard the teachings of the Sages; immediately, he took it upon himself to carry forward the Way through all eternity and vowed to extinguish the doctrines of Śākyamuni and Laozi.
He abolished fermented meats and wine and composed several dozen treatises to refute heterodox views. At seventeen, he read the preface to the *Zizhi lu* (Record of Self-Knowledge) and...
In the *Zhuchuang suibi* (Random Notes from the Bamboo Window), he wrote: "I did not slander the Buddha; rather, I took the treatises I had composed and burned them.

At twenty years of age, I expounded upon the *Analects* and attained great awakening to the mind-dharma of Confucius and Yan Hui. In winter, my father passed away; hearing of the Original Vow of Kṣitigarbha, I gave rise to the aspiration for transcendence."
At twenty-two, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of nianfo (Buddha-recitation) and burned more than two thousand pieces of his draft writings.
At twenty-three, he listened to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. At twenty-four, within a single month, he dreamed of Hanshan three times; the Master then traveled to Caoxi.
Unable to follow [Master Yunqi] from afar, he instead received the precepts of renunciation from Master Xueling, who was given the name Zhixu. Master Xueling was a disciple of Master Han.
At the age of twenty-five, he resided at Mount Jing and attained realization of the Way. At twenty-six, he received the Bodhisattva precepts. At twenty-eight, his mother fell critically ill;
he cut flesh from his own arm four times, yet she could not be saved. His grief pierced to the very core of his lungs and liver. [He attended to] the funeral arrangements.
Having finished [his studies], he burned his brushes and inkstones and vowed to head for the deep mountains. He subsequently secluded himself at Songling.

Suffering from a severe illness in Guanzhong, he applied the methods of Chan meditation to seek rebirth in the Pure Land. At the age of thirty, he emerged from seclusion and began composing works such as the *Jiyao of the Vinaya* (Vini Shi Yi Jiyao).
At thirty-two, he devoted himself to the study of the Tiantai school. At thirty-seven, he composed the *Ullambana*.

New Commentary. At the age of thirty-nine, he composed the *Combined Commentary on the Brahma Net Sutra*. At the age of forty-one, he composed the *Textual Exegesis of the Great Buddha-Topknot Dhāraṇī*.

Among the various works authored by the Master include the *Treatise on the Refutation of Emptiness*, the *Commentaries on the Three Sutras*, the *Essentials of Consciousness-Only*, the *Direct Explanation of the Eight Essentials of the Dharma Characteristics School*, the *Essential Explanation of Amitābha*, the *Meaning of the Assembly of the Lotus Sutra*, the *Commentary on the Meaning of the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, and the *Awakening of Faith*.
Including the *Liegang shu* and other works, there were forty-eight titles comprising approximately three hundred volumes.
At the age of fifty-seven, he entered parinirvāṇa at Lingfeng. Three years later, his disciples opened the sarcophagus for cremation and beheld him sitting upright and majestic;
his hair had grown long enough to cover his ears, and his countenance was as if alive. After the cremation, his teeth remained entirely intact, so they did not dare to proceed [with their disposal].
The Posthumous Bequest: "The remains [of the Master] shall be enshrined in a bone-stupa to the right of the Great Hall.
This concludes the three prefaces by the masters. △ Fourth, the Main Exposition, which is divided into two parts: First, the Preface to the Dharma-gate; Second, the Preface to the Commentary.
The first part is further divided into two: First, a General Preface to the Many Gates; Second, a Specific Elucidation of the Pure Land School. △ Now, the first [part].

[Preface] To begin with, the Buddhas take pity on the deluded masses and bestow their transformative teachings according to their capacities. Although the return to the source is non-dual, the expedient means are manifold.
[Commentary] "To begin with" (*yuanfu*) is an introductory phrase. "The Buddhas" refers to the Dharmakāya, Sambhogakāya, Nirmāṇakāya, and Nairmāṇikakāya. The Nirmāṇakāya...
The Buddhas of the *sahā* (common) lands are the *nirmāṇakāya* (response bodies). The Buddhas of the lands of skillful means are the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward bodies).

The Buddhas of the lands of true reward are the *dharmakāya* (dharma bodies). The Buddhas of the lands of tranquil light are the *dharmakāya*. Furthermore, each single body possesses all four lands, and each land possesses all four bodies;
the perfect interfusion of body and land is inconceivable. "Compassionate mindfulness" refers to the Buddhas.

There are three types of *maitrī* (loving-kindness): those conditioned by sentient beings (*sattvālambana*), those conditioned by phenomena (*dharmālambana*), and those without conditions (*anālambana*).

*Maitrī* conditioned by sentient beings takes conventional designations as its object. *Maitrī* conditioned by phenomena takes real dharmas as its object. *Maitrī* without conditions takes the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) as its object.

The *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) compassionately regards the six classes of ordinary beings through *maitrī* conditioned by sentient beings. The *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) compassionately regards the nine realms through *maitrī* conditioned by phenomena. The *dharmakāya* and *sambhogakāya* [compassionately regard] through *maitrī* without conditions.

It is out of compassionate mindfulness for the sentient beings of the ten realms. As for those who are deluded: the six classes of ordinary beings are deluded regarding the Truth of Reality (*satyadharma*), while the followers of the Three Vehicles are deluded regarding the Middle Way.
Because they are deluded regarding the Truth, they falsely create illusory existence; thus there is birth-and-death with distinct segments (*paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa*).

Because they are deluded regarding the Middle, they falsely cling to illusory emptiness; thus there is birth-and-death through transformation (*pariṇāma-jarāmaraṇa*). Due to the suffering of these two forms of death, they give rise to [retribution].
"Third, it is compassion and sympathetic concern. 'According to capacity' refers to the capacities for the four *siddhāntas*.
Regarding *siddhānta*: *Siddha* means 'universal,' which is a term from the Chinese language; *tān* refers to *dāna*, a term from the Sanskrit language, meaning 'giving.
Combining these Chinese and Sanskrit terms, we have *siddhānta*. There are four kinds: namely, the world-view *siddhānta*, the person-oriented *siddhānta*, and the..."

The therapeutic standpoint (*yathā-saṃtāna-siddhānta*) and the ultimate standpoint (*paramārtha-siddhānta*). "Faculties" (*maki*) refers to the spiritual capacities (*indriya*). The Tathāgata observes these faculties and adapts his teaching accordingly.

To cause those who have not yet planted roots of goodness to plant them, he teaches according to their inclinations; this is the worldly standpoint (*loka-siddhānta*), which accords with the faculty of joy.
To cause those who have already planted roots of goodness to increase them, he teaches according to what is appropriate for them; this is... [the therapeutic standpoint].

The *puruṣa-siddhānta* (human standpoint) is for those with the potential to produce wholesome roots; it causes those already grown to reach maturity and is taught according to what is needed as an antidote.

The *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (antidotal standpoint) is for those with the potential to destroy unwholesome roots; it causes those already matured to attain liberation and is taught according to the principle.
The *paramārtha-siddhānta* (ultimate standpoint) is for those with the potential to enter into the principle; it is also called the "four benefits" (*catur-anuśamsa*), and is also known as...
The four types of followers: because there are these four capacities, the three bodies are manifested as skillful means for their instruction.
"Returning to the source is non-dual" means returning to the single ultimate. "Skillful means" refers to the means of the four *siddhāntas*.
"Many gates" refers to the sixteen gates of the four teachings. This concludes the initial general introduction to the many gates.

Therefore, it is better than anything else to faithfully aspire and single-mindedly hold fast to the Name.
[Commentary] This, moreover, selects the sixteenth practice—single-mindedly holding fast to the Name—from among the sixteen sublime contemplations because it is simple, easy, stable, and reliable.

To establish this as a daily practice—does this not reveal that the single method of holding the name universally accommodates the three capacities, encompasses both phenomena and principle without omission, and unifies all teachings and schools without exception? Is it not truly inconceivable?
[Commentary] Regarding the "encompassing of phenomena and principle": the single phrase of the Great Name constitutes the four kinds of pure lands.

Therefore, it is called "Comprehensive" (She). As for that which unifies the teachings and the school: the single thought-moment of the mind-nature is the great fundamental principle of the Dharma-realm.
If a person simply recites the name of Amitābha Buddha, this is termed the unsurpassed, profound, and wondrous Chan. Therefore, it is called "Unifying the School" (Tongzong).

It spans horizontally across the eight teachings and penetrates vertically through the five periods. Therefore, it is called "Unifying the Teachings. This concludes the section on the Dharma-gate of the Preface.

【Preface】 Throughout antiquity, there have never been periods lacking those who produced commentaries and sub-commentaries. As time has passed, these have mostly fallen into obscurity, with but a few remaining.

The Venerable Master Yunqi composed the *Sūcāo* (Commentary and Sub-commentary), which is vast, profound, and subtle. The Master Uncle Youxi composed the *Yuanchong Cāo* (Sub-commentary on the Perfect and the Centered), which is lofty and deep.
Vast and profound. It is like the sun and moon in the midst of the sky; all who have eyes behold them. [Commentary] The text consists of two sections.

The first, from "In ancient times, Yunqi... onwards, introduces the recent era. As for "Yunqi": *Note: The term "Yunqi" (雲棲) refers to the Chinese Buddhist master Zhuhong (株宏), whose posthumous title was Hongwu (洪武). The mountain named Mount Lianchi is the site of the Dharma-center of Master Lianchi. The Master’s name was Zhuhong; his courtesy name was Fohui.
He was a native of Renhe in Hangzhou and his secular surname was Shen. He entered the monastic order at the age of thirty-one and studied under Nianhua Bianrong.

Master Xiaoyan Bao attained enlightenment. In the fifth year of the Longqing era of the Great Ming, he went to Yunqi to beg for alms; seeing that the mountains and waters were elegant and refined, he settled there.
He authored works such as the *Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra* (*Mituo Shuchao*). He passed away in the fortieth year of the Wanli era at the age of eighty-one.

Those who refer to Yunqi as *upādhyāya* did so because they received the precepts from him. Regarding the *Shuchao*:
"Sū" refers to elucidating the meaning of the sūtras, while "Chao" refers to further explaining the *shu*. It is vast and profound.
"Zhe" (The One) praises his vast and expansive principles as well as his refined and meticulous prose. "Youxi" (Deep Creek) is a place name;

it refers to Mount Tiantai, specifically Youxi Gaoming Temple, which was the site of practice for the Great Master Chuandeng. The Master’s secular surname was Ye. In his youth, he left the household life under the guidance of Chan Master Ying’an.
He authored works such as the *Yuanzhong chao* (Commentary on the Perfect Center) and the *Wusheng lun* (Treatise on Non-arising), and widely propagated the practice of nianfo (Buddha-recitation).
Dharma Gate. Each time he ascends the seat, celestial music resounds in the void, heard by the entire assembly. Regarding the *Yuanzhong chao* (Excerpts from the Perfect [Teaching]):
using the principle of the Perfect Teaching, it is an excerpted commentary on Master Dayou’s *Brief Explanation of Amitābha* from Beichen Monastery in Suzhou.
The phrase "lofty, profound, vast, and extensive" praises its perfect principle as being both lofty and profound, and its Middle Way as being broad and extensive. Sun and Moon.
The "Middle Heaven" serves as a metaphor to reveal the vastness and profound depth of the meanings contained in those two books.
The phrase "all who have eyes behold it" indicates that those two books can only benefit those with prior learning; they cannot benefit beginners.

Therefore, they are not essential commentaries on this sutra, for this sutra is one that universally encompasses practitioners of all three capacities. This concludes the initial preface to the ancient commentaries.

△ Second, the introduction, which is now explained in two parts: first, the formal introduction of the causes and conditions; second, the clarification of the reasons for its distinctiveness. △ Now, the first part.

[Introduction] Specifically, because the text is voluminous and the meaning is manifold, its boundaries are unfathomable. Consequently, those of initial capacity and shallow understanding find it difficult to develop faith and aspiration.
Therefore, I shall not again presume upon my own mediocrity and folly to restate the essential interpretation.
△ Second, clarifying the point of their differences.
[Preface] I do not dare to compete with the two elders in asserting difference, nor is it necessary for me to insist on being the same as them. It is like looking at something from the side.
As for the formation of peaks: viewed horizontally, they appear as ridges; viewed vertically, none are fully exhausted. This is the true realm of Mount Lu.
One must simply ensure that each person has personally seen Mount Lu for themselves.

[Commentary] This section consists of two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the illustration by means of a metaphor. Within the illustration, the metaphor is presented first. Su Dongpo’s poem on visiting Mount Lu says:
“Seen from the front, it forms a ridge; seen from the side, it forms peaks. From afar or near, high or low, each is different.
I do not recognize the true face of Mount Lu, Simply because my body is within these mountains. Within this poem...
This matter possesses a principle. Regarding it from the perspective of phenomena (*dharma*): when one’s body is within a mountain, one cannot see the entire landscape of Mount Lu;
thus it is said, "One does not know the true face of Mount Lu, precisely because one's body is on this very mountain. Regarding it from the perspective of principle (*tattva*):
Dongpo was one who had realized the Way (*bodhi*), and he used this phenomenon to manifest that principle. Viewing the peaks from the side... [the text continues with] horizontal...

"Beholding the mountain ridges, where near and far, high and low, each differ"—this means that whether viewed from the side or from across, these aspects of distance, proximity, height, and depth are all formed by the nature of mind (*cittatā*).
"Not knowing the true face of Mount Lu" means not knowing the original face of the nature of mind.
"It is simply because one's body is within this mountain" means that the body is within the nature of mind.
For this reason, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Once deluded, one takes this as the mind and is certain to be confused, regarding it as being within the physical body.
One does not know that from the physical body outward, including the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, all are objects manifested within the wondrously luminous mind."

In this context, viewing the mountain from the side as peaks and viewing it from the front as ridges is a metaphor for the various commentaries and sub-commentaries, each of which elucidates the Buddha’s mind;
yet none of them exhaustively captures it, because its essence is fundamentally an inexhaustible treasury.

Even though none of them are exhaustive, they nonetheless ensure that each person has personally seen Mount Lu; that is to say, even if one does not fully exhaust the Buddha’s mind, one nevertheless...

This does not lose the Buddha’s intent. What is the Buddha’s intent? It means that each person, through mindfulness, reaches the state of "one mind undisturbed," personally awakens to the true face of the nature of mind, personally attains birth in the Pure Land, and personally beholds the true realm of Ultimate Bliss—only then will it be finished.
The second preface, the present commentary, is now concluded. This concludes the first major section, the meaning of the preface.

△ Second, the explanation of the sūtra, which is further divided into two parts: first, the fivefold profound meaning (*pañca-gambhīrārtha*); second, the formal explanation of the sūtra text. The first part is further divided into five sections: first, the explanation of the title; second, the discernment of the essence (*tattva*);

third, the clarification of the primary tenet (*mūla-siddhānta*); fourth, the clarification of the power and function; fifth, the clarification of the characteristics of the teaching (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*).

First, the clarification of the first section, the explanation of the title, which is further divided into two parts: first, the general presentation of the established title; second, the specific explanation of its common application.
Separate. △ Now, the first [section].
【Commentary】 First, the explanation of the title. This sutra is titled after the person who speaks and the person spoken to.
【Sub-commentary】 Among the seven ways of establishing titles, this is the case where it is named after a single person. Question: Regarding the speaker and the one spoken to...
"All are Buddhas. Why are they called "persons"? Answer: A Buddha is the ultimate person.

△ Second, the detailed explanation of the general and specific names has two parts: first, the explanation of the specific names; second, the explanation of the general name. The first part [the explanation of the specific names] further has three sections:
first, the explanation of the character "Buddha" (佛); second, the explanation of the character "to preach" (說); third, the explanation of "Amitābha. △ Now, the first section.

[Commentary] "Buddha" refers to the teaching master who can expound the Dharma in this land. That is, Śākyamuni, who, by virtue of the power of his great compassionate vows, was born into the world of the five turbidities;
he awakened those yet to awaken (awakening others) through his own prior awakening (self-awakening), knowing all dharmas and seeing all dharmas (the perfection of awakening).
[Commentary]: "The Teacher of the Doctrine" refers to the master of the four teachings; that is, the three bodies (trikāya) of Śākyamuni Buddha.

"The power of the great compassionate vow" refers to the three conditions of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. "The world of the five turbidities" refers to the four kinds of defiled lands.

Regarding the three types of awakening: these refer to the three awakenings within the four teachings. That is to say, in the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) teaching, one attains self-awakening through the contemplation of analytical emptiness;

one turns the wheel of the Dharma regarding the truth of birth-and-death and the means of deliverance to awaken others; and entering extinction upon the exhaustion of conditions constitutes the fulfillment of awakening.

In the *Pratyekabuddha* (Shared) teaching, one attains self-awakening through the contemplation of the essence of emptiness; one turns the wheel of the Dharma of both birth-and-death and non-arising to awaken others; and [upon the] exhaustion of conditions...
Entering cessation constitutes the fulfillment of self-awakening (*svabodhi*). In the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), one awakens oneself through the three successive contemplations;
turning the wheel of the Dharma of the three vehicles constitutes awakening others (*parabodhi*); and exhausting the twelve grades of ignorance constitutes the fulfillment of awakening.

In the Perfect Teaching (*samyak-saṃbuddha-yāna*), one awakens oneself through the three contemplations in a single mind; turning the wheel of the Dharma of the four teachings constitutes awakening others; and exhausting the forty-two [grades of] ignorance...

The exhaustion of ignorance within the categories [of existence] constitutes the fulfillment of awakening. "There is no dharma he does not know" refers to the ultimate realization of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"There is no dharma he does not see" refers to the ultimate realization of the Buddha-eye. The explanation of the character "Buddha" is complete.
△ Second, the explanation of the character "to speak" (shuo).
[Commentary]: To speak means to express what one harbors in one's heart. The Buddha harbors the intent to deliver sentient beings.

When the capacity of sentient beings to attain Buddhahood has matured, he speaks the Dharma that is difficult to believe, causing them to achieve ultimate liberation; therefore, it is called "speaking" (or "delighting").

[Commentary] Those whose capacity for attaining Buddhahood has matured are not the capacities of the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles; rather, they are the capacities of the Buddha-realm of the Perfect Teaching (Enkyō).
"Ultimate liberation" means that in a single thought-moment of resonance, there is a single Buddha. The explanation of the character *shaku* (釋) is complete.
△ Third, the explanation of Amitābha has two parts: first, clarifying the Guide; second, clarifying the Brahma-flower. △ Now, the first part.

【Commentary】 Amitābha refers to the Guide of that land as described. By means of his forty-eight vows, he receives those sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha with faith and aspiration, causing them to be born in the World of Ultimate Bliss and forever attain the stage of non-retrogression.
[Commentary]: "The Guide of that land" refers to the guides who lead one through the four kinds of pure lands.

"Permanently attaining the stage of non-retrogression" means the perfect realization of the three types of non-retrogression. The explanation of "non-retrogression" will appear in the subsequent text. This concludes the clarification of the Guide.
△ Second, explaining the Chinese and Sanskrit names.
[Commentary]: The Sanskrit term is Amitābha; this is translated here as "Immeasurable Life" (Wúliàngshòu). It is also called "Immeasurable Light" (Wúliàngguāng).

In essence, his merit and wisdom, spiritual powers and supernatural faculties, the adornments of his primary and secondary bodies, and his preaching of the Dharma to transform and deliver beings—each and every one of these is immeasurable.
[Commentary] "Sanskrit" (Banyu) refers to the language of Brahmā. Because the language of India is identical to that of Brahmā, it is called "Sanskrit.
At the beginning of the kalpa, the devas of the Ābhāsvara Heaven descended to India; therefore, their language is the same as that of Brahmā.

"Light-life" (Kōju) refers to the light and life of the three bodies (*trikāya*); this will be explained in the subsequent text. The three bodies are the four lands (*catasraḥ bhūmayaḥ*), and the four lands are the four... [text fragment ends].
Therefore, both merit and wisdom pertain to all four teachings. Merit and wisdom refer to the six *pāramitās* of the four teachings:
the first five *pāramitās* constitute merit, while *prajñā* constitutes wisdom. Supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) refer to the six supernatural powers of the four teachings.

The Path refers to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) of the four teachings. Powers refer to the ten powers (*bala*) of the four teachings. The Bases refer to the four kinds of pure lands.
"Correct" refers to the primary and attendant elements of the four lands. "Adornment" refers to the two adornments of merit and wisdom.

"Preaching the Dharma" means that both the primary and attendant elements are able to preach the Dharma. "Transformation and deliverance" refers to the transformer and the transformed, the deliverer and the delivered.
"Immeasurable" means inconceivable. Because it is inconceivable, it cannot be measured by the mind; because it is beyond deliberation, it cannot be...

Regarding the measure of discourse: it is not only that the three aforementioned lands are inconceivable; even within the Land of Common Residence, every single phenomenon one might mention is inconceivable.
Because they are inconceivable, it is said that the four lands are perfectly interfused. This concludes the explanation of the specific names.
△ Second, the explanation of the general title.

[Commentary]: All that issues from the golden mouth is generally termed "Sūtra. In contrast to the aforementioned five characters, this is a case where the general and the specific are combined to form the title.

Regarding the three categories of teaching (*jiao*), practice (*xing*), and principle (*li*), each has both general and specific aspects, as explained extensively in the *Tiantai Zang* (The Tiantai Canon).
[Commentary: This explains the general meaning of the character "sūtra" (*jing*) while simultaneously distinguishing its general and specific applications.

"As explained in the *Tiantai Zang*" refers specifically to the explanation of the character "sūtra" found in the Tiantai teachings—that is, it points back to the preceding passage explaining the term "sūtra. The major section on the "Explanation of Names" is hereby concluded.
△ Second, the exposition of the essence (*tattva*). The *Miaozong* states: "Explaining the names" means explaining the provisional names that can express [the reality].
"Expounding the essence" means revealing the actual substance (*vastu*) signified by those names. This is intended to ensure that students have a point of reference;

this is precisely the subtle intent behind Tiantai’s exposition of the essence. Within this section, there are two parts: first, the presentation of the names; second, the formal exposition. △ Now, the first part.
[Commentary] The second section distinguishes the essence (*tattva*). All Mahāyāna sūtras take *bhūtatathatā* (the true mark of reality) as their primary essence.

[Sub-commentary] The *Guanjing shu* (Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra) states: "Essence refers to the fundamental substance. The *Śāstra* says: "Except for the *bhūtatathatā* of all phenomena, everything else is the work of Māra.
Mahāyāna sūtras take *bhūtatathatā* as their seal and as the primary essence of the sūtra. The *Miaozong chao* (Sub-commentary on the Miaojue jing) explains: "All..."
The Dharma abides in neither arising nor ceasing; it is neither existent nor empty; it has no agent and no object;

it is free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of names, and free from the characteristics of mental objects. Being free from all such characteristics is called the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of formlessness.
Since it is termed the true characteristic, it is also called the true substance, the true power, the true activity, and even the true beginning and end.
Ultimate equality. Since these ten dharmas are real, they are the true arising, the true Buddha, the true reliance, and the true correctness.

A single form or a single fragrance is none other than the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). One should know that the true mark is the total illumination of the entire body, which is called the true mind (*tathatā-citta*) and is also termed original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*).
Because the essence of awakening is all-pervasive, all phenomena are real. To point to its essential core: it does not depart from what is manifest before one.

The thought of discrimination—this very thought is original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*); this enlightenment is the essence of the sutra. Therefore, the subsequent section examines the mind to discern the essence.
Furthermore, "Mahāyāna sutras" distinguishes them from Hīnayāna sutras. The Hīnayāna has three seals: impermanence, non-self, and [the peace of] nirvana.
These two seals seal *saṃsāra*. The single seal of quiescence seals *nirvāṇa*. In the Hīnayāna, because *nirvāṇa* and *saṃsāra* are distinct, they are each sealed separately.
In the Mahāyāna, because *saṃsāra* is itself *nirvāṇa*, only the single Seal of True Reality (*bhūtatathatāmudrā*) is required.
"Seal" (*mudrā*) means faith; it also refers to an official tally or seal. That which is expressed accords with this [seal], whether in the two vehicles, Great or Small.
All vehicles may be trusted. The initial presentation of the names is concluded.
△ Second, the formal discussion. Generally speaking, all dharmas are identical with the true mark (dharmatā). The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "All dharmas have such characteristics, nature, and so forth.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction," and so on. Now it is said:
"The single thought-moment before us" is an interpretation based on the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*). This interpretation contains three points:

First, the *Wenju* states that if one were to interpret this according to the Buddha-dharma, the doubt would be too lofty; if one were to interpret it according to the dharma of sentient beings, the doubt would again be too broad.
Therefore, interpreting it according to the mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*) present before us is the most immediate and relevant. Second, this constitutes the primary interpretation.
A single phrase of the great name of myriad virtues is itself emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle Way;
it is the secret treasury of the three virtues realized by all Buddhas, the essential core of the Buddhas' minds. Therefore, the subsequent text states:
"One utterance of 'Namo Amitābha Buddha' is the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi attained by our Original Teacher. Furthermore, these three aspects are beneficial.
For those who practice Zen, it is easy to attain awakening and entry. All phenomena are fundamentally tranquil; it is only the mind that is itself restless.

If the mind is not restless, the myriad phenomena will remain as they are, and the essence of the true mark (*dharmatā*) will manifest. Within this, there are three parts: first, clarifying that the nature and measure are without marks;
second, clarifying that the nature-body is perfectly accomplished; and third, clarifying that the nature is fully endowed with pervasive activity. These are the three sections.
The single character "nature" (性) within the phrase "the nature of the mind in this one thought-moment" distinguishes its essence, attributes, and function. △ Now, the first [section].
【Commentary】 The nature of the mind in the present one thought-moment of ours does not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between.

It is not of the past, not of the present, and not of the future. (Students must investigate deeply and apply rigorous pressure in this manner; they must not merely let it pass by as mere words or intellectual principles.)
[Commentary] "The nature of the mind in the present single thought-moment" specifically refers to the essence of a single recitation of the Buddha’s name. The *Wusheng lun* states:
"The perfectly interfused essence of the Dharma-realm acts as my single thought-mind; therefore, the mind with which I recite the Buddha's name is in its entirety the Dharma-realm itself.
This extends to the vast, ordinary mind of daily life, which the *Miaozong chao* identifies as "discrimination."
This is the general title for the three categories. The three categories specifically manifest the three truths.

"Mind" (xin) refers to the function of the unchanging following conditions, analogous to waves upon water. "Nature" (xing) is the essence of the following conditions while remaining unchanging, analogous to the moist nature of the waves.
These correspond to the two meanings of "quiescence and illumination" discussed below in the subsequent text.
The two meanings of radiance and longevity are non-dual in essence and function; thus it is said that they are eternally quiescent and eternally illuminating.

"Not abiding in the three places" and "not belonging to the three periods of time" refers to what the *Miaozong* calls the fact that the mind-dharma is neither produced nor extinguished in its own place. This "own place" is—
This refers to the very substance itself. Since the substance of the mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*) cannot be apprehended, it does not exist within, without, or in between.
It is like a wave being identical to moisture; one cannot find a wave apart from moisture, for it does not exist outside the moisture, inside the moisture, or in between them.
Because the substance of the mental phenomena is neither arising nor ceasing, they do not belong to the three periods of time. This is like [the waves] upon the sea.
The waves appear to have past and future, yet the entire wave is simply water; fundamentally, no three periods of time can be found.

Furthermore, it does not abide in these three locations; therefore, it is said to be "transversely pervasive. It was originally not of the three periods of time; therefore, it is able to "vertically exhaust" them.

Because it vertically exhausts them, it is called "quiescence. Because it is transversely pervasive, it is called "illumination. Because it illuminates, it is called "light. Because it is quiescent, it is called "longevity. As the ancient masters said:
The ten ages of past and present do not depart from the present thought; the boundless oceans of lands are not separated by a single hair-tip.
Therefore, it is called "Immeasurable Light and Life.
[Commentary: It is neither blue, yellow, red, nor white; neither long, short, square, nor round; neither fragrance, nor flavor, nor touch; nor is it a phenomenon (*dharma*).
[Commentary] This refers to what the *Miaozong* calls the absence of the characteristics of subject and object. "Subject" refers to the six sense organs; "object" refers to the six sense fields.
It is illustrated by the analogy that the initiator is water and the initiated is waves. Since waves and water are one and the same moist nature, they are neither subject nor object.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgatagarbha is the fundamentally wondrous, perfect, and complete mind. It is not mind, it is not emptiness..."
Earth, water, fire, and wind are not the six sense organs; they are not the six sense objects; they are not the six consciousnesses; they are not the Four Noble Truths;
they are not the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination; they are not the Six Perfections; nor are they the Four Virtues, and so forth.
[Commentary] When sought, it is utterly unobtainable, yet one cannot say it is non-existent. It fully manifests the thousand suchnesses of the hundred realms, yet one cannot say it is existent.
[Commentary]: This refers to what the *Myōshū* calls the "neither existent nor non-existent" characteristic. It is likened to waves upon water: they are neither existent nor non-existent.
Because the waves are entirely water, they are not existent; because the water entirely constitutes the waves, they are not non-existent.

Since both existence and non-existence are negated, all four propositions (*catuskoṭi*) are absent. Because the four propositions are absent, one is free from the hundred negations (*śata-apavāda*). Therefore, it is called the "pure reality."

This refers to "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*). If one searches for them, they are utterly unobtainable. This means that, following the preceding text regarding the three locations and three periods of time, they cannot be found.

It cannot be said that they do not exist; for although they lack characteristics, they possess essence and function. "Possessing the creation of the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses" (*śata-dhātu-sahasra-tathatā*):
"Possessing" refers to inherent possession (*li-jù*), meaning that within a single moment of mind, the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses are fundamentally possessed.
This is analogous to the principle that water inherently possesses waves. "Creation" refers to phenomenal creation;

it means that the nature of mind, following conditions, creates the phenomena of the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses. This is analogous to water encountering wind and moving, thereby giving rise to the phenomenon of waves.
"The hundred realms" refers to the ten dharma-realms; as each realm possesses its own ten dharma-realms, there are thus one hundred realms.

Furthermore, there are the "ten suchnesses," namely: such appearance, such nature, such substance, such power, such activity, such cause, such condition, such fruit, such retribution, and such ultimate equality from beginning to end.
Each of the hundred realms possesses its own ten "thusnesses" (yūrūshī), resulting in one thousand such instances.

Furthermore, there are one thousand provisional names, one thousand primary retributions (*zhengbao*), and one thousand environmental retributions (*yibao*), totaling three thousand. Additionally, there are the three thousand as inherent in principle (*lijù*) and the three thousand as manifested in phenomena (*shìzào*), constituting two layers of three thousand.
Thus, the ancient masters said: "There are two layers of three thousand: those inherent in principle and those manifested in phenomena."

The three thousand [realms] coexist within a single thought-moment. That they "cannot be said to exist" means that although the hundred realms and thousand phenomena are distinct, they are but the one True Suchness (tathatā), and each lacks an independent self-nature (svabhāva) that can be apprehended.

This is illustrated by the analogy of waves: although the waves are distinct, they are but the one nature of moisture, and each lacks an inherent nature that can be apprehended. Therefore, it is said that they cannot be said to exist.
[Commentary: It is free from all objects of thought, conceptual discrimination, and the characteristics of speech and writing;
yet, these objects of thought, conceptual discrimination, speech, and writing do not exist as having a separate intrinsic nature apart from this [freedom].

[Commentary]: This *Miaozong* (Exquisite Commentary) states that the mental dharmas are, in their very place, free from the characteristic of verbal expression, free from the characteristic of names, and free from the characteristic of mental conditions.
It is, for example, like waves and water: in their essential substance, they are without verbal expression, without names, and without mental conditions.
"To be free from all characteristics of conceptualization, discrimination, language, and letters" means to be entirely free from the aforementioned characteristics of clinging to objects,
mental deliberation, discrimination, language, and letters— whether they pertain to what is internal, external, or intermediate. Furthermore,
these characteristics of conceptualization, discrimination, language, and letters do not possess an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) that exists separately from this [freedom].
This means that all aforementioned objects of cognition, conceptualizations, and so forth, are by nature fundamentally detached.
They are not detached because they possess a nature; rather, they are fundamentally unobtainable. Therefore, it is said that they are detached from this "non-nature.
If they possessed a nature, they could not be detached. This is illustrated by waves upon water: their very self-nature is moisture, and they are not detached from this moisture.

There is no separate nature of waves that can be apprehended. This is because it is free from the pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) of ordinary beings; for that conceptualization is fundamentally empty.

It is not only free from this, but also free from the partial truth of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), as well as all marks of discursive thought, discrimination, language, and letters.
Furthermore, it is free from the "mere Middle" (*butong zhongdao*) of Bodhisattvas, which consists of all discursive thought, discrimination, language, and letters.

Regarding the characteristics of syllables (*akṣara-lakṣaṇa*): through these two kinds of objective referents and so forth, there arises the attachment to phenomena outside the [true] realm (*dharmagrāha*), which constitutes the pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*) of the noble ones.

Taken together with the aforementioned ordinary beings, these constitute the ignorance of the five stages (*pañca-vāsabhūmi-avidyā*). This ignorance of the five stages is by nature fundamentally detached, for it is originally unobtainable.
It is like waves upon water; they take moisture as their own nature, yet they are detached from that moisture.
As for its nature, there is no separate nature of waves to be found. If it were a substantial nature, then one could not be free from it;
because one cannot be free from it, sentient beings would be unable to become Buddhas. The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "This Dharma cannot be understood through conceptualization or discrimination.
The *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* states: "Therefore, all phenomena have, from the very beginning, been by nature detached [from such conceptualizations]."
It cannot be fully expressed by any words or written characters. It is free from the mind’s攀缘 (pariniśraya/ālambana), devoid of all marks, ultimately equal, and is solely this one mind;
it is called *tathatā* (suchness). As for what is called *tathatā*, even this is without marks.
However, among all forms of verbal expression, this is the ultimate: using words to dispel words.

These preceding four sections collectively employ the absolute truth (*paramārtha-satya*) to refute both ordinary sentiments and the conceptual understandings of the sages, thereby revealing the full measure of the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*). The final section concludes by establishing the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

[Commentary]: In brief, to be detached from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) is precisely to be all dharmas. Because they are detached, there are no marks; because they are identical, there is no absence of marks.
Having no other choice, we provisionally name this the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
[Commentary] This concludes the formation of the true reality (*dharmatā*) within the Perfect [Teaching]. To summarize:

"to speak by way of essentials" means that "being free from all marks is itself all phenomena" refers to the aforementioned discussion of marklessness, which—by way of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)—destroys ordinary sentiments and the conceptualizations of the holy, but does not destroy any phenomena of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). It does not subvert the conventional truth.

Therefore, it is not a partial truth; because it is free from emotional attachments and intellectual interpretations, it is not a partial conventionality. Because it is not partial, it possesses the meaning of the Perfect (yuan).

Because it is free [from attachment], there is no "form" (xiang); because it is identical [to reality], there is nothing that is not form. By following the Truth (zhen), there is no form—this is not a partial negation.

By following the Conventional (su), there is nothing that is not form—this is not a partial affirmation. Because it does not lean toward either of the two extremes, it is the Middle Way. Since it is thus perfect...

The Middle Way is also the perfect Truth (paramārtha-satya) and also the perfect Conventional (saṃvṛti-satya). Because there is no other way, we have provisionally given it the name "Reality" (bhūtatathatā).

Reality has no name, yet there is nothing that does not name it; we have merely provisionally established this name and called it Reality. This concludes the initial clarification that the nature and magnitude [of reality] are without marks.

△ Second, the clarification of the perfect accomplishment of the essential nature (*svabhāva*). Regarding "essential nature," it refers to that which universally encompasses all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Regarding "perfect accomplishment" (*pariniṣpanna*), it reveals the original possession by sentient beings and the perfect realization by the Buddhas—the body that is fully perfected and truly established.
This section consists of three parts: first, the general heading; second, the detailed exposition; third, the summary conclusion.
[Commentary] The essence of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is neither quiescence nor illumination; yet it is quiescent while constantly illuminating, and illuminating while constantly quiescent.
[Sub-commentary] This is a general indication that the nature and essence of the Middle Way simultaneously negates the two extremes and simultaneously illuminates the Two Truths.

Because negation and illumination are simultaneous, it says "yet again" (ér fù). Because quiescence and illumination are non-dual, it says "constantly quiescent and constantly illuminating. As for "quiescence":

The essence that remains unchanging while following conditions is the "nature" (xing) mentioned in the preceding text; its function of illuminating while remaining unchanging yet following conditions is the "mind" (xin) mentioned in the preceding text.
Since it is solely this single mind, it is said to "simultaneously negate" (shuang zhe); since it is fully endowed with both essence and function, it "simultaneously illuminates" (shuang zhao).
Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The wondrously luminous original mind of the Tathāgatagarbha is free from both identity and difference."
"This is precisely 'not being identical'"; this is the general heading. The following eight phrases provide the specific exposition.

Among these eight phrases, the first four discuss only the qualities of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*); the middle two phrases discuss both intrinsic nature and cultivation (*bhāvanā*) together; and the final two phrases discuss only the qualities of cultivation."
Regarding "intrinsic virtue" (xingde), it applies throughout the six stages of realization. As for "cultivated virtue" (xiude), there are both inverse cultivation and direct cultivation;
here we discuss only direct cultivation, while inverse cultivation is subsumed within intrinsic virtue. Within direct cultivation, there are both cause and fruit; here we discuss only the fruit.
This realm is the Buddha-realm because it arises through dependent origination.
[Commentary: It is illumination within stillness; it is conventionally named the Land of Constant Still Light. It is stillness within illumination; it is conventionally named the Pure Dharma-body.
[Commentary] These two phrases clarify that the present single thought-moment of the sentient being’s mind-nature is itself the body and land of the Tathāgata.
Regarding "Eternally Quiescent Light" (*nitya-praśānta-ābhāsa*): it is the secret treasury of the three virtues inherently possessed. "Eternal" (*nitya*) is the virtue of the Dharma-body;

"quiescent" (*praśānta*) is the virtue of liberation; "light" (*ābhāsa*) is the virtue of prajñā. Because this is the principle-substance realized by all Buddhas, it constitutes the land. As for the land, there is...
The meaning of movement: therefore, it is both stillness and illumination. This phrase emphasizes the word "stillness. As for the "Pure Dharma-body," this refers to the inherently pure Dharma-body.
Since the "body" (kāya) carries the sense of responding to conditions, it is both stillness and illumination.
This phrase emphasizes the word "illumination."
[Commentary] Furthermore, "illumination-quietude" is metaphorically named the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); "quietude-illumination" is metaphorically named the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

[Sub-commentary] These two phrases clarify that the nature of the mind is also the Tathāgata’s two bodies: the Dharma-body and the Reward-body. The first phrase refers to the character "quietude" (*jì*);

therefore, it corresponds to the Dharma-body, as it takes up the meaning of the Dharma-body's lack of marks (*animitta*). The second phrase refers to the character "illumination" (*zhào*); therefore...
[This] corresponds to the *saṃbhogakāya*. This is because the *saṃbhogakāya* possesses the characteristic of having marks (*sanimitta*). Question:

In the previous two phrases, the *dharmakāya* was associated with the term "correspondence" (*he*). Why, in these two phrases, is the *dharmakāya* associated with "quiescence" (*jì*)? Answer: The *dharmakāya* possesses two meanings: "following conditions" (*suiyuan*) and "being without marks" (*wuxiang*).

In the preceding [section], the discussion was based on the body and land (*kāya-bhūmi*); therefore, the land was associated with quiescence, as it takes "unchangingness" (*avikāra*) as its essence. Now, however, the discussion is based on the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*.
Commentary: Since the merging of the Dharma-body with tranquility constitutes the essence of the Reward-body, these first four lines discuss only the qualities of the nature (xing-de).
The final two lines discuss the nature and cultivation (xing-xiu) in combination.

[Commentary] Furthermore, the quiescent illumination of inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*) is called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); the quiescent illumination of cultivated virtue (*bhāvanā-guṇa*) is called the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
[Sub-commentary] "Inherent virtue" refers to the essential nature of the virtues originally possessed by the mind-nature; it points to the preceding four lines.

Although these constitute the Dharma- and Reward-bodies along with their lands and divisions, they represent the state of original endowment (*li-jù*). Having not yet encountered the power of cultivation and refinement, their functional manifestation (*shi-yòng*) has not yet been realized. It is like...
Gold within ore has not yet been formed for practical use; therefore, whether it be quiescence or illumination, both are collectively termed the *dharmakāya*.

As for the cultivation of merit, this refers to the wisdom of initial enlightenment (*prātibodha*) which illuminates the principle of original enlightenment (*mūlapratibodha*). When delusions are exhausted and wisdom is perfected, the inherent qualities (*prakṛtiguṇa*) are fully manifested.

Like gold extracted from ore, whether characterized by quiescence or illumination, it is collectively termed the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*). The latter two lines discuss only the cultivation of merit.
[Commentary:

Furthermore, the cultivation of merit characterized by illumination and quiescence is called the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*); the cultivation of merit characterized by quiescence and illumination is called the Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

[Commentary] The Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is the self-enjoyment reward body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*), which consists of the four wisdoms and their mental factors (*cittavastu*). It is also called the Dharma-gate Body (*dharmamukhakāya*).
The *Miaozong* states: "The eighty-four thousand *dhāraṇīs* are the hair; the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is the topknot; the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the head;
great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is the eyes; the untainted (*anāsrava*) is the nose; the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are the mouth; and the forty unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*)..."
The Dharma is the teeth; the two types of wisdom are the hands; the Tathāgatagarbha is the abdomen; the three samādhis are the waist; and meditative concentration and wisdom are the feet.
It is clearly understood by oneself alone, yet not seen by others; therefore, it is "harmonized in stillness" (he-ji). This refers to the response-body and transformation-body.

This refers to the *paranirmāṇakāya* (body of transformation for others), which manifests forms throughout the ten realms to respond to and transform all beings; therefore, they are depicted together.
Furthermore, if one masters the preceding four lines, one will know that all sentient beings are fully endowed with the wisdom, virtues, and marks of the Tathāgata’s body and land.

If one understands the middle two phrases, although the principle is complete, it must rely on cultivation to be manifested; yet this manifestation through cultivation is itself the manifestation of the nature.
If one understands the final two phrases, then one knows that the merit of the virtues of cultivation is not in vain. Furthermore, although this clarifies the Buddha-realm, [it applies to all].
The nine [aspects] are likewise manifested together; this is a specific clarification. What follows is a summary of the one mind. [Commentary:
Tranquility and illumination are non-dual; body and land are non-dual; nature and cultivation are non-dual; reality and response are non-dual; there is nothing that is not the true mark (*dharmatā*).

[Commentary]: Although the preceding sections have distinguished between quiescence and illumination, body and land, nature and cultivation, reality and phenomena, and the true and the responsive, they all reside within a single thought-moment;
therefore, it is said they are "non-dual. This concludes the explanation of the perfect realization of the essential nature.
△ The nature of the three insights is fully pervasive and all-encompassing. This section has two parts: first, receiving the preceding and initiating the subsequent; second, the actual exposition.
△ Now, the first part.
【Commentary】The true mark (dharmatā) is non-dual, yet it is also not non-dual.
[Commentary] This承接 (inherits) the principle of non-duality from the preceding text and introduces the reality of non-non-duality in the subsequent text.
That is to say, this nature of mind not only lacks two distinct characteristics, but also lacks the characteristic of non-duality.

△ Second, the actual manifestation. [Commentary: Therefore, the entire substance acts as the support and acts as the principal; it acts as the practice and acts as the reward; it acts as itself and acts as another;

even extending to the speaker (Śākyamuni) and the spoken (Amitābha); the savior (the Buddha) and the saved (sentient beings); the one who can believe (the mind) and that which can be believed (the Dharma); the one who can aspire (to joy and aversion) and that which can be aspired to (Sukhāvatī); and the one who can maintain (the three karmas) and that which can be maintained (the Name).

It can give rise to the three provisions and the four pure lands they produce; it can praise Śākyamuni and all other Buddhas, as well as Amitābha’s primary and secondary realms. There is nothing herein that is not sealed by the authentic seal of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
[Commentary] Regarding the term "inherently complete" (xingju): it means that all phenomena are fundamentally and inherently complete within the nature.
If the nature were not complete [with them], how could phenomena be produced? It is like wood, which inherently contains all possible vessels and is thus able to produce all kinds of vessels.
If the vessels were not inherent within the wood, they could not be made. Since the wood can produce all vessels, every vessel is essentially wood. In reality, this is so.
When all phenomena manifest as marks, then every phenomenon is the true mark (*dharmatā*). Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"The Tathāgatagarbha is the primordial luminosity and the wondrous mind; it is the mind itself, it is emptiness, and it is earth, water, fire, and wind.

For this reason, when it is said that the entire substance acts as the support (*āśraya*) and the supported (*āśrita*), it means that the entire nature, substance, and magnitude act as such; it is not merely a small portion.
There is not a single thing that is not sealed by the True Seal of the Real Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

This means that whichever phenomenon one may take up—even a single atom, a single mustard seed, a single incense stick, or a single flower—all are the spiritual texts (*lingwen*) sealed by the totality that is vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive.
Since they are all vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive, it is said that "phenomenon and phenomenon are unimpeded. If this is so for even a single atom, [it holds for all].
Thus, a single phrase of the Great Name is itself the manifestation of the entire body of reality, vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive. Therefore, the subsequent text states:
"One utterance of 'Namo Amitābha Buddha' is the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi realized by our Original Teacher.
Since it is what the Tathāgata has realized, it is the essence of the Mahāyāna sūtras and the authentic seal of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).

Therefore, the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "The Mahāyāna refers to the three great aspects—essence (*tǐ*), characteristics (*xiàng*), and function (*yòng*)—which are that upon which all Buddhas ride.
This concludes the explanation of the pervasive activity inherent in nature. Part Two: Discerning the Essence through Investigation within the Fivefold Profound Meaning.
△ Section Three: Clarifying the Tenet (*zong*). Master Tiantai has a section titled "Distinguishing the Tenet and the Essence" (*zhì zōngtǐ yī*).
I now record it here for the convenience of students. Some say that the tenet is identical to the essence, and the essence is identical to the tenet.
This is not accepted here. Why? Because while the tenet is dual, the essence is non-dual. If the essence were dual, it would not be the essence. If the tenet...

Non-duality means that the thesis itself is not the thesis. It is like beams and pillars being the structural framework of a house, while the void of the house is what is occupied by those beams and pillars.
One should not say that the beams and pillars are the void of the house, nor that the void of the house is the beams and pillars.

If the essence of the thesis were one with its object, the fault would be as follows; if the essence of the thesis were different from its object, then the two things would exist in isolation, and the thesis would not [establish its meaning].

The school that reveals the essence: the essence is not the essence of a school, and the school is not the essence. If the school were not the essence, there would be no seal against error and inversion;

if the essence were not the school, the essence would be narrow and incomplete. To claim that all phenomena exist separately outside of the *dharmatā*—such that the school and the essence are different—is a fault of this nature.
Now, it is said that they are not different, yet they are different; thus there is a school. They are not one, yet...

Because it is one, it possesses substantiality. I now record this text to clarify the meaning of the essence of the school (*zongti*). However, whether [the specific application] is employed or not is permissible.
This is divided into three parts: first, a general discussion of the meaning of the school; second, a formal elucidation of the school's core tenets (*jingzong*).
The three [sections] conclude with the cause and effect. △ Now, the first.

【Commentary】 The third section clarifies the fundamental tenet (*zong*). The tenet is the essential path for cultivation; it is the pivotal mechanism for realizing the essence and the governing principle of the myriad practices.
If the main rope is pulled, all the tassels are displayed; if the collar is grasped, the sleeves follow. Therefore, following the realization of the essence, one must next...

Discourse on the Thesis. [Commentary]: This summarizes the intent of the discourse on the thesis. The thesis is like the pivot of a door or the trigger of a crossbow. The opening and closing of a door depend upon the pivot;
the discharge of an arrow depends upon the trigger. Therefore, it is said that [the thesis] is the pivot and trigger for realizing the essence of true reality (*dharmatā*).

Indeed, all four teachings discuss the essential path; they all discuss the pivotal mechanism; they all discuss the governing principles. "Gang" (the net) is a metaphor for the governing principles of the four teachings;

"ling" (the collar) is a metaphor for the garment of the three patiences. In the Tripitaka Teaching, the analytical contemplation of emptiness (*vibhajya-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) is taken as the essential path of practice.
It captures the pivotal mechanism of the essence of partial truth and serves as the guiding principle for the myriad practices of the three vehicles within the Tripitaka teachings.
If one lifts this main cord, then all the various items of the eight categories of the Tripitaka teachings will be displayed;

if one pulls this collar, then the lapels and sleeves of the robe of the two types of patience regarding phenomena and their arising will naturally follow. In the Shared Teaching, the contemplation of the emptiness of essence is taken as the essential path of practice.
The "Assembly" (*hui*) is the pivot of the true essence and the guiding principle for the myriad practices of the three vehicles within the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*).

If one lifts this main rope, then all the various items of the eight dharmas of the Shared Teaching will unfold; if one pulls this collar, then the lapels and sleeves of the two types of patience regarding phenomena and birth (*shengfa erren*) of the Shared Teaching will naturally follow.
The Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), by means of the successive three contemplations, brings about the convergence of the "but-midway" (*danzhong*) and the true aspect (*shixiang*).

The essence consists, for the Bodhisattva’s myriad practices, of the eight dharmas of the Separate Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*), where the collar and sleeves of the three successive patiences arrive spontaneously.
In the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna*), by means of the single mind and the threefold contemplation, one realizes the essence of the true reality (*dharmatā*) within the perfect center.

This is exclusively the myriad practices of the Tathāgata, also called the "Secret Cause of the Tathāgata. In the eight dharmas of the Perfect Teaching, the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) serves as the robe; the preceding three are provisional.

The latter one is the reality (*satya*). Because provisional means are established for the sake of reality, there are the distinctions of the four teachings. When the provisional is opened to reveal the real, there is only the single reality;
thus it is said that this is the pivotal mechanism for realizing the essence of the true mark (*dharmatā*). This concludes the general discussion of the essential tenets.

△ Second, the section correctly elucidating the core tenets of the sutra, which is divided into two parts: first, a brief indication of the three requisites; second, an extensive explanation of the three requisites.
△ Now, the first part. [Commentary:
This sutra takes faith, aspiration, and the holding of the name as the essential core of practice. Without faith, it is insufficient to initiate aspiration.
Vows alone are insufficient to guide one's practice; the mere holding of the name is not a sublime practice sufficient to fulfill one's vows and realize what one has faith in.
In the sutra, the environment and its inhabitants are first presented to engender faith; next, one is exhorted to arouse vows to guide practice;
and finally, the holding of the name is shown as the direct path to ascending to the stage of non-retrogression.

[Commentary] The text is divided into two sections. The first section formally identifies the three requisites, none of which may be lacking. The passage beginning with "In the sutra... serves as the scriptural proof.
Generally speaking, these three requisites are common to all four teachings; however, that which is believed, aspired to, and practiced differs among them.

In the Tripitaka Teaching (Āgama-yāna), the object of faith, aspiration, and practice is the partial truth (pradeśa-satya). In the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna), the object of faith, aspiration, and practice is the very truth itself (tathatā).

In the Separate Teaching (biejiao), the "Middle" (zhong) alone constitutes faith, aspiration, and practice; in the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), the "Perfect Middle" constitutes faith, aspiration, and practice.

It is not that other [teachings] lack these, but rather that they do not accord with the specific capacities of those beings. In this sutra alone, the name "Holding through Faith and Aspiration" is established as the cause of the primary doctrine (zong), while the Pure Land is the fruit of that doctrine.
By citing the cause, the fruit is subsumed; therefore, it is designated as "Holding through Faith and Aspiration."

The essential point is this: it is not that other teachings are not to be trusted, but rather that they are not suited to the present time and circumstances. Furthermore, those [other teachings] are "vertical" (sequential) expositions;
