while the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) is indeed "horizontal" (simultaneous), it only accommodates those of superior faculties. Only this sutra is suited to the time and suited to the capacities of beings.

Moreover, it is a "horizontal transcendence," universally encompassing all three levels of faculties, elucidating all four teachings (*sijiao*), and is the very essence within the essence of the essential points.
△ Second, the detailed explanation of the three provisions, in two parts. First, the general heading; second, the specific explanation. △ Now, the first [the general heading].
【Commentary】 Faith consists of faith in oneself, faith in others, faith in the cause, faith in the fruit, faith in phenomena, and faith in principle.

Vow consists of wearying of and detaching from the Sahā world, while joyfully seeking the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Practice consists of upholding the Name with single-mindedness and without distraction.

△ Second, the detailed explanation has three parts: first, the explanation of the six faiths; second, the explanation of the two gates; third, the explanation of the sublime practices. The first part [the explanation of the six faiths] further has six sections:
first, faith in oneself, up to sixth, faith in the principle. △ Now, the first.

[Commentary] "Believing in oneself" means believing that the single thought-moment of my present mind (the student must here exhaust all traces of a thieving mind; one must not be casual) is fundamentally neither a physical lump of flesh nor a shadow of external conditions.
Vertically, it has no beginning or end; horizontally, it transcends all boundaries. Throughout the day I follow conditions, yet throughout the day I remain unchanging.
The empty space of the ten directions and the lands as numerous as motes of dust are, from the very beginning, objects manifested within the single thought-moment of my own mind.

Although I am currently mired in delusion and confusion, if I were to turn my mind back for even a single moment, I would certainly attain the inherently present Ultimate Bliss of my own mind; of this there is no doubt.
"Contemplating this is called 'faith in the self' (taking the nature of mind as the self). [Commentary:

Among these six types of faith, there is the subject that can believe and the object that is believed. This 'faith in the self' precisely clarifies the mental state of the single thought-moment that is capable of believing;
hence it is called 'faith in the self. It takes the nature of mind as the self; it is the self of the other."
This is the mind that directly confronts the object; it is not the deluded thought that takes a reflected image as its condition. The subsequent five stages of faith are what is believed.

This mental factor of faith likewise has the entire dharma-realm as its substance; therefore, it is said to "vertically exhaust [the past] and horizontally pervade [the present]. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:
"The nature of this mental factor of faith is clear and limpid; its intrinsic nature is pure clarity. Because it is free from faults and transcends all that is non-virtuous, it is called 'clear'."

"Pure. It is vertically pervasive and horizontally unobstructed; therefore, it is called "inherently pure" (*prakṛti-viśuddha*). As for the "fleshly lump," this refers to the heart as a mass of flesh within the abdomen;
it is the heart among the five viscera and is a provisional mind composed of the four great elements. It is the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the eighth consciousness.

This is also the "floating dust" mental faculty (*manas-indriya*). Regarding "conditioning images" (*yuan-ying*): "conditioning" (*yuan*) refers to the act of grasping at objects, indicating the perceiving aspect (*darśana-bhāga*).
"Images" (*ying*) refers to that which is perceived, indicating the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*). All eight consciousnesses possess an object of perception;

here, it specifically refers to the objective aspect perceived by the sixth consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*), which is the reflection of the *dharma-dhātu* (mental objects) transformed by its own consciousness. Therefore, it is called "conditioning images."

The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "To falsely recognize the reflected images conditioned by the six sense-objects as the characteristics of one's own mind" refers to the aforementioned passages concerning [the mind] being "within" or "without," and so forth.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*'s investigation of the mind in seven locations completely refutes this deluded attachment to reflected images.

Because sentient beings do not understand the relationship between the subject that perceives (*ālambaka*) and the object perceived (*ālambana*), from time immemorial they have universally taken the object to be the subject; hence it is said, "to recognize."
The thief acts as one's son; this is like mistaking a reflection for one's head. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

Ānanda said, "The Tathāgata has now questioned me regarding the location of the mind. I have used my mind to investigate and pursue it, and that which performs this investigation, I shall take to be the mind.
The Buddha said, "Ha! Ānanda, this is not your mind. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, "This is not my mind."
"What should this be called? The Buddha told Ānanda, "This is a false perception of the characteristics of external objects that deludes your true nature.
From your beginningless past until your present life, you have mistaken a thief for your own son, thereby losing your original permanence and undergoing the cycle of rebirth.
You should examine these words: although Ānanda says he is able to investigate, in reality he has already fallen into that which is being investigated."
This is because it is of the nature of that which is cognized. Furthermore, the shadows cast by the five sensory objects when they have subsided are easy to discern;
however, to merely remain still while guarding the empty shadow is the most difficult to analyze and deconstruct. As the Sūtra says:

"Even if you cease seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and inwardly maintain a state of profound seclusion, this is still merely a matter of the conceptual shadows of dharma-objects. I am not commanding you to insist that this is not the mind; rather, it is simply that within your own mind...
Examine this closely. If there were a nature of discrimination apart from the external objects before you, that would indeed be your true mind. (Text) The nature of the mind is like a mirror;
the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) that can perceive is like the light of the mirror, and the perceived-image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) is like the reflection in the mirror.

While a reflection of something with form is easy to understand, a reflection without form is most difficult to comprehend. It is like how a reflection within a mirror that contains a form is easily known.

One must not fail to recognize that there is a reflection of the void returning from within forms; this is the fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) of sentient beings, and one must not treat it with casual negligence.
"Vertically without beginning or end, and horizontally transcending all boundaries" means that vertically it exhausts the three periods of time.
It extends horizontally throughout the ten directions. The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "To contemplate that distant past is as if it were today.
This means that events from kalpas as numerous as motes of dust in the past are all contained within the present single thought-moment;

likewise, the future event of disciples attaining Buddhahood is also contained within the present single thought-moment. Is this not vertical exhaustion? Furthermore, it is like a person who has lost their way...
That is to say, it is not the east, nor the south, nor the west, nor the north. Originally, it is merely a single thought transformed by deluded objects;
yet what the awakened person calls the "correct" east, south, west, and north—is this not a single thought transformed by enlightened emotion?
Thus one can see that a single thought horizontally pervades the ten directions. Throughout the day, while following conditions, throughout the day there is no [delusion].

"Transformation" refers to the arising of delusions, the creation of karma, and the undergoing of retribution throughout one's entire life due to the conditions of the two attachments to self and phenomena.
Thus, there are two kinds of birth-and-death; yet, [the Tathāgata-garbha] is not transformed by these two kinds of birth-and-death. This is illustrated by the analogy of ice and water:
though they follow the conditions of cold and warmth, their moist nature does not change. Or like space: though it follows the conditions of light and darkness, its empty nature remains as it is.
It is unchanging. The empty space of the ten directions and the lands as numerous as motes of dust are, fundamentally, objects manifested within the single thought-moment of my own mind.

This precisely refers to the states of delusion and awakening within a single thought-moment. The directional characteristics of east, south, west, and north that are transformed by these states are such that the state of deluded emotion manifests the *sahā-loka* (the shared world), while the state of awakened emotion manifests the *upāya-bhūmi* (the land of skillful means), the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (land of real reward), and the *dharmatā-niṣyanda* (land of tranquil light). — *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* (The Great Buddha-Top Scripture)
It says: "The void arises within the Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean. The minute dust-motes of the worlds of outflows are all produced dependent upon the void.
When the bubble ceases, the void was originally non-existent; how much more so the various realms of the three states of existence. It further says:

"The empty space of the ten directions is born within your own mind, like a fragment of cloud appearing within the vast clarity of the great sky. Regarding those who are muddled, confused, and deluded: "muddled" refers to the absence of... [text truncated]

"Clarification" refers to the two attachments to self and dharmas. "Delusion" refers to the two delusions regarding the True and the Middle. "Inversion" refers to the eight inversions of ordinary beings and sages.
"Affliction" refers to the afflictions of the five stages of abiding. Because of attachment to self, one is deluded regarding the Truth, whereby there arise the four inversions of ordinary beings.
The two delusions of view and thought arise because of attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). Being deluded regarding the Middle Truth (*madhyasatya*), there are the four inversions of the sages;

from this, the dust-sand-like ignorance (*avidyā*) arises, and by means of this, the two kinds of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) exist. If one turns the mind for even a single thought-moment, [one attains liberation].

Regarding those who will certainly attain birth in the *Sukhāvatī* inherently possessed within their own minds: if one turns the mind through the contemplative practices of the four teachings, one will be born in one of the four kinds of impure lands;
however, by turning the mind through the practice of Buddha-remembrance (*nienfo*), one transcends horizontally to the pure land of the West.

This means that if one upholds the Name until reaching the state of "single-mindedness without distraction" (*shixin buluan*), then at that single thought-moment, the mind of self-clinging is turned back, and [birth is assured].
One will certainly attain birth within the mind of non-existence; this is the two kinds of Ultimate Bliss—*upāya-sāṃbhoga* (convenient co-residence)—which are inherently possessed.

If one reaches the principle of single-mindedness without distraction, then in a single thought the mind of attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) is turned back, and one will certainly attain birth within the mind of non-dharmas;
this is the two kinds of Ultimate Bliss—*śānta-prabhāsa* (tranquil light) and *dharmatā-vipāka* (true retribution)—which are inherently possessed. Such a judgment is definitive in principle.
To have no doubt regarding the facts is called "faith in oneself. This concludes the first section, "Faith in Oneself.
II. Faith in Others.
[Commentary] As for "faith in others," it means having faith that Śākyamuni Tathāgata certainly has no deceptive speech, and that the World-Honored Amitābha certainly has no falsehood.
I pray that the broad and long tongues of the Buddhas of the six directions will provide no equivocal words, but accord with the true instructions of all Buddhas.
Resolving my mind to seek birth [in the Pure Land], I shall have no further doubt. This is called "trusting others" (taking the teachings as the other).
△ Third, the cause of faith. [Commentary:
Regarding the cause of faith: one must have deep faith that even calling the Name while distracted serves as the seed for attaining Buddhahood; how much more so when the mind is not distracted?
How could one not be born in the Pure Land? This is called the cause of faith (taking the recitation of the Buddha’s name as the cause).
△ Fourth, the fruit of faith.
[Commentary] Regarding the fruit of faith: one has deep faith that the gathering of all virtues in the Pure Land arises entirely from the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha.

Just as planting melon seeds yields melons and planting bean seeds yields beans, and just as a shadow necessarily follows a form and an echo necessarily responds to a sound, there is never any fruitlessness.
This is called the fruit of faith (taking that which has already arisen as the fruit).
△ Five: Matters of Faith.

[Commentary] Regarding matters of faith: because one has deep faith that the present single thought-moment before us is inexhaustible, one knows that the worlds of the ten directions manifested by the mind are likewise inexhaustible.
Truly, there exists the Land of Ultimate Bliss beyond hundreds of thousands of billions of lands.
It is supremely pure and adorned; it is not like the allegories of Zhuangzi. This is called the "matter of faith" (taking the objective realm as the matter).

[Commentary] That the single thought-moment before us is inexhaustible is because it vertically exhausts and horizontally pervades all things. As for the fact that the worlds of the ten directions manifested by the mind are also inexhaustible:
if one relies on the single thought-moment of the self-grasping mind, then the Shared World (*sahā-loka*) is manifested.
Regarding the world: if one relies on a wholesome mind, then a wholesome world appears—namely, the three happy realms.

If one relies on an unwholesome mind, then an unwholesome world appears—namely, the three miserable realms. This serves as a general metaphor for the spatial orientations perceived by a deluded person;
because these extend vertically through time and horizontally across space, they are inexhaustible. If one relies on a single moment of mind that clings to phenomena, then spatial directions appear.
There are the *byin* (nirmāṇa) worlds and the *shih-pao* (vipākaphala) worlds.

Because there are degrees of lightness and heaviness in the clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) and thickness and thinness in ignorance (*avidyā*), there are nine grades of persons in the stage of skillful means (*upāya*) and forty-two grades of persons in the stage of true retribution (*vipākaphala*). What they perceive differs;

this is a general metaphor for the spatial characteristics perceived by those who have attained awakening. It is likewise vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive, and thus cannot be exhausted. If one relies on that which is free from clinging—
When the mind manifests, it appears as the world of serene light (*sukhāvatī*); it has no verticality that can be fathomed and no horizontality that can be encompassed.
This is called truly exhausting the vertical and encompassing the horizontal. Therefore, the preceding text says: "Vertically there is no beginning or end;

horizontally it transcends all boundaries. It is like a person who is neither deluded nor awakened; fundamentally, there is no verticality or horizontality to be distinguished. Truly, the Land of Ultimate Bliss exists.

"Beyond ten trillion lands" refers to the four lands mentioned above; because they manifest solely based on the mind, and because the mind is substantially real, the lands are also substantially real.
Therefore, the Land of Ultimate Bliss truly possesses these four lands situated beyond ten trillion lands.
"Most supremely pure and adorned" means that the four lands are perfectly interfused (*yuanrong*); thus, their adornment is spontaneously perfected.
His son was surnamed Zhuang and named Zhou. As for "parables" (*yuyán*), this refers to the *Nanhua jing* (The Scripture of Southern Florescence).

"Parable" (*yù*) means to entrust or to rely upon; it refers to words that rely upon one thing to explain another. Although these names exist, originally there were no such events. For example, it is said:
"There was a man named Chaos who was born without the seven apertures. People took pity on him and bored them for him. Once the seven apertures were present, Chaos died."
Thus, although such names exist, there is in reality no such person.
The Buddha’s teaching that the Western World of Ultimate Bliss truly exists is therefore not like those allegories. This concludes the section on faith.

△ Section Six: The Analysis of Faith in Principle is divided into two parts. First, clarifying that the nature of the mind has no external realm; second, clarifying the non-obstruction of phenomena with phenomena.
△ Now, the first part. [Commentary]:
Regarding "faith in principle," it means to have deep faith that the ten trillion lands do not, in reality, transcend this present, infinitesimal moment of my own consciousness.
"Mind is outside [of objects]," yet in reality, the single thought-mind before us has no external realm. [Commentary:
This mind-nature having no exterior is also because the nature of objects has no exterior; this is because mind and object are non-dual in nature. Regarding "a mere moment" (*ji-er*):
the *Treatise on Birth and Non-Birth* states that the mind which recites the Buddha's name is extremely subtle and weak, and is therefore called "a mere moment."

By stating "it does not go outside," it clarifies the reason why luminosity does not emerge from outside the mind. Although this single thought-moment is subtle and weak, it is the entire substance of the dharma-realm;
it is fundamentally vertical and pervasive throughout, truly having nothing external. Therefore, it is said that it does not go outside.
This concludes the initial clarification that the nature of the mind has no exterior.
△ Second, the clarification of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena. [Commentary]:

Furthermore, one should deeply believe that the Western Land—including its environment (*āśraya*), inhabitants (*adhiṣṭhāna*), principal figure (*nāyaka*), and retinue (*parivāra*)—are all reflections manifested within the single thought-moment of my present mind.

The entirety of phenomena is identical to principle; the entirety of delusion is identical to truth; the entirety of cultivation is identical to nature; and the entirety of the other is identical to oneself. This is my own mind.
Because it is all-pervasive, the Buddha-mind is also all-pervasive, and the mind-nature of all sentient beings is likewise all-pervasive. It is like a single room with a thousand lamps:

the lights interpenetrate one another, mutually encompassing each other in infinite layers without mutual obstruction. This is called "believing in the principle" (taking the *dharmadhātu* as the principle).

[Commentary] The text is divided into two sections. The first section correctly elucidates the metaphors through the following illustrations. It correctly demonstrates that [the mind] possesses the four dharma-realms:

"a single thought" refers to the dharma-realm of principle; "images" refer to the dharma-realm of phenomena; "the entirety of phenomena is principle," etc., refers to the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena;
and "because my mind is pervasive," etc., refers to the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena. This also serves as an illustration.
The mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. "Support" (yi) refers to the environmental support, namely the adornments of the four lands.

"Principal" (zheng) refers to the primary retribution, namely the principal figures and their retinues within the four lands. "Principal" (zhu) refers to Amitābha’s three bodies; "retinue" (ban) refers to the people and so forth.
"Reflection" (ying) is a name derived from a metaphor, meaning that this single thought-moment of the mind-nature has four aspects: the support, the environment, the principal, and the retinue.

The "companion" (the object) is the *nimittabhāga* (image-part), like a reflection in a mirror. The "single thought-moment" (the subject) is the *darśanabhāga* (seeing-part), like the luminosity of the mirror.

The "mind" (*citta*) is the *svasaṃvittibhāga* (self-verifying part), like the surface of the mirror. The "nature" (*prakṛti*) is the *svasaṃvittisaṃvittibhāga* (part that verifies the self-verifying part), like the bronze of the mirror.

These four parts are but a single mind; therefore, it is said that "the entirety of phenomena is itself principle," and so forth. "The entirety of phenomena is itself principle" means that the entirety of the *nimittabhāga*...
The "matter" refers to the principle of the three internal divisions. It is illustrated by the analogy of a complete mirror and its reflection; the "complete delusion" is the copper of the mirror.

That "the complete delusion is itself the truth" means that the delusion of the two divisions—subject (seeing) and object (appearance)—is itself the truth of the two internal divisions. These are the two divisions of subject and object.

This refers to the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), because the dependent is like an illusion. It is analogous to the light of a mirror and the reflection in a mirror, for they are identical with the surface of the mirror itself.

"The entirety of cultivation is the nature" means that the cultivated virtues of the three parts (*trikalpa*) are identical to the realized inherent virtues of the *svasaṃvedana-bhāga* (self-verifying part).
This is analogous to how the reflection, the light, and the surface of the mirror are all identical with the bronze of the mirror. "The entirety of the other is the self" means:
It is not only my own *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect); rather, it is manifested by my mind. Thus, even the *nimitta-bhāgas* of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others are also manifested by my mind;
this refers to the manifestation of the *sāmānya-vijñāna* (common consciousness). Regarding the "common consciousness":

the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment) is common within the common, while the *upapatti-vipāka* (the body) is uncommon within the common. Therefore, it is said that "my mind is pervasive. As for the phrase "because my mind is pervasive," etc.:
This means that my own mind-king and its mental factors pervade the four lands; the Buddha’s mind-king and its mental factors also pervade the four lands;
and the mind-kings and mental factors of all sentient beings likewise pervade the four lands. This is based on the principle that the entire object is identical to the mind;

hence it is said, "Because my mind pervades," and so forth. If, however, one bases this on the principle that the entire mind is identical to the object, then it is further said, "Because my object pervades."
The realm of the Buddha is all-pervasive, and the nature of the realm of all sentient beings is likewise all-pervasive.

This is illustrated by the analogy of the fire seen by hungry ghosts, which is water seen by humans, and is also lapis lazuli seen by devas and humans; therefore, it is said that "phenomena and phenomena are unimpeded" (*shishi wuai*).
For example, the metaphor of a thousand lamps in a single room serves to manifest this unimpededness of phenomena and phenomena. "A single room" is a metaphor for...

The objective aspect of the dependent retribution (依報相分) is likened to a thousand lamps; the objective aspect of the primary retribution (正報相分)—namely, the bodies of the Buddha, oneself, and sentient beings—is likewise represented by the lamps.

The light symbolizes the mind that remains unchanging while following conditions (不變隨緣). The empty space within the room symbolizes the nature that follows conditions while remaining unchanging (隨緣不變).

The mutual pervasiveness of each light symbolizes that upon the objective aspect of the Buddha, there exists the objective aspect transformed by one's own mind—the objective aspect of the self (我心所變相分). This is the objective aspect of the self (我相).

Furthermore, there are the *nimitta-bhāga* (perceived objects) manifested by the mental states of sentient beings. Upon these *nimitta-bhāga*s of sentient beings, there are also the *nimitta-bhāga*s manifested by the Buddha’s mental states.

The Buddha’s *nimitta-bhāga* is the Land of Peaceful Light (*śānta-prabhāsa-kṣetra*). The *nimitta-bhāga*s of sentient beings refer, for the time being, to the Land of True Reward (*samyaktva-vipāka-kṣetra*) and the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-kṣetra*).
My own *nimitta-bhāga* refers, for the time being, to the Land of Shared Residence (*sahā-loka-kṣetra*). These four lands are all situated within one [reality].

Therefore, it is said that they are mutually inclusive in successive layers without mutual obstruction. Furthermore, since the four lands are situated within a single location, they are called "co-resident" (*tongju*).
Since all four lands are established for the sake of sentient beings, they share the same skillful means (*upāya*).
Since all four lands are the fruition of true practice, they are equally the land of true recompense (*shibao*). Since the four lands are nothing other than the one mind, then...

Furthermore, it is the sole, quiescent light. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "The realm of purity within the shared dwelling; the ultimate and conventional truths are perfectly interfused, beyond measure.
Only those who believe in this manner can be said to have faith in the principle. This concludes the first explanation of the six types of faith.

△ Second, the explanation of the two gates is divided into two parts. First, the explicit clarification of the two gates; second, the clarification of the matters of adoption and rejection regarding phenomena and principle.
△ Now, the first part.

【Commentary】 (The following clarifies the vow: Having established such faith, then this Sahā world is precisely the defilement manifested by one's own mind, and the principle of that mental defilement...
One should cultivate weary detachment [from saṃsāra]. The Land of Ultimate Bliss is the purity manifested by one's own mind;
since it is one's own mind that is pure, one ought logically to aspire for it (this being the principle underlying the phenomenon).
[Commentary] This passage correctly elucidates the two gates of aspiration: joy and revulsion. These two gates exist both horizontally and vertically.
Now, as for "aspiration," it refers to the four great vows. These four great vows are generated in reliance upon the Four Noble Truths.

Relying upon the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), one says: "I vow to deliver infinite sentient beings. Relying upon the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), one says: "I vow to exhaust all afflictions (*kleśa*)."
To sever [defilements] by relying on the Truth of the Path, one says: "I vow to study the immeasurable Dharma-gates.

To rely on the Truth of Cessation, one says: "I vow to realize the unsurpassed Buddha-way. The first two vows constitute the gate of wearying detachment (*vidveṣa*), while the latter two constitute the gate of joyful seeking.
Since the Four Noble Truths pervade the four teachings, the Four Great Vows likewise pervade the four teachings. This is the vertical exposition; now, regarding the Pure [Land]...
This is the "Horizontal Treatise on the Lands. It means that when one feels weary of and seeks to leave behind all [realms], the four lands of the Sahā world are completely relinquished;
when one joyfully seeks and aspires toward all [realms], the four lands of Sukhāvatī are completely attained.

Through complete relinquishment, the afflictions of the five stages of abiding are severed without being severed; through complete attainment, the fruits of Buddhahood of the four teachings are realized without being realized. Therefore, subsequently...
The text states: "One perfectly perceives the three bodies and perfectly realizes the three non-regressions," and so forth. Having established such faith, one initiates a vow based upon that faith.

Since one has already believed that all lands manifest in dependence upon the mind, one understands that the four kinds of defiled lands of this Sahā world are evoked by one's own fundamentally non-existent defiled mind—namely, the defilements of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), and the defilements of the sands of *kleśas* (*rajas-kleśa*).

Ignorance is a defilement; yet, since it is a defilement that is fundamentally non-existent, it is only logical that one should feel weary of it and seek liberation from it—this is not beyond the scope of reason.
Furthermore, one should know that the four kinds of pure lands of Sukhāvatī are evoked by one's own inherently existing pure mind.

This refers to superior wholesome karma, which brings about the purity of co-residence (*sahabhāva-viśuddhi*); the wisdom of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā-jñāna*), which brings about the purity of skillful means (*upāya-viśuddhi*);

the wisdom of the contemplation of wondrous provisionality (*prajñapti-viśuddhi*), which brings about the purity of the true reward (*dharmatā-viśuddhi*); and the wisdom of the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-vipaśyanā-jñāna*), which brings about the purity of the tranquil light (*śāntaprabhā-viśuddhi*).

Since these purities are inherently possessed, it is logically appropriate to seek them with joy, as they do not lie beyond one's capacity. This concludes the initial correct explanation of the two gates.

II. Clarifying the Principles and Matters of Adoption and Rejection. This section is divided into two parts. First, the formal clarification of the two refutations of attachment. Now, the first part. [Commentary]:

One must weary of defilement and abandon it until reaching the ultimate; only then is there nothing further to abandon. One must delight in purity and adopt it until reaching the ultimate; only then is there nothing further to adopt.
(This is the principle underlying the matter. Thus, the *Miaozong* states: "If adoption and rejection reach their limit, they are not different from non-adoption and non-rejection."

[Commentary] The text is divided into two sections: the first provides the formal explanation, while from "Miaozong" (The Sublime Commentary) onwards, it cites scriptural evidence. Now, as for "taking and abandoning":
this refers to employing the merit of the Path Truth’s *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to take up the Cessation Truth and abandon the two truths of Suffering and Origination.

While all four teachings discuss taking and abandoning, the first three are provisional and are thus set aside without further discussion. Here, we shall discuss them according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

Because there are six levels of "immediacy" (*jiji*), it is said that "relinquishing reaches the ultimate" and "attaining reaches the ultimate," and so forth. However, these two characters, "ultimate" (*jiujing*), also carry two meanings.

If one discusses the six immediacies, one must reach the stage of *Miaojue* (Wonderful Enlightenment), where the merit of cultivation is fully accomplished and the inherent nature is perfectly manifested;

thus, the emotions of grasping and relinquishing are emptied, and it is said that [the Pure Land] is then "not present. This is the vertical perspective. If discussing from the gate of the Pure Land, it is a horizontal perspective.

Such a person merely attains rebirth in the Pure Land and is thus called "ultimate. This is because the defilement of the Sahā world has been ultimately abandoned, and the purity of the Pure Land has been ultimately attained;
for by means of the perfect, pure, and quiescent light, one perfectly ascends to wondrous enlightenment.

Therefore, the subsequent passage on the Vow states: "From this point on, ordinary sentient beings, within the state of non-retrogression through mindfulness, transcend and exhaust the forty-one causal stages.
This is still an explanation in terms of phenomena (*dharma*). If one were to discuss it from the perspective of principle (*tattva*), how could it be limited merely to rebirth?

However, precisely at the moment of reciting the Buddha’s name, there is correspondence in a single thought-moment and perfection in a single thought-moment; there is correspondence in every thought-moment and perfection in every thought-moment.
Regarding the citations in the *Miaozong* (The Sublime Commentary), the *Miaozong Chao* asks:

"The ultimate principle is subtle and wondrous—neither defiled nor pure, neither grasping nor rejecting. Now, by establishing defilement and purity, one causes people to grasp and reject; since this deviates from the subtle principle..."
This would then not be the Supreme Vehicle (Agrayāna). Therefore, the answer says: "If grasping and rejecting reach their ultimate limit, they are no different from non-grasping and non-rejecting.

This objection uses a specific attachment to challenge the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). From the perspective of the Perfect Teaching, every single instance of grasping and every single instance of rejecting is none other than the wondrous principle.
"Che" (徹) means a carriage track. This concludes the formal explanation.
△ 2. Refuting Attachment.

[Commentary]: Even if one does not engage in the practice of acceptance and rejection, yet merely adheres to non-acceptance and non-rejection, this is to cling to principle while abandoning phenomena.

Since phenomena are abandoned, principle is likewise incomplete. If one realizes (through faith) that all phenomena are themselves principle, then both taking (through aspiration) and rejecting are likewise principle.
This is precisely the principle. To either grasp or reject is nothing other than the Dharma-realm; therefore, following faith, the Vow is clarified.
[Commentary] There is a class of practitioners in the world who, though they likewise practice mindfulness of the Buddha, do not resolve to seek birth [in the Pure Land].

These are mostly those who cling to a partial understanding of the principle. Yet they fail to realize that even while claiming to "value the principle," they have already grasped at it; thus, they do not vow to seek birth.
This is already the matter of relinquishing; yet grasping and relinquishing remain distinct. What, then, is meant by "neither grasping nor relinquishing"?
If one realizes that phenomena are mutually unimpeded (*amitābhā-dharmadhātu*), then whatever is picked up at random is none other than a phenomenon, and the whole is entirely principle (*tattva*).

Therefore it is said: "Grasping is also principle; relinquishing is also principle. Whether grasping or relinquishing, every instance is the dharma-realm of mutual non-obstruction. Thus, next is faith.
This is the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of all phenomena, which clarifies the vows of acceptance and rejection. The explanation of the two gates is concluded.

△ Third, the explanation of the section on "Sublime Practice" is divided into two parts: first, the direct clarification of the sublimity of practice; second, the comparative evaluation of the sublimity of practice. △ Now, the first part.

[Commentary] Regarding the statement "to hold fast to the name with single-mindedness and without distraction": a name is used to invoke virtue, and since that virtue is inconceivable, the name is likewise inconceivable.
Because the merit of the name is inconceivable, even calling upon it in a distracted manner constitutes planting the seed of Buddhahood;
yet by holding it fast, one attains the stage of non-retrogression (for those who have faith simply believe, while those who deliberate and analyze are incapable).

[Commentary] "A name is that which summons virtue. "Name" refers to a provisional designation (*prajñapti*). "Virtue" refers to actual merit. "Summons" means to call out by means of a name and its characteristics.
"Virtue that is inconceivable" means that the merits of Amitābha Buddha are fundamentally beyond thought and mind, and beyond verbal discussion.
Since the actual merit is inconceivable, the Buddha’s provisional name is likewise so.
It is inconceivable. It is only through the provisional name "inconceivable" that one comes to know that the nature of our own mind is fundamentally inconceivable.
Because the nature of the mind is inconceivable, it is designated as the seed for attaining Buddhahood.

If one can maintain single-mindedness without distraction, one will certainly ascend to the stage of non-retrogression. This concludes the initial section clearly elucidating the excellence of practice.

△ Second, the section on comparing the excellence of practice, which is divided into two parts: first, showing the inferiority of various practices; second, uniquely revealing the excellence of upholding the Name.
△ Now, the first part.

[Commentary]: However, the various sutras present the practices for the Pure Land in ten thousand variations and a thousand differences, such as contemplating images, contemplating visualizations, prostrating, and making offerings.
Cultivating the five repentances, the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), and so forth—when each of these practices is perfected, one will be reborn in the Pure Land.
[Commentary] Contemplating the image refers to the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*. Contemplating the visualization refers to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Sixteen Contemplations).

Prostrating, making offerings, and performing the five repentances refer to the "Ten Great Vows of the King of Vows" from the *Bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna*, namely: first, paying homage to all Buddhas; and so on.
1. Mindfulness of the Buddha; 2. Praising the Tathāgata; 3. Extensively cultivating offerings; 4. Repenting of karmic obstacles; 5. Rejoicing in merit; 6.
Requesting the turning of the Wheel of Dharma; 7. Requesting the Buddha to remain in the world; 8.
Constantly following and learning from the Buddha; 9. Always acting in accordance with sentient beings; 10. Universally dedicating all merits. These are the six recollections.
First, mindfulness of the Buddha, the compassionate teacher. Second, mindfulness of the Dharma, the mother of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Third, mindfulness of the Sangha, the field of merit for humans and devas. Fourth, mindfulness of heaven, characterized by long life and peace and happiness.

Fifth, mindfulness of precepts, which purify body and mind. Sixth, mindfulness of giving, which universally relieves poverty. The *Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations* states that there are three kinds...
Sentient beings shall attain rebirth [in the Pure Land]. First, they maintain a mind of loving-kindness and refrain from killing, fully observing all precepts and practices.
Second, they read and recite the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras. Third, they practice the six mindfulnesses and dedicate their merit through making vows.
Possessing these merits, even for as little as seven days, one shall immediately attain rebirth. However, all these practices depend entirely upon dedication and the making of vows.
One should aspire for rebirth; merely attaining the aspiration for rebirth is itself the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha (*nien-fo*).

These various dharma-gates do not encompass a wide range of capacities and are not easy to undertake; therefore, they are inferior to the practice of holding the name. Nevertheless, those who uphold the Name must not lack these various practices.
This concludes the initial demonstration that these various practices are inferior.
△ Second, the excellence of holding the name alone.
[Commentary]: Holding this single dharma of the name alone encompasses the widest range of capacities and is the easiest to undertake.
Therefore, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, speaking spontaneously without being asked, singled it out for the Great Wisdom Śāriputra. It may be called the foremost among all skillful means.

It is a sūtra of skillful means (the *Xingjing*); it is the unsurpassed definitive meaning among all definitive teachings (the *Jiaojing*); it is the most perfectly sudden among all perfectly sudden principles (the *Lijing*). Thus it is said:

"When a pure pearl is cast into turbid water, the turbid water cannot fail to become clear; when the name of the Buddha is cast into a distracted mind, the distracted mind cannot fail to become the Buddha.
(These are the words of an ancient master on the ultimate perfection.)

[Commentary]: There are three kinds of excellence in the practice of upholding the Name. Its capacity to encompass all capacities is vast; its method of entry is easy—this constitutes the excellence of the practice (*shimyo*).
The three phrases beginning with "the foremost skillful means" constitute the excellence of the principle (*rimyo*).

Furthermore, its ability to perfectly encompass all practices, including the three contemplations, the ten stages of the vehicle, the seven categories of the path of cultivation, and immeasurable Dharma gates, constitutes its perfect excellence (*enmyō*). Possessing these three excellences, it stands alone...
It is supremely wondrous. Regarding the "first expedient means": because every thought-moment is itself Buddha, one does not fall into the various practices of the Three Vehicles.
Regarding the "unexcelled definitive meaning": because every thought-moment is itself Buddha; "definitive meaning" refers to the manifestation of the supreme ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
"Buddha" is precisely the unexcelled supreme ultimate truth. Regarding the "most ultimate, perfect, and sudden": because every thought-moment...
Because he is the Buddha himself, he does not fall into gradual succession. As for the "pure pearl," it refers to the water-clearing pearl;

since this pearl has the power to clarify water, it serves as a metaphor for how the name of the Buddha has the power to bring about Buddhahood. This concludes the third explanation of "wondrous practice.
This concludes the second section, which correctly elucidates the core tenet of the sutra.
△ Third, the summary of cause and effect. [Commentary:

Taking faith, aspiration, and the holding of the Name as the true cause of the One Vehicle, and taking the four kinds of Pure Lands as the wondrous fruit of the One Vehicle—since the fruit must necessarily follow when the cause is raised, faith, aspiration, and the holding of the Name are established as the orthodox teaching of this sutra. Its...
The characteristics of the four kinds of pure lands are detailed in the *Miaozongchao* and the *Fannwang jing xuanyi*; they are not fully described here.
One should wait for the subsequent commentary based on the main text, where they shall be briefly indicated.
[Commentary] The *Fahua xuanyi* takes the cause and effect of the One Vehicle as its central tenet (*zong*). Therefore, this concludes by returning to cause and effect.
The third major section, "Clarifying the Central Tenet," is finished.
△ Section Four: Explaining the Power and Function, divided into three parts. First, a general statement of the power and function; second, a detailed explanation of the power and function;
third, a comparative judgment of the power and function. △ Now, the first part.
[Commentary] The fourth section clarifies the power and function (*balakārya*). The power and function of this sutra consist in the non-retrogression of those who attain rebirth there.
[Sub-commentary] "Power and function" refers to the merit of this sutra. "Power" (*bala*) signifies "merit" (*guṇa*), and "function" (*kārya*) signifies "virtue" (*guṇa*).
This sutra takes rebirth as its merit and non-retrogression as its virtue. As the sutra says: "All sentient beings who are born there are all *abhiṣikta* (non-retrogressing)."
They are irreversible. Among them, there are many who are in their last birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*);

their number is so vast that it cannot be known by calculation, but can only be described as immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*). This is the great power and function of this sutra.
The general indication of its power and function is now complete.
△ Second, the detailed explanation of the power and function, which is divided into two parts. First, the four signs of rebirth; second, the four meanings of non-retrogression.
Regarding the first [of these], there are again two sections: first, a general indication; second, a detailed exposition. △ Now, the first.
[Commentary] There are four lands for rebirth, each discussed in terms of nine grades. For now, I shall briefly clarify the characteristics of attaining birth in these four lands.
[Sub-commentary] As for the four lands: first, the Land of Common Dwelling of Ordinary Beings and Sages; second, the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder;

third, the Land of True Reward and Non-obstruction; and fourth, the Land of Eternal Quiescent Light. These four lands are explained through the two meanings of purity and impurity, and horizontal and vertical.
In the subsequent text, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of these names. First, regarding "the common abode of ordinary beings and sages":
if we refer to this land, it consists of the three realms, the nine stages, and the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).

These are originally the result of the outflowing karma of ordinary beings—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or imperturbable—and yet sages also dwell therein. There are two aspects to this cohabitation.
There are two kinds of sages: the Real and the Expedient. The Real refers to those who have already realized the fruits of the Three Vehicles but have not yet entered *nirvāṇa*.

The Expedient refers to those who manifest their arrival in the three higher lands. Because these two types of sages dwell together with ordinary beings, it is called "Ordinary Beings and Sages Dwelling Together.
This is not the case in the Pure Land; there, ordinary beings are exclusively those who attain birth through the practice of *nianfo* (mindfulness of the Buddha).

This is not a realm of outflowing karma (*sāsrava-karma*). There are only humans and devas; there are no four evil destinies (*apāya*), no heavens of the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-dhātu*), no heavens of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*), and no heavens of the Māra kings.

All beings enter exclusively the group of those destined for rightness (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*); there is no group of those who are not so destined (*aniyata-rāśi*) nor the group of those destined for error (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*).

It is simply because they have not yet exhausted their afflictions of views and thoughts that they are termed "ordinary beings" (pṛthagjana). It should be understood that even among the sages there are both provisional and ultimate [levels].

Regarding the second, the stage of "residual skillful means": if we refer to this land, it is the dwelling place where the noble assemblies of the Three Vehicles who have transcended the triple world cultivate the path of skillful means;

they have merely escaped the *pariccheda* (segmented) death but have not yet avoided the *pariṇāma* (transformation) death, and while they have exhausted the afflictions of views and thoughts, they have not yet...
Because they have eliminated only the secondary afflictions, it is called "having a remainder. Nine types of people are born in this land:

namely, those of the *pitaka* (Tripitaka) teaching, the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), the three vehicles of the *sūtra* (Shared) teaching, the three stages of the worthy ones (*śaikṣa*) of the distinct teaching, and the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) of the perfect teaching. If one refers to the Pure Land, then they merely depart from the triple world of this Sahā world.

They do not depart from the Land of Ultimate Bliss’s Shared Residence (*sābhisamskāra-sādhāraṇa*). They are perfectly free from the two deaths and have completely severed the five abodes of ignorance.

Among these nine grades of beings, they are exclusively Bodhisattvas; although there are those called Śrāvakas, they are not of fixed nature. They are merely named Śrāvakas because they have severed the delusions shared with ordinary beings.
Because their residual afflictions have not yet been exhausted, they are for the time being called those with "residual lands of expedient means.

Third, regarding those in the "true retribution of non-obstruction": because they give rise to cultivation from the entirety of their nature, they experience a true retribution that accords with that nature.
Matter and mind are sovereign, and dust-like worlds mutually contain one another; this is the realm where Bodhisattvas of the forty-one stages dwell, and their bodies are able to manifest lands.

The land also manifests its form; it does not contravene the nature of reality (dharmatā) and is adorned in accordance with that nature, as in the *Avataṃsaka*’s "Ocean of the Establishment of the Dharma-realm.
Fourth, the Land of Eternal Quiescent Light refers to the secret treasury of the three virtues realized by the Tathāgata:

"Eternal" is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), "Quiescent" is liberation (*vimukti*), and "Light" is wisdom (*prajñā*). Furthermore, all three virtues are eternal, for their nature is without transition.
Therefore, the three virtues are all quiescent, for they are free from defilement; the three virtues are all luminous, for they are supremely pure and bright.
This is the dwelling place of the Pure Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). In terms of wisdom, it is called the "body" (*kāya*); in terms of principle (*tattva*), it is called the "land" (*kṣetra*).

Body and land are of one suchness (*tathatā*); there are not two distinct characteristics. There is no state of mutual separation or difference here, yet it truly pervades all distinct realms. By means of...
Regarding the distinct realms: because there is no other place for their establishment apart from these, each is discussed in terms of nine grades.

In the *Tongju* (Shared) realm, the two delusions of views and thought-and-affection (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) are divided into nine grades; in the *Fangbian* (Provisional) realm, the delusions of dust-like afflictions (*rajas-kleśa*) are divided into nine grades;
and in the *Shibao Jiguang* (True Reward and Quiescent Light) realm, ignorance (*avidyā*) is divided into nine grades. This concludes the initial general presentation.
△ Second, the specific explanation.

[Commentary]: If one upholds the Name but has not yet severed the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), then according to whether their state is distracted or concentrated, they are divided into three grades and nine ranks within the Land of Common Dwelling (*sahā-loka-dhātu*).
[Commentary] This refers to the signs of rebirth in the Land of Common Dwelling. Regarding "view-delusions" (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and "thought-delusions" (*vicikitsā-kleśa*):

"view" refers to the five sharp afflictions (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-kleśa*), while "thought" refers to the five dull afflictions (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*). As for the five sharp afflictions: the first is the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), which is the false identification of the four great elements as a self.

2. Extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*): This refers to the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism. Failing to realize that this body is fundamentally without self, one gives rise to these extreme views.
3. False view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*): To deny the existence of the causes and effects of good and evil, and so forth. 4. Adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*):
This refers to not denying cause and effect, yet regarding what is not a cause as a cause; failing to understand the true cause, such as the observances of cows, dogs, and so forth.
When a disciple of the Buddha clings to the characteristics of precepts and fails to understand the emptiness of self, this is likewise subsumed under the "clinging to precepts" (śīlavrataparāmarśa).

The five types of clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) refer to regarding that which is not a fruit as being a fruit—namely, taking the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, and the state of non-perception to be *nirvāṇa*.
The five dull afflictions (*pañca-nivaraṇa*) are greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt; all are called "afflictions" (*kleśa*) because they are driven by the mind.
The eight consciousnesses act as kings; these [afflictions] are what the kings employ. This is the general discussion.

To discuss them specifically, according to the three realms and the four truths, there are eighty-eight delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). Regarding the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*), across the nine stages, there are eighty-one grades.
One should examine the numerical categories of these dharmas; however, as they are not essential here, they are not recorded. If one were to discuss...

To emerge vertically from the triple world necessarily requires the exhaustion of delusions; this [practice], however, is to emerge horizontally from the triple world by being reborn while still carrying one's karma.
"Whether distracted or concentrated" refers to the stage of name (myōji-i) for the distracted, and the stage of contemplative practice (kan-gyō-i) for the concentrated.
The "three ranks" refer to the superior, middling, and inferior; the "nine grades" consist of three sets of three, totaling nine grades.

[Commentary]: If one maintains the practice of single-mindedness and non-distraction regarding the ultimate reality, the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*) will naturally fall away first, and one will be born in the Pure Land of the Remaining Trace of Expedient Means (*upāya-śeṣa-vimala*).

[Sub-commentary]: "Single-mindedness and non-distraction regarding the ultimate reality" means that the self-grasping is empty and one is not disturbed by the delusions of views and thoughts; thus, the delusions of views and thoughts...

Regarding "the karmic destiny falls first": this refers to entering the stage of semblance realization (*sādharmya-avasthā*). The practitioner’s intention lies in *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation); there is no deliberate intent to sever delusions.
Because the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) is subtle, it is severed later; because the attachment to self (*ātman-grāha*) is coarse, it falls away first.

As for "then being born in the Pure Land of Expedient Means": this means transcending horizontally from this defiled land of shared habitation to the Pure Land of Expedient Means in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

[Commentary]: If one reaches the ultimate principle with a single-mindedness that is undisturbed, and suddenly shatters even one grade of ignorance, up to forty-one grades, then one will be born in the Pure Land of True Reward Adornment and also partially realize the Land of Constant Quiescent Light.

[Commentary]: "The principle of single-mindedness without distraction" means that, based on the practice of single-mindedness without distraction, one directly perceives the Middle Way and the true reality (*dharmatā*), remaining undisturbed by the attachment to phenomena of the two extremes.
"Ignorance" refers to delusion; it is being deluded regarding the two extremes.

Because they do not penetrate the true reality (*dharmatā*), it is called ignorance (*avidyā*). If one breaks through even a single grade of this ignorance, one enters the first stage, the Dwelling of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpādavihāra*).
If one reaches the forty-first grade, one realizes the Perfect Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). These are all stages of partial realization;

those who are born in the Pure Land of Real Reward Adornment (*sambhogakāya-vipākālaṃkāra-śuddhakṣetra*) are said to transcend horizontally from this defiled land of cohabitation to the Pure Land of Real Reward in Sukhāvatī.
Furthermore, those who have partially realized the Land of Constant Quiescent Light are so named in reference to what they have realized;
it is this very land that Mañjuśrī, Nāgārjuna, Zhiyi, and Yongming occupied. They were the ones who attained it.
[Commentary] If ignorance is completely severed and exhausted, this is the supreme and ultimate true recompense (*sambhoga-kāya*), the ultimate *śānta-prabhāsa* (tranquil light).

[Sub-commentary] "Supreme and ultimate true recompense" refers to the highest grade of the True Recompense Land (*sambhoga-kṣetra*). "Ultimate tranquil light" refers to attaining the Perfect and Wondrous Enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), which is the ultimate secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa-guhya-kośa*).
While the previous three lands all speak of "rebirth," this— (Note: The provided text ends mid-sentence; the translation reflects the partial nature of the source.)

Regarding the statement "is": the former refers to the stage of cause (*hetu-bhūmi*), wherein ignorance (*avidyā*) is not yet exhausted; thus, up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), there is still birth.
This is why Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Sudhana, and others all made vows to seek birth [in the Pure Land].
The present refers to the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*), where ignorance is forever severed; hence it is said, "is. The four aspects of rebirth are concluded.
△ Second, the four meanings of non-retrogression. Regarding non-retrogression, there are generally only three types;
here, one additional type—ultimate non-retrogression—is added to manifest the merit of the Buddha’s name and the inconceivable merit of the *dharmadhātu* dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Furthermore, these three types of non-retrogression are common to all four teachings (*catur-yāna*), yet they involve both affirmation (*anujñā*) and negation (*pratiṣedha*). If we discuss them in terms of affirmation:

Consideration: Each of the four teachings has its own three types of non-retrogression. If we analyze them by contrasting them: in the two teachings of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and the *Vaipulya* (Shared), there is only non-retrogression in terms of position (*avasthāna*).

In the *Distinct* (Separate) teaching, one realizes non-retrogression in practice (*caryā*) at the stage of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi-prayoga*), and realizes non-retrogression in mindfulness (*smṛti*) upon ascending to the stages (*bhūmi*).

In the *Perfect* (Round) teaching, one fully realizes the three types of non-retrogression from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*). This is identical to those who attain birth in the Pure Land while still carrying their karmic hindrances (*saha-karma-upapatti*).
It is uniformity.

[Commentary] There are four meanings of non-retrogression: first, non-retrogression in a single thought-moment, whereby one destroys ignorance, manifests the Buddha-nature, and is born directly into the Land of True Reward.
[This refers to] partial realization of the *śāntaprabhāsa* (the Land of Tranquil Light).

[The *Chao* states: "Non-retrogression in every thought-moment" means that with each successive thought, one flows into the ocean of awakening; it is also called the "nature of co-arising," because one equally realizes the *dharmakāya*.
"Destroying the obscuration of non-manifestation to reveal Buddha-nature" means that by means of the wisdom of the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*), one destroys fundamental ignorance.

This clarifies and manifests the three kinds of Buddha-nature: the manifestation of the Dharma-body is the Buddha-nature as the direct cause; the realization of Prajñā is the Buddha-nature as the revealing cause;

and the attainment of liberation is the Buddha-nature as the conditional cause. It is also called the perfect arousal of the three minds and the perfect realization of the three virtues, whereby one opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

[Commentary] Second is non-retrogression in practice. Once the afflictions of views and thought have fallen away, the "dust-sand" [afflictions] are likewise shattered. One is born into the Land of Expedient Means and advances toward the ultimate fruit.

[Sub-commentary] "Non-retrogression in practice" means that one constantly delivers sentient beings and does not fall into the stages of the Two Vehicles. "The dust-sand [afflictions] are likewise shattered" means...
“Dust-like sands” refers to the attachment to the teachings of the Two Vehicles. This attachment to the teachings obstructs the path of transformation;
because such paths of transformation are as numerous as dust and sands, one cultivates the contemplation of the provisional (jia-guan) precisely to shatter this delusion.

When this delusion is exhausted, the Knowledge of the Modes of Phenomena (mārgajñatā) is accomplished, whereby one constantly delivers sentient beings without falling into the stages of the Two Vehicles.

[Commentary] The three stages of non-retrogression involve being reborn while still carrying one's karmic burdens within the Land of Common Residence (*sahā-lokadhātu*). There, one takes form within a lotus flower and is forever separated from conditions for retrogression.

[Sub-commentary] Regarding "non-retrogression in stage": if we speak in terms of this world, it requires that the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-kleśa*) be emptied and the fruit of the Two Vehicles be realized.
One does not fall into the stage of ordinary beings; thus, one’s name and rank do not regress.

Now, within the gate of mindfulness of the Buddha, while still carrying the two karmas—good and evil—from immeasurable kalpas, one horizontally transcends from this defiled land of cohabitation to the pure land of cohabitation in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
There, within the ponds of the seven treasures, one is born by transformation from a lotus flower. "Permanently departing from conditions for regression" means that one constantly beholds the Buddha.

They are forever free from conditions for regression in thought, as they constantly hear the Dharma; they are forever free from conditions for regression in practice, as they are always accompanied by those in the stage of "one more birth" (*ekajātipratibaddha*);
and they are forever free from conditions for regression in status. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "The phenomena are the great causal conditions, and the principle is the secret treasury.
Thus, this constitutes the perfect realization of the three non-regressions. The following text provides a formal judgment and comparison of the power and function of this stage.

[Commentary]: Fourth, there is ultimate non-retrogression. It does not matter whether one is in a state of focused concentration or a distracted mind, whether one possesses awareness or lacks it, or whether one understands or does not understand.

If even the name of Amitābha, or the names of the Buddhas of the six directions, or the title of this sutra passes once through the ear, then even after ten million kalpas, one will ultimately be delivered and liberated by virtue of this.
It is like hearing the sound of a "poison-smeared drum"; whether far or near, all are affected.
If one eats even a small amount of gold while in mourning, it will certainly not be digested.
[Commentary] This specifically reveals the inconceivable merit of the Buddha’s name. "To pass through" (jīng) means to experience; "to pass through the ear" means to hear it.
That those who ultimately attain liberation by means of this are like the old man in the time of the Buddha. It is like a drum smeared with lethal poison.
This belonged to King Prasenajit and was used for military expeditions. Poison was smeared upon the drum;

when it was sounded on the battlefield, one's own army possessed a method to neutralize the poison, whereas the enemy army did not. Upon hearing its sound, they all perished. This serves as a metaphor proving that the attainment of fruition is not in vain.
Just as eating even a small amount of *vajra* (diamond) ensures it will certainly not be digested, this illustrates that the seed of Buddhahood is not in vain. Second, a specific clarification.
The section on the function of power is concluded.
△ Third, the comparative evaluation of the function of power has three parts: first, pointing out the function of power; second, the formal evaluation of the function of power;

and third, the comparative measurement of the function of power. The intent of these three sections is like a government court’s adjudication of a case: first, one must examine and determine the facts.
First, one must identify the offense; second, one must adjudicate the crime according to the Vinaya; third, one must weigh its gravity.
One should strive to ensure that people’s hearts are won over. If one decides cases in this manner, they will become irrevocable "iron cases. Otherwise, one becomes a blind official.

[Commentary] Furthermore, those who are born through the remaining traces of karma and dwell together in purity, as well as those who have attained the stage of non-retrogression, all share the same rank as those in their final birth (the *ekajātipratibaddha*).
They shall all, in one more life, necessarily attain the rank of Buddhahood.
[Commentary]: "Merely bringing karma with one to be born in the Shared Pure Land" refers to those who have attained non-retrogression at the stage of realization.

"Merely" (*shiki*) means "beginning. This indicates that while they do not sever the power and function of the [higher] three lands, they are nonetheless judged to be among those who, within the Shared Land, begin by being born there with their karma still present and attain non-retrogression in their realized status.
These are individuals such as Zhang Zhonggui and others. All of them... [and so forth].
This points out the two kinds of power and function shown in the sutra. First, [the practitioners] are all together with those in the stage of being next to Buddhahood (*upapadya-bodhisattva*).
The sutra says: "Sentient beings who hear this should make a vow, wishing to be born in that land, so that they may be gathered together in one place with such supreme and virtuous people.
Second, they will all necessarily attain the rank of Buddhahood in their next life. The sutra says: "The multitude..."
All those who have been born [in this state] are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive).

Among them, there are many who are in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*), and their number is so vast that it cannot be known through calculation; one should read the subsequent commentary in detail for this.
It is not only the case with Zhang Zhonggui and others, but even parrots, starlings, and the like are also thus. This is as determined by the examination of their transgressions.
[Commentary]:
Now, "supreme goodness" in one place refers to being born in the Land of Common Dwelling; this already implies being born in the three higher lands.

"Being born to succeed the Buddha in one lifetime" refers to non-retrogression in rank; this already implies the perfect realization of the three types of non-retrogression (based on the *Liaoli lun*).

[Commentary] This is the correct judgment regarding the power and function [of the teachings]. That is to say, the first [stage], "the supreme good gathered together," refers to the horizontal manifestation of the four lands (*catur-bhūmi*).
The second, "one life remaining before Buddhahood" (*ekajāti-pratibaddha*), refers to the perfect realization of the three non-regressions (*tri-avaivartika*).

Since there is the horizontal manifestation of the four lands and the perfect realization of non-regression, one then perfectly transforms the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), perfectly severs the five abodes of ignorance (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*), perfectly cultivates the myriad practices (*sahasra-pratipatti*), and is perfectly...
