When the faculty of hearing gives rise to auditory consciousness, one personally hears the perfect sound; like space sealing space, this is called "hearing."

[Commentary]: True reality (*dharmatā*) is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Therefore, it is neither the "self" of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), nor is it the "non-self" of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

Regarding Ānanda’s not destroying conventional designations, there are three kinds of self: namely, the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), the pride of self (*ātma-māna*), and the self as a name (*nāman-ātman*).
Ānanda has merely destroyed the view of self and the pride of self, but has not destroyed the self as a name; therefore, he remains...
Regarding the statement that "the ear faculty gives rise to ear-consciousness," there are two kinds of ear faculties:

first, the *pudgala-śarīra-indriya* (the physical sense organ), which is the coarse external appearance and constitutes the remote objective aspect (*viprakṛṣṭa-nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness; second, the *paramārtha-indriya* (the ultimate sense organ), which is the subtle internal appearance.

This is the direct objective part (*sākṣāt-svabhāga*) of the eighth consciousness; the ear-consciousness arises based upon this ultimate sense organ (*paramārtha-indriya*). "To personally hear the perfect sound" means to hear directly from the Buddha.
"Personally hearing" refers to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the ear-consciousness; "perfect sound" refers to the objective part (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the ear-consciousness.
By relying on the Buddha’s fundamental essence, it transforms its own objective part, which constitutes the direct object-condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*); therefore, it is called "direct."

Listen! As for "emptiness sealing emptiness": because the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is without marks, it is like emptiness; because the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) is without arising, it is also like emptiness.
Since these two parts are in essence but a single mind, how could there be "is" or "is not" within them?
Therefore, it is said that "emptiness seals emptiness."
[Commentary] Time has no substantial reality. Because the paths of teacher and disciple are in harmony, and the speaking and listening are complete, it is called "one time.
[Sub-commentary] That "time has no substantial reality" means there is no real entity to point to. It is merely established provisionally based on dharmas such as form and mind;
this very reality of what lacks reality is the true mark (*dharmatā*). Furthermore, its duration is not fixed; it arises in accordance with karma.
It appears like a dream lasting three watches, wherein twenty years of affairs are accomplished within seven days in a cave, yet a thousand years have already passed in the world;
since duration is thus indeterminate and unstable, it is said to lack substantial reality.

According to the Buddha’s teaching, the encounter between the capacity of the disciple and the resonance of the Dharma—from "Thus have I heard" to "having paid homage, they departed"—is collectively termed "at one time."
[Commentary] Self-awakening, awakening others, and the perfection of the practice of awakening—this Great Teacher of humans and devas is named Buddha.

[Sub-commentary] The character "in" (在) was briefly explained in the *Shu* (Commentary); it is now supplemented here. The *Wenju* (Textual Exegesis) on the *Buddhāvatamsaka-sūtra* says: "Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining..."
The general term is "being present" (*zài*). "Being present" is equivalent to "abiding" (*zhù*). We shall now explain "being present" by means of "abiding. There are four types of abiding:

namely, the celestial abiding (*devasthāna*), the Brahma abiding (*brahmasthāna*), the noble abiding (*āryasthāna*), and the Buddha abiding (*buddhasthāna*). The Buddha is the one who abides; these four dharmas are that which is abided in.
The dharmas are what can be abided in, while places such as Śrāvastī are the locations where one abides.
[Commentary]: Śrāvastī means "Hearing Things" (聞物). It is the name of a great kingdom in Central India, where King Prasenajit resided.
The king’s crown prince was named Jeta, which means "Victorious in Battle" (戰勝). The king’s minister was named Sudatta, which means "Giver to the Lonely" (給孤獨).
The Elder Sudatta spread gold to purchase the prince’s grove to provide for the Buddha and [the Sangha].

The monk Jeta sighed with emotion and offered the remaining small portion of land that had not yet been laid out; therefore, it is called both Jetavana (Jeta’s Grove) and Anāthapiṇḍika-ārāma (Garden of the Benefactor of the Destitute).
[According to the] *Chao* (Commentary): "Central India" refers to Madhyadeśa (Middle India). The *Mingyi ji* (Collection of Names and Meanings) states: "Formerly called Shendu, or..."
*Xiandu* (賢豆): Following the correct phonetics today, it should be called *Indu*. In this [language], it is called the "Land of the Moon.

This is because the sages and worthies govern all things like the moon shining upon them; hence it is called *Indu*. *Pusini* (波斯匿) means King "Victorious Army" (*Śatānīka*), as his military forces surpassed those of other nations.
*Jita* (祇陀) means "Victory in Battle," for he was born at the time when King Śatānīka’s troops emerged victorious.
Therefore, it is said that he was victorious in battle. Regarding the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada’s purchase of the grove by spreading gold:
there was an elder in Rājagṛha named Sudatta (Śāntanu). The Elder Sudatta was his friend. One day, [Sudatta] was arranging a marriage for his son.
Upon arriving at his house, he saw that it was more bustling and chaotic than usual, so he asked the reason for this.
Sudatta replied, "Tomorrow morning I am inviting the Buddha to provide a meal for the Sangha; I am now preparing the offerings in advance. Sudatta asked, "Who is called the Buddha?
Sudatta said, "Do you not know? Prince Siddhārtha, the son of King Śuddhodana, studied the Way on the Snowy Mountains and attained realization..."

He has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. He possesses the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, is fully endowed with the three types of knowledge (*vidyā*), the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), the ten powers (*bala*), and the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).
He has one thousand two hundred and fifty disciples and is currently preaching the Dharma at the Veṇuvana Monastery outside the city. Sudatta—
Upon hearing of the Buddha, the hairs on his body all stood on end; he leaped for joy and could not rest even upon his pillow.
Suddenly seeing the break of dawn, he rose and departed the city. After traveling no great distance, the sky suddenly turned dark.
He then suspected, saying, "Could it be that some malevolent spirit is deluding me? Suddenly, he heard a deity in the air proclaim: "Proceed steadily forward; do not delay."
The merit of taking a single step forward surpasses the gift of the seven treasures filling seven chariots.
Before Su-datta had traveled far, he beheld the Tathāgata, resplendent with a golden hue, majestic and dignified, walking back and forth outside the Bamboo Grove.
Suddenly he saw a man who circumambulated the Buddha three times and prostrated before him three times. Sudatta also circumambulated the Buddha three times and prostrated before him three times.

The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they immediately realized the first fruit of enlightenment (*srotāpanna*). They then requested the World-Honored One to come to the kingdom of Śrāvastī the following year to preach the Dharma.
The Buddha said, "I have already accepted King Bimbisāra’s invitation for next year. They then invited him again for the year after that.

The World-Honored One granted his consent. He then asked whether there was any grove outside the city of Śrāvastī that was lush and excellent, secluded from the clamor of the world, and suitable as a dwelling place for his thousand followers.
Sudatta replied, "I only pray that the World-Honored One will not reject me; I shall personally provide it.
Sudatta returned to his country, proclaiming [the news] along the way until he reached his own land, yet everywhere he looked, he found nothing good.

"As for a location, only the Prince’s garden can accommodate a thousand people; its groves are lush and beautiful, and it is one *yojana* in circumference. However, the Prince is not a seller of gardens.
Tomorrow, come to the Prince’s residence and speak to him regarding the purchase of the garden. Sudatta followed his instructions accordingly.
When he arrived, the Prince teased him, saying, "If you cover the ground of the garden entirely with gold, then I shall sell it to you. Sudatta indeed acted as instructed.
Regarding his words: "I shall spread gold upon the ground. As he was nearly finished spreading it, the Prince heard that Sudatta had been speaking of laying out the garden until its completion.
The Prince then became suspicious and went in person to the site of the garden.
Seeing that gold was everywhere, with the exception of only one small corner, he asked Sudatta, "You have not yet finished spreading it; I will not sell you the garden. Sudatta replied, "No."
It was not that he could not afford it; rather, he was merely calculating how much gold would be required.

When the Prince saw that Sudatta had not a single thought of retreating from his resolve, he asked for the reason. Sudatta praised the Tathāgata’s merit, wisdom, physical marks, and majestic spiritual power as being inconceivable.
He said, "I have already invited the Buddha to come to my country next year to preach the Dharma; therefore, I am purchasing this land."
The garden was offered to the Buddha and the Sangha. The Prince sighed with deep emotion and said, "Since this is so, you and I, the two of us, shall together accomplish this undertaking.
Until it has been spread across the remaining ground and all the trees, let them be made my offering."
Therefore, it is collectively referred to as the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. This concludes the initial designation of the time and place of the Dharma assembly in the sutra text.
II. Invoking the Great Assembly to Hear Together (in three parts): 1. The Assembly of Śrāvakas; 2. The Assembly of Bodhisattvas; 3. The Assembly of Deva and Human Beings.
[Commentary] Regarding the citation of the great assembly hearing together: this means it was not heard by a single person alone; therefore, the great assembly is cited as hearing together.
This constitutes the "accomplishment of the assembly. There are two kinds of *śrāvakas*:

first, the *śrāvaka* of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), who is one who awakens to the Path upon hearing the sound of the Buddha’s teaching on the Four Noble Truths; second, the *śrāvaka* of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), as [described] in the *Lotus Sūtra*.
It says: "By means of the sound of the Buddha-way, cause all to hear. Regarding "Bodhisattva," the correct term is *bodhisattva*.
Because this land [China] prefers brevity, it is simply called "Bodhisattva. This translates as "Awakened Sentient Being" (*jue youqing*). There are two explanations.

If taken in terms of one's own practice (*svayam-ācāra*), although they have attained awakening, their emotional afflictions (*kleśa*) are not yet exhausted; therefore, they are called "Awakened Sentient Beings. If taken in terms of...
"Transforming others" refers to awakening sentient beings. These three groups collectively encompass the seven classes of disciples of the Tathāgata:
namely, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, and [upāsikās].
Upāsikā. These seven assemblies are further divided into the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, resulting in fourteen assemblies. Within these fourteen assemblies, each is again divided into four groups:
first, the initiating assembly (*pravartaka-gaṇa*), referring to those who initiate profound transformation;

second, the assembly of those for whom the teaching is intended (*pratipannaka-gaṇa*), referring to those who hear the Dharma and obtain benefit; third, the assembly of shadows and echoes (*chāyā-pratibimba-gaṇa*), referring to those who practice the cause while carrying the fruit; fourth...
Regarding the assembly that forms karmic connections (*karmabandha*). Those who form connections and establish the seeds [of enlightenment] are as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:

when the Greatly Pervasive Victorious and Wise Buddha (*Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū*) had his sons lecture on the Dharma for him, those who at that time gave rise to the aspiration were the assembly that initiates the path; those who heard the Dharma and attained the Way were the assembly that was suited to the occasion (*tatkālādhimukta*) at that time;

and those who heard the Dharma but were not yet delivered, yet encountered one another life after life, were the assembly that forms karmic connections at that time. Since it was so for that Buddha, it is likewise now.
The Buddha is likewise. Four times fourteen makes fifty-six assemblies; therefore, it is said that "the great assembly heard together.
[Commentary:
The Śrāvakas are placed first because they manifest the supramundane aspect, because they constantly follow [the Buddha], and because the Buddha-dharma relies upon the Saṃgha for its transmission.
The Bodhisattvas occupy the central position because their characteristics are not fixed, because they do not follow [the world] constantly, and because this symbolizes the meaning of the Middle Way.
The devas and humans are arrayed behind because they possess worldly characteristics, because they comprise a mixture of ordinary beings and sages, and because they serve as external protectors.
[Commentary] This clarifies the reason for the sequential listing of the assembly. Question: The *śrāvakas* belong to the Hīnayāna; for what reason are they listed first?
The *bodhisattvas* belong to the Mahāyāna; for what reason are they listed next? Therefore, it is said that the *śrāvakas* occupy the foremost position, and so forth.

"Because they manifest the characteristics of transcending the world" means that by shaving their hair and beards, wearing the shaven-headed tonsure, and donning the square-cut robes, they represent the sages and saints who have transcended the mundane world.

This is because it represents the characteristic of the victory banner. As for those who constantly follow him—these one thousand two hundred who have already attained the Way—they constantly attend the Buddha to manifest the virtue of the Teacher.

Regarding the fact that the Buddha-Dharma relies upon the Sangha for its transmission: this is because the future Dharma and the two Jewels rely upon the Jewel of the Sangha for their widespread propagation.
As for the Bodhisattvas situated in the center whose positions are not fixed: Bodhisattvas may be either ordained or lay.
Regarding Bodhisattvas: there are lay Bodhisattvas, there are Bodhisattvas born in this land, and there are Bodhisattvas who should come from other directions;
thus, their manifestations are not fixed. As for "not always following": the Bodhisattva takes the benefit of sentient beings as his primary task;
he follows where there is benefit in this place, and does not follow where there is no benefit in this location. This expresses the Middle Way. [The passage on] the Śrāvakas' delight...
Nirvāṇa. While devas and humans delight in birth and death, the Bodhisattva does not lean toward either; thus, he represents the Middle Way.
As for the listing of devas and humans at the end to represent worldly phenomena, whereas the Śrāvakas represent supramundane phenomena, here they represent worldly phenomena.
Regarding those of mixed categories, the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings therein are mostly Bodhisattvas appearing in the world. As for the officials who provide external protection:
The śrāvakas serve as internal protectors, while devas and humans serve as external protectors.
△ First, regarding the assembly of śrāvakas, there are three parts: first, clarifying their categories and indicating their number; second, defining their stages and extolling their virtues;
third, listing the names of the leaders. △ Now, the first part.
Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty persons.
[Commentary: "Together with" (yǔ) means "in common. The *Śāstra* explains "common" through seven aspects: namely, being at the same time, in the same place, and observing the same precepts.
One mind, one vision, one path, and one liberation. According to the four teachings, the *śrāvaka* (Tripitaka) teaching consists of seven "samenesses":

namely, being equally moved by the time of the Buddha’s appearance; being together at the Deer Park location; sharing the same Prātimokṣa precepts; sharing the same all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); sharing the same untainted right view (*anāsrava-samyagdṛṣṭi*);

sharing the same factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*); and sharing the same nirvana. The *pratyekabuddha* (Shared) teaching consists of two sets of seven, distinguished by the sharpness or dullness of their faculties; the *bodhisattva* (Distinct) teaching has no such [shared] categories.

The measure is seventy-one, because it involves both self-cultivation and the transformation of others. The perfection is one hundred and seventy-one, because the initial resolve and the ultimate goal are not two different things.
Regarding "Great" (*mahā*): in Sanskrit it is *mahā*, which here means "vast," "many," or "supreme.

It is called "Great" because it is revered by celestial kings and great beings (for instance, the Brahma King was the teacher of Ājñātakauṇḍinya, and Śakra was the teacher of Kāśyapa). It is called "Many" because its knowledge and understanding are extensive, encompassing both internal and external scriptures. It is said to transcend the nine [stages].
Fifteenth, because his knowledge and vision are superior, he is said to be "victorious. Now, when we speak of "great," it encompasses many such victories.

As for the twelve hundred and fifty followers, they were originally Great Beings (Mahāsattvas) of the Dharma-body who appeared in the world to assist the Buddha in his transformative work, leading ordinary beings into sainthood.
First, he manifested as an outsider following the path of craving and views, desiring to lead the "milk" into "curd. Furthermore, he manifested as one of the Three Piṭakas...

One thousand two hundred and five [recitations] lead the curd into the ghee; again, one thousand two hundred and five *vaipulya* Prajñāpāramitā [recitations] lead the ghee into the clarified butter (*sarpis*);
again, one thousand two hundred and five *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* [recitations] now lead the defiled back to the pure.
Furthermore, he also manifested the Pure Land as the one thousand two hundred and fifth [transformation].

△ The commentary divides this into two parts: first, clarifying the categories; second, indicating the number. The first part further has two sections: first, a general heading; second, a detailed explanation.
△ Now, the first section.
[Commentary] A *mahābhikṣu* is an ordained person who has received the full precepts (*upasampadā*).
[Sub-commentary] "Full precepts" refers to the precepts that fully embody the three truths. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are ten kinds of precepts:
first, the "unimpaired precept. If one commits a root offense, it is broken and ruined and thus unfit; if one does not commit such an offense, it is called "unimpaired. Second...
1. Unbroken precepts: If one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, it is like a vessel that is cracked; if one does not commit such an offense, it is called "unbroken. 2. Unpierced precepts:
If one commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense, it is like a vessel with holes; if one does not commit such an offense, it is called "unpierced. 3. Unmixed precepts:
To dwell on thoughts of breaking the precepts is called "mixed"; not dwelling on them is called "unmixed. 4. Precepts following the Path.

First is the precept of conformity to the principles of the Truths, which is naturally free from transgression. Second is the precept of non-attachment, wherein the two vehicles have exhausted their views and afflictions and are thus unstained by attachment.
Seventh is the precept of mastery, so called because the Bodhisattva attains mastery over the wondrous functions of transforming others.
1. The precepts praised by the eight knowledges (*jñāna*): the bodhisattva’s *pien-chu* (offenses) are without deficiency, and they are constantly praised by the wise.

2. The precepts that accord with meditative concentration (*samādhi*): abiding in concentration, their outward conduct is naturally and constantly tranquil; they spontaneously refrain from transgressions. 3. The precepts of full completion:

employing the Middle Way, their wisdom universally enters into all phenomena, such that there is no precept that is not fully prepared. Regarding these ten precepts, the first six belong to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

The precepts of ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) are the seventh and eighth; these are the conventional precepts (saṃvṛti-satya) of the bodhisattvas. The ninth and tenth are the middle-truth precepts (madhyama-satya) of all Buddhas.
Those who have left the household life are fully endowed with the precepts of ultimate truth. Having left the home of common dwelling, they are fully endowed with the precepts of conventional truth.
Having left the home of expedient means, they are fully endowed with the precepts of middle truth—this refers to leaving the home of true retribution (sambhoga-niṣyanda). This is the general summary.
[End of section].
△ Second, the detailed explanation has two parts: first, explaining the three meanings of *bhikṣu*; second, explaining the six harmonies of the monastic community (*saṃgha*).
△ Now, the first part.

[Commentary]: The term *bhikṣu* (biqiu) is a Sanskrit word that contains three meanings: 1. **The Mendicant** (*bhikṣu*): Sustaining oneself with a single alms-bowl and possessing no stored wealth, one focuses exclusively on seeking the essential means of liberation.
2. **The Destroyer of Evil**: Through the observation of correct wisdom, one destroys the evil of afflictions (*kleśa*) and does not fall into the attachments of craving or views.

3. **The Terrorizer of Māra**: Upon generating the resolve for enlightenment and receiving the precepts, the ritual of full ordination (*karmavācanā*) is accomplished; at that moment, Māra is terrified.

[Commentary] "One bowl for the sustenance of the body" means that one constantly practices begging for food to sustain physical life. "Having nothing stored away" means that one seeks only the food of the Dharma to sustain the life of wisdom.

"Dedicatedly seeking the essential way of transcendence" refers to transcending the Land of Common Residence (tongju), the Land of Expedient Means (fangbian), the Land of Real Reward (shibao), and the Land of Peaceful Light (jiguang).
"Observing with correct wisdom" refers to the correct wisdom of the three contemplations (sanguan). [This] breaks...
"Afflictions that are evil" refers to destroying the evils of the five dwelling grounds (*pañca-vāsanā-bhūmi*). "Not falling into craving and views":

craving refers to the delusions of thought (*klesha-āvaraṇa*), while views refer to the delusions of vision (*dṛṣṭi-āvaraṇa*). There are [delusions of] co-residence (*sahabhū*), of the stage of expedient means (*upāya-bhūmi*), and of true retribution (*vipāka-bhūmi*).

There are four kinds of Māras: namely, the Māra of afflictions, the Māra of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the Māra of death, and the celestial Māra (*devaputra-māra*). In Sanskrit, this is called *karma*. This...

Regarding the "Method of Practice": this refers to ascending the altar to receive the precepts. Once the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of one motion and three proclamations) has been completed, the four Māras are all struck with fear.
△ Second, explaining the six harmonies of the monastic community (*saṃgha*).

[Commentary]: "Saṃgha" (僧). In full, it is called Saṃgha; this translates as "harmonious assembly. Because they collectively realize unconditioned liberation (*asaṃskṛta-vimukti*), it is termed "harmony in principle" (*li-he*).
They dwell together in body, are without dispute in speech, share mutual joy in mind, possess identical understanding in view, practice the precepts together, and share benefits equally.
This refers to the harmony of names and phenomena.

[Commentary] Regarding the division of the Mahayana and Hinayana schools in India, both the harmony of principle (*li*) and the harmony of phenomena (*shi*) are categorized as either Mahayana or Hinayana.
Furthermore, there are four types of *saṃgha*: first, the "non-gradual" *saṃgha*, referring to those who have broken the precepts; second, the "dumb sheep" *saṃgha*, who do not understand...

Regarding "those who possess the Dharma": these are the three types of pure *saṃgha*, the persons on the seven stages of expedient means, and the four types of true *saṃgha* who have already entered the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*).
This concludes the initial clarification of categories.
△ Second, indicating the number. [Commentary]:

Regarding the "one thousand two hundred and fifty people": the three Kāśyapas, including their disciples, total one thousand; Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, including their disciples, total two hundred;
and Yaśas and his companions number fifty. All of them were the first to attain liberation after the Buddha’s realization of the Way.
[He] was liberated. Moved by the Buddha’s profound kindness, he constantly followed him.
[Commentary]: Kāśyapa means "Great Tortoise Clan" (Mahā-kauṣṭhila); this is his surname. There were three brothers:
first, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, which means "Pumpkin Grove" (*kapittha-vana*), so called because he resided in that grove; it is also called "Pumpkin Hunchback," as there was a hunch on his chest.
1. Kauṇḍinya: Because he was as humpbacked as a *kapittha* fruit. 2. Gayākāśyapa: This is the name of a mountain, namely Elephant Head Mountain (*Gajapadaka*), located outside the city of Rājagṛha;
because he studied the Way on this mountain, he is so named. 3. Nadīkāśyapa: This means "river.
Because he studied the Way by the side of a river, he was named after the river. These three men together erected a pillar for the *stūpa* during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha; therefore, even now...
They were bound together as brothers. Initially, they were non-Buddhist practitioners who worshipped fire; later, they encountered the Buddha’s transformation and realized the fruits of the Path.

Regarding the teacher and disciples: the teacher is the holy artisan, while the disciples receive their natural endowments from him. Śāriputra is here called "Body-Son" (Shenzi) and also "Śārikā" (Qulü).
Maudgalyāyana is here called "Mung-bean Clan" (Caishu Shi); this was a Brahmin surname. Yaśas is [Ya]... [text ends].
Excluding the son of the elder Śreṣṭhin and adding Kauṇḍinya and the other four, there are thus one thousand two hundred and fifty-five people;
this is merely stating the approximate number. One should consult the *Śākyapuṭa* or the *Miaozhenji* for further details.
These are not recorded here in full. The initial section of the sutra clarifies the classification and enumeration [of the arhats].
△ Second, the delineation of their status and praise of their virtues:
they are all Great Arhats (whose status and whose virtues are) known to all.
[Commentary] Regarding "known by all": initially, he was known by those with craving and views; at the time of his renunciation, he was known by those of the Tripitaka teachings;
at the time of the Vaipulya, he was known by those of the four teachings; and at the time of the Prajñāpāramitā...

Furthermore, [the Buddha] was known by the assemblies of the three teachings; at the time of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Nirvāṇa* sūtras, he was known only by the assemblies of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

This is not merely because he was known by the assemblies of the Shared Residence (*tongju*), but also because he was known by the assemblies of the Expedient Means (*fangbian*) and the True Reward (*shibao*).
Ultimately, his fundamental nature is that which is known by the assemblies of the Peaceful Light (*jiguang*).
△ The commentary is divided into two parts: first, the delineation of the stages; second, the praise of virtues. △ Now, the first part. 【Explanation】 "Arhat" also encompasses three meanings: 1.
Worthy of Offerings (*arhat*), which is the fruit of the mendicant (*bhikṣu*); 2. Slayer of Thieves (*arhat*), which is the fruit of destroying evil;

3. Non-arising (*anuppāda*), which is the fruit of terrifying Māra. Furthermore, there are those liberated through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*) and those liberated both ways (*ubhaya-to-bhāga-vimukta*), as well as those free from doubt (*akathaṃkathī*).
Liberation is of three different kinds. This is now the liberation of being free from doubt; therefore, it is called "Great.
Furthermore, he is originally a Great Being of the Dharma-body who manifests as a śrāvaka; because he realizes this inconceivable dharma of the Pure Land, it is called "Great."

[Commentary] The text is divided into three sections. First, the three meanings of "Arhat. Next, the phrase "Furthermore" clarifies that among the three types of Arhats, this one is the "Great" (Mahā).
Then, the phrase "Moreover, originally" explains the "Great" by revealing the fundamental through the manifested traces. Within the first section, there are also three meanings:
the previous term "Bhikṣu" is a name based on causes, while the current term "Arhat" is a title based on results; thus, cause and result correspond to one another. Cause...

Since these three [qualities] are complete, the fruit likewise contains all three. Furthermore, as the six types of Arhats represent the stages leading to Buddhahood, the Buddha is the ultimate Great Arhat;
thus, among his ten titles, he is called "Arhat," and he is also the ultimate Bhikṣu.

As for the Arhat liberated through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*), they enter directly by taking emptiness as their object and realize only the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). During the causal stage, they cultivate the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) regarding their own nature.

The one who can destroy all non-Buddhists (tīrthika) and is liberated through both parts (ubhayatobhāgavimukta) practices both the phenomenal and the ultimate, possessing the three types of supernormal knowledge (traividyā) and the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa);

by practicing the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) in common during the causal stage, they are able to destroy the non-Buddhists who possess the five supernatural powers (pañcābhijñā). This is the one liberated through non-doubt (akopyadharman-vimukta).

He thoroughly mastered the Tripitaka and the four Vedas, as well as astronomy and geography. During his causal stage, he cultivated the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), whereby he was able to defeat the Vedic non-Buddhists;
these are also called the "three kinds of foundations of mindfulness. The foundations of mindfulness are the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness.

As for the "foundations of mindfulness by nature" (*svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna*), this refers to practicing only the four foundations of mindfulness and the seven categories of the path factors (*mārgāṅga*) to sever delusions and realize the truth, without cultivating [the other two types].

Regarding the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): this refers to the various dhyānas and samādhis being cultivated together with the four applications of mindfulness;

thus, one becomes fully endowed with the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*) and the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*). Regarding the application of mindfulness as an object: this means that one can further penetrate both mundane and supramundane dharmas and resolve the doubts of the multitude;
therefore, one is able to defeat the Vedas and the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). These non-Buddhists are also divided into three types: namely, the small, the medium, and the [great].
The "Great" [non-Buddhist] refers to those who claim omniscience; these are minor non-Buddhists who merely assume the title of "Omniscient One.
The "Supernatural Power" (ṛddhi) non-Buddhists possess only the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) that are tainted by outflows (*sāsrava*).

The "Veda" non-Buddhists are major non-Buddhists who have mastered astronomy, geography, and the four Vedas, while also attaining the five superknowledges. *Veda* is translated here as "Book of Wisdom" (*jñāna-grantha*). There are...

There are four kinds; therefore, they are called the Four Vedas. Regarding the "unveiling of the traces to reveal the fundamental": if one refers to the manifested traces, there is the assembly of śrāvakas;
if one refers to the fundamental gate, their number is truly immeasurable. For instance, Subhūti is actually a manifestation of the Buddha Śvetaketu;
thus it is said that he is fundamentally a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body manifesting as such. This concludes the delineation of the stages.
△ Second, praising his virtues.
[Commentary] Because he turned the wheel of the Buddha’s teaching and extensively benefited humans and devas, he was well-known to the masses.
[Sub-commentary] "Turning the wheel" is a name derived from a metaphor; there are four types of wheels—gold, silver, copper, and iron—and the Wheel-Turning Kings likewise...

There are four kings, which metaphorically represent the four Buddhas—the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, the Transformation-body, and the Emanation-body. The wheel represents the Wheel of the Four Teachings. Regarding those who turn the wheel from the Buddha:
some turn the Four Truths of Arising and Ceasing from the Transformation Buddha; some turn the Four Truths of Non-arising from the Response Buddha;
some turn the Four Truths of the Immeasurable from the Reward Buddha; and some turn the [Four Truths of] the Unconditioned from the Dharma Buddha.
He manifests the Four Noble Truths; he may turn them suddenly, gradually, secretly, or indeterminately.

He may manifest in the form of a Buddha, or manifest in the forms of Bodhisattvas and others. He may turn the four kinds of Four Noble Truths among humans, or turn the three kinds of Four Noble Truths—namely, the Shared, the Distinct, and the Perfect—among the heavens.
Or, he may turn the two kinds of Four Noble Truths within the stage of Expedient Means. Namely:
Regarding the Separate and Perfect [teachings], or those in the Real Reward Land and the Land of Quiescent Light, who turn one kind of Four Noble Truths to extensively benefit humans and devas:
there are four types of devas. First, worldly devas, such as various kings and the like; second, devas by birth, the various devas of the three realms;
third, pure devas, namely the followers of the Two Vehicles; and fourth, devas of principle, namely Bodhisattvas. These great beings may also exist among human beings.

Alternatively, he may be among the four deva realms, initiating the four benefits of a Tathāgata to extensively benefit all beings; thus, he serves as a true and virtuous spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) for the great assemblies of the four lands.
To hear his name is called "knowing" him; to see his face is called "recognizing" him. This concludes the second section of the sutra, which delineates the stages and extols his virtues.
△ Third, listing the names of the leaders:
The Elder Śāriputra (here translated as "Son of Śarī"), Mahāmaudgalyāyana (Great Maudgalya), and Mahākāśyapa (Great Kāśyapa).
Mahākātyāyana (Great Ornament), Mahākauṣṭhila (Great Knees), Revata (Star),
Cūḍapanthaka (Successor of the Path), Nanda (Joy), Ānanda (Rejoicing), Rāhula (Obscuration), Gavāmpati (Ruminator),
Piṇḍola Bharadvāja (Immovable Sharp Faculties), Kālodāyin (Black Light), Mahākapphiṇa (Hare Star), Bakula...
Rāhula (Good Appearance), Aniruddha (Free from Poverty), and other such great disciples. [Commentary]:
Śāriputra is here called "Body-Son" (Shenzi) or "Pupil-Son" (Zubazi). He was named after his mother;

because she was the most intelligent among women, and because the mark of intelligence resides in the pupils of the eyes—the very source of the "pupil"—he is called "Pupil-Son. As for "Body-Son" (Shenzi)...
As for "Śāriputra": his mother’s physical form was beautiful, and he was born from her body; thus he is called "Son of the Body" (Śarīraputra).

His father gave him the name Upatiṣya, which translates as "Discourse on Meaning" (Lunyi). Having obtained a wife through discourse on meaning, he was named after that discourse; this serves to highlight the virtues of his father.

Śāriputra: "Śāri" refers to his father; "Putra" (translated as *li*, meaning "benefit") refers to his mother. Because both parents are manifested together, he is called Śāriputra; "putra" means "son. Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Mahā" means "great.
"Maudgalyāyana" is a clan name (*gotra*); it is translated as "Bean-herder" (*mudga*). It is also rendered as "radish," for this was the food of ancient seers, and the clan was named accordingly.
His personal name was Kolita; "Kolita" is the name of a tree, specifically the *kovidāra* tree, from which he was named. He was so called because he prayed under that tree [for a son].
The deity obtained a son and named him accordingly. Because there were many who shared that name, he is distinguished here by his greatness.

○ Mahākāśyapa, the Great Kāśyapa, is also translated as "Wave of Light" (Guangbo). The light from the bodies of ancient seers surged like a calamity, capable of eclipsing other lights so they could not appear;
hence he is called "Wave of Light. Kāśyapa’s bodily radiance likewise eclipses other objects. He is also translated as...

Daiguī (Great Tortoise) was his clan name. His ancestors had practiced the Way, and a numinous tortoise responded by bearing a divine chart; because the clan was named according to this virtue, he was called Guī (Tortoise).
His personal name was Pipalā; "Pipalā" is the name of a tree. Having prayed to the tree and obtained a son, he was named after it.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-saṃgraha* (Fǔfǎzàng jīng) states that after the parinirvāṇa of Vipaśyin Buddha, the golden images on the stūpas were damaged and decayed.
At that time, there was a poor woman who found a golden bead. She requested a craftsman to fashion it into a bowl. The goldsmith was delighted;

once he had finished polishing and refining it for the Buddha, he made a vow to become her husband for ninety-one kalpas. Throughout these periods, whether among humans or in the heavens, their bodies were always golden in color and their minds constantly experienced bliss.
In his final birth, he took rebirth in the family of the Brahmin Nyagrodha in the kingdom of Magadha.
The poor woman was none other than the Bhikṣuṇī Jinguang (Golden Light). ○ Mahākātyāyana: "Great Ornamented One.
He is also translated as "Fan-sheng" (Fan-rope) or "Haojian" (Good Shoulder). He is also named Kāla; Kāla means "Victorious Thought" in this language.
O Mahākoṣṭhila, the Great-Thighed One, was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra. From the past, he had always been victorious in debate over his sister;

however, once she became pregnant, he could no longer defeat her in discussion. Knowing that the one she carried was a man of wisdom, he realized that even when the eloquence was merely entrusted to another, it was already so superior—how much more so when the child had emerged from the womb!

He immediately left the household life and went to South India, where he studied the eighteen great sūtras. He had no leisure even to trim his nails, such was his devotion. Thus say the people of the world.
He was called the Brahmacārin Dīrghanakha. Having completed his studies, he returned home and asked where his nephew was. People told him that he had become a disciple of the Buddha.

He became greatly arrogant, thinking, "My nephew has been renowned throughout the five regions since he was eight years old; what kind of spiritual arts does that śramaṇa possess to have seduced my sister's son?
He went straight to the Buddha’s location and meditated for a long time, yet he could not gain entry into even a single dharma.
Citta said to the Buddha, "I do not accept any dharma. The Buddha asked, "Do you see this acceptance? This placed him in a position of defeat on both counts:
if he saw acceptance, it contradicted his previous statement that he did not accept anything; if he did not see acceptance, he had no way to prevail over the Buddha.
He then lowered his head and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. Upatiṣya (Vipula) said, "A star is the father."
His mother prayed to the stars and gave birth to him; he is also called Li-yue (Vītaśoka) or Jia-he-ho (Saṃghāta). The *Śāstra* states:
While staying overnight in an empty pavilion, he saw two ghosts contending over a corpse. He told them that whether they judged according to principle or against principle, neither would escape harm.
Therefore, he answered according to the facts. The larger ghost pulled off its hands and feet, while the smaller ghost took the corpse and restored it to them.
Having finished eating, he wiped his mouth and departed. Because of his afflictions, he did not know whose body it was; thus, he became suspicious of this body.
"If it is my own body, why does it pull itself out as I watch? If it is another's body, why does it follow me? Thinking thus, he questioned everyone he encountered.
"Do you see my body? The assembly of monks replied, "This person is easy to deliver. [The Buddha] said, "This body was originally the remains left by another;
it does not belong to oneself. Immediately, he attained the Way. Therefore, it is said: "A provisional combination.
*Cuḷapanthaka* (translated as "Successor of the Path") refers to these two brothers. The elder brother was named *Mahāpanthaka*. According to the customs of the Western Regions, the mother—
While pregnant, she returned to her natal home and gave birth on the road; therefore, he was named Jidao (Continuing the Way).
Bandhula means "Little Jidao," as he was his younger brother. ○ Nanda means "Joy"; this refers to Sundarananda.
Sundarī means "Lovely" or "Elegant," and she was his wife. He was born on the ninth day of the fourth month and was shorter than the Buddha.
[He was] four fingers [taller]. If there were those among the multitude who did not recognize him, they would say, "The Buddha has come.
In the kingdom of Magadha, there was a naked ascetic (nirgrantha) of great intelligence whom the people called a "wise man. He had been silenced while debating with Śāriputra;

a virtuous mind arose within him, and he desired to leave the household life to enter the Buddha’s Dharma. Seeing that Nanda’s appearance and features were exceptionally magnificent, he sighed and said:
The short and small bhikṣu’s wisdom was difficult to fathom; how much more so for one who is dignified and majestic! Nanda was then ordained and left the household life.
○ As for Ānanda, he is called "Joyous" (Qingxi), or "Delight" (Huānxǐ), or "Untainted" (Wǎnrǎn). He was born at the time the Tathāgata attained enlightenment;
King Śuddhodana was greatly rejoiced, and King Śuklodana announced, "A son has been born. The entire nation celebrated with joy, and thus he was named.

Ānanda, the Joyful One, followed the Buddha into the dragon palace in the heavens; because he saw the male and female dragons and celestial maidens without his mind being stained by attachment, he is called "Unstained" (Araṇa).
Rāhula is said to be "one who covers and obstructs. In the past, he blocked a mouse hole for six days;
now he remains in his mother’s womb for six years—therefore, he is called "Covering and Obstructing. When Yaśodharā became pregnant, all the Śākyas were filled with resentment.
For what reason did this happen? Desiring to punish and kill her, malicious rumors filled the roads. The precious woman Gopīla was slightly recovered by the testimony [of others].
Thereupon, she cast herself into a fire pit and made a great vow: "If I have committed a wrong, may mother and son perish together;
if I am truly innocent, may Heaven bear witness. She embraced her child and threw herself into the pit; the fire transformed into a pool, and a lotus flower supported their bodies.
The king and the people of the country finally ceased their doubts. Later, when the Buddha returned to his home country, Yaśodharā had Rāhula offer the *modaka* (joyful ball) to the Buddha.
Because Rāhula was of such tender age, he went directly before the great assembly to present it to the Buddha;
Yaśodharā used this to quell the slander. Since the slander arose because of her son, she spoke of "concealment and obstruction. ○ Regarding Gavāmpati, it is said:
The "ox-chewer" (Go-mukha) is also called the "Ox-King. Because he had mocked a śramaṇa in a previous life and uttered an evil word, he was reborn as an ox for five hundred lifetimes.
Even after the ox had finished eating, it would constantly pant and belch; because this residual retribution had not yet been exhausted, people of the time called him the "ox-chewer.
Pindola Bharadvāja is called the "Immovable One with Sharp Faculties. "Immovable" is a name...
"Also" (*ya*) refers to the lineage. "Sharp faculties" (*li-gen*) is the clan name; it may also be translated as "heavy banner. Among the eighteen Brahmin clans, this is one of them.
*Kālodāyin* means "Black Light" (*Hei-guang*). This is because his facial complexion was coarse and dark. Furthermore, his black color shone with a brilliance that differed from ordinary blackness.
When he went out at night to beg for food, people were startled and terrified; therefore, the Buddha prohibited walking about at night.
Mahā-Kapphiṇa: As for "Kapphiṇa," it means "born under the constellation Kṛttikā. His parents prayed to the Kṛttikā star when he was born;
furthermore, he resided in the same room as the Buddha at the potter’s house, and thus he is called Kṛttikā. Bakkula: As for "Bakkula," it means "of handsome appearance."
Some say his form was magnificent; others say he was large and robust. Because his appearance was upright and handsome, he was called "Good Appearance" (Sundara).
○ *Aniruddha* means "One Without Poverty," and is also called "As One Wishes. The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states:
During the final dharma period of Puṣya Buddha, there was a famine in the world. A pratyekabuddha went out begging with an empty bowl and obtained nothing. A poor man saw him...

He was filled with grief and lamentation, saying, "O Noble One, would you accept some millet porridge? He immediately offered him what he had been eating. After the man had finished eating, he performed the eighteen miraculous transformations.
Later, as he went out to gather more millet, a rabbit leaped up and embraced his back; it then transformed into a corpse, leaving him without a companion to escape.
Waiting for darkness, he returned home; when he set the body down on the ground, it instantly became a golden man. He pulled out its fingers and used its feet.
Taking from it, one never exhausts it; for ninety-one kalpas, the retribution of its fruit will be sufficient.

Therefore, he is named "The One Without Poverty. [Commentary]: Because his virtue and seniority are both venerable, he is called an "Elder" (sthavira). The Venerable Śāriputra is foremost in wisdom among the assembly of śrāvakas.
The Venerable Maudgalyāyana is foremost in supernatural powers. The Venerable Kāśyapa possesses a golden light upon his body; he transmitted the Buddha’s...
Cixin (Mind-Seal) was foremost among the patriarchs; Touduo (Alms-Seeker) was foremost in ascetic practice. Wenshi (Ornamented) was of Brahmin descent and foremost in doctrinal debate.
Dakui (Great-Knee) was foremost in answering questions. Xingxiu (Constellation) was foremost in being free from confusion and error.
Jidao (Successor of the Way) possessed dull faculties and could only retain a single verse, yet his eloquence was inexhaustible and he was foremost in upholding the meaning [of the teachings].
1. Venerable Ānanda: the Buddha’s own younger brother; foremost in physical appearance. Venerable Nandika: the Buddha’s cousin;
served as his attendant and was foremost in extensive learning (*bahuśruta*). Venerable Channa: the Buddha’s son; foremost in secret conduct (*guhyacaryā*). Venerable Gavāmpati:
due to harsh speech in a previous life, he experienced this residual retribution; yet he was foremost in receiving offerings from the devas.
First, the Venerable Aśvajit, who has long dwelt in the world, is foremost among those worthy of offerings in the final age as a field of merit.

Second, the Venerable Kālodāyin, acting as the Buddha’s messenger, is foremost in teaching and transforming others. Third, the Venerable Revata, is foremost in his knowledge of the lunar mansions and celestial bodies.
The Venerable Śāriputra was foremost in longevity; the Venerable Aniruddha, also a younger cousin of the Buddha, was foremost in the divine eye.
These and others were his constant followers; they were originally Great Beings of the Dharmakāya who manifested as śrāvakas to serve as a retinue of influence and response.
Now, having heard of the merit of being gathered into the Pure Land, one attains the benefit of the ultimate *siddhānta*;
the Path increases and births are diminished, and as one purifies the Buddha-land for oneself, one is further called a member of the assembly for whom the teaching is truly suited.

[Commentary]: One who is honored both for virtue (*guṇa*) and seniority (*vassa*) is called an *sthavira* (Elder). This means that both their virtue and seniority are great, and both are aged. There are three kinds of elders:
the elder by age (*vṛddha-sthavira*), the elder by nature (*dharmatā-sthavira*), and the elder by office (*kṛta-sthavira*). Here, it refers to the two types—the elder by age and the elder by nature;
therefore, it is said they are "honored both for virtue and seniority. [Regarding] the Venerable Śāriputra’s wisdom...
Regarding the first [of the three]: from the day he was in his mother’s womb, his wisdom resided in his mother’s mouth; at eight years of age, he ascended the throne and was peerless in debate;
within seven days, he attained a thorough mastery of the Buddha-dharma; thus he is called "the foremost.

Furthermore, he is the foremost in all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the foremost in the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the foremost in the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). The term "foremost" refers to the citation of each individual virtue.

This is merely to illustrate various preferences. ○ Regarding the Venerable Maudgalyāyana, foremost in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*): "Supernatural" (*shen*) refers to the nature of the heavenly mind; "power" (*tong*) refers to the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*). Because this innate wisdom illuminates all things with unimpeded penetration, it is called *ṛddhi*. There are six kinds: first, the power of transformation at will (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*), also called the power of the feet (*pāda-ṛddhi*); second, the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); third, the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*); fourth, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)... [text continues]... fifth, the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*); sixth, the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*). Among these, the first five are mundane, while the last one is supramundane. Furthermore, within the first five, the first four are mundane, while the last one is both mundane and supramundane. As for the Venerable Maudgalyāyana, he was foremost in the first [the power of transformation at will]. This is because his mental concentration was extremely sharp and clear, and his physical body was extremely light and agile. Consequently, whenever he desired to travel to a distant place, he would simply focus his mind on it, and he would arrive there in an instant. It is like a person who, when they wish to go somewhere, merely thinks of it and arrives immediately. Therefore, he was called "foremost in supernatural powers. Regarding the term "foremost": it means that among all those who possess such powers, he was the most superior. As for the Venerable Śāriputra, foremost in wisdom: "Wisdom" refers to the nature of discernment (*pravicaya*). Because he could distinguish between right and wrong, and because he could penetrate the profound meanings of the Dharma, he was called "wisdom. Furthermore, there are two types of wisdom: first, the wisdom of hearing and contemplation (*śrutamayī-prajñā* and *cintāmayī-prajñā*); second, the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Among these, the former two are mundane, while the latter one is supramundane. Moreover, within the first two, there are again two types: first, the wisdom of hearing; second, the wisdom of contemplation. Among these, the former is shallow, while the latter is deep. Furthermore, within the wisdom of contemplation, there are again two types: first, the wisdom of inference; second, the wisdom of direct realization. Among these, the former is indirect, while the latter is direct. Regarding the Venerable Śāriputra, he was foremost in the wisdom of direct realization. This is because his faculty of wisdom was extremely sharp and clear, and his understanding of the Dharma was extremely profound and subtle. Consequently, whenever he heard a single verse or a single phrase of the Dharma, he could immediately understand its underlying meaning and penetrate its essence. It is like a person who, upon seeing a precious jewel, immediately knows its value and can distinguish its true worth from that of a common stone. Therefore, he was called "foremost in wisdom. Regarding the term "foremost": it means that among all those who possess such wisdom, he was the most superior. As for the Venerable Ānanda, foremost in learning: "Learning" refers to the nature of retention (*dhāraṇī*). Because he could receive, hold, and never forget the teachings he had heard, he was called "learning. Furthermore, there are two types of learning: first, the learning of the words; second, the learning of the meaning. Among these, the former is the literal text, while the latter is the underlying principle. Moreover, within the learning of the words, there are again two types: first, the learning of the extensive scriptures; second, the learning of the concise summaries. Among these, the former is voluminous, while the latter is brief. Furthermore, within the learning of the meaning, there are again two types: first, the learning of the conventional truth; second, the learning of the ultimate truth. Among these, the former is provisional, while the latter is real. Regarding the Venerable Ānanda, he was foremost in the learning of the conventional truth. This is because his faculty of memory was extremely sharp and clear, and his capacity for retention was extremely vast and great. Consequently, whenever he heard the Buddha preach the Dharma, he could immediately receive and retain it all without omission. It is like a vessel that, when filled with water, can hold it all without leaking. Therefore, he was called "foremost in learning. Regarding the term "foremost": it means that among all those who possess such learning, he was the most superior. As for the Venerable Upāli, foremost in the Vinaya: "Vinaya" refers to the nature of discipline (*vinaya*). Because he could thoroughly understand the precepts and regulations, and because he could skillfully apply them to resolve disputes, he was called "Vinaya. Furthermore, there are two types of Vinaya: first, the Vinaya of the prohibitions; second, the Vinaya of the applications. Among these, the former concerns the rules of conduct, while the latter concerns the methods of adjudication. Moreover, within the Vinaya of the prohibitions, there are again two types: first, the heavy offenses; second, the light offenses. Among these, the former are grave, while the latter are minor. Furthermore, within the Vinaya of the applications, there are again two types: first, the Vinaya of the Sangha; second, the Vinaya of the individual. Among these, the former concerns the community, while the latter concerns the person. Regarding the Venerable Upāli, he was foremost in the Vinaya of the Sangha. This is because his understanding of the disciplinary rules was extremely thorough and precise, and his skill in applying them was extremely adept and unhindered. Consequently, whenever there were disputes or violations within the Sangha, he could always provide a definitive resolution. It is like a skilled judge who, when faced with a legal case, can immediately determine the verdict without error. Therefore, he was called "foremost in the Vinaya. Regarding the term "foremost": it means that among all those who possess such mastery of the Vinaya, he was the most superior. As for the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, foremost in ascetic practices (*dhūta-guṇa*): "Ascetic practices" refers to the nature of austerity (*saṃlekha*). Because he could sever worldly attachments and cultivate a life of purity, he was called "ascetic practices. Furthermore, there are twelve types of ascetic practices: first, wearing robes made of discarded rags (*pāṃsukūla*); second, wearing three robes (*traicīvarika*); third, begging for food (*piṇḍapātika*); fourth, eating only one meal a day (*ekāsanika*); fifth, refusing food after the proper time (*khalupaścādbhaktika*); sixth, living in the forest (*āraṇyaka*); seventh, living under a tree (*vṛkṣamūlika*); eighth, living in an open space (*ābhyavakāśika*); ninth, living in a charnel ground (*śmāśānika*); tenth, sitting while sleeping (*naiṣadyika*); eleventh, sitting in any posture (*yathāsaṃstarika*); twelfth, wearing clothes made of felt (*nāmatika*). Among these, the first five are related to food and clothing, while the latter seven are related to dwelling and sitting. Moreover, within the first five, there are again two types: first, the practice of contentment; second, the practice of frugality. Among these, the former is satisfied with what is obtained, while the latter reduces what is used. Furthermore, within the latter seven, there are again two types: first, the practice of seclusion; second, the practice of vigilance. Among these, the former avoids the world, while the latter guards the mind. Regarding the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, he was foremost in the practice of seclusion. This is because his detachment from the world was extremely firm and resolute, and his dedication to solitude was extremely profound and steadfast. Consequently, whenever he lived in a mountain or a forest, wild beasts would not harm him, and spirits would protect him. It is like a lotus flower growing in the mud, which remains untainted by the filth. Therefore, he was called "foremost in ascetic practices. Regarding the term "foremost": it means that among all those who practice austerities, he was the most superior. As for the Venerable Rāhula, foremost in the training of disciples (*śiṣya-vinaya*): "Training of disciples" refers to the nature of instruction and guidance. Because he could teach and transform sentient beings according to their capacities, he was called "training of disciples. Furthermore, there are two types

The supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are: first, the power of the divine ear; second, the power of knowing others' minds; third, the power of recollecting past lives; fourth, the power of the divine eye; fifth, the power of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*); and sixth, the power of the knowledge of the non-arising of outflows (*anutpādajñāna*).

The first five are possessed by outsiders, ordinary worldlings, and spirits alike; the sixth belongs only to noble ones (*ārya*). As for what is called "the foremost," it refers to such acts as subduing dragons or burning the Hall of the True Dharma (*Saddharmasabhā*).
Therefore, it is called "the foremost. Regarding the Venerable Kāśyapa, who received the Buddha’s mind-seal and was foremost in the practice of *dhūta*, Lord Wang Jing asked Chan Master Fohuiquan:

【Explanation】 The Dharma-gate of the Pure Land universally encompasses the three faculties (of faith, understanding, and practice). It is absolute, perfectly interfused, inconceivable, and completely inclusive.
This dharma-gate transcends all phenomena; it is profoundly deep and difficult to believe (having never been spoken of before). Therefore, it is specifically addressed to those of great wisdom.
Without the foremost wisdom, one cannot immediately attain freedom from doubt (it can be seen that both correct wisdom and ordinary folly are both inconceivable).

[Commentary] Regarding the "universal inclusion of the three faculties": if categorized according to the four teachings, the *Zang* (Āgama) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings include those of dull capacity but not those of sharp capacity, and they include the Small Vehicle but not the Great Vehicle.
The *Bie* (Distinct) and *Yuan* (Perfect) teachings include the Great Vehicle but not the Small Vehicle.

Only this single gate universally includes the three faculties, fully encompassing both the sharp and the dull. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Those of the highest-highest faculty cannot transcend it..."
Even those of the lowest capacity can reach this realm. Regarding that which is "independently perfect and inconceivable," Cheshu said:
"One must know that a single phrase of 'Amitābha Buddha' fully embodies the fourfold core principles:
first, taking 'mind-only' as the principle; second, taking 'Buddha-only' as the principle; third, taking 'independent perfection' as the principle; and fourth..."
It takes the transcendence of emotion and departure from views as its fundamental tenet. That "the Buddha is entirely the mind" is the tenet of Mind-Only;

that "the mind is entirely the Buddha" is the tenet of Buddha-Only. As for being "unconditioned by dependence," it means that the nature of the mind vertically exhausts all time and horizontally pervades all space, such that there is nothing external to it.

The Buddha, too, is vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive, with nothing external to him; each [of these] is likewise without exteriority, which constitutes being "beyond all relativity. As for "perfect interfusion":
the nature of the mind pervades all places, yet this does not hinder the Buddha-nature from also pervading, nor does it hinder the nature of all phenomena from pervading.

The Buddha-nature pervades all places, yet this does not hinder the nature of the mind from also pervading, nor does it hinder the nature of all phenomena from pervading. Thus, each and every one is without obstruction.

They are unimpeded; each is without destruction or confusion. This is what is meant by "perfect interfusion" (*yuánróng*). Now, combining this with "absolute transcendence" (*juédài*) as perfect interfusion constitutes a single school.
Absolute transcendence is itself perfect interfusion, and perfect interfusion is itself absolute transcendence; this is the school of absolute transcendence and perfect interfusion.
For those who have transcended emotion and left behind views, it is simply that, regarding the absolute transcendence of mind and Buddha, they have already surpassed ordinary emotions and—
It transcends noble views. If one considers the perfect fusion of mind and Buddha, it completely encompasses the four propositions and harmonizes the hundred negations;

it is especially beyond the reach of ordinary sentiment or noble views, being the school that transcends emotion and leaves behind views. This summarizes the essential principle of these four propositions.
This is the orthodox principle of the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha. Therefore, it is called inconceivable.
Regarding the phrase "perfectly encompassing and perfectly transcending all dharma-gates": there are immeasurable dharma-gates, yet they do not exceed four gates, namely, the gate of existence.
The Gate of Emptiness; the Gate of Both Being and Emptiness; the Gate of Neither Being nor Emptiness. Now, the school of the Buddha alone perfectly encompasses the Gate of Being;
the school of Mind-Only perfectly encompasses the Gate of Emptiness; the school of Perfect Interfusion perfectly encompasses the Gate of Both Being and Emptiness;
and the school of Absolute Transcendence perfectly encompasses the Gate of Neither Being nor Emptiness. This is what is meant by "perfectly encompassing all."

All dharma-gates. Furthermore, by means of the school of Mind-Only, it perfectly transcends the gate of existence; by means of the school of the Buddha alone, it perfectly transcends the gate of emptiness;

by means of the school of absolute transcendence, it perfectly transcends the gate of both existence and emptiness; by means of the school of perfect fusion, it perfectly transcends the gate of neither existence nor emptiness.
This is what is meant by "perfectly transcending all dharma-gates. Moreover, when correctly and perfectly gathered, it is immediately perfect.

Transcendence. When one transcends through perfect completeness, one is immediately gathered within that completeness; this simultaneous non-obstruction of perfect transcendence and perfect gathering is contained within this single phrase, "Amitābha Buddha.
Therefore, it is said to be profoundly deep and difficult to believe; it is spoken specifically for those possessed of great wisdom.
Regarding the two who are inconceivable—the one of perfect wisdom and the one of common ignorance: the one of perfect wisdom is inconceivable because their realization is ultimate;
the one of common ignorance is inconceivable because they simply do not employ thought. Anyone other than these two cannot avoid conceptualization.
This concludes the initial clarification of the intent behind the summons.

△ Second, the correct explanation of the sutra text is divided into five parts: first, the explanation of the western direction; second, the explanation of the dependent retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*); third, the explanation of the primary retribution (*mūla-vipāka*);

fourth, the re-explanation of the two types of existence; fifth, the explanation of the current preaching of the Dharma. The first part [the explanation of the western direction] is further divided into two: first, the direct explanation.
Second, dispelling doubts. △ Now, the first [section].
【Commentary】 "The West" refers to the direction directly westward, indicating the present location. "Ten million billion" means that ten million is called a *koṭi* (億);
here, it refers to ten million accumulated to the point of being a billion (*koṭi*). "Buddha-field" refers to the trichiliocosm, which collectively constitutes—
All are transformed by a single Buddha. To speak of this land specifically:

a single Mount Sumeru, with one continent each to the east, west, south, and north, all illuminated by the same sun and moon and surrounded by a single Iron Ring Mountain (Cakravāḍa), is called a single "four-continent world" (cāturdvīpaka).
One thousand sets of four continents are called a small chiliocosm; one thousand small chiliocosms are called a medium chiliocosm;
and one thousand medium chiliocosms are called a great trichiliocosm. To the west, beyond a hundred trillion such buddha-fields, lies this world of Ultimate Bliss.

[Commentary] "Horizontal" means intersecting with the straight west. "Intersecting" (互) means to pervade. That is to say, it extends horizontally to the straight west, indicating that it is level with this world-system.
"The place where he manifests" refers to the land where Amitābha Buddha manifests his birth; it is the Land of Common Residence (*sahā-loka-dhātu*).
Regarding the one continent each in the east, west, south, and north: to the east of Mount Sumeru is a continent named Pūrvavideha.

This is called *Videha* (Victorious Body), because the bodies [of its inhabitants] are exceptionally superior. To the south of the mountain is named Jambudvīpa; this is translated as "Victorious Gold.
To the west of the mountain is named Aparagoyānī; this is translated as "Cattle-Trade," because cattle serve as their currency. To the north of the mountain is named Uttarakuru;
this is translated as "Superior Place," because it is superior to the other three continents. That which is surrounded by a single Iron Ring Mountain (*Cakravāḍa*) refers to these four...
Beyond the continents lies a great ocean. Beyond the ocean lies a mountain named Cakravāḍa (Small Iron Ring Mountain). This mountain is made entirely of iron and encircles these four continents.
That which is called "one four-continent world" is so named because the Cakravāḍa Mountains encircle the Great Bitter Salt Ocean.
Within the four continents of the world, there are seven golden mountains that encircle the fragrant ocean. In the midst of these seas stands Mount Sumeru;
on its slopes dwell the Four Heavenly Kings, and at its summit is the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Above these are the Yāma Heaven and the Tuṣita Heaven.
The Nirmāṇarati Heaven and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven constitute the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). Above these, one enters the three heavens of the First Dhyāna of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*);
this is called a single four-continent world system (*cāturdvīpaka*).

A thousand such four-continent world systems is called a small thousandfold world system (*sāhasracūdika lokadhātu*), which consists of one thousand first-dhyāna heavens covered above by the second-dhyāna heavens; this is termed a small thousandfold world system.
A thousand "small thousands" constitutes one thousand second dhyāna heavens, which is covered above by a third dhyāna heaven; this is called a medium chiliocosm.
A thousand "medium thousands" constitutes one thousand third dhyāna heavens, which is covered above by a fourth dhyāna heaven and a single heaven of the four formless realms (ārūpyadhātu);
this is called a great chiliocosm. It contains ten billion sets of four continents. Beyond this—
Thus, one hundred trillion *koṭis* of Buddha-lands to the west is precisely the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*). This concludes the formal explanation.
△ Second, Dispelling Doubts. [Commentary] Question:
For what reason is the Land of Ultimate Bliss located in the west? Answer: This is not a good question. Even if the Land of Ultimate Bliss were in the east, it would still be the same.

You have further asked why it is located in the east. Is this not mere frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*)? (A wondrous answer indeed; for those who answer in such a way only add to frivolous proliferation.
Moreover, when viewed from eleven trillion buddha-fields, it is still in the east. Why should this be a cause for doubt?
[Commentary] The explanation of the Western Quarter is concluded.

△ Second, the explanation of the dependent retribution (niśraya-vipāka) also has three parts: first, the formal explanation of the world; second, the specific clarification of the pure and the defiled;
third, the indication of the realm of cohabitation (sahā-lokadhātu). △ Now, the first part.
[Commentary] There is a world named Sukhāvatī. This introduces the name of the land as the "recompense-environment" (*niṣyanda-bhājana-loka*).

It is called a "world" (*loka-dhātu*) because it is defined vertically by the three periods of time to distinguish its temporal duration, and horizontally by the ten directions to determine its spatial boundaries. Thus, it is the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
In Sanskrit, it is called *Sukhāvatī*. It is also translated as "Peaceful Nurturing" (*Ān-yǎng*), "Peaceful Bliss" (*Ān-lè*), "Pure Tranquility" (*Qīng-tài*), and so forth;
it refers to that which is eternally free from all suffering and represents the foremost state of security. This shall be explained in detail below.

[Commentary]: Regarding "world" (*loka-dhātu*): "world" (*loka*) refers to the three periods of time; "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to the ten directions. Because these intersect both horizontally and vertically, it is called a "world.
This will be explained extensively below, as clarified in the subsequent section on suffering and pleasure. The formal explanation of "world" is now complete.
△ Second, a specific explanation of the pure and the defiled.

[Commentary]: There are four kinds of Buddha-lands, each divided into the pure and the defiled (all errors corrected). In the Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages, that where the five turbidities are heavy is the defiled.
The five turbidities (pañca-kaṣāya) are light [in this land], which is pure (the Western Land is a "pure co-residence" because ordinary beings are treated as sages).

[Commentary]: This is the aspect of purity and defilement within this land of co-residence. Regarding the five turbidities: the nature of water is originally clear, yet it becomes turbid due to the dust of afflictions (kleśa).

These afflictions have no substantial body; they possess characteristics only by depending upon the water of nature. First is the turbidity of the eon (kalpa-kaṣāya), which consists of the other four turbidities.

1. The *utsada-kalpa* (age of increase) has intensification as its essence and unceasing fervor as its characteristic. 2. The *kleśa-kaṣāya* (impurity of afflictions) has the five dull fetters (*mūla-anuśaya*) as its essence and the tormenting of mental agitation as its characteristic.
3. The *sattva-kaṣāya* (impurity of sentient beings) has the conjunction of the three conditions as its essence and the non-ceasing of saṃsāra as its characteristic.

4. The *dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya* (impurity of views) has the five sharp fetters (*tīkṣṇa-anuśaya*) as its essence and erroneous knowledge and distorted understanding as its characteristic. 5. The *āyuḥ-kaṣāya* (impurity of lifespan)... [text truncated]

Turbidity (*kaṣāya*) has the triad of lifespan, warmth, and consciousness as its substance. Its characteristic is the shortening of the years and the reduction of the life span. Regarding the distinction between light and heavy, pure and defiled:

if the turbidity of the three miserable realms is heavy, the land is defiled; if the turbidity of the human realm is light, the land is pure. Furthermore, within the human realm, there is both purity and defilement.

The heavens of the Path of Gods are pure; the heavens of desire are defiled. The heavens of dhyāna are pure; the Sahā world as a whole is entirely defiled because it is characterized by suffering, emptiness, and impermanence.
The Land of Ultimate Bliss as a whole is pure because ordinary beings therein are equal to the sages.
[Commentary]: The Land of Skillful Means with Remainder is defiled for those who enter through the analysis of emptiness and the clumsy vehicle;

it is pure for those who enter through the realization of essential emptiness and the skillful vehicle (the Western Land is a pure land of skillful means because it consists of those of the Small Vehicle who have turned their minds [toward the Great Vehicle]).

[Commentary]: This refers to the characteristics of the "Pure-Defiled" stage of the Expedient Means (*upāya*). Nine types of people are born in the Land of Expedient Means: namely, those of the *Hīnayāna* (the Two Vehicles) within the *Tripiṭaka*, those of the Three Vehicles within the *Pāramitā* [Vehicle], the Three Sages of the Distinct Teaching, and the Ten Faiths of the Perfect Teaching.
All of these have already severed the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), yet they have not yet shattered ignorance (*avidyā*);

they merely reside temporarily in the Land of Expedient Means. If they belong to the *Hīnayāna* of the *Tripiṭaka*, they receive the contemplation of analytical emptiness (*vibhaṅga-śūnyatā-dhyāna*), sever views and thoughts, and transcend the birth-and-death of limited segments (*paricchinna-bhava*).
As for those who enter by way of the ocean [of birth and death]: what they perceive is defiled, because their attachment to dharmas is heavy and their contemplative wisdom is crude.

If, however, one belongs to the Three Vehicles and, receiving the practice of the contemplation of the emptiness of essence, cuts off the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*) and crosses the ocean of birth and death with its limited segments to enter [the path], what they perceive is pure, because their attachment to dharmas is light and their contemplative wisdom is skillful.
Furthermore, the "defilement" of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-yāna*) refers to not yet attaining [ultimate realization].

Because it is the Middle Way, the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) is pure; because it thoroughly realizes the Middle Way. Furthermore, the Separate Teaching is defiled because it does not realize that [phenomena] are immediately the Middle.

Only in the Ten Faiths of the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao) is what is seen pure, for ignorance has already been subdued. Regarding "analytical emptiness" (xi-kong) and "essential emptiness" (ti-kong):
by analyzing this body into the four great elements and the five aggregates, one finds that a self or anything belonging to a self cannot be obtained; therefore, it is so called.

Analytical emptiness (*vibhāga-śūnyatā*). As for essential emptiness (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), it is not only that the self is empty; phenomena (*dharma*) are likewise like illusions, being empty in their very essence. Therefore, it is called "essential emptiness.
Sukhāvatī is a pure land of skillful means (*upāya-viśuddha*), because it is for those of the Hīnayāna who have turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna].

[Commentary]: The Land of True Reward and Non-obstruction is defiled for those who enter through the sequential threefold contemplation, but pure for those who enter through the single-mind threefold contemplation (the Western Land is the pure land of true reward because that which is realized is perfect and sudden).

[Commentary] The Real Reward Land (*sambhoga-kāya*) is the dwelling place of Bodhisattvas of the forty-one stages of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), including those of the distinct ten stages (*bie shidi*) as well as the two types of awakening—Equal Enlightenment (*dengjue*) and Wondrous Enlightenment (*miaojue*).

As for the "Successive Three Contemplations" (*cidi san guan*), these are cultivated according to the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*); specifically, it is said that during the ten stages of faith (*shixin*), one cultivates the analysis of emptiness (*xikong*).

I have humbly observed that one cultivates the emptiness of essence (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) during the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) to sever the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), thereby entering the stage of skillful means (*upāya*).

During the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*), one cultivates the contemplation of the provisional (*parikalpita*) to shatter the "dust-sand" [afflictions].
