During the Ten Transferences (*daśa-pratipatti*), one cultivates the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) to subdue ignorance (*avidyā*). At the First Ground (*prathamā-bhūmi*), one shatters ignorance and realizes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
One has merely begun to enter the stage of true retribution; because wisdom is not yet perfectly integrated (*yuanrong*), the characteristics of the land perceived therein appear defiled.

The practice of the "single mind and three contemplations" is that cultivated by Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). This means contemplating that the single thought-moment is ultimately ungraspable—this is called emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

That subject and object remain distinct and manifest—this is called the provisional (*upādāya-prajñapti*). Although subject and object remain distinct and manifest, their nature is eternally empty of itself.
Emptiness and the provisional are non-dual; this is called the "Middle. It is three yet one, and one yet three; this is termed the "Threefold Contemplation of the One Mind.
When this contemplation is perfected, one is able to completely sever the three delusions and completely realize the three virtues.

Thus, at the very first stage of the "Abiding in the Resolve," one immediately shatters ignorance, realizes the three virtues, and enters the stage of True Reward. Because the wisdom of contemplation is perfectly interfused, that which is perceived...
The nature of the land is purity. Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) is the pure land of true retribution (*sambhogakāya*), because that which is realized there is perfect and sudden.

[Commentary: The Land of Eternal Quiescent Light (*nitya-prabhāsvara-dharmadhātu-kṣetra*): for those who have partially realized it, it is defiled; for those who have fully and ultimately realized it, it is pure (the Western Land is the purity of quiescent light, because its enjoyment is identical to that of the Buddha).

[Commentary] This land is the realm where the Tathāgata dwells. If one considers the distinct stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*), although it is termed "ultimate" in the fundamental teaching, it merely involves the severance of twelve grades of ignorance;

thus, it remains a stage of partial realization (*pradeśa-prativedha*). Therefore, it is said that those at the stage of partial realization are still defiled, as their ignorance is not yet exhausted.
Ultimate, complete realization, however, is Perfect Sublime Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), wherein all [ignorance] is exhausted.

The "Source of Illumination" (*myōgen*) is the ultimate, pure, and perfect Great Enlightenment. The Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Gokuraku*) is the Pure Land of Quiescent Light (*jakukōjō*), because its enjoyment (*ujyō*) is identical to that of the Buddha.
Thus concludes the separate explanation of the pure and the defiled.
△ Third, the three fingers point to the Land of Common Residence.
[Commentary] What is now called the World of Ultimate Bliss specifically refers to the Pure Land of Common Residence;

it is also that which horizontally encompasses the aforementioned three types of pure lands (because this is the realm of common residence within the sutra, and because the superior roots of goodness are gathered therein).
[Commentary]: Regarding the horizontal possession of the three aforementioned Pure Lands: this means that all superior virtuous persons assemble in one place.

When the Buddha is in the Shared Residence (sahā-loka), it is the Land of Tranquil Light (prabhāsvara-kṣetra); when a Bodhisattva is in the Shared Residence, it is the Land of True Reward (vipāka-bhūmi-kṣetra);

and when a Śrāvaka is in the Shared Residence, it is the Land of Expedient Means (upāya-kṣetra). Furthermore, the Shared Residence horizontally possesses the three aforementioned lands; the Land of Expedient Means horizontally possesses the two aforementioned lands.

The *shibō* (true recompense) realm horizontally possesses the first of the upper [three] lands; the *jakukō* (tranquil light) realm horizontally possesses the last three; the *shibō* realm horizontally possesses the last two;

and the *hōben* (expedient means) realm horizontally possesses the last one. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "In the pure realm of the shared dwelling (*tōkyū*), the ultimate and conventional truths are perfectly interfused (*en'yū*), beyond measure.
This concludes the second explanation of the *e-hō* (environmental retribution). The small characters are the marginal notes of Great Master Jiecheng.

This treatise discusses cultivated virtues (*bhāvanā-guṇa*), not inherent virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*). As for inherent virtues, every single atom naturally possesses the four kinds of pure and impure Buddha-lands. Now, this discussion is based on the three factors of faith, aspiration, and practice; for the name of Amitābha is inconceivable.

It enables ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) to experience a co-residence (*sahā-vāsa*) in Ultimate Bliss that is supremely pure. This is something not found in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions; that Ultimate Bliss is uniquely possessed by this Sahā-world alone. This is precisely the essential principle of the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss (the same applies to all subsequent explanations of its meaning).

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "all atoms are fully endowed with Buddha-lands": all phenomena are mind-only, and atoms are likewise mind-only. Because the mind is pure, the land is pure; because the mind is defiled, the land is defiled. This is the spontaneous principle; therefore, it is said that they are "naturally and inherently endowed."
Although the Pure Land is said to be cultivated through merit, it is also inherently possessed by nature; it does not exist outside of nature.

△ Third, the explanation of the primary retribution and the teaching lord has three parts: first, clarifying the single and triple bodies; second, clarifying the transcendence of emotion and departure from views;
third, pointing out the transformation body. △ Now, the first part.
[Commentary]: "There is a Buddha named Amitābha" introduces the name of the primary teacher as the subject of the exposition. The translation is provided below with a detailed explanation.

A Buddha possesses three bodies (*trikāya*), each of which may be considered either singular or plural. The *dharmakāya* (Dharma-body) is singular, referring to the principle of reality (*tathatā*) realized.

The *sambhogakāya* (Enjoyment-body) is singular, referring to the merit and wisdom that constitute the capacity for realization. The *nirmāṇakāya* (Transformation-body) is singular, referring to the manifested marks, signs, and physical forms. Dharma...

Regarding the "repetition of the body" (*kāya-punarukta*): the Body of Essential Nature (*svabhāva-kāya*) is pure by nature and the sublime, ultimate Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*) free from defilement. Regarding the "repetition of the enjoyment body" (*saṃbhoga-kāya-punarukta*):

it consists of the enjoyment body for one's own benefit (*svasaṃbhoga-kāya*) and the enjoyment body for the benefit of others (*parasaṃbhoga-kāya*). Regarding the "repetition of the transformation body" (*nirmāṇa-kāya-punarukta*):

it consists of the transformation body that manifests birth (*janma-nirmāṇa-kāya*), the transformation body that appears as another being (*parātman-nirmāṇa-kāya*), the transformation body of the Buddha-realm (*buddha-dhātu-nirmāṇa-kāya*), and the transformation body that conforms to various types of beings (*yathā-jāti-nirmāṇa-kāya*).

[Commentary] Within the context of the three bodies taken individually: that which is called "the principle of reality realized" is the principle of suchness (*tathatā*), the self-nature pure *dharmakāya*, and the essence of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
It is the virtue of the *dharmakāya* within the secret treasury of the three virtues.
That which is the "merit and wisdom by which realization is attained" is the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*), the *saṃbhogakāya* of self-enjoyment, and the true mark.
This is the primary application [of the three virtues]. Among the three virtues, it consists of the two virtues of *prajñā* (wisdom) and *vimukti* (liberation).

"Merit" (*guṇa*) refers to the virtue of liberation; "wisdom" (*jñāna*) is *prajñā*. It is also termed the twofold adornment of merit and wisdom. As for the physical marks, secondary characteristics, and forms that are manifested:
This refers to the form and appearance of the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body) up to the form and appearance of the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) according to the various types of beings.

Regarding the "three bodies," the word "furthermore" (*fù*) means "repeatedly. As for "inherently pure" (*svabhāva-viśuddha*), this is the *dharmakāya* of intrinsic virtue; it is the very principle of reality (*tathatā*) realized above.
Because its nature is fundamentally pure from the beginning, it is called the "inherently pure *dharmakāya*. This is the original state of sentient beings.

The source is the inherently true Buddha-nature. This body encompasses both cause and effect. That which is "stainless and supremely wondrous" is the Dharma-body of cultivated virtue (*bhāvanā-śīla*).
"Stainless" means being free from the defilements of the five abodes; it is the ultimate emptiness of severed virtue (*prahāṇa-śīla*).

"Supremely wondrous" means reaching the pinnacle of the wondrousness of the three wisdoms; it is the ultimate fulfillment of the wisdom-virtue (*jñāna-śīla*). When the efforts of cultivated virtue are completed, the inherent virtue (*prakṛti-śīla*) is perfectly manifested.
Therefore, it is said that this is the "Dharmakāya of the Ultimate Sublime Freedom from Defilement. This body belongs exclusively to the fruit.

As for the self-enjoyment [body], it is the ultimate, true fruit of the two virtues of wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*) of Amitābha. Regarding the virtue of wisdom, it is the perfection of bodhi, returning to non-attainment.

Regarding the virtue of abandonment, it is the complete exhaustion of the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra*), wherein the two types of death are forever extinguished. As for the other-enjoyment [body], it is the [fruit] of the stages...

Regarding the superior Bodhisattvas: according to the measure of their own minds, they perceive the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) within the atoms of the lands. As for the multiplication of transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*):

"manifesting birth" refers to the manifestation of the eight phases [of a Buddha's life]; "responsive manifestation" refers to appearing in accordance with sentient beings, like the moon reflected in water. This is the Buddha-realm.

This refers to manifesting the body of the Buddha-realm according to the various types of beings; that is, manifesting in accordance with the nine realms. This concludes the section on the single and multiple three bodies.
△ Second, clarifying the transcendence of emotion and the departure from views.

[Commentary]: Although one may distinguish between the single and the triple bodies, in reality they are neither one nor three; yet they are three and one. They are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither simultaneous nor separate.
Transcending all faults and severing all contradictions, they are inconceivable (this refers to the nature-endowment).
[Commentary]: This section is intended to prevent people from failing to grasp the meaning and thereby giving rise to dualistic views regarding the "three" and "one. Thus, it refutes such notions.

That is to say, although the single and multiple aspects of the three bodies are explained, these are all discussed in accordance with conventional sentiment; as for the ultimate reality, [it is beyond such distinctions].
Two do not form a pair, nor does one remain solitary; there is no conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) regarding three or one.

Fearing that people might again cling to "neither one nor three," it is further said that it is "both three and one. If the conditions for the four *siddhāntas* are encountered, there is no hindrance to speaking of three or speaking of one;
this is the inherent meaning of opening and closing. It is neither vertical nor horizontal, neither simultaneous nor distinct.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "What is called the 'Secret Treasury'? It is like the character *i*. If its three dots are aligned horizontally, they do not form the character *i*;
if they are vertical, they do not form the character *i*; and if they are separate, they also do not form the character *i*.
Only when they are like the three eyes on the face of Maheśvara does it become the character *i*. The Buddha is also like this; so too is the dharma of liberation."
Nirvāṇa is not [the Tathāgata’s body]. The body of the Tathāgata is also not nirvāṇa. Mahāprajñā is also not nirvāṇa.
These three dharmas being distinct from one another is also not nirvāṇa. I now abide in these three dharmas; for the sake of sentient beings, this is called "entering nirvāṇa.
It is like the world's letter *i*. Zhan’an’s commentary states: "The letter *i* in the West has a new..."
The old *i* (the ancient form of the letter *i*). This old *i* is arranged vertically and horizontally like blazing fire or scattered droplets of water;

each part is discontinuous, serving as a metaphor for the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*) of other teachings. This new *i* has its fine strokes connected, being neither vertical nor horizontal, serving as a metaphor for the inconceivable Three Virtues of the Perfect Teaching (*vairocanayāna*).
That this [new form] is neither vertical nor horizontal, yet not separate, is precisely what adopts the perspective of the Perfect Teaching.
This is the meaning. To speak of the three bodies is not a verticality like water droplets; to speak of the one is not a horizontality like blazing fires.
To speak of the one is not to conflate them; to speak of the three is not to separate them. It transcends the faults of the four propositions and cuts off the errors of the hundred statements.
Regarding "inconceivable": "si" (思) refers to mental thought, and "yi" (議) refers to verbal deliberation; it cannot be [grasped by] these.
One cannot conceive of it as definitely one; one cannot conceive of it as definitely three; one cannot conceive of it as definitely neither three nor one;
and one cannot conceive of it as definitely both three and one. These constitute the four fundamental propositions.

Each proposition contains its own set of four propositions, resulting in sixteen propositions (four times four). When categorized according to the three periods of time, there are forty-eight propositions.
Furthermore, when the already arisen and the not yet arisen are combined, there are ninety-six phrases; adding the four fundamental phrases, they total one hundred.

Because the Buddha-body is fundamentally free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of names and words, and free from the characteristics of mental objects, it is called "inconceivable."
△ Third, pointing out the transformation body that manifests birth.

[Commentary: The present mention of Amitābha Buddha specifically refers to the transformation body manifesting birth within the Land of Common Residence (for this treatise emphasizes cultivated merit, as it is perceived within this Land of Common Residence).
Furthermore, this very body is simultaneously the reward body and the dharma body (because the Buddha-body appears according to the four lands in their horizontal arrangement).
[Commentary] Question: Regarding the present mention of Amitābha Buddha, among the single, dual, and triple bodies (trikāya), to which body does he belong? Answer:

The present mention of Amitābha Buddha specifically points to the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya). This is because there might be doubt that it is neither the dharma-body nor the reward-body (saṃbhogakāya).
Therefore, it is further said that "reverting and returning" refers to the immediate manifestation of the Dharma-body. The three bodies are not separate from one another;

they are likened to the substance of a pearl, its luster, and its reflection, which do not exist apart from each other. Yet, although they are inseparable, they do not hinder each from being perceived according to the capacities of sentient beings.

This concludes the section on the Transformation Body (Nirmāṇakāya) within the Three Bodies of Instruction. This also concludes the major section explaining the Primary Retribution Body (Sambhogakāya).
△ A fourfold explanation of the two kinds of existence.

[Commentary] Furthermore, when both the world and the Buddha speak of "existence," they do so by way of four meanings (the four *siddhāntas*). To specifically indicate the actual realm and cause it to be sought with joy (*loka-siddhānta*);
to provide truthful instruction and cause one to focus single-mindedly (*puruṣa-siddhānta*); to distinguish it from that which is not a *gandharva-nagara* (mirage city) or a solar reflection...

It is not a provisional manifestation or a biased display (it is not Māra). It is not a shadow-like reflection or a false appearance (it is not the mundane). It is not the preservation of the "true" in a partial or exclusive manner (it is not heterodox).

Because it destroys Māra, heterodoxy, the provisional, and the Lesser Vehicle, it is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the therapeutic standpoint). [Note: "Not provisional" refutes the errors in the *Huayan he lun*; "not heterodox" refutes the habitual delusions accumulated in the末代 (final age). These two analytical distinctions are of great significance.
Because it perfectly manifests the inherent nature and causes one to realize it deeply, it is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the standpoint of ultimate truth).
[Commentary] The "City of Gandharvas" (Gandharvanagara) refers to a city manifested by the illusory power of gandharvas;

these are frequently found in vast wildernesses and deep mountains, as well as in phenomena such as mirages and sea-spirits' cities, all of which are manifestations of demonic vapors. "Mirage" (marīci) refers to the warm vapors rising from level ground during springtime that appear to be water from afar but vanish upon closer inspection.
These are not instances of expedient manifestations or indirect teachings. —From Master Li’s *Huayan Jing Tanxuan Ji*.
This is the *Yanhe lun* (Treatise on the Harmonization of the Profound). It states that the Western [Pure Land] is a provisional manifestation (*upāya*) shown for those of inferior faculties;
it is not the case that the shadow of the dharma-objects perceived by the sixth consciousness—which is empty and illusory—is the "Mind-Only Pure Land" or the "Self-Nature Amitābha.

This [treatise] refutes sentient beings of the末代 (final age) who take the shadows of dharma-objects perceived by the sixth consciousness to be the Mind-Only Pure Land and the Self-Nature Amitābha, asserting that the West exists outside the mind. To preserve the truth, this is the *Zang* (Treasury/Concealed).
The "Guaranteed True" refers to the *nirvāṇa* of the *parikalpita-nirvāṇa* (the provisional city). The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "I now guarantee this matter for you;
it shall never be in vain. "Exclusive" (*piān*) refers to the exclusive truth of the Tripitaka teachings; "merely" (*dàn*) refers to the mere-middle of the Separate Teaching (*biéjiào*).
This refers to the two kinds of existence in the Western Land; these are the wondrous existence of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), which is neither partial nor provisional.

Because it destroys the demonic, the heterodox, and the expedient teachings of the Lesser Vehicle, it serves as a benefit for the destruction of evil. To fully manifest the inherent nature and enable deep realization:

the two types of retribution—the environment and the inhabitants—of the West are all things inherently possessed within my own mind. If one does not attain rebirth there, one cannot obtain their reception.
Function. At the time of rebirth, that which is inherently possessed is fully manifested; therefore, it is called "the benefit of entering into principle.
△ Fifth, the explanation of preaching the Dharma in the present.

[Commentary] The phrase "the one currently preaching the Dharma" distinguishes [this Buddha] from the aforementioned two types of existence—the environment and its inhabitants—which are either past and already extinguished or future and not yet formed (in contrast to this land, Śākyamuni will not long remain, and Maitreya has not yet been born;
thus, there is no present Buddha to rely upon). One should, therefore, rightly resolve to be reborn there to personally behold him and hear the Dharma, so as to swiftly attain perfect enlightenment.
[Commentary]: In this land, Śākyamuni has already passed away and Maitreya has not yet been born; in that land, Amitābha currently dwells and preaches the Dharma.

Therefore, one should resolve to attain birth there. This concludes the explanation of the current preaching [of the Dharma]. This concludes the main section of the formal commentary on the scriptural text.
△ Third, the conclusion of the meaning of the introduction.
[Commentary: Furthermore, "The two existences are present" constitutes the introduction for encouraging faith. "The world is named Sukhāvatī" constitutes the introduction for encouraging aspiration.

"The Buddha’s name is Amitābha. This is the preface to the wondrous practice of encouraging the holding of the Name. Furthermore, "Amitā" (Amitābha) prefaces the Buddha; "Saying the Dharma" (the act of reciting) prefaces the Dharma;
"the present ocean-like assembly" prefaces the Sangha. That the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha share the same true reality (dharmatā) prefaces the essence.

From this [referring to the Three Jewels as one essence], one gives rise to faith, vows, and practice—this prefaces the school. Once faith, vows, and practice are perfected, one will certainly attain rebirth, see the Buddha, and hear the Dharma.
The Prologue. Taking only the single Buddha-realm as the object of focus (this is the true guide) and not mixing it with other matters constitutes the characteristics of the introductory teaching.
The words are concise, yet the meaning is comprehensive. The initial Prologue section is concluded.
[Commentary] To "conclude by setting forth the meaning of the introduction" means to conclude by setting forth the significance of the *utthāna* (the originative cause).

Now, an *utthāna* must necessarily set forth the causal conditions for a single sutra. Since the significance of a single sutra does not exceed the fivefold profound meaning (*pañca-vidha-gambhīrārtha*), he points specifically to these five stages.
Each point is clearly elucidated. Regarding the fact that the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha share the same *dharmatā* (real mark):

the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are the Three Jewels of Sustenance (*shouzhi sanbao*), whereas the *dharmatā* is the Three Jewels of Essential Unity (*yiti sanbao*). As for saying they are "the same," the Buddha is the ultimate *dharmatā*.
The Dharma is that which can express the true reality (*dharmatā*); the Sangha is that which partially realizes the true reality. Therefore, they are said to be "identical.

Regarding the statement that "only the single Buddha-realm is the object of focus": this means that the nature of mind (*cittatā*) only takes the Buddha-realm as its object of perception, and arises solely through the Buddha-realm as its condition, without being mixed with other matters;
that is, the nature of mind does not fall into the nine realms. Now, the mind is fundamentally unarisen.
Birth necessarily follows conditions. If one follows the conditions of the Buddha-realm, then the whole body is the Buddha.
If one follows the conditions of the nine realms, the whole body is the nine realms. Even if one follows the dharma-realm of a bodhisattva, it is still like discarding gold to carry hemp.
How much more so for the six classes of ordinary beings and the three miserable realms—should one not be cautious? Therefore, it is called the "True Southern Guide.
The *Lotus Sūtra* is a teaching of pure unity without admixture; this scripture shares the same flavor as the *Lotus Sūtra*, yet they do not appear at the same time.
Although its words are brief, the meaning of the five stages is complete. Thus ends the first section, the Introduction, of the major outline of the sūtra text.
△ Second, the Main Body of the Teaching (Zhengzongfen) has three parts: first, an extensive exposition of the wondrous fruits of the environment and inhabitants of that land to inspire faith;

second, a specific exhortation for sentient beings to seek rebirth therein to give rise to the vow; third, a formal demonstration of the practitioner’s upholding of the Name to establish the practice.
Faith, Vow, and the Upholding of the Name constitute the essential purport of this sutra. Faith and the Vow constitute the wisdom-aspect of the practice.
Holding the Name is called "the practice of practice. Whether one attains birth [in the Pure Land] or not depends entirely on the presence or absence of faith and aspiration;

the high or low grade of one's rank depends entirely on the depth or shallowness of holding the Name (these words are as immovable as a mountain). Therefore, wisdom-practice serves as the precursor, while practice-practice is the primary cultivation—like the eyes and feet working in tandem.
△ The first section has two parts: first, the excellence of the environment; second, [the excellence of the inhabitants].

The retribution of the primary fruit is wondrous. △ This first section further has two parts: first, the inquiry and explanation; second, the extensive explanation. △ The first part further has two sections:
first, the inquiry; second, the explanation. △ Now, the first [of these].
Śāriputra, for what reason is that land called "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī)?
△ Second, the explanation [of the name] has two parts: first, the explanation based on the subject who experiences; second, the explanation based on the objects experienced.
△ Now, the first.
The sentient beings of that land have no manifold sufferings; they experience only various joys. Therefore, it is named "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī). [Commentary:

The bliss of the Pure Land is an inconceivable bliss that transcends all relative conditions (*atyanta-apratītya*). This is because there is no suffering with which it might be contrasted. Now, bliss is manifested in opposition to suffering.
Since there is no suffering in the Pure Land, how can it be called "bliss"? It is only in contrast to the extreme suffering of the Sahā world that it is so designated.
This reveals the purity of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

△ The commentary is divided into four parts: first, a brief explanation of sentient beings; second, a general discussion of suffering and happiness; third, a specific explanation of suffering and happiness;
fourth, a concluding reference to the Shared Residence. △ Now, the first part.

[Commentary]: "Sentient beings" refers to all those capable of experiencing [the results of karma], from ordinary humans up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksaṃbodhi). For now, we shall speak specifically of human beings.
By taking the lowest of the low as an example, one may infer the cases of the higher levels (this inconceivability of the Pure Land school lies herein).

[Commentary]: "Sentient beings" (sattva) briefly possesses three meanings: first, birth in a multitude; second, the arising of manifold dharmas, namely the five aggregates (skandhas) and the four great elements (mahābhūtas);
third, birth through the confusion of afflictions (kleśa). Sentient beings in the Land of Ultimate Bliss possess two of these meanings; they lack the meaning of "receiving birth."
"Equal to the Awakened One" (等覺者) means being equal to a Buddha; thus, everyone from the Bodhisattvas in their final birth (補處菩薩) downward may be so named.

This refers to all beings from the highest level of Equal Awakening down to the common people, who are all termed "sentient beings" (眾生). The phrase "using the lowest of the low as an example for the highest of the high" (以下下例上上者) means "by way of analogy" (例) or "in general" (概).
It signifies that from the common people up to those at the stage of Equal Awakening, they are all generally those who will attain Buddhahood within a single lifetime.
△ Second, a general discussion of suffering and pleasure. [Commentary]:

In the Sahā world, suffering and pleasure are intermingled. In reality, suffering is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), because it oppresses both body and mind; pleasure is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
Because it does not endure for long, that which is neither suffering nor pleasure is the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), as its nature is one of constant flux.

That land is eternally free from the three types of suffering; it is not like the "pleasure" in this land that exists only in contrast to suffering. Therefore, it is called "Supreme Bliss" (the term "Supreme Bliss" serves to illuminate and transcend all sufferings).
[Commentary] *Saha* means "able to endure" (*kṣānti*). This is because the sentient beings of this land are able to endure suffering.

These three types of suffering are also called the three feelings (*vedanā*). Regarding the feeling of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*), it is "suffering upon suffering" (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*): this is because this body is already the fruit of suffering, and further suffering is added to it;

hence it is called "suffering upon suffering. The feeling of pleasure (*sukhavedanā*) is "the suffering of change" (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*); that which does not abide for long is the pleasure that stands in contrast to suffering.
One cannot abide for long; even abiding for long turns into suffering. Neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensations are the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*).

That which is "by nature shifting and flowing" refers to the shifting and flowing of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), for it ultimately ends in transformation and extinction. These three types of suffering, when considered in terms of phenomena, are restricted to the triple world (*tridhātu*);
when considered in terms of principle, they pervade the four lands (*catur-bhūmi*). There is no peace in the triple world; it is like a burning house.

That which is suffering as suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) is like a provisional city of transformation; it cannot be dwelt in for long and is thus characterized by the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).

Although the true recompense land of the serene light is free from the suffering and pleasure of birth-and-death and nirvana, because the characteristics of thought have not yet been exhausted and the suffering of conditioned transformation (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) has not yet been transcended, it remains [subject to] the suffering of conditioned existence.
In the four lands of Ultimate Bliss, one is forever free from these three types of suffering; because its enjoyment is equal to that of the Buddha, it is not like this world.
Regarding suffering, there is also pleasure.
△ Third, the specific explanation of suffering and pleasure has two parts: first, the formal explanation of the four lands; second, pointing out the excellence of practice.
△ Now, the first part.
[Commentary] To distinguish them briefly: in the Shared Residence [heavens], the five turbidities are slight and there are no eight sufferings of the分段 (fen-duan) [birth-and-death cycle].
One experiences only the pleasures of being free from illness and old age, traveling with sovereign ease, and the gathering of all virtues, such as celestial food, celestial garments, and so forth.
[Commentary] To analyze this superficially is not yet to speak with full detail. Regarding "segmented" (bun-dan): in this land, there is segmented birth-and-death (*paricchinna-saṃsāra*).

"Segment" (*bun*) refers to a limit; it means that the lifespan has extensions and contractions. "Segmented" (*dan*) refers to a physical mass; it means that the body has large and small dimensions. As for the "eight sufferings":

the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of [being separated from] what is loved... [and so forth].

The suffering of separation from what is loved, the suffering of encountering what is hated, and the suffering of the proliferation of the five aggregates. The former seven are specific, while the latter one is general.
In that land, these various sufferings are transformed into various joys; therefore, it is named "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī).

[Commentary] The essence of the skillful means (*upāya*) is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). It is free from the suffering of sinking into emptiness or stagnating in quiescence; rather, one experiences only the bliss of sporting with supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-vikrīḍita*).

[Sub-commentary] The sages of that Land of Skillful Means all receive the contemplation of the essence of emptiness according to the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*), and skillfully attain entry through realization.

Because these are all Mahāyāna bodhisattvas, and because the four lands are perfectly interfused, there are no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas of the *saṃghāṭa* or *neyāya* vehicles who sink into partial emptiness or stagnate in the suffering of quiescent extinction.
In this land, those of the two vehicles are obstructed by the partial emptiness of nirvāṇa and do not give rise to the great resolve;
therefore, it is considered suffering. In that land, the opposite is true: they merely enjoy the play of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
Purifying the Buddha-lands and maturing sentient beings, they equally enjoy happiness.

[Commentary: When the contemplation of the mind of true recompense reaches perfection, there is no longer suffering characterized by separation or lack of integration; one experiences only unimpeded, inconceivable bliss.

[Commentary] That land is the Land of Actual Reward (*sambhoga-kāya*). All who have realized entry through the threefold contemplation of the single mind according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) experience only unobstructed bliss and the like, because their wisdom is perfectly interfused;
thus, they are free from the suffering of separation and lack of fusion characteristic of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*).
[Commentary] In the ultimate realm of tranquil light, there is no leakage of the dharma-body nor the suffering of the continuous flow of conditioned existence;
one experiences only the perfect, ultimate bliss that accords with the nature of reality.
[Commentary] "Ultimate equality" refers to the ultimate land of tranquil light (*śāntaprabhāsa*), where principle and wisdom are non-dual and body and land are of one suchness.
Regarding the phrase "the Dharma-body permeates and the true permanence flows forth," this refers specifically to the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*).

Although it is called "ultimate" according to the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*), according to the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpannavyavahāra*), it is still but a stage of partial realization; there remains the suffering of permeation and flowing forth. The Dharma...
Regarding "the body’s seepage and so forth": this refers to the inconceivable death and rebirth (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*) of a Bodhisattva.

Because ignorance is not yet exhausted, the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) are not yet exhausted. Because the conditions are not yet exhausted, the water of the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) continues to seep and flow.
Since the enjoyment in that land is equal to that of a Buddha, they experience only the bliss of the equality of nature (*tathatā*). This is the fourth [section] of the formal explanation.
The section on the lands concludes.
△ Second, pointing out the excellence of practice.

[Commentary]: However, because sentient beings dwelling in the Land of Common Residence possess the same roots of goodness and merit from upholding the Name as the Buddha, they fully purify the four lands.
"One fully experiences all joys" (this is precisely the Pure Land School of Ultimate Bliss).
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "because the roots of goodness and merit from holding the Name are identical to those of the Buddha":

this means that at the very moment one correctly recites the Name, one takes the Buddha’s roots of goodness as one’s own roots of goodness, and the Buddha’s merit as one’s own merit; therefore, it is said they are "identical to the Buddha."
The Sutra says: "One cannot be born in that land by means of few roots of goodness, merit, or karmic conditions.
If there are good men or good women who, upon hearing the name of Amitābha Buddha, hold fast to his title with single-mindedness and without distraction, they shall immediately attain rebirth.
Since it states that few roots of goodness do not lead to birth, yet immediately follows by saying that holding the name can lead to birth, this is clearly evident.

To uphold the name of the Buddha is to possess manifold roots of goodness and manifold merits; because such merit and goodness are so abundant, one is able to perfectly purify the four lands and fully receive all forms of bliss.
This does not mean that perfect purification and full reception occur only after being born in the Pure Land; rather, it occurs at the very moment of mindfulness of the Buddha.
When a single thought accords with reality, there is a single thought of pure reception; when every thought accords with reality, there is every thought of pure reception. Therefore, it is said:
This is the excellence of practice. The third section, the detailed explanation of suffering and bliss, is concluded.
△ Fourth, the conclusion pointing to the Land of Common Dwelling.
[Commentary] Furthermore, the supreme excellence of Ultimate Bliss does not reside in the three higher lands, but rather in the Land of Common Dwelling. This is because the former...
Thus, the ten directions coexist, yet they defer to its extraordinary excellence; even those below may compare themselves with this land.
This is why ordinary beings enter with ease and composure, transcending horizontally to leap over [the realms]. When the Buddha spoke of suffering and joy, his intention lay herein.

[Commentary] "Yielding" (遜) means to defer. All Buddha-lands in the ten directions possess the Land of Common Residence (*sahā-loka-dhātu*), yet one must yield to the supreme excellence and uniqueness of the common residence of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Furthermore, below this, one may compare the suffering and happiness of this land [of Jambudvīpa]. "Superior" (優) means excellent.

The scope of its inclusion is most extensive; therefore, one enters with ease. The initial application is most simple; therefore, one proceeds with composure. Every thought-moment is itself the Buddha;
therefore, one transcends horizontally. One does not fall into the nine realms; therefore, one surpasses them. The Buddha’s intention in speaking of suffering and bliss lies precisely in this:

within the Land of Common Residence (*sahā-loka*), one detests suffering and seeks bliss, abandoning defilement to return to purity. The first part of the sutra text, explaining [the Pure Land] by way of the subject who experiences it, is concluded.

△ Second, an explanation based on what is experienced (this also serves as a further explanation of the preceding statement that "there is no suffering, but only the experience of various joys"; the detailed explanation of this single section below follows the same principle).

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the land of Ultimate Bliss is adorned with seven tiers of railings along its borders, seven tiers of jeweled nets in the space above, and seven rows of trees surrounding the open grounds;
all are composed of the four precious substances and encircle it on every side. For this reason, that land is called Ultimate Bliss.
[Commentary] Regarding the adornments of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), one should consult the *Mahā-amitābha-sūtra* and the *Sūtra on the Sixteen Contemplations*;

they are not recorded here in full. △ The commentary is divided into three parts: first, a general explanation of the supreme realm; second, a detailed exposition of the four lands; third, a section of questions and answers for refutation.
The Sentiment. △ Now, the first part. [Commentary:
The seven layers represent the seven categories of the path-factors (mārga). The four jewels represent the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
That they surround it on all sides indicates that this is the dwelling place of immeasurable Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Since they are all made of the four jewels, one’s own merit is profound.
Surrounding it on all sides, other worthy sages are everywhere; this is the true internal and external causal condition for this Land of Ultimate Bliss.
[Commentary] The text is divided into two sections. The first briefly explains the scriptural passage. "Manifest" (biao) means to reveal; it reveals the cause by means of the fruit.
The seven categories refer to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), which will be explained in the subsequent text.

These seven categories do not transcend morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). The railings represent morality, for they prevent transgressions; the nets represent concentration, for concentration covers the mind;
and the rows of trees represent wisdom, for the tree of the Path is lofty and far-reaching. Regarding the four jewels: although the jewels in that land are truly immeasurable, it is only said...

The four jewels symbolize the four virtues. This land is a shared realm of expedient means where only the four inversions exist; hence it is said that both ordinary beings and sages possess these four inversions.
In that land, however, as a shared realm, every person truly possesses the four virtues. As for "permanence," it is because of immeasurable life.
"Joyful" means that one experiences only various forms of bliss. "Self" means possessing immeasurable light and the eight masteries (*vaśitā*).
"Pure" means that the pure land is free from defilement. As for the eight masteries: first, the ability to manifest a single body as many bodies;
second, the ability to pervade the great trichiliocosm with a body the size of a single atom; third, the ability to manifest a massive body and travel vast distances with ease.
Fourth, they are able to manifest as immeasurable types of beings while constantly dwelling in a single land; fifth, their various faculties function interchangeably;

sixth, they attain all dharmas yet remain without the notion that there are any dharmas; seventh, they can explain the meaning of a single verse for immeasurable eons; eighth, their bodies pervade all buddha-fields.
It is like empty space. In the subsequent text, it is stated that he makes offerings to ten trillion Buddhas in other directions and returns to his own land at the time of the meal;
this refers precisely to these eight great sovereigns (*mahāvaśitā*).

Regarding the phrase "the depth of one's own merit," this means the cause of manifold roots of goodness is profound. Regarding "the pervasiveness of other worthies and sages," this means manifold... [text ends].
The conditions for merit and virtue are powerful; all of these are manifestations of the great name of myriad virtues in a single phrase. This concludes the general explanation of the supreme realms.
△ Second, the specific elucidation of the four lands, divided into two parts: First, the horizontal and vertical dimensions of the four lands. Second, the circularity of the four lands.
Rong: Now, if one speaks in terms of the inherent virtue (*xingde*), it is neither horizontal nor vertical. What is now called "horizontal" and "vertical" refers to the cultivated virtue (*xiude*).
Although one distinguishes between the inherent and the cultivated, the cultivation arises entirely from the inherent nature, and the cultivation is entirely contained within the nature.

If one speaks in terms of rebirth in this land, whether by reciting the name, or by performing meditative visualization, one may be born in the Land of Common Dwelling (*tongju*) or be born in the higher realms.

Third: collectively, these are termed "horizontal transcendence. If one considers those lands in relation to the three higher stages—whether entering from the stage of shared residence or proceeding upward—there is both horizontal and vertical progression, because the capacities of sentient beings are not uniform.
Those with sharp faculties enter horizontally; those with dull faculties advance vertically.
If one enters transversely, one cultivates the sudden and perfect *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, and the distinction between the stage of semblance and partial realization is discussed.

If one advances vertically, one cultivates the gradual *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, and there is the differentiation between "immediate emptiness" and "wondrous provisional. Although these are distinguished as transverse and vertical, [they are ultimately unified].

Being perfectly complete both horizontally and vertically, it is distinct from the three preceding teachings; therefore, the *Jiaoguangzong* (Outline of the Doctrines and Contemplations) establishes three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* according to the pedagogical methods (*huayi jiao*).
Here, we shall consider only the two types—sudden and gradual—the *wuding zhiguan* (contemplation of the indeterminate) being included therein as well.
△ Now, the first [section].

[Commentary] These adornments belong to the Pure Land of Shared Dwelling (*sābhisamskāra-sādhāraṇa-vihāra*). They are produced by superior wholesome karma and are also produced by the perfected practice of the five grades of contemplation (*pañca-krama-śikṣā*).
Their substance consists of the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) that are sublime and wondrous due to dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
[Commentary] This clarifies the cause and effect of the Land of Common Dwelling (*sahā-loka*). Taking the two types of response as the cause, the substance of the land is the effect.
This land is exclusively horizontal and lacks vertical progression. These adornments collectively refer to the two retributions—the environment and the inhabitants—of the four lands.

"Superior wholesome karma" specifically refers to the Land of Common Dwelling; it is that which is induced solely by the invocation of the Name, and it is also the cultivation of the five [virtues] of the Perfect Teaching.
This chapter concerns the karmic fruition of contemplative practice. To single-mindedly recite the Name as a superior wholesome karma means that every thought-moment is itself the Buddha;
it is the immediate antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for my own attainment of Buddhahood.
It is called "dominant" specifically because the dominant condition subsumes the three preceding conditions. This is wholesome karma.
This refers to the untainted wholesome karma of the Middle Way. Regarding the "five grades of contemplation," these are:

rejoicing, reciting and chanting, explaining and teaching, practicing the six perfections concurrently, and practicing the six perfections correctly. These two types of practice serve as the causes capable of inducing [rebirth], while rebirth in the Pure Land of Shared Dwelling constitutes the result induced.
As for "having the five sublime sensory objects produced by conditions as its essence": "produced by conditions" means—
This refers to phenomena produced by causes and conditions. "Exquisite and wondrous" means it is not the coarse and evil nature of the Sahā world.
The "five objects" refer to form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch. "Substance" refers to the essential nature of the land.
[Commentary: The Land of Expedient Means is that which is evoked by the wisdom of the contemplation of emptiness, and it is also evoked by the three contemplations in their semblance form.
It takes as its essence the five sense objects of the untainted (anāsrava) wondrous ultimate truth.
[Commentary] This clarifies the cause and effect of the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-bhūmi*). As for the cause, it is both horizontal and vertical.

The vertical refers to that which is evoked by the wisdom of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-darśana-jñāna*). The horizontal refers to the three contemplations in their semblance (*pratirūpa-tri-vipaśyanā*). Regarding "the contemplation of emptiness," this is not the emptiness of existence in the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*);

rather, it is the emptiness of the Middle Way and the provisional (*parikalpita*) in the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-śāsana*). The "three contemplations in their semblance" refer to the single mind (*ekacitta*).
The three contemplations are for those who have entered the stage of semblance realization. The "wondrous ultimate truth" is not a partial truth, but rather the inconceivable truth.

Regarding the "five dusts free from outflows": they are free from the outflows of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*), the outflows of [afflictions as numerous as] motes of dust (*rajas-āsrava*), and the outflows of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
This refers to the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) that are untainted (*anāsrava*) within the middle way.

[Commentary: The Land of True Reward and Purity is brought forth by the wisdom of the sublime contemplation of the provisional (*miao-jiaguan*). It is also brought forth by the partial realization of the three contemplations.
Its essence consists of the inexhaustible five sensory objects of the sublime conventional truth (*miao-sudi*).
[Commentary: This clarifies the cause and fruit of the *sambhogakāya* (Real Reward Land). "Exquisite provisional contemplation" refers to the inconceivable provisional contemplation;

it is the provisional [aspect] that is simultaneously the Middle and the Empty. This is explained from a vertical perspective. "Partial realization of the three contemplations" refers to the stage of partial realization of the three contemplations within a single mind.
This is explained from a horizontal perspective. "Exquisite conventional truth" refers to the inconceivable conventional truth.
This is the Truth (satya). It is the conventional reality that is itself the Middle Way and the Real. Regarding the "inexhaustible five sense objects" (pañca-viṣaya):
whichever single object one grasps, it contains all objects; that is to say, within each and every object there are all objects, and within each and every mind there are all minds.
Within each and every atom are all minds; within each and every mind are all atoms. Within each and every atom are all lands;
and it is likewise for all the atoms within those lands, and so forth.

[Commentary]: The Land of Constant Quiescent Light is that which is realized through the wisdom of the Middle Way (Madhyamaka), and it is also that which is realized through the ultimate threefold contemplation (*trivipaśyanā*).
It takes as its essence the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) that accord with the nature of the wondrous Middle Truth (*madhyama-satya*).

[Commentary] This clarifies the cause and effect of the Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*). "The Middle as Contemplation" refers to the middle that is simultaneously emptiness and the provisional;
it is discussed in terms of the vertical dimension. "The Ultimate of the Three Contemplations" refers to the ultimate stage of the three contemplations within a single mind;
it is discussed in terms of the horizontal dimension. "The Subtle Truth of the Middle" refers to the inconceivable middle.

This is the truth; it is the very midst of both the ultimate and the conventional. "The five sense objects that accord with the nature" refers to the five sense objects that are inconceivable and perfectly interfused in accordance with the nature.
This concludes the initial explanation of the four lands in terms of their horizontal and vertical dimensions.
△ Second, the clarification of the perfect interfusion of the four lands.
[Commentary: This distinction is made for the sake of easy understanding. In reality, the adornments of the four lands are all phenomena produced by causes and conditions;

there is nothing that is not immediately empty, provisional, and middle (this refers to the nature upon which cultivation arises). Therefore, the pure realm of the Shared Land of Ultimate Bliss is the perfect interfusion of the ultimate and the conventional.

"Immeasurable" (this treatise maintains that cultivation is complete and resides within the nature; only in this way is it the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss). All subsequent sections follow this pattern. [Commentary]:
To facilitate easy understanding, this analysis is made. By making this sequential analysis of the four lands: the Land of Common Dwelling is dependent origination;
the Land of Expedient Means is the identity with emptiness; the Land of Real Reward is the wondrous provisional; and the Land of Silent Radiance is the identity with the Middle Way.

If one relies on the ultimate principle, the four lands are without exception perfectly interfused. Therefore it is said that the adornments of the four lands are none other than the dharmas produced by causes and conditions.
That "none are not produced by causes and conditions" means that the four lands are, in essence, only the Land of Common Dwelling (*sahā-loka*).

That "none are not identical with emptiness" means that the four lands are, in essence, only the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-bhūmi*). That "none are not identical with the provisional" [means that the four lands are, in essence, only the Land of Ultimate Bliss].
"Those [four lands] are but the one land of true recompense (*samyak-vipāka*). "There is nothing that is not the Middle" means the four lands are but the one land of tranquil light (*śānta-prabhā*).

Below this, the text cites the realm of perfect interfusion to verify the principle of perfect interfusion. "The perfect interfusion of the real and the conventional" refers to the perfect interfusion of the three truths (*tri-satya*).
"People" represents the phenomena produced by causes and conditions; it refers to the Land of Common Dwelling (*sahā-loka-dhātu*).

Furthermore, the Śrāvaka represents "emptiness" (śūnyatā), which is the land of skillful means (upāya-bhūmi). The Bodhisattva represents "provisional existence" (prajñapti), which is the land of true recompense (vipāka-bhūmi).

The Buddha represents "the Middle Way" (madhyamā-pratipad), which is the land of serene light (prabhāsvara-bhūmi). If it were not for the principle of perfect interfusion (yuanrong), how could there be such a realm of perfect interfusion?
Ordinary beings and sages dwell together in one place without obstruction; therefore, it is called "perfectly interfused. It cannot be limited.
Regarding "measure": it cannot be delimited by means of three sequential cognitions. In the subsequent passages where the principle is revealed, all shall follow this model.
This concludes the separate clarification of the four lands.
△ Third: Refuting [the objection] through Question and Answer. [Commentary: Question:

If the Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*) consists solely of the principle of nature (*dharmatā*), how can it possess such adornments? Answer: Each and every adornment is the entire body of the principle of nature;
each and every aspect of the principle of nature is fully endowed with adornment. Only then is it the ultimate fruit of reliance (*niśraya-phala*) of all Buddhas. If...
The Land of Tranquil Light does not possess the five superior and subtle sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).

How does it differ from the partial truth of the *dharmatā*? [Commentary]: This is likely because people do not realize that the Land of Tranquil Light is the principle within phenomena themselves, and thus fall into a biased view.
These questions and answers are established to prevent this. Indeed, the Land of Tranquil Light originally does not exist outside the three lands, nor does it exist within them.
Within the lands, because the *sambhogakāya* (the land of serene light) fundamentally has no location, it is the essential substance (*dharmatā*) of the principle of the three lands.

Therefore, the answer states: "Each and every adornment is the entire body of the rational nature of serene light; each and every rational nature is fully endowed with the adornments of the three lands.
As the sutra says: "The dwelling place of all Buddhas is named the Constant Serene Light. This is spoken from the perspective of the Tathāgata’s own portion.

The three lands are entirely perfected within the Land of Peaceful Light (*śānta-prabhāsa*). Conversely, from the perspective of sentient beings, the Land of Peaceful Light is entirely manifested as the three lands;

this is merely due to the differences in their karma—what does it have to do with the lands having high or low status? Furthermore, ordinary people see only the Land of Common Residence (*sahā-loka*) and do not see the three higher lands;
*śrāvakas* see only the two lower lands and do not see the two higher ones; and Bodhisattvas see [only] the lower [land].
Third: [the bodhisattvas] see the Land of Quiescent Light partially, whereas only the Buddha sees the four lands completely.

If the Land of Quiescent Light were outside the magnificent adornments of the other three lands, what difference would there be between it and the partial truth of the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) of the Lesser Vehicle?

The second section of the sutra, explaining [the lands] in terms of what is experienced and enjoyed, is concluded. The first major heading, consisting of the inquiry and the explanation, is now finished.
△ Second, the detailed explanation has two parts: first, the individual explanation of that which is received; second, the combined explanation of the receiver and that which is received.
△ First part, again, has two sections: first, the explanation of the place of birth; second, the concluding indication of the Buddha’s power. △ Now, the first section.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, in the land of Ultimate Bliss there are ponds made of the seven treasures, filled with water possessing the eight meritorious qualities.
The bottoms of these ponds are entirely covered with ground of golden sand, and their four-sided steps and walkways are composed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
Above are multi-storied pavilions, likewise adorned with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, musaragalva, red pearls, and agate.

Within the ponds, lotus flowers are as large as chariot wheels; those that are blue emit a blue light, those that are yellow emit a yellow light, those that are red emit a red light, and those that are white emit a white light—subtle, wondrous, fragrant, and pure.
[Commentary] *Vaidūrya* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "blue-colored gem. It is also called "not far" (*avidūra*), because it is not far from the city of Vārāṇasī.
It is also called *kāca* (glass) or *sphaṭika*. This is translated as "water-jade" (*shuiyu*) or "white pearl."
It resembles crystal; there are both red and white varieties.
△ In the commentary (*shū*), there are four sections: first, a general indication that this differs from others; second, an explanation of the water with eight virtues;
third, an explanation of how it fills the interior and so forth; fourth, an explanation of the flower-wheels and so forth. △ Now, the first section.
[Commentary] Above, the dwelling place was explained; now the birthplace is explained. The jewel ponds are composed of gold, silver, and so forth, unlike the earth and stone of this world.
(The absolute bliss [of the Pure Land] must be discussed through contrast for the sake of sentient beings in a defiled age.)
[Commentary] "That which differs from this land of earth and stone" means that it is not only that the precious metals differ from the earth and stones;

rather, there is a vast distinction between the ordinary and the holy. This land is the result of the tainted karma of ordinary beings, whereas that land is formed by the untainted pure karma of sages and is further adorned by the power of Amitābha’s vows. This land is like a prison.
As for the hells, that land is like a celestial palace; how could they possibly be compared?
Regarding the mention of gold, silver, and the seven treasures, the jewels in that land are truly immeasurable; it is merely spoken of as "seven" in accordance with what ordinary people here value.
Even the water of eight virtues is described as being "similar" to the common waters of this land, speaking only of their resemblance. As for the celestial palaces of this land—
Even the precious waters cannot be fathomed; how much less can the realm of the Sage be measured by ordinary sentiments?
This is because every single dharma one might grasp from that land is none other than the three bodies and four virtues of Amitābha, without the slightest distinction.
All subsequent passages are to be understood in this manner.
△ Second, explaining the water of eight virtues. [Commentary]: As for the eight virtues:
first, it is clear and limpid, unlike the turbidity found here; second, it is cool and refreshing, unlike the extremes of cold and heat;

third, it is sweet and delicious, unlike salty, bland, or inferior flavors; fourth, it is light and soft, unlike that which is heavy and hard; fifth, it is moist and lustrous, unlike that which is parched or putrid.
1. Fading away; different from permanence. 2. Peace and harmony; different from sudden calamity. 3. Eliminating hunger and thirst; different from cold and heat. 4. Nurturing the sense faculties;
different from impairing the sense faculties, as well as from baleful influences, increasing illness, drowning, and so forth.
[Commentary] The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Sixteen Contemplations) states: "The water of eight virtues arises from the King of Wish-fulfilling Jewels and divides into fourteen branches.
Each branch displays the wondrous colors of the seven treasures. This mani-water flows among the flowers and ascends and descends along the trees;
its sound is subtle and exquisite, expounding upon suffering, emptiness, impermanence, non-self, and the pāramitās. There is no [end].

The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "When those bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas enter the jewel pond, if they wish for the water to reach their ankles, the water immediately reaches their ankles;
even if they wish for it to drench their bodies, it naturally drenches their bodies; if they wish for it to recede, the water immediately recedes.
Thus, it accords spontaneously with their wishes, opening the spirit and gladdening the body, washing away the defilements of the mind, and purifying [the senses]."
It is bright, clear, and pure. Waves rise up, producing immeasurable and spontaneous wondrous sounds; according to their respective capacities, there are none who do not hear them.

The commentary states that regarding the eight meritorious qualities (*aṣṭāṅga-guṇa*), while the actual merits of the precious waters are truly immeasurable, these eight kinds are briefly set forth here to accord with the common understanding of ordinary beings.
First, it is limpid and clear, unlike the turbid waters of this world. Those precious waters of that land are not...
However, its own substance is clear and pure, and it is further able to clarify the bodies and minds of all sentient beings. Thus, a sutra says:
"It opens the spirit and delights the body, washing away the defilements of the mind. The water of this region, however, is not only unable to wash away the defilements of the mind;
its own substance is turbid, and it can further cause everything else to become turbid. Second, regarding the difference between clarity-and-coolness and coldness-and-heat:
The waters of that land are not only inherently cool themselves, but can also cool all things;
for those who bathe in these waters are freed from all feverish afflictions. The waters of this region, however, cannot remove affliction;

they are themselves cold or hot, and furthermore, they cause everything to become cold or hot. Regarding the three types of sweet flavors as opposed to the salty, bland, and inferior tastes: in that land...
The water of that place is not only sweet in its own essence, but it is also sweet to all;
those who drink this water leave suffering behind and attain happiness. The water of this region, however, cannot cause one to leave suffering and attain happiness;

its own essence is salty, bland, or of inferior taste (the sea is salty, rivers are bland, and other waters are of inferior taste), and furthermore, it is salty or bland to everyone. Moreover, it is light and soft, whereas [the other] is heavy and hard.
The waters of that region are not only light and soft in their own essence, but they are also light and soft to all things;
for those who bathe in these waters, both body and mind become tranquil and at ease. The waters of this region, however, do not provide such tranquility;
they are heavy in their own essence and heavy to all things. They possess five qualities of moisture—namely, stagnation, decay, discoloration, and so forth—whereas the waters of that region...
Water: Not only is its own substance moist and refreshing, it further moistens and refreshes all things.
Those who drink this water do not fail to obtain benefit. The water of this region, however, does not even possess the quality of *siddhānta*;

its own substance is putrid and discolored, and it further causes everything else to become putrid—(“putrid” meaning foul-smelling; “rotten” meaning decayed; “discolored” meaning the color has changed over time)—and it corrupts the harmony of the six flavors.

As for the turbulent waters of this region, the waters of that land are not only free from turbulence; their very nature is peaceful and harmonious, and they further bring peace and harmony to all things.
As a sutra says: "With subtle ripples and eddies, they flow calmly and slowly. Upon hearing the sound of these waters, all attain the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).
The waters of this region, however, are not only incapable of preaching the Dharma; their very nature is turbulent, and they are furthermore violent.
It subdues all [afflictions]. Seventh, regarding the removal of hunger and thirst while producing a different kind of coldness:

the water of that region not only removes the hunger and thirst of the physical body (*rūpakāya*), but also removes the hunger and thirst of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This is because those who drink this water are able to attain immeasurable samādhis and eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
The water of this region, however, not only fails to provide the joy of the Dharma (*dharmaprīti*), but itself produces a natural coldness. Furthermore...
Furthermore, regarding the two bodies of cold and raw-colored phenomena, the eight types of nourishment for the sense faculties, and the various impairments of the sense faculties,
as well as the increase of malignant diseases, drowning, and so forth— while the waters of that region not only nourish the physical body and its sense faculties,
they are also able to nourish the sense faculties of the Dharma-body, namely faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; such is not the case with the waters of this region.

Not only does it fail to nourish the two bodies, but it further damages the sense faculties, leading to drowning and death, as well as illness caused by baleful influences (the term *lei* meaning "disharmony," and *li* meaning "contradiction"). This concludes the second clarification on the water of eight virtues.
"△The three types of supernormal knowledge (trividyā) fill its interior," etc.

[Commentary: It is filled within; it differs from being parched or overflowing. Its floor is pure golden sand, differing from muddy silt. The stairways consist of four jewels, differing from bricks and stones.
"Tier" (bìjí) refers to a step; "path" (dào) refers to a level thoroughfare; "pavilion" (lóu) refers to a multi-storied building; "tower" (cēnlóu) refers to a high, peaked structure.
The "pavilion" refers to a pavilion made of the seven treasures, which differs from the wood, earth, vermilion, and green used here in this land.

These pavilions serve as dwelling places and venues for Dharma assemblies. Once the lotus buds in the precious ponds have blossomed, one may ascend to the four banks, enter the Dharma assembly, see the Buddha, and hear the Dharma.

[Commentary: It is filled to the brim, unlike that which is either parched or overflowing. The waters of that region not only fill it completely, but can also perfectly accord with the intentions of people.

As the Sūtra says: "When those Bodhisattvas and the assembly of Śrāvakas enter the precious pond, if they wish for the water to submerge their feet, the water immediately submerges their feet; if they wish for it to reach their waists, it immediately reaches their waists."
Even when one wishes for the water to return to its original state, it immediately returns; its temperature is harmonized, naturally according to one's will.

The waters of this region not only do not comply with human desires—being either parched or overflowing—but when parched, they cannot be utilized, and when overflowing, they further cause destruction to all things. The bottom is pure gold.

Regarding the sands being different from the muddy silt: at the bottom of those ponds in that land, there may be golden sand, or silver sand, or sand of a single jewel, even up to sand of immeasurable jewels and so forth.
In this world, the bottoms of the ponds consist purely of muddy silt;
it cannot be seen with the eyes nor smelled with the nose. One may then ascend the four banks and enter the Dharma assembly, where one beholds the Buddha and hears the Dharma.
It is not merely that one ascends the four shores of the east and west;

rather, one ascends the shore of the four virtues (*caturguṇa*), enters the Dharma-assembly of the four lands (*caturkṣetra*), beholds the Buddhas of the four bodies (*caturkāya*), and hears the Dharma of the four teachings (*caturdeśanā*). Thus concludes the section on the "Three Clarities (*trividyā*) being fully present therein."
△ Fourth, the Flower-Wheel and so forth. [Commentary:
As for the "Flower-Wheel," it refers to the Golden Wheel of a Cakravartin King, forty *li* in diameter; this is stated by way of citing the smallest possible size.

However, according to the *Contemplation Sūtra* and the *Assembly on Infinite Life*, its actual dimensions are truly immeasurable, due to the bodies [of beings] within the Pure Land of Shared Residence.
This is because their characteristics are not uniform: the blue is called *utpala*, the yellow is called *kumuda*, the red is called *padma*, and the white is called *puṇḍarīka*.
Because the bodies born therein possess radiance, the lotus calyxes likewise possess radiance.
However, the lotuses of Sukhāvatī have immeasurable colors and light; this has been stated only briefly. Their subtle and wondrous fragrance—
"Pure. This briefly extols the four virtues of the lotus. To be substantial yet formless is called "subtle" (*wei*); to be unimpeded is called "wondrous" (*miao*).
Being formless, it is free from defilement; hence it is "pure. If the lotus calyx is thus, the birth-body (*janmakāya*) may likewise be known as wondrous.

[Commentary]: Regarding "flower wheels," these are lotuses in the pond as large as chariot wheels. A "chariot wheel" refers to the Golden Wheel-Treasure (*cakraratna*) of a Golden Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*).
There are four types of wheel-turning kings: those of gold, silver, copper, and iron. A Golden Wheel-Turning King wields a golden wheel and rules over the four continents;
he possesses the seven treasures and a thousand sons. This occurs when the human lifespan is eighty-four thousand years.
They are transformed and guided solely by the ten virtuous deeds. The golden wheel-jewel is forty *li* in diameter;
this refers to the smallest lotus flower. According to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (Sixteen Contemplations Sutra) and the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, in the assembly of the Tathāgata Amitāyus:
The sizes explained therein are truly immeasurable, because the physical forms of the sentient beings dwelling there are not equal.

Regarding the "immeasurable light and color of the lotus flowers in the Land of Ultimate Bliss," it means that not only are the lotus flowers immeasurable, but even their light is immeasurable and their color is also immeasurable.
This is also a brief description; it is not merely a brief description of the lotus flowers, but rather—

Regarding the jeweled ponds within the lattices of the walking-avenues, the golden sands, the virtuous waters, and so forth—whether their light, their color, their basis, or their perfection—each is described briefly.
This is because this sutra excises the redundant and adopts only the essential.
As for the brief praise of the four virtues of the lotus, the merits of the lotus are likewise immeasurable; they do not consist merely of the four virtues of being subtle, fragrant, pure, and clean.
"Substance without form": substance refers to the essential nature of the seven treasures; "without form" means it does not have a fixed size or shape, but conforms to the mind as one desires.
"That which is unimpeded is called wondrous" means that because it conforms to the mind as one desires, it is inconceivable.
"Without form, it is not a mundane object": since it conforms to the mind as one desires, its entire being is solely... [the Dharma-nature].
The *Sūtra* says: "This seeing and its objects are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi. Therefore, it is said that because they are not defilements, they are pure.
Since the lotus calyx is subtle, wondrous, fragrant, and pure, the body produced from it is likewise subtle, wondrous, fragrant, and pure.
This concludes the initial explanation of the place of birth in the sūtra text.
△ Second, the summary indicating the Buddha’s power:
"Śāriputra, the Land of Ultimate Bliss is thus adorned with the accomplishment of such meritorious virtues.
△ The commentary divides this into three parts: first, the explanation based on the Buddha; second, the explanation based on the rebirth [of beings]; third, the explanation based on non-duality. △

First: [Explanation] This clarifies the superior dwelling places, the birthplaces, and the various adornments, all of which are accomplished through the merits of Amitābha Buddha’s great vows and great practices that accord with his true nature (this meaning refers to the Buddha). Therefore, they are able to universally adorn the four kinds of pure lands and universally encompass [all beings].
[This practice] enables all ordinary beings and sages throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time to attain rebirth.
[Commentary]: Regarding adornment, there is that which adorns and that which is adorned. Great vows constitute the adornment of wisdom;

great practices constitute the adornment of merit and virtue. These two are the means of adornment. The qualities that accord with the nature (*dharmatā*) constitute the nature that is adorned. This nature comprises the three truths.

Co-residing [in the realm of birth and death] is the nature of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), for one has not yet seen the ultimate truth. Expedient means (*upāya*) is the nature of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), for one has not yet reached the Middle Way.
The Real Reward Land and the Land of Peaceful Light are the nature of the Middle Truth (*madhyama-satya*), for ignorance (*avidyā*) has already been shattered.
Regarding vows, there are both general and specific types. Generally, there are the four great vows; specifically, there are the forty-eight vows, as well as the ten great vows, and so forth. Now...

By subsuming the particular within the general, these do not exceed the four great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna*). These four vows correspond to the Four Noble Truths, and as the Four Noble Truths are divided into the four teachings, there are thus four teachings and four vows.

Based on the vows, practice arises; since practice is likewise divided into the four teachings, we now take the vows and practices of the Tripitaka Teaching to adorn the Pure Land of Shared Residence, and the vows and practices of the Shared Teaching to adorn the Pure Land of Expedient Means. As for the Distinct Teaching...
The vows and practices adorn the Pure Land of True Reward; the vows and practices of the Perfect Teaching adorn the Pure Land of Dharma-Nature Light.
Furthermore, by means of the first three teachings, one adorns the four lands in sequential order; by means of the Perfect Teaching, one adorns the four lands in their perfect interpenetration.
These two kinds of adornment must necessarily be cultivated from the perspective of sentient beings; therefore, they are able to universally encompass the ten [stages].

This refers to all ordinary and holy beings throughout the three periods of time. Now, the *tongju* (shared) realm universally encompasses the ordinary and holy beings of the *Zang* (Tripitaka) teaching;

the *fangbian* (expedient means) realm universally encompasses the ordinary and holy beings of the *Tong* (Shared) teaching; the *shibao* (recompense for reality) realm universally encompasses the ordinary and holy beings of the *Bie* (Distinct) teaching;

and the *jiguang* (dharma-realm of tranquil light) realm universally encompasses the ordinary and holy beings of the *Yuan* (Perfect) teaching. Now, by means of the *tongju* realm, it universally encompasses the ordinary persons of the four teachings. By means of the... [the square... [text truncated].

Thus, the [Land of] Expedient Means universally encompasses both the sages of the Separate and Shared [Teachings] as well as the ordinary beings of the Distinct and Perfect [Teachings]. The [Land of] Real Reward universally encompasses the sages of the Distinct and Perfect [Teachings].

The [Land of] Quiescent Light encompasses only the sages of the Perfect Teaching. Now, by means of these four lands in their sequential order, all ordinary beings and sages are universally encompassed in their respective stages.

If, however, one considers the four lands in their perfect fusion, they universally encompass all throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time; therein, everyone exclusively invokes the Name.
It brings about the perfect fusion of ordinary beings and sages, enabling them to attain rebirth. The first section, explaining [the term] in relation to the Buddha, is concluded.
△ Second, explaining it in relation to rebirth.

【Commentary】 Furthermore, the Buddha, by means of his great vows, acts as the cause for the manifold roots of goodness in sentient beings; by means of his great practices, he acts as the... [text continues]
