The conditions for generating abundant merit cause those who maintain the Name with faith and aspiration to achieve such virtues in every thought-moment (this meaning refers to "arising").
Yet these are all already accomplished; they are neither of the present nor of the future (who can truly take this responsibility?).
[Commentary] This explains, from the perspective of sentient beings, the accomplishment of such adornments of merit.
The forty-eight vows are the cause for manifold roots of goodness; the six perfections and myriad practices are the conditions for manifold merit and virtue.

By means of these vows and practices, the Buddha adorns sentient beings with the four kinds of pure lands, and further, by means of these vows and practices, he brings them to full adornment and completion.
A single phrase of the Great Name: therefore, for those who hold the name with faith and aspiration, the Buddha’s four lands are entirely subsumed within my own four lands;
the Buddha’s vows and practices are entirely subsumed within my own vows and practices.

Thus, in every thought-moment, one perfectly purifies the four lands, perfectly realizes the three bodies, and perfectly realizes the three non-regressions, attaining Buddhahood in a single lifetime—all of which are already accomplished.
"That which is neither of the present nor of the future" refers to the Amitābha within my own mind, who has long since been fully perfected;

it does not wait for me to achieve perfection now or in the future. This is analogous to a father-king who has already brought the world to completion and merely awaits the prince’s accession to the throne.
This concludes the section on the "approximate birth."
△ Third, the explanation by way of non-duality. [Commentary:

This means that the various adornments of Amitābha serve as the sovereign objective basis (*ālambana*), which brings forth the various adornments within the minds of sentient beings (wherein nature and characteristics are perfectly luminous, completely eliminating the boundaries and limits of the Dharma-gate). Thus, the Buddha is entirely the sentient being, and the other is entirely the self. Therefore, it is said: "To achieve suchness."
The Adornment of Merit (the two meanings mentioned above are in fact one meaning). [Commentary]:
This refers to the two meanings of the Buddha’s birth mentioned above; they are harmoniously integrated into a single meaning.
When the Adornment of Amitābha acts as the predominant substantial cause (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it serves as the objective realm of the predominant condition for sentient beings. Condition.

There are four kinds: namely, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

As for "dominant," it possesses a dominant power and function. There are three kinds of objects: first, the objective realm (*svabhāva-viṣaya*); second, the realm with a substantial core (*sadravya-viṣaya*); and third, the realm of solitary images (*pratibimba-mātra-viṣaya*).
Regarding the objective realm, there are two types: first, that which lacks a primary substance; this refers to Amitābha’s Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) and—
The bodies, lands, and their adornments manifested by our eighth consciousness are themselves the objective essence (bǎnzhì jìng), and they also serve as the dominant condition (adhipatipratyaya).
Second, there are those with an objective essence, namely the objects of the five sensory realms (pañca-viṣaya) manifested by the first five consciousnesses.
The "object with a shared substance" (*sabhāga-viṣaya*) is also of two kinds: first, when the mind takes the mind as its object, it is called a "true shared-substance object";

second, when the mind takes form (*rūpa*) as its object, it is called a "semblance shared-substance object. These correspond to the sixteen contemplations (*ṣoḍaśākāra*) and so forth based on the Sūtras. The "solitary image object" (*kevala-pratibimba-viṣaya*) is also of two kinds:
first, the "solitary image without a real basis," such as when one contemplates the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit; second, the "solitary image with a real basis," which is...
This refers to practices such as meditative contemplation based on the sūtras.

"Bringing forth the adornment of one's own mind for the sake of sentient beings" means that, relying upon this substantial object as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), one transforms and brings forth various adornments within one's own mind. There are two types of "bringing forth."

First is "concomitant with the original" (*sahaja*), which refers to the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) realizing suchness (*tathatā*). Second is "transformed concomitance," which refers to the manifestation of the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*).
Now, the adornments of the four lands are inherently possessed by one's own mind; they cannot arise spontaneously without conditions.

At present, relying upon the Buddha’s primary substance as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), the eighth consciousness transforms and gives rise to an objective aspect that lacks a primary substance. The first five [consciousnesses]...

The transformations of consciousness give rise to objects that possess a substantial basis (*sabhāva-viṣaya*). The sixth consciousness gives rise to objects that appear as if possessing a substantial basis (*sadṛśa-sabhaava-viṣaya*).
Both are perceived through one's own transformations; therefore, it is said that "one's own mind is adorned with various [ornaments].

When the Buddha is entirely identical to birth, the adornment of the Buddha’s substantial basis is precisely the adornment of the sentient being’s substantial basis, and the adornment of the Buddha’s appearance-as-a-substantial-basis is precisely that of the sentient being.

Born with the adornment of substance, in which the other is entirely oneself: the Buddha is the Amitābha within the hearts of sentient beings, and I am the sentient being within the heart of the Buddha.
Since the mutual inclusion of the Buddha and myself is thus established, the same applies to the inclusion of all Bodhisattvas and all people;
therefore, it is said that such matters are accomplished in every respect.
It is unimpeded; it is the adornment of inconceivable merit. The initial separate explanation of that which is received is concluded.
△ Second, the combined explanation of the receiver and that which is received, which has two parts. First, the clarification of enjoyment by way of the five faculties and the five objects.
Next, the enjoyment [of the Dharma] is clarified by way of the faculty of hearing and the object of sound. △ This section has two parts: first, the actual clarification;
second, the concluding demonstration. △ Now, the first part.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, in that Buddha-land, celestial music constantly plays in the air; below, the ground is made of gold; in between, during the day...
Six times during the night, it rains *mandārava* flowers (adorning the void above and the golden earth below).
The sentient beings of that land always at dawn each take a robe-sack filled with various wonderful flowers to make offerings to ten trillion Buddhas in other directions;
then, at the time of eating, they return to their own land to eat and walk in meditation.
△ The commentary is divided into two parts: first, the combined topical outline; second, the explanation of the scriptural text. △ Now, the first part.

【Explanation】 "Joy" refers to the sensory object of sound. "The ground" refers to the sensory object of form. "Flowers" refer to the two sensory objects of form and fragrance. "Food" refers to the sensory object of taste.

"Carrying flowers, scattering flowers, and walking in meditation" refer to the sensory object of touch. It should be understood that the five faculties of sentient beings correspond to these five sensory objects.
[Commentary] The five faculties of sentient beings experience these five kinds of pure objects; therefore, it is said that the "five faculties and five objects clarify experience.
△ Second, the explanation of the sūtra text is divided into four parts. First, the explanation of "constantly producing celestial music," etc. Second, the explanation of the *mandārava* [flower].
Flowers, etc. The third interpretation refers to the times for eating and so forth. The fourth interpretation refers to eating, walking, and practicing *caṅkrama*.

△ Now, the first [interpretation]. 【Commentary】 "Constantly performing" refers to the six periods of the day. That which has gold for its ground is a realm adorned with the seven treasures, whose substance is gold.
The divisions of the day—beginning, middle, and end—are called the three periods of the day. The divisions of the night—beginning, middle, and end—are called... [the three periods of the night].
Because there are three periods of the night, it is said that there are six periods of day and night. However, in that land, both the environment and its inhabitants possess their own radiance;

they do not rely on the sun and moon to distinguish day from night. The division of time is merely a provisional designation made in accordance with the conventions of this region (one may conform to the conventions of this region for comparison, but one must not follow the subjective views of this region).
[Commentary]: Regarding "constantly playing celestial music," in this land, the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) have heaven as their limit;

therefore, they are called "celestial music," "celestial garments," "celestial food," and so forth. However, the music of that land cannot be compared to that of heaven. As the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
The music of the world’s emperors and hundreds of thousands of musical instruments—
from that of the Wheel-Turning Sage Kings up to the celestial music of the sixth heaven— each successively surpasses the other by billions of times.

Yet the ten thousand kinds of musical sounds in the sixth heaven do not equal even one-tenth of a billionth part of the single kind of sound produced by the various seven-jeweled trees in the Land of Immeasurable Life.

Regarding this so-called "heavenly music," there are two aspects: first, it accords with the common sentiments of people in this world; second, it is the music of the Heaven of Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha*).
This is because within the Buddha-land, any phenomenon one might mention is, in its entirety, the three bodies and four virtues of Amitābha.
There is no difference whatsoever; it should be understood that the ground is made of gold and so forth.
△ Second, the explanation of the *māndārava* flowers and others. [Commentary]:
*Māndārava* means "pleasing to the mind" (*cittānukūla*) in this language, and is also called "white flower. *I-kuei* (衣裓) refers to a vessel for holding flowers. "Various wonders" (*zhòng miào*)...
The flowers do not refer solely to the *mandārava* type; they should be understood as the four kinds of flowers in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, representing the four stages of the causal path.
Offering them to the Buddhas of other directions signifies that through the true cause, one hastens toward the ultimate fruit, for the virtue of the fruit is all-pervading.

Furthermore, the mention of "ten million billion Buddhas" in reference to the Sahā world is intended to show that once one has been born in Sukhāvatī, one returns to make offerings to Śākyamuni and Maitreya.
None of these are difficult. If empowered by the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of Amitābha, how could anything be too distant to reach?

[Commentary] Regarding the "four flowers" in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: the *Lotus Sūtra* states, "At that time, the World-Honored One entered the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings.
At that moment, the heavens rained down *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, and *mañjuṣaka* flowers."
They scattered *sa* flowers and *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers over the Buddha. Regarding *mahāmandārava*, this is translated as "Greatly Pleasing";
*mañjūṣaka* is translated as "Gentle," and *mahāmañjūṣaka* as "Greatly Gentle. These represent the four stages of the causal position.
The four flowers manifest the four kinds of true causes—the stages of the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten transferences, and the ten grounds—of the Bodhisattva.

Making offerings to the Buddhas of other directions symbolizes those who, through the assembly of true causes, are hastening toward the ultimate fruit; thus, they offer exquisite flowers to the Buddhas.
This signifies that all true causes tend toward the fruit of Buddhahood. Why is it that one makes offerings to Buddhas in other directions?
This signifies that the merit of the fruit is omnipresent in all places. The remainder of the text may be understood accordingly.

△ Third, the explanation consists of three parts: first, "at the time of eating," etc. This section further divides into three: first, clarifying that the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) are inconceivable;
second, clarifying the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*dharmadharmāpratighāta*); third, clarifying the profound depth of the Dharma-gates (*dharmamukha*). △ Now, the first part.
[Commentary: "At the time of eating" refers to early morning; hence it says "immediately. This clarifies that his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) are inconceivable:
without leaving that land, he constantly pervades the ten directions, without needing to spend time traveling back and forth.
[Commentary] Regarding the inconceivable supernormal power (*ṛddhi*): among the six supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), there is the supernormal power of psychic travel (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*).

It is also called the supernormal power of the sphere of psychic manifestation (*ṛddhiviṣaya-jñāna*) and the supernormal power of mastery over the mind (*kāmacārābhijñā*). It has three types: first, "reaching" (*gamana*), which means the body is able to fly like a bird without obstruction;
it makes the distant near, reaching a destination without traveling; one vanishes here and appears there, or vanishes there and appears here. First.
Mindfulness can reach the worlds of the ten directions. Second is transformation: the large can be made small, and the small can be made large;

the one can be transformed into many, and the many can be transformed into one. Third is the noble power of *ṛddhi*: manifestations appear without limit, and responsive transformations are unfathomable.
This is the supernormal power (*ṛddhi-pāda*) of one's own strength; it is already unfathomable. How much more so when relying on the supernatural power of the Tathāgata—how could it be conceivable?
Therefore, without leaving that land, they constantly pervade the ten directions, without needing to spend time traveling back and forth. As for "traveling" (*yú*): [it refers to]...
"Transcendence. This does not mean returning to one's own country after time has passed.
△ Second, clarifying the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena.
[Commentary] This text reveals that within a single sound of the Pure Land, a single atom, a single kṣaṇa, and even across a single step or the snap of a finger, all [are non-obstructed].
It penetrates without obstruction throughout the Triple Gem of the ten directions.
[Commentary] The aforementioned "supernormal power" (*ṛddhi*) was explained in terms of phenomena; here, it is revealed in terms of principle.

This supernormal power is not a penetration achieved through deliberate effort, but is rather the spontaneous nature of reality (*dharmatā*), the principle of the dharma-nature. This passage reveals that a single sound or a single... of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
"Dust" refers to any phenomenon whatsoever that one might pick up. In the Pure Land, any phenomenon one might pick up is ultimately pure *tathatā* (suchness).
This *tathatā* is without discrimination and without boundaries; it encompasses the inexhaustible Triple Gem throughout the ten directions.
All are contained within this single dharma. The Triple Gem of the ten directions is likewise ultimately pure *tathatā* (suchness).
Since *tathatā* is without differentiation and without limits, it fully encompasses the inexhaustible Triple Gem of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. If this one dharma is thus, so it is with all others.
All phenomena are thus. Therefore, one can stride across and snap the fingers, mutually penetrating one another without obstruction.

Because of this unobstructed penetration, one does not leave that land while constantly pervading the ten directions; returning to the kingdom to make offerings to the Buddhas occurs simultaneously and without hindrance.
Thus it is said: "This my place of enlightenment is like a celestial jewel, wherein the Three Jewels of the ten directions appear as reflections."
[In the] midst, my own reflection appears before the Triple Gem; with head touching their feet, I take refuge and pay homage.
△ Third, the profoundness of the Dharma-gate. [Commentary:
Furthermore, it reveals that while being in the Sahā world involves heavy defilements and evil obstructions, it is not separated from Sukhāvatī, yet it is separated. To be born in Sukhāvatī...
In the Land of Bliss, merit is exceedingly profound; it is both separated from and not separated from the Sahā world.
[Commentary] The Sahā world is like a prison: though not separated, it is separated. The Land of Ultimate Bliss is like a celestial palace: though separated, it is not separated.
This concludes the section beginning with "At the time of eating."
△ Fourth, the explanation of eating and walking meditation (caṅkrama). [Commentary:

Regarding eating and walking meditation: when food arrives, one eats with mindfulness without needing to make arrangements. When the meal is finished, the bowl departs without the need for laborious lifting or wiping.
One simply walks upon the golden ground, enjoying the delights of flowers and music, progressing in cultivation spontaneously and naturally.

[Commentary] Regarding the passage on "walking for alms-food," the intent is to manifest that there is no need for artificial arrangement or contrivance, nor the labor of lifting, wiping, cleaning, or washing.
There are no worldly conditions that obstruct the Way; there is only the golden ground for walking and the enjoyment of flowers and music as superior conditions that assist the Path.
This concludes the initial correct exposition of the sutra text.
△ Second, the summary and indication.
Śāriputra, the Land of Ultimate Bliss is thus adorned with the accomplishment of such meritorious virtues. [Commentary]:
The sutra text has first concluded its explanation of the enjoyment [of the land] by means of the five faculties and the five sense objects.

△ Second, the enjoyment [of the Dharma] is clarified in terms of the ear faculty and the object of sound. Because the ear faculty is most acute in this region, it is explained in detail specifically regarding the Dharma-sound.
In reality, however, the Land of Ultimate Bliss encompasses all capacities within the Dharma-realm;
each of the five sensory objects is perfectly wondrous, giving rise to all Dharma-gates.
[Commentary]: The five faculties of sentient beings each possess varying degrees of sharpness or dullness.

For instance, the sentient beings in the land of the Buddha Gandhottamakūṭa have such sharp faculties of the tongue that the Tathāgata Gandhottamakūṭa performs buddha-work by means of fragrant food. Furthermore, there are those who perform buddha-work by means of celestial robes;
this is because their faculty of the body is sharp. In this world, the faculty of the ear is the sharpest; therefore, Śākyamuni Buddha [performs buddha-work] by means of sound.
Sound performs the work of a Buddha. Thus, the *Buddhottamasikhara Sutra* states: "The true essence of the teaching in this land is pure within hearing and sound.
For this reason, this sutra specifically addresses the Dharma-sound of Amitābha to extensively clarify its enjoyment. If one investigates the ultimate reality, however:

The Pure Land perfectly encompasses all capacities within the Dharma-realm; thus, all five sense objects are perfect and wondrous, each capable of giving rise to all Dharma gates—not merely the single object of sound.
Furthermore, there are two parts: first, the detailed explanation; second, the summary. In the first part, there are two sections: first, the sounds that transform sentient beings;

second, the sounds that transform insentient things. In the first of these, there are again two sections: first, the benefit of the Dharma through the voices of birds; second, the brief exposition through inquiry and explanation.
△ First. Furthermore, Śāriputra, in that land there are always various wonderful birds of diverse colors:
white cranes, peacocks, parrots, śāris, kalaviṅkas, and saṃjīvakas. These various birds, throughout the six periods of day and night...

At that time, a harmonious and elegant sound issues forth. This sound expounds and clarifies the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, and such dharmas as these.
When the sentient beings of that land hear this sound, they all recollect the Buddha, recollect the Dharma, and recollect the Sangha.
△ The commentary is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the birds' voices; second, the explanation of the benefits of the Dharma. △ Now, the first part.
【Explanation】 "Various and wondrously multicolored" means numerous and beautiful. Below, six types are briefly enumerated. Śāri: formerly translated as *qiúlù* (crane).
Master Qí said it refers to the spring oriole; this may well be so. Kalaviṅka: here translated as "wonderful."

Regarding sound: before it has even emerged from the egg, its voice already surpasses that of all other birds. As for the *saṃjīva* (co-life) bird, which has two heads on a single body, their perceptions are distinct yet their karmic retribution is shared.
These two types [of birds] exist in places such as the Snow Mountains of the Western Regions; those who cherish and admire them here have merely described them based on their resemblance.
As for the six times they emit their sounds, one knows that in the Pure Land, night is not defined by the roosting of birds.
This is because those born from within lotus flowers inherently lack the state of slumber and do not require lying down at night.
[Commentary] Regarding the various wondrous birds of mixed colors: they are not only numerous, but also beautiful. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (Sixteen Contemplations Sutra) states:
"The King of Wish-fulfilling Jewels emits a subtle, golden light;

this light transforms into birds of a hundred precious colors, whose harmonious calls are plaintive and elegant, constantly praising the mindfulness of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. Master Qi was...
The Yuan dynasty Chan Master Chushi Fanqi was surnamed Zhu and was a native of Xiangshan in Ningbo.
As for the claim that he was "the spring oriole," the *Xizhai shi* (Poems from the Western Studio) states: "The śarīra is the spring oriole; his cultivated brows are like lacquer-drawn pupils.

This may well be so, yet it cannot be definitively settled. Regarding the "bird of wondrous sound" (*māyūrapakṣin*) before it has emerged from its egg, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "It is like the kalaviṅka..."
The kalaviṅka bird, while still within its eggshell, surpasses all other birds in its song. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
"In mountains, valleys, and vast wildernesses, there are many kalaviṅkas that produce wondrous sounds;
neither devas, nor humans, nor kinnaras can equal them, except for the voice of the Tathāgata. [This refers to] the saṃjīva, which has one body and two heads. Consciousness...

Regarding those with identical retributions: in Sanskrit they are called *jīvajīvaka*, which translates as "living" (*sheng*). The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* (Sheng Tianwang Jing) calls them "life-giving life" (*shengsheng*).

Alternatively, it translates as "life-force" (*ming*). The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* (Fahua Jing) calls them "life-and-life" (*mingming*). The *Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra* (Zabaozang Jing) names them "shared-life" (*gongming*).
Although their mental consciousnesses are distinct, they share a single retributive life-force. These various birds are all those cherished and admired here in this world.
Regarding their similarity: although their names are similar, their essential natures (tattva) are, in fact, different.

They are like the precious birds born from the King of Wish-Fulfilling Jewels (*cintāmaṇi-rāja*), who were originally emanations of Amitābha. This concludes the initial explanation of the birds' cries.

△ Second, the explanation of the benefits of the Dharma, which is further divided into three parts: first, the explanation of the *mārga-pakṣya-dharmas* (factors of the path); second, the explanation of the *sama-dharmas*; and third, the explanation of mindfulness of the Three Jewels.

The first section [on the factors of the path] is further divided into two: first, the formal explanation; second, the analytical discussion. The first [of these] has seven sub-sections; the first is the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
2. The four right efforts; 3. The four bases of power; 4. The five faculties; 5. The five powers; 6.
The seven factors of enlightenment; 7. The eightfold noble path. △ Now, the first [section].

[Commentary] The fivefold roots refer to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣikā dharmāḥ*). These are: first, the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*);

second, the foundation of mindfulness of sensation (*vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna*); third, the foundation of mindfulness of the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*); and fourth, the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), "mindfulness" (*smṛti*) is the wisdom that performs the contemplation, and "foundations" (*upasthāna*) are the objects of that contemplation.

There are four teachings [regarding them]. This section specifically clarifies the foundations of mindfulness according to the Tripitaka Teaching (*piṭakavāda*), because they are precisely what should be employed within the gateway of wearying detachment (*nirveda*).

Because the Buddha, when approaching his parinirvāṇa, repeatedly entrusted this matter to us, it must be applied correctly. One who is able to sever the desires of this Sahā world will attain rebirth;
if these desires are not severed, rebirth is difficult to achieve. It is like riding a horse: one must first loosen the halter. To launch a boat, one must first pull out the anchor.
If the anchor is not pulled out, how can the boat be launched? If the halter is not loosened, how can the horse move? [The same applies to] desire.
If one does not sever [the bonds], how can one attain rebirth? Although many people recite the Buddha’s name, those who attain rebirth are few;
this is precisely because they have not severed their craving and desire. Regarding the entrustment made when the Buddha was about to enter *nirvāṇa*:

when the Buddha was on the verge of entering *nirvāṇa*, Ānanda asked the Buddha, "While the Buddha is in the world, we dwell relying upon the Buddha. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, what shall we rely upon to dwell? The Buddha replied: "Rely upon..."
The four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*). First, the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) refers to contemplating the impurity of the body.
There are seven kinds of contemplation on impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*): 1. Impurity of the seed (*bījāśubhatā*): This body initially arises from a single thought of desire.
2. Impurity of conception (*upapatty-aśubhatā*): At the time of taking birth, one gathers the two drops—red and white—from the parents; consciousness enters therein and undergoes [conception].
1. Impurity of birth; 2. impurity of the dwelling place, meaning that while in the mother’s womb, one dwells below the stomach and above the intestines; 3.
impurity of being consumed by food, because while in the womb, one consumes only the mother’s blood; 4. impurity of initial birth, as one emerges from the birth canal.
1. The bloody garments fall away together, leaving a foul and chaotic mess. 2. The entire body is impure;

within the thin skin, pus and blood fill it completely, while excrement and urine overflow the belly, and maggots cover the whole body, with filth streaming from the nine orifices. 3. Ultimately, it is impure.
After death, the body swells and rots; dogs drag it and pigs pull at it, with bones and flesh strewn about. Constantly practice this contemplation;

it can sever craving for the *sāṃsārika* world and accomplish the pure karma of Sukhāvatī. This is the foremost sublime practice among the gates of wearying detachment and renunciation, which those who cultivate the path of purity must not fail to know.
Second is the application of mindfulness to sensation (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*), which means contemplating that sensation is...

Regarding suffering: there are three types of feeling—namely, painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Painful feeling is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); pleasant feeling is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*);
and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). As for the three applications of mindfulness of mind:

This refers to contemplating that the mind is impermanent because the four types of mind—greed, hatred, delusion, and those with equal proportions—constantly fluctuate. Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*): this refers to contemplating that all phenomena are without self. "Phenomena" refers to the phenomena of the five aggregates and so forth; they are devoid of a self or anything belonging to a self. This means contemplating that the body in the Pure Land is ultimately pure. In contrast to the seven kinds of impurity in the Sahā world, one briefly clarifies the seven kinds of purity and resolves to generate the bodhicitta.

Taking birth is pure, as he sits upright upon a lotus throne; his dwelling is pure, consisting of the joy of dhyāna and the delight of the Dharma;

△ Second, the Four Right Efforts.
[Commentary]: The four right efforts are: first, the abandonment of unwholesome states that have already arisen; second, the non-arising of unwholesome states not yet arisen;
third, the arising of wholesome states not yet arisen; and fourth, the increase and cultivation of wholesome states that have already arisen.
[Commentary]: "Right Effort" refers to right diligence (*samyag-vīrya*). "Evil that has already arisen" refers to the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava* and *bhāvanā-āsrava*).

"Evil not yet arisen" refers to the afflictions of the dust-like sands and ignorance (*avidyā*). "Good not yet arisen" refers to the Knowledge of the Paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). "Good that has already arisen" refers to the Omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Regarding "Right Effort for the Pure Land," it means that with every thought, one does not [forsake] even a single phrase of the Buddha’s name.
Abandonment. To maintain mindfulness at every moment without interruption is right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*).
△ 34. The Four Bases of Psychic Power (*ṛddhipāda*). [Commentary]: The four bases of psychic power are:
first, the base of psychic power of desire (*chanda-ṛddhipāda*); second, the base of psychic power of energy (*vīrya-ṛddhipāda*); third, the base of psychic power of mind (*citta-ṛddhipāda*)...
The bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*). [Commentary:

As for the bases of power, they are so called because all that is wished for is accomplished. They are also called the four bases of miraculous power (*ṛddhipāda*) because they are able to give rise to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
"Wish as one desires" (*chanda-ṛddhipāda*) refers to the longing, yearning, and delight directed toward the object of contemplation. "Diligence as one desires" (*vīrya-ṛddhipāda*)...
Regarding the object of observation, it is refined and not mixed; it advances and does not retreat. "Mind as desired" (*cittakāma*) is also called "mindfulness as desired" (*smṛtikāma*);
it is the mind dwelling correctly and single-mindedly upon the object of observation. "Contemplation as desired" (*vitarkakāma*) is also called "wisdom as desired" (*prajñākāma*);
it is the mind not wandering or scattering from the object of observation. ○ Regarding the "basis of power of the pure land" (*śuddhakṣetrarddhipāda*).
To joyfully seek the Land of Ultimate Bliss is the fulfillment of one’s desire; to advance directly without retreating is diligence;
for each phrase to be clearly distinct is the fulfillment of the mind, as well as the fulfillment of contemplation.
△ Four or five faculties.
【Explanation】 Regarding the five faculties: having faith in the right path and the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).

Diligently seeking the right path and all wholesome factors conducive to enlightenment without ceasing is called the faculty of vigor (*vīryendriya*). Mindfulness of the right path and all wholesome factors conducive to enlightenment...

The Dharma. To have no other thoughts is called the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*). To collect the mind within the right path and the various wholesome dharmas that assist the path, remaining in association with them without distraction, is called the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*).

To contemplate the Four Noble Truths, such as suffering and so forth, for the sake of the right path and the various wholesome dharmas that assist the path, is called the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).

[Commentary] The "right path" refers to the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). Because it can destroy the four inversions, it is called the right path. The "auxiliary path" refers to other supportive practices;
that is, practices such as giving (*dāna*) and observing the precepts (*śīla*) are called the auxiliary path. The text is easy to understand.

Regarding the statement that the contemplation of the four truths, such as suffering, is called the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*): this refers to the sixteen aspects of contemplation (*ṣoḍaśākāra*). The preceding four foundations of mindfulness constitute the general [category].

It possesses the four truths. This specifically reveals the four truths. What constitutes their general possession? That is to say, the body, sensation, mind, and phenomena that are observed constitute the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
The means of observation—impurity, suffering, impermanence, and non-self—are the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*). The four inversions (*viparyāsa*) are the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).

The non-arising of the four inversions is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*). What constitutes their specific revelation? Each of the four truths specifically reveals four modes of contemplation.

The four sets of four constitute sixteen contemplations; thus, they are explained separately. One should contemplate these numerical categories of the Dharma. Regarding the five faculties of the Pure Land:

to have faith in this single phrase of the Buddha’s name is the lotus root of the nine grades of rebirth. To maintain this without ceasing from moment to moment is called the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*).
To have no other thoughts is the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*). To remain with a single mind without distraction is the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*).
The suffering and accumulation [of the world] of Sahā are severed; the path and cessation of Sukhāvatī are accomplished. This is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
△ Five. The Five Powers (*pañcabala*).

【Explanation】 As for the five powers: when the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) increases, it is able to destroy doubt and confusion, to destroy all false beliefs, and to destroy the afflictions (*kleśa*).

The faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) increases and is called the power of faith (*śraddhābala*). It destroys various forms of physical and mental indolence and accomplishes the great task of transcending the world.

The faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*) increases and is called the power of diligence (*vīryabala*). It destroys all wrong thoughts and achieves all meritorious qualities of right mindfulness that transcend the world.

The faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) increases and is called the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*). It destroys all distracted thoughts and gives rise to all [virtuous] activities. The faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*) increases and is able to destroy discursive thoughts and give rise to all [meditative] objects.

Cultivating meditative concentration is called the power of concentration (*samādhi-bala*). When the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) increases, it is able to obstruct both the universal and specific afflictions and give rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*);
this is called the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*).

[Commentary] As for the five powers, they refer to the functional capacity of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) when increased, which is able to destroy the five hindrances. When the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) increases...
"Lengthy and so forth" means that through clear and distinct contemplation, right faith naturally increases and false faith naturally perishes;
thus, the four inversions do not arise, which is why it is called "destroying afflictions. Regarding "the faculty of diligence increases and so forth":
bodily diligence destroys bodily indolence, verbal diligence destroys verbal indolence, and mental diligence destroys mental indolence, thereby accomplishing transcendence.
The great matters of the world pertain to body, speech, and mind. Regarding "the growth of the faculty of mindfulness" (*smṛtīndriya*) and so forth:

it refers to the growth of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), which destroys the false mindfulness of the four inversions and accomplishes the supramundane wisdom of impurity, the wisdom of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), and so forth—namely, the virtues of the four wisdoms.

Regarding "the growth of the faculty of concentration" (*samādhīndriya*) and so forth: it is able to destroy the distracted thoughts of the desire realm and brings about the attainment of mundane *dhyāna*.

The four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and so forth; or the supramundane contemplations on principle, the six subtle gates (*ṣaḍ-sūkṣma-dvāra*), the sixteen special victories (*ṣoḍaśa-viśeṣa-jaya*), and so forth—these are called the power of concentration (*samādhi-bala*).
As for the growth of the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) and so forth, it is able to obstruct the pervasive delusions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).

Regarding the "afflictions common to all": because they are severed equally by the three vehicles. Furthermore, they can obstruct the specific afflictions of the "dust-like" ignorance so that they do not arise;
these specific afflictions are severed only by Bodhisattvas and are not severed by the two vehicles. This gives rise to the untainted wisdom of the true reality.
Regarding the "five powers of the Pure Land": first, through single-mindedness without distraction, one is not afflicted by the Saha world.
It is movement.
△ 6–7. The Factors of Enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
[Commentary]: The seven factors of enlightenment are also called the seven limbs of awakening. When wisdom contemplates all phenomena, it is well able to discern and distinguish them.
To discern truth from falsehood and not mistakenly adopt deceptive phenomena is called the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

When one diligently cultivates the various path-phenomena, being well able to awaken to them and not mistakenly engaging in fruitless asceticism, but always maintaining a diligent mind within the practice of the true Dharma, this is called the awakening factor of diligence (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
If the mind attains joy in the Dharma, being well able to awaken to this joy—
To take no delight in inverted dharmas, but to abide in the true joy of the Dharma, is called the awakening factor of rapture (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

When one eliminates the afflictions of various views, being able to discern well and remove all falsehoods without damaging the genuine roots of goodness, is called the awakening factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
When one abandons the attachment to objects of perception, being able to discern well that which is abandoned...
The realm of the false and unreal is never again recollected; this is called the awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

When entering various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), one is skillfully able to discern that these absorptions are provisional and false, giving rise to no attachment, views, or deluded thoughts; this is called the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
When cultivating the supramundane path, one is skillfully able to discern how to always maintain the balance between concentration and wisdom, or when the mind...
If [the mind] sinks, one should constantly attend to the three awakening factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, and joy to observe and arouse it.

If the mind becomes agitated, one should constantly attend to the three awakening factors of equanimity, relinquishment, and concentration to restrain and hold it. Thus, one brings them into a state of balanced harmony.

This is called the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*). [Commentary: Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment, they are also called the seven limbs of awakening. In Sanskrit, *bodhi* means "perfect awakening" (*samyag-bodha*) in Chinese.
This refers to the aforementioned arousal of true, outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), which is never absent from moment to moment; hence it is called a "limb of enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣa*).
Regarding "wisdom contemplates all phenomena" (*dharmas*): "all phenomena" refers to the true and false phenomena, such as the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and so forth.
Those that are associated with outflow-free wisdom are true phenomena; those not so associated are termed false and deceptive phenomena. One diligently cultivates the various paths.

Regarding "the Dharma and so forth": the dharmas of the path are the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*). If they are associated with untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), they are called beneficial true dharmas;

if they are not associated [with such wisdom], they are merely fruitless ascetic practices. Regarding "if the mind attains the joy of the Dharma and so forth": [this refers to the attainment of such states].
If it is joy associated with untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), it is the true joy of the Dharma; yet even this joy of the Dharma is not permitted to be clung to.
If it is associated with the four inversions (*catur-viparyāsa*), it is called inverted joy.

If one eliminates various views, afflictions, and so forth, one thereby severs the delusions of view, such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and extreme views. True roots of goodness are untainted wisdom itself.
Regarding "if one abandons what is seen, what is thought of, what is clung to, and so forth":

"what is seen, what is thought of, and what is clung to" refers to the objects of what is seen, what is thought of, and what is clung to—namely, the characteristics of the body and the characteristics of the self as grasped by the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). These are "false and unreal."

This object is originally non-existent; it appears to exist only because of attachment through thought. It is, therefore, an image transformed by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and is thus called unreal.
As for "giving rise to the various dhyānas and so forth," these refer to the four dhyānas and eight samādhis, which are mundane meditations;

hence they are called false and provisional. "Not giving rise to craving or views": craving refers to the delusions of affliction (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*), while views refer to the delusions of wrong understanding (*dṛṣṭy-āvaraṇa*); both are termed delusive.

Regarding "perception": if one cultivates supramundane paths and so forth, these seven categories of the factors of enlightenment are precisely the factors of the path for transcending the three realms.
If the mind sinks, then concentration (*samādhi*) exceeds wisdom (*prajñā*); if the mind is restless, then wisdom exceeds concentration.
None of these can give rise to the truth. When concentration and wisdom are balanced, one is still yet constantly illuminating, and illuminating yet constantly still;

thus, one is able to give rise to the truth. ○ Regarding the "Factor of Enlightenment of the Pure Land": a single thought in accord with reality is a Buddha; every thought in accord with reality is a Buddha.
This is precisely the factor of enlightenment of the Pure Land.
△ 7–8. The Factors of the Noble Path. [Commentary:

The eight factors of the noble path are also called the eightfold right path. Cultivating the contemplation of untainted practice (*anāsrava-caryā*) and clearly perceiving the Four Truths is termed Right View (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*).
Contemplating with an untainted mind, initiating awakening and cognition, and exercising deliberation constitutes [Right Resolve].
Causing [the roots of goodness] to increase and enter into Great Nirvana is called Right Thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).

Using untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) to eliminate the four types of wrong livelihood and encompassing all vocal actions while abiding within all right speech is called Right Speech (*samyag-vāc*).
Using untainted wisdom to eliminate all wrong bodily actions and abiding within pure right bodily action is called Right Action (*samyak-karmānta*). Using untainted wisdom to penetrate...
To abide in pure and right livelihood by eliminating the five types of wrong livelihood within the three modes of action is called right livelihood.

(The five wrong livelihoods all concern gain and honor: first, falsely manifesting extraordinary or strange appearances; second, speaking of one's own merits; third, divining good or bad fortune and preaching the Dharma for others; fourth, raising one's voice and displaying an air of authority to inspire awe and respect in others; fifth, speaking of the offerings one has received to stir the hearts of people.
To apply oneself with diligence and vigor to cultivate the path to Nirvāṇa in association with untainted wisdom is called right effort.
Mindfulness associated with untainted wisdom that correctly attends to the noble path and the factors conducive to enlightenment is called right mindfulness.
Concentration associated with untainted wisdom through the attainment of meditative absorption is called right concentration.
[Commentary]: Regarding the "eightfold noble path" (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), which is also called the "eightfold right path," this is the correct path practiced by the sages (*ārya*).
It is called "right" (*samyak*) because it consists of untainted (*anāsrava*) noble dharmas; it is called "path" (*mārga*) because it leads directly to *nirvāṇa*.

As for "practicing untainted contemplations of the formations and so forth," the "untainted contemplations of the formations" refers to the sixteen aspects of the contemplation of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path (*duḥkha-samudaya-nirodha-mārga-ṣoḍaśākāra-vipaśyanā*). One practices these contemplations.

It only ascends; it cannot leak downward. Therefore, it is called "contemplation of the outflow-free" (*anāsrava*). Because the eye of wisdom is clear and distinct, it is called "right view" (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the phrase "associated with the outflow-free mind" and so forth: the outflow-free mind is precisely the knowledge of the Four Noble Truths.
This is collectively termed the "mind of omniscience" (*sarvajñā-citta*). Regarding "contemplative arousal":

it refers to the activation of the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths (*catur-ārya-satya*), the awakening to and deliberation upon the objects of the Four Noble Truths, for the purpose of increasing the four types of knowledge (*jñāna*), severing delusions, and realizing the truth.

As for "removing the four wrong livelihoods and so forth with untainted wisdom" (*anāsrava-prajñā*): the four wrong modes of livelihood (*mithyājīva*) are as follows: first, the "mouth-food," which refers to crookedness and flattery.

First is seeking profit through power and influence, acting as a messenger to the four quarters. Second is seeking profit through the mouth, referring to various incantations and divinations of good and bad fortune.
Third is seeking profit by looking upward, meaning sustaining one's life by observing the stars and constellations.

Fourth is seeking profit by looking downward, such as cultivating fields and gardens or compounding medicinal decoctions. These four ways of seeking gain with a deviant mind to sustain one's life are therefore called "deviant" (*mithyā*).
Life. Departing from these four perversions, one exclusively practices begging for alms, speaks truthful and real words, restrains all vocal karma, and abides in right speech.
By means of untainted wisdom, one eliminates all perverse bodily karma;

that is to say, since there is not even non-killing, non-stealing, and non-sexuality [in the sense of mere absence], how much less could there be the karmas of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct? Therefore, it is called "pure and right bodily karma."
Regarding "using untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) to universally eliminate [unwholesome conduct]" and so forth:

whereas the two preceding [perfections] eliminate [faults of] body and speech individually, this one eliminates all three types of action (*karma*) universally, because the five forms of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*) pertain to all three types of action. Since they are eliminated by means of untainted wisdom, it is called "pure right livelihood" (*viśuddha-samyagājīva*).
Regarding "exerting diligence associated with untainted wisdom" and so forth, this refers to the practice of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
At that time, the wisdom of selflessness (*anātma-prajñā*) stands before one, preventing the arising of the grasping at a self; this is called right diligence on the path to *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding "being associated with outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) and mindfulness of the right path," etc., it means practicing the right path and the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), taking outflow-free wisdom as a whole for right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).
Regarding "being associated with outflow-free wisdom and entering meditative concentration (*samādhi)," it refers to entering meditative concentration.

Previously, we first raised the topic of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), which is capable of giving rise to untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*). Regarding the "right path to the Pure Land":
a single phrase of the Buddha’s name is the direct path to the Pure Land.

These categories of the path (mārga-aṅga) are practiced based on the four truths of arising and ceasing (and thus possess the merit of correcting errors); these are the path-categories of the Tripitaka Teaching.

They are practiced based on the four truths of non-arising; these are the path-categories of the Shared Teaching. They are practiced based on the four truths of the immeasurable; these are the path-categories of the Distinct Teaching.
The *Mārga-varga* (Chapter on the Path). It is practiced in reliance upon the unconditioned Four Noble Truths; that is, the *mārga-varga* of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

[Commentary] As for the *mārga-varga*, it is the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) among the Four Noble Truths. In the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, nothing is found that does not fall within the Four Noble Truths.
This is the World-Honored One’s wondrous wisdom for benefiting others; it is like prescribing medicine according to the illness.
If the illness of views and afflictions is heavy, he teaches the Four Truths of Arising and Ceasing. If the illness of views and afflictions is light, he teaches the Four Truths of Non-Arising.
If the illness of ignorance is heavy, he teaches the Four Truths of the Immeasurable. If the illness of ignorance is light, he teaches the Four Truths of Non-Action.
The Great Master Zhiyi classified these as the Four Teachings and the Four Truths. Regarding the "Zangjiao" (Store Teaching), this refers to the Tripitaka Teaching:
the *Catuṣpariṣat-sūtra* and other texts constitute the Sūtra Piṭaka; the *Vinaya* constitutes the Vinaya Piṭaka; and the *Abhidharma* constitutes the Śāstra Piṭaka.

This is called the Tripitaka of the Hīnayāna, established by name according to phenomena (*dharma*). The latter three teachings are Mahāyāna, established by name according to principle (*tattva*). This teaching...
The "Shared Teaching" (Tongjiao) exclusively elucidates the four truths of arising and ceasing, the twelve links of dependent origination, and the six perfections as phenomena.

It is called "Shared" because it is common to both the Great and Small Vehicles: those of dull faculties share it with the preceding Tripitaka Teachings, while those of sharp faculties share it with the subsequent Distinct and Complete Teachings. Therefore, it is termed "Shared."
This is the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna, which elucidates the Four Truths of Non-arising, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and so forth. As for the "Distinct Teaching" (Bie-jiao):

it is called "distinct" because its doctrine, principle, wisdom, abandonment, practice, stages, cause, and fruit differ from those of the preceding *Zang* (Āgama) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings, and differ from the subsequent Perfect Teaching (*Yuan-jiao*). Thus, it is distinct.
The Dharma of the Bodhisattvas alone elucidates the immeasurable Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and so forth. As for the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao):
it is called the Perfect Teaching because its teaching, principle, wisdom, abandonment, practice, stages, cause, and fruit are all perfectly interfused;

thus, it elucidates the Unconditioned Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and so forth. Regarding the Four Noble Truths of Arising and Ceasing: in the Truth of Suffering, there are the three [phases] of arising, abiding, and ceasing.

They undergo mutual transition. The Truth of Origination consists of greed, hatred, delusion, and their equal combination; these four states of mind are in constant flux. The Truth of the Path consists of antidotes that are easily subverted.
The Truth of Cessation consists of the extinction of existence and its return to non-existence. It is the same for the sentient beings of the Pure Land.

If those of a lesser disposition ripen first, they will certainly hear the Four Noble Truths of Arising and Ceasing and receive the factors of the Path of Arising and Ceasing; they naturally belong to the *Pitaka* (the Tripitaka).

Therefore, it is said that one practices based on the four truths of arising and ceasing; this refers to the *dharmapada* (factors of the path) of the Tripitaka Teaching. As for the four truths of non-arising:

the truth of suffering is like an illusion and like a transformation, lacking the characteristic of oppression. The truth of origination is like an illusion and like a transformation, lacking the characteristic of conjunction.

The truth of cessation, which is *nirvāṇa*, is like an illusion and like a transformation, lacking the characteristic of arising. The truth of the path is [like an illusion and like a transformation, lacking the characteristic of origination], just as the truth of origination is.

Like illusions and like transformations, they possess no dual characteristics. If one is a practitioner of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), they will certainly hear of the Four Truths of Non-arising and receive the Path Factors of Non-arising;
therefore, it is said that they cultivate "in reliance upon the Four Truths of Non-arising," which refers precisely to the Path Factors of the Shared Teaching.
Regarding the immeasurable Four Noble Truths: suffering has immeasurable aspects because the retributions of the ten realms are not the same;

origination has immeasurable aspects because the afflictions of the five abodes are not the same; the path has immeasurable aspects because the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are not the same;
and cessation has immeasurable aspects because the various pāramitās are not the same. This is according to the Separate Teaching (biejiao).
The capacity [of the practitioner] is such that they definitively hear the immeasurable Four Noble Truths and receive the immeasurable factors of the path; therefore it is said:
"If one practices in reliance upon the immeasurable Four Noble Truths, this is precisely the distinct factors of the path. As for the Unconditioned (anabhisaṃskāra) Four Noble Truths:

all four truths are the true mark of Thusness (tathatā), being unconditioned and non-active; therefore they are called "unconditioned. Regarding the truth of suffering, the aggregates (skandhas) and sense bases (āyatanas) are all thusness, and there is no suffering to be found.
Regarding cessation (*nirodha-satya*): afflictions are fundamentally pure; there is no accumulation to be severed. Regarding the path (*mārga-satya*):

extremes and deviance are all inherently the Middle Way; there is no path to be cultivated. Regarding cessation (*nirodha-satya*): birth and death are themselves *nirvāṇa*; there is no cessation to be realized.

For those with the capacity for the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), they will certainly hear of the Four Truths of Non-action (*wu zuo*) and receive the Path-factors of Non-action; therefore, it is said that they rely on non-action.
One cultivates the Four Truths to perfect the factors of the path. This concludes the detailed analysis of the four teachings.
II. Detailed Analysis of the Four Lands. [Commentary]:

The factors of the path in the *Hīnayāna* (Zàng) are called the "Dharma-gate of Half-Characters. Since the defilements are light in the Pure Land, they seem unnecessary; this is for those of small capacity.
Regarding those who mature first: some may use them temporarily. The "Stages of the Common Path" (*sādhāraṇa-mārga*) is called the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna;

it is what all three vehicles (*triyāna*) receive in common, and it is frequently taught in the *Sahā* Pure Land. The "Stages of the Distinct Path" (*viśeṣa-mārga*) is called the unique Dharma of the Bodhisattvas;

it is frequently taught in the *Upāya-saṃbhoga* Pure Land. The "Stages of the Perfect Path" (*pariniṣpanna-mārga*) is called the Unsurpassed Buddha-Dharma. For those of sharp faculties, regarding these four...
"In the Pure Land, all shall hear [the Dharma]" (this is precisely the Pure Land School of Ultimate Bliss). [Commentary]:
"The teaching of the half-syllables" is a metaphor for the partial principles of the Hīnayāna, which are not complete. Regarding "the turbidity is light in the Pure Land":
the Pure Land is originally free from turbidity; it is only because sentient beings from the Sahā world are born in that land that there is slight turbidity.
It is as follows: that which seems unnecessary may be used temporarily if one possesses the seeds of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) that have already matured;

however, if one lacks such seeds, it need not be used regularly. Regarding the "initial gate of the Mahāyāna," this refers to the initial gates of both the Separate (Bebhidya) and Complete (Yuan) Teachings.
It is frequently explained in the context of the Shared Pure Land because the sentient beings of the Shared Land still possess the afflictions of views and thoughts (dṛṣṭi- and bhava-āsrava).
This is the discourse on the Chapter on the Path of Non-arising. Regarding "the Dharma unique to Bodhisattvas," this refers exclusively to the practices performed by Bodhisattvas.

Regarding "mostly taught in the shared expedient [land]," this means it is not used in the two higher lands. Regarding "the Chapter on the Perfect Path being heard in all four lands," this refers to the fact that it is heard throughout all four lands.
Because the four lands are perfectly interfused, this is the fundamental tenet of the Pure Land. Thus, in the Land of Common Residence, all four teachings are present;

in the Land of Expedient Means, there are only the Separate and Complete Teachings; in the Land of Real Reward, there is only the Complete Teaching; and in the Land of Tranquil Light, there is neither teaching nor non-teaching.
The analysis is complete. The explanation of the Path Factors (Dharmapada) is finished.
△ Second, the explanation of "and so forth" (ādi).
[Commentary: Regarding "and so forth," it refers to the previous foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), and bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

It also includes the remaining four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), the six perfections (*pāramitā*), the ten powers (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and the immeasurable dharma-gates. Although the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) exhaustively encompass all dharmas, yet...
As capacities and conditions vary, he employs various methods of exposition and synthesis; though names and meanings differ, he expounds everything according to what the listeners wish to hear.
Thus, he causes those who hear him to take refuge in the Triple Gem, resolve upon Bodhicitta, and subdue and extinguish their afflictions.

[Commentary] The text is divided into two sections: first, the direct explanation of the text; second, the clarification of the opening and closing [of the categories]. First, the direct explanation: Regarding the "four means of attraction" (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*):

first, attraction through giving; second, attraction through kind speech; third, attraction through beneficial conduct; and fourth, attraction through common purpose. By means of these four dharmas, one gathers and attracts sentient beings.
Regarding the "six perfections" (*ṣaṭ pāramitāḥ*): giving overcomes stinginess and greed; ethical discipline overcomes the violation of precepts.
Patience overcomes anger and resentment; diligence overcomes indolence; meditative concentration overcomes distraction; and wisdom overcomes ignorance.
Regarding the "ten powers," these are the ten kinds of intellectual power of the Tathāgata. The first is the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna-bala*).
2. The power of knowing karma; 3. The power of knowing meditative concentrations; 4. The power of knowing the faculties; 5. The power of knowing inclinations; 6. The power of knowing elements; 7.
The power of knowing the paths leading to various destinations; 8. The power of recollecting past lives; 9. The power of the divine eye; 10.
The power of the exhaustion of outflows. Regarding the four fearlessnesses: 1. Fearlessness regarding omniscience. At...

1. Fearlessness in the knowledge and vision of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-jñānadarśana-vaiśāradya*). Because one has thoroughly exhausted and realized the five abodes (*pañca-vihāra*). 2. Fearlessness in the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vaiśāradya*).

Because one has thoroughly known and taught the phenomena that obstruct the path (*mārgāvaraṇa-dharma*). 3. Fearlessness in teaching the obstacles to the path (*antarāyika-dharma-vaiśāradya*). Because one is able to know and teach the path that exhausts suffering (*duḥkhakṣayamārga*).
These four encompass the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) and other qualities, all of which possess the four methods of instruction (*catasro deśanāḥ*). Fearing prolixity, they are not detailed here.

Record. Second, the clarification of opening and closing. "Though the inclusion of dharmas is exhaustive" means that within the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) all dharmas are fully present, and within all dharmas the factors of enlightenment are fully present.
"Sentient capacities and conditions are unequal" refers to the four teachings and four types of capacity, with the four *siddhāntas* serving as the conditions;
hence they are said to be unequal. Regarding the various differences in names and meanings through opening and closing: if it concerns the capacity for the *Hīnayāna* (Tripitaka) teaching...

For those with the capacity for the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), they open the categories of the path of non-arising (*anutpāda*), as well as immeasurable Dharma-gates such as the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the six perfections (*pāramitā*). The same applies to the Distinct and Perfect Teachings.

To expound and elaborate upon these is called "opening" (*kai*); not to expound them is called "closing" (*he*). Furthermore, if the conditions and capacities of the audience favor extensiveness, then...
He extensively expounds the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, thereby accomplishing immeasurable Dharma-gates.

If the capacity and conditions of the listeners favor brevity, he instead expounds the path-factors (mārga-aṅga), accomplishing the six perfections, the four means of integration, and so forth; thus their names differ.

According to the names, the meanings are revealed, and the meanings themselves also vary. In summary, whatever they wish to hear, there is nothing he does not expound clearly, fully exhausting what is appropriate for each case. No... [text ends]
Since they have not yet arrived, this causes those who hear [this teaching] to perfectly recollect the Triple Gem, perfectly give rise to the three minds, and perfectly sever the three delusions.
This concludes the second explanation of the equal dharmas.
△ Third, the explanation of mindfulness of the Triple Gem, which has two parts: first, the formal exposition; second, the analytical discussion. △ Now, the first. [Commentary:

Because one clearly perceives that the compassionate majesty [of the Buddha] is inconceivable, one recollects the Buddha. The joy of the Dharma enters the heart, and the flavor of the Dharma becomes sufficient.

Therefore, one recollects the Dharma. Having heard and received it together, one cultivates and realizes it with a single mind; thus one recollects the Sangha (these three phrases each possess four benefits, as seen in detail below in the explanation of the recollection of the Triple Gem).

[Commentary] This passage correctly clarifies the causes and conditions for mindfulness of the Three Jewels. "To see clearly" means to be born in the Pure Land and personally behold the three bodies (*trikāya*) of Amitābha.
For those of the two capacities of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and *Pratyekabuddha* vehicles, they see clearly the inconceivable compassion and majesty of Amitābha’s transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Therefore, they practice mindfulness of the Buddha; upon hearing the Dharma of the vehicle-vehicle chapters, their hearts enter into the joy of the True Truth (*satyadharma*).

Because the flavor [of the Dharma] is sufficient, one contemplates the Dharma (*dharmānusmṛti*). Because one hears and receives [the teachings] together with the sages and worthies of the *pitaka* and the *pāṭha*, and dwells within the same land practicing and realizing with a single mind, one contemplates the Sangha (*saṃghānusmṛti*).

If one possesses the capacities of either the Distinct or the Perfect [vehicles], one clearly perceives that the compassion and majesty of Amitābha’s two bodies—the recompense body and the dharma body—are inconceivable;
thus, one contemplates the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*). Upon hearing the factors of enlightenment of the Distinct and Perfect paths, the joy of the Dharma enters the heart.
Within the mundane world, one contemplates the Dharma because it is replete with the flavor of the two truths.

One contemplates the Sangha because one hears and receives [the teachings] together with the sages and worthies of the Separate and Perfect Teachings, practicing and realizing them with a single mind within the lands of Expedient Means, True Reward, and Ultimate Reward. Thus concludes the explicit explanation.
△ Second, a comparative analysis. [Commentary:

The capacity for mindfulness is itself the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*). That which is the object of mindfulness—the Three Jewels—possesses both distinct characteristics (*bhinnalakṣaṇa*) and a single essence (*ekasvabhāva*), as well as the meanings and principles of the four teachings (*catuṣparyāya*).
The differences between the provisional and the real regarding the three truths should be understood as they were analyzed above in the section on the factors of the path (*mārga*).

[Commentary]: This distinguishes between the subject that recollects (*nominative*) and the object that is recollected (*objective*). "The subject that recollects is the three contemplations" distinguishes the subject that recollects.

This refers to the emptiness through analysis in the Tripiṭaka Teaching, the emptiness of essence in the Shared Teaching, the sequential [emptiness] in the Distinct Teaching, and the single mind in the Perfect Teaching.
Regarding the phrase "the Three Jewels as objects of mindfulness" below: when distinguishing the objects of mindfulness, they differ;

there are the Three Jewels of distinct characteristics, the Three Jewels of identical essence, and the Three Jewels of the four teachings, the Three Jewels of the three truths, and the provisional and real Three Jewels, as explained in the preceding passage by means of the four...

The analysis of the stages of the path (*mārga*) according to the four realms of reality (*catur-bhūmi*) should be understood accordingly. Regarding the distinct-characteristic Three Jewels (*pṛthak-lakṣaṇa-triratna*):

the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) constitute the Buddha Jewel of the four teachings; the teaching, wisdom, and severance constitute the Dharma Jewel of the four teachings;

and the noble ones and sages of the three vehicles constitute the Saṅgha Jewel of the four teachings. Regarding the single-essence Three Jewels (*eka-svabhāva-triratna*): true suchness (*tathatā*) as awakened realization is the Buddha Jewel; the entire body as the norm...
Thus, [the wisdom] is the Jewel of the Dharma; the harmony of principle and wisdom constitutes the Jewel of the Sangha. Regarding the meaning of the four teachings:
their distinct characteristics and their single essence each comprise four teachings. The distinct characteristics are easily understood.

As for the "single essence," the wisdom that performs the contemplation is the Buddha-jewel, the principle that is the object of contemplation is the Dharma-jewel, and the harmony of the subject and object is the Sangha-jewel. The "meaning" refers to the one...

"Essence" (*tǐ*) refers to the [ultimate] nature. "Meaning" (*yì*) refers to the distinct characteristics (*biéxiàng*). Regarding the "Three Truths": in the *Zàng* (Āgama) and *Tōng* (Shared) teachings, they are the Three Jewels of the Single Truth of Reality (*zhēndì*).

In the *Bié* (Distinct) teaching, they are the Three Jewels of the Three Truths in Succession (*cìdì*), which are sequential and discrete; furthermore, these constitute the Three Jewels of the Conventional Truth (*sùdì*).

In the *Yuán* (Perfect) teaching, they are the Three Jewels of the Three Truths within a Single Mind (*yīxīn*), which are perfectly interfused; furthermore, these constitute the Three Jewels of the Middle Truth (*zhōngdì*). This is the provisional and the real.

Regarding this: the first three teachings are provisional (*upāya*), while the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*) is the reality. The distinct characteristics (*pṛthag-lakṣaṇa*) are provisional, while the single essence (*eka-rasa*) is the reality. Within the first three teachings, the single essence is collectively provisional;
only the single essence of the Perfect Teaching is the reality. Furthermore, to distinguish the four lands (*catur-bhūmi*): the Land of Common Dwelling (*sahā-loka-dhātu*) possesses all [four];

the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-kauśalya*) excludes the *Hīnayāna* (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha) and the Shared Teaching (*samāna-yāna*); the Land of Real Reward (*bhūtakoṭi-vipāka*) excludes the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*); and the Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhā*) [excludes the previous three].
Furthermore, regarding the distinguishing characteristics: there is no recollection and no realization; there is neither three nor one, yet it can universally manifest all things.

This concludes the third explanation of "recollection" regarding the Three Jewels in the commentary. This completes the first section of the sutra text concerning the Dharma-benefit of the birds' cries.
△ Second, the interrogation, explanation, and brief manifestation.
"Śāriputra, do not say that these birds are actually born as a retribution for their sins. Why is this?
In that Buddha-land, there are no three evil realms. Śāriputra, in that Buddha-land, even the names of the evil realms do not exist; how much less could there be such beings?"
How much more so for those that are real? All these various birds are transformations produced by Amitābha Buddha, intended to cause the sound of the Dharma to flow forth.

△ The commentary divides this into three parts: first, a question-and-answer refuting doubts; second, a question-and-answer revealing the benefits; third, pointing out and indicating the significance.
[The] Finger. △ Now, the first [section]. [Commentary:
The inquiry and the explanation may be understood. Question: Are names such as "white crane" not names for the evil realms? Answer:

Since these are not retributions for transgressions, each and every name expresses the ultimate merit of the Tathāgata (the inconceivable dharma-realm of names being thus). That is to say, they are the ultimate white cranes and so forth.
There is nothing that is not a virtuous quality of nature; how could it be an ill repute?
[Commentary] This is the resolution of residual doubts regarding the "ill repute.

While the doubts concerning the reality of phenomena (*dharmas*) have been largely clarified through the interrogation and explanation in the Sūtra, the fact that there is no name for the evil realms remains obscure. Therefore, the question is asked: "Are the white cranes and so forth not evil?"
Regarding the names of the paths: why do you say that even the names of the evil realms do not exist? The answer is:

since the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are not retributions for sin, their provisional names (*prajñapti-nāman*) are likewise not evil names. That which is not a retribution for sin is a retribution for goodness; that which is not an evil name is a good name.
A retribution for goodness is the ultimate merit of the five aggregates; a good name is the ultimate merit of provisional names.
Virtue. Therefore it is said that each and every name explains the ultimate virtues of the Tathāgata.

"Each and every name" refers to the provisional names of the Buddha, as well as the provisional names for even such things as white cranes. "Explains" means to use provisional names to elucidate and manifest the true Dharma.
"Ultimate virtues" refers to the virtues realized by the Tathāgata, who has reached the exhaustion of the ten dharma-realms.

Regarding what is called "the ultimate white crane" and so forth: since the Buddha has realized the nature of the dharma-realm to its ultimate limit, that which is ultimate in one thing is ultimate in all things.
To the Buddha, he is the ultimate Buddha; to the white crane, it is the ultimate white crane;

this is also the ultimate śarīra, and the ultimate dung beetle, and so on. There is nothing that is not a sublime designation for the virtues of the nature (dharmatā-guṇa). This applies to the ten realms.

The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all the functional virtues and activities inherently present within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). The provisional names of the ten realms (*daśa-dhātu*) are likewise the beautiful designations inherent in their nature.
How could they be merely the provisional names for the evil paths of the Sahā world? Therefore, it is said that the Dharma-realm of names is inconceivable.
The first section, consisting of questions and answers to dispel doubts, is concluded.
△ Second, the question and answer revealing the benefits. [Commentary] Question:

What is the significance of manifesting as various birds? Answer: There are four *siddhāntas* (teachings) for this purpose (in this sutra, all *siddhāntas* are the ultimate truth [*paramārtha-satya*] while encompassing the three lower *siddhāntas*).

Ordinary beings take pleasure in these various birds; thus, he manifests them in accordance with their inclinations to cause them joy. Furthermore, even birds preach the Dharma, causing those who hear it to give rise to wholesome roots. Therefore, [he does not manifest as such for other reasons].
One should conceive of the bird as inferior in order to counteract the discriminative mind;
thus, the bird is Amitābha, causing one to realize that the Dharmakāya is equal, being neither incomplete nor uncreated.
[Commentary] The text is easy to understand. "The bird is Amida" means that the bird is the Dharmadhātu-garbha-body (the body as the treasury of the Dharma-realm).

This causes those who hear the Dharma to awaken to and enter the Dharmadhātu-garbha-body, wherein there is not a single dharma that is not fully present and not a single dharma that is not created; thus, one attains the benefit of entering into principle.
This explanation of *siddhānta* (the established tenet) shows that within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), all three lower *siddhāntas* are fully contained. It is transcendent...

Because this sutra differs from other sutras. Other sutras possess the four teachings and the four *siddhāntas*; this sutra, however, consists purely of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*) and the four *siddhāntas*.
The Perfect Teaching is the teaching of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and the Buddha is the personification of the ultimate truth.

Within the Perfect Teaching, one realizes the four *siddhāntas* through partial realization; therefore, within the ultimate truth, the three lower *siddhāntas* are fully contained. This is partial realization.
The four *siddhāntas* are explained in the text below. The section on "Question and Answer Revealing Benefits" is concluded.
△ Third, "Pointing Out and Indicating. [Commentary]:
