Herein, it is revealed that the subtle sounds of wind, trees, nets, and so forth, as well as all phenomena of the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-dharmin*), whether provisional or real, are, in their very essence, [the Dharma-body].
These three bodies and four virtues of Amitābha Buddha are entirely without distinction (which may be called the pointing finger toward the Dharma-realm).
[Commentary] "Pointing finger toward the Dharma-realm" refers to words that directly indicate the Dharma-realm. The Dharma-realm is precisely one's own self-nature.
Regarding the phrase "manifesting therein" and so forth: within the section on the wondrous unity of the environment and its inhabitants, it manifests the six sense objects of Sukhāvatī.

This is the realm [of Amitābha]. A gentle breeze is the dust of touch (*spraṣṭavya*). Tree nets are the three dusts of form, odor, and taste (*rūpa*, *gandha*, *rasa*). Sound is the dust of sound (*śabda*).
"Provisional" refers to provisional phenomena, which are the dust of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*). "Real" refers to real phenomena, which comprise the preceding five dusts.

Among these six dusts, whichever single phenomenon one may take up, its entire substance is none other than the three bodies (*trikāya*) and four virtues (*caturguṇa*) of Amitābha; there is not the slightest deviation.

It is distinct. Since these are the three bodies and four virtues of the Buddha, they are also the three bodies and four virtues of sentient beings, and likewise the three bodies and four virtues of myself;
there is not the slightest difference between them. Therefore it is said: "Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.

Thus, this serves as the pointer to the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and it is also the *siddhānta* of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). (End of Section Two of the Sūtra Text)
The brief explanation of the interpretation is complete. This concludes the major section on the sounds that transform sentient beings.
△ Second, the sounds that transform insentient things:
"Śāriputra, in that Buddha-land, when a gentle breeze stirs the various rows of jewel trees and the jeweled nets, they produce [sounds]..."
Subtle and wondrous is this sound. It is like a hundred thousand kinds of music playing simultaneously;
those who hear this sound naturally give rise to thoughts of mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Sangha.
△ The commentary is divided into two parts. First, the causes and conditions for mindfulness of the Three Jewels; second, the four benefits of mindfulness of the Three Jewels.
△ Now, the first part.
【Explanation】 Sentient and insentient beings alike proclaim the wondrous Dharma. The factors of the Path and the immeasurable Dharma-gates of the Four Teachings are simultaneously expounded.
It is said that according to their respective capacities, each understands [the teaching], enabling those who hear it to bring the Triple Gem to mind.
[Commentary]: Sentient and insentient beings alike are entirely the wondrous essence of Amitābha. When the wind moves the trees and nets, they fully manifest the Buddha’s broad and long tongue.
Although the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma with a single voice, sentient beings understand it according to their respective types. Nevertheless, although each...
Explanation: In the end, they all return to the single essence of the Triple Gem. This concludes the clarification of the causes and conditions for mindfulness of the Triple Gem.
II. Clarifying the Four Benefits of Mindfulness of the Triple Gem. Regarding these four benefits, in this land there are both horizontal and vertical dimensions.

"Horizontal" refers to a single person of sharp faculties; "vertical" refers to the six stages of realization for those of dull faculties. In that land (the Pure Land), there is only the horizontal and no vertical, because [of the nature of that realm].
One is born in the Pure Land because one is certain to attain Buddhahood in a single lifetime; therefore, we now discuss only the four benefits of partial realization.
[Commentary] Recollecting the Three Jewels is to obtain benefit from the *siddhānta*. When an ordinary person first hears this, their entire body leaps with great joy;

this is the benefit of joy, as they enter into communion with the vital energy of the Three Jewels. They will certainly be able to give rise to the bodhicitta; this is the benefit of generating wholesome roots.
By this, the afflictions are subdued and extinguished; this is the benefit of destroying evil. One realizes the single essence of the Triple Gem; this is the benefit of entering into principle.
The initial detailed explanation is concluded.

[Commentary] "Reciting the Three Jewels is to obtain benefit from the *siddhānta*" is a general heading indicating the direct realization of the Three Jewels as one essence (*ekakāya-triratna*), whereby the four benefits are perfectly attained.

Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) have two stages of contemplative practice: those who are external ordinary beings, and those whose realization is similar [to that of the noble ones], who are called internal ordinary beings.
Having suddenly shattered ignorance and for the first time heard the principle of Buddha-nature, one naturally experiences a surge of joy that pervades the entire body;

therefore, in the Separate Teaching (Pratideśanīya-yāna), this is called the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi). Having suddenly entered the ranks of the sages and attained resonance with the "vital energy" (qi-fen) of the Three Jewels in their single essence, the Bodhicitta is thereby awakened;
therefore, in the Perfect Teaching (Ekayāna), this is called the Abiding Stage of Resolving the Mind (Cittotpāda-vihāra). It is from this point that [the distinction] arises.
To shatter the afflictions of ignorance is termed the "benefit of overcoming evil" in reference to the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).

To realize the single essence of the Three Jewels—namely, the three virtues, the three bodies, and so forth—is termed the "benefit of entering the principle" in reference to the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*). Furthermore, as stated in the preceding text, one recollects the Three Jewels.

The three phrases beginning with "clearly perceiving the Buddha’s compassionate majesty" each possess these four benefits. This is because seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma are received together at the same time.

Furthermore, although the intent of these four benefits lies in the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), in reality they are common to all four teachings, for they contain the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) of the four teachings and because all four teachings are ultimately perfect.
One should explain this according to the four teachings and the six stages of realization (*liu ji*). (From the *Sūtra*)
Section Two: The Conclusion of the Transformation of Insentient Beings through Sound. The first major section, the specific explanation, concludes.
△ Second, the summary:
"Śāriputra, that Buddha-land is adorned with such accomplished merits and virtues."
△ The commentary is divided into two parts: first, the explicit elucidation of the wondrous realm of Mind-Only; second, the refutation of ignorance and delusion. △ Now, the first part.
【Explanation】 This is reiterated layer upon layer to inspire deep faith that all adornments are produced from the seeds of the Teacher’s vows and practices.
All that is manifested by wisdom is induced by the pure karma of ourselves; it is a transformation of consciousness alone (*vijñaptimātra*).

The Buddha-mind and the [ordinary] mind arise in mutual relation as shadow and substance, like the light of many lamps, each pervading yet appearing as one (in which nature and characteristics are perfectly luminous). The entirety of principle constitutes phenomena, and the entirety of phenomena is identical to principle.
The entirety of nature gives rise to cultivation; the entirety of cultivation resides within nature (the cultivation of Buddha-nature is entirely the arising of nature, which is cultivation).
This may also be contemplated deeply and at length. [Commentary] Regarding "causing deep faith": the faith of the three teachings—*Āgama*, *Vaipulya*, and *Pratyekabuddha*—is all shallow faith.

This, however, is the faith of the perfect and interfused non-obstruction of phenomena with phenomena; therefore, it is called "deep faith. Regarding "all adornments": the adornments of the four lands.
This is "adornment. That which is accomplished through vows and practice refers to that which is accomplished through the vows and practices of the four teachings.
Taking this as the cause, that which is manifested by the All-Knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) refers to what is manifested by the All-Knowledge when the fruit is perfected.

This clarifies that the adorned objective aspect (nimittabhāga) is a transformation of the Buddha-mind; the entire adornment is the Buddha-mind itself, all of which is evoked by the pure karma of us sentient beings.
Taking this as the cause, that which is "transformed by consciousness-only" continues until the fruit is established as "transformed by consciousness-only.
This clarifies that the manifested *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) is the adornment of the minds of sentient beings; the entirety of the adornment is, in fact, the mind of sentient beings.

Regarding the statement that the minds of Buddhas and the minds of sentient beings mutually serve as the shadow and the substance, it may also be said that the objects of Buddhas and the objects of sentient beings mutually serve as the shadow and the substance.

Because the entire realm is mind, this refers to the Buddha’s adornments as the objective reality (*bhāva-viṣaya*), yet they exist within the minds of sentient beings as purely projected images (*pratibimba-mātra-viṣaya*).
Conversely, the adornments of sentient beings are the objective reality, yet they exist within the Buddha’s mind as purely projected images.
Thus, the Buddha is Amitābha within the minds of sentient beings; he is named the Amitābha of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-amitābha*).
Sentient beings are the people within the Buddha’s own mind; they are called "sentient beings of self-nature. Therefore it is said:
"I vow to deliver sentient beings of self-nature," and so on, up to "I vow to accomplish the Buddha-way of self-nature. As it is for one person, so it is for many.
Whether one takes up a single speck of dust or a single dharma, all are this very realm. The nature of dharmas is inherently thus.
This is not a matter of artificial construction; it is the same for all four lands, not merely the Real-Response Land (*sambhoga-kṣetra*).

To clarify this further through analogy, it is like the light of many lamps: though each lamp’s light pervades its own room, they appear as one and are indistinguishable, yet in reality, each lamp has its own distinct light.
So too, the Buddha-mind and the sentient beings’ minds together transform the adornments of the four lands; they appear as one and are indistinguishable, yet [they remain distinct].
Rather, each person has their own distinct adornment. However, because shared karma produces shared aspects, these appear difficult to distinguish;
yet consider how humans see water while ghosts see fire—this illustrates distinct karma and distinct aspects. Thus, all is but mind, and all is but adornment.

The realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena (shishi wuai) is easy to understand. That "the principle completely constitutes the phenomena, and the phenomena are identical to the principle" means that the mind completely constitutes the environment, and the environment is identical to the mind.
It is like when ice completely becomes water, and the ice is identical to the water.

"Entirely from nature arises cultivation; entirely within nature lies cultivation. This means that while the adornments are fully inherent within nature, they arise to constitute the adornments of cultivated virtue;
yet these adornments of cultivated virtue remain entirely within the nature of the mind, never departing from the mind, for the nature of the mind has no exterior.
It is like the entire ocean forming waves: the entire wave is in the ocean, never departing from the ocean. Therefore it is said:
"The land is purely mind; Amitābha is one's own nature. This is also something that should be contemplated deeply and for a long time. This principle is subtle and profound;
it cannot be understood by those of false or shallow intelligence.
△ Second, rebuking and refuting ignorance and delusion.

[Commentary: Alas! To abandon this Pure Land and instead discourse separately on the "Pure Land of Mind-Only" is to willingly fall into the derision of being like a rat that has become a bird or a mouse that has become a hawk.
(To speak of the mind while separated from the land is certainly but the delusive thought of conditioned shadows. The first section, on the excellence of the environment, is concluded.
[Commentary] "Shu" (rat) refers to the sound of a rat's cry; it is a metaphor for those who, while practicing *ha-tan* (the practice of "just this"), do not penetrate *myō-u* (wondrous existence).
"Chō" (bird) refers to the sound of a bird's cry; it is a metaphor for those who, while practicing *ha-tan*, do not penetrate *shinkū* (true emptiness).

"Kō" (to mock) means to deride. These are ancient metaphors used by past sages, hence they are called "kō. Worldly people do not understand the principle that things are "just this," nor the mind that is "just this" regarding the earth.

To depart from this inconceivable Pure Land and instead cling to the delusory thoughts of conditioned reflections (*ālambana-chāyā*), taking them to be the "Mind-Only Pure Land" or the "Self-Nature Amitābha," is nothing more than the talk of mice and birds. These "conditioned reflections and delusory thoughts" are the shadows grasped by the sixth consciousness;
for while consciousness is like a mirror, that which it perceives is like a reflection—merely a dharma-object (*dharmaviṣaya*) devoid of substantial reality.
This is precisely what people nowadays refer to as the "original face" prior to the kalpa of emptiness (*śūnyakalpa*), beyond the limit of *Vaiśravaṇa*. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"Even if one is detached from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and internally maintains a state of profound stillness, it is still merely a reflected phenomenon of the discrimination of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*).
To be deluded by this and take it for the mind is to categorically deny that the Western [Pure Land] exists outside of the mind."
Thus ends the second summary of the sūtra text; the first major section, "The Subtlety of the Environment," is concluded.

△ Second, "The Subtlety of the Primary Reward" (the Buddha’s own body), in two parts: (1) Deeply Accordant with the Buddha’s Mind; (2) Initial Inquiry and Explanation of the Name and Title; (3) Separate Explanation of the Principal and the Retinue. △ Within the first part, there are two sections:
(1) The Inquiry; (2) The Explanation. △ Now, the first [section]: the inquiry.
"Śāriputra, what do you think? For what reason is that Buddha named Amitābha? [Commentary:
This sutra specifically demonstrates the sublime practice of holding the name; therefore, it poses a question to explain the significance of the name.
It intends for people to have deep faith in the great name of myriad virtues, which is inconceivable, and to hold it with single-minded devotion, free from further doubt or hesitation.
[Commentary]: Regarding the Tathāgata’s investigation and explanation of the name: this sutra clearly reveals that upholding the name constitutes a sublime practice;
therefore, it specifically investigates and explains it. It intends for people to have deep faith in the magnificent name of myriad virtues, which is the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*).
To uphold it with a single mind inherently possesses the tenfold contemplative methods (*daśa-yāna-dharma*); it perfectly encompasses and completely transcends all phenomena.
Therefore, it is said that there is no longer any doubt of a second [name].
△ Second, the explanation has two parts: first, an explanation based on light; second, an explanation based on lifespan.
"Amitābha" translates directly as "Immeasurable. Originally, it is ineffable. The Original Teacher, through the two meanings of light and lifespan, encompasses all immeasurable [qualities].

As for its measure (its certainty and excellence): its light extends horizontally throughout the ten directions, and its lifespan reaches vertically through the three periods of time. This horizontal and vertical interpenetration is the very substance of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

To take up this substance and manifest it as the body and land of Amitābha is, in fact, to take up this substance and manifest it as the name of Amitābha (one must quickly believe and enter into this).
Therefore, the name of Amitābha is none other than the fundamental awakening and rational nature of sentient beings. To hold the name...
This is the union of initial awakening with the fundamental awakening; thus, the initial and the fundamental are non-dual, and the sentient being and the Buddha are non-dual.
Therefore, in a single thought-moment of correspondence, one is a Buddha; in every thought-moment of correspondence, one is a Buddha.
[Commentary] This anticipatory indication of the merit of the Name is inconceivable; it causes people to single-mindedly uphold it without doubt.
"Amitābha" is a direct translation of the meaning "Immeasurable. Translating from Sanskrit into Chinese [is as follows]: "Immeasurable" means fundamentally beyond thought and calculation.
Because it is inconceivable, it cannot be expressed in words; this is the purport of the gate of True Suchness (tathatā-mukha).

Although it cannot be spoken of, it does not obstruct verbal expression. Therefore, the Original Teacher, based on the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*), encompasses all immeasurables through the two meanings of light and longevity.
Through the meaning of longevity, he encompasses all immeasurables that are ineffable;
through the meaning of light, he encompasses all immeasurables within verbal expression. Light, moreover, extends horizontally throughout the ten directions.
"Quiescence" means that the nature of the mind is tranquil yet constantly illuminating. "Life-span" means that the nature of the mind is illuminating yet constantly quiescent.

When the horizontal and vertical dimensions penetrate each other, this is the essence of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Within the horizontal there is the vertical, and within the vertical there is the horizontal;
this is the essence of the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm. The essence of the Dharma-realm is precisely the unchanging nature of the mind that constantly conforms [to conditions].
Conditions. Following conditions yet remaining eternally unchanging, this is the great governing principle of the ten realms and the true essence of the ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*).

Therefore, as the ancient masters said: "The perfectly interfused substance of the Dharma-realm constitutes my single thought-moment; thus, my mind that recites the Buddha's name [is that very substance]."

The entire body is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). When this body is manifested as the body and land of Amitābha, then Amitābha’s three bodies (*trikāya*) and four lands (*catasraḥ bhūmayaḥ*) are produced by a single thought-moment (*ekacittakṣaṇa*), just as when one takes ink to form a painting, the entire painting is nothing but ink.
When this body is manifested as the Name, then the entire Name is produced by a single thought-moment, just as when one takes ink to write characters, the entire character is nothing but ink.
The characters are also ink; the name and title are precisely original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). This is "the mind is itself the Buddha.

The union of initial enlightenment with original enlightenment is the non-duality of subject and object. That initial and original enlightenment are non-dual, and that sentient beings and Buddhas are non-dual, refers solely to this present single thought-moment of the nature of mind.
When this present single thought-moment is constantly in resonance with the Buddha’s name, then in that single thought-moment...
One should attain Buddhahood in a single thought-moment; in every successive thought-moment one accords with reality and attains Buddhahood, for one does not follow the conditions of the nine realms.
△ Now, first, this is explained in terms of light.
Śāriputra, the light of that Buddha is immeasurable; it illuminates the lands of the ten directions without any obstruction.

For this reason, he is named Amitābha. △ The commentary divides this into two parts: first, explaining that the Buddha’s light is immeasurable; second, clarifying that the Buddha’s light is unobstructed. Regarding the first part:
First, an explanation based on realization; second, an explanation based on vows; third, a distinction between the three bodies. △ Now, the first. [Commentary:

The nature of the mind is quiescent yet constantly illuminating; therefore, it is "light" (the essential core of the minds of all Buddhas). Now, one thoroughly realizes the immeasurable substance of the nature of the mind.
Therefore, his radiance is immeasurable.
[Commentary] "The nature of the mind is quiescent yet constantly illuminating" clarifies the essence of the realized principle (*tattva*). In the section "Discerning the Essence," it says:
"The essence of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is neither quiescence nor illumination, yet it is quiescent while constantly illuminating. This is precisely what Amitābha has realized.
The true aspect (*dharmatā*) is unchanging yet constantly follows conditions. Because it can follow defiled and pure conditions to fully create the ten dharma-realms, it is called "radiance.
To thoroughly realize the immeasurable essence of the mind-nature refers to the merit of the wisdom that is capable of realization.
"Thoroughly realizing" means, by means of the threefold contemplation within the one mind, realizing the threefold wisdom within the one mind, starting from the stage of names.
From initial realization up to ultimate realization, the essence of the immeasurable wisdom and virtue of the mind-nature is fully manifested;
therefore, its radiance is immeasurable. That which is the essential core of the minds of all Buddhas is precisely this very mind-nature of the present single thought-moment.
△ Second, the explanation by way of vows. [Commentary:
All Buddhas have thoroughly penetrated the essential nature and all illuminate the ten directions; thus, they may all be called "Immeasurable Light.
However, because their powers of aspiration during the causal stage differ, distinct names are established according to causes and conditions. Amitābha was the Bhikṣu Dharmākara, who made four...
The eighteenth vow is the vow that his radiance shall constantly illuminate the ten directions; now the fruition has been realized exactly as vowed (one may awaken to the Buddha within the mind).
[Commentary] This section clarifies that distinct names are established according to the conditions of the four *siddhāntas*. If one were to explain this solely in terms of realization:
Thus, the essence of all Buddhas is identical, and it is impossible to establish distinct names for them. To establish a distinct name necessarily relies upon causes and conditions;
otherwise, one falls into the error of causelessness. As for "causes and conditions," they refer to the four *siddhāntas* (purposes) established for the sake of sentient beings.
Amitābha being the Bhikṣu Dharmākara is the *loka-siddhānta*. His making of the forty-eight vows is likewise [for the sake of] sentient beings.

This refers to the *puruṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint for individuals). "Possessing the vow that light constantly illuminates the ten directions" refers to the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of remedial treatment).
"Now the fruit has been realized as vowed" refers to the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the standpoint of ultimate truth). One may thus awaken to the Buddha within the mind.
This indicates the benefit of entering into the principle.
△ Third, distinguishing the three bodies.
[Commentary] The radiance of the Dharma-body is without boundaries; the radiance of the Reward-body accords with true nature. This is the Way of all Buddhas.
The same applies to the radiance of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body): there are those that illuminate one *yojana*, ten, a hundred, or a thousand;

those that illuminate a single world-system, or ten, a hundred, or a thousand world-systems. Only the Amitābha [Buddha] shines universally upon all directions—this is the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss—and thus he is specifically named "Immeasurable Light" (*Amitābha*).
Nevertheless, the three bodies (*trikāya*) are neither identical nor different; this distinction is made only for the sake of enabling sentient beings to obtain the four benefits.

[Commentary] The text is divided into two sections. The first is the primary refutation. The section beginning with "However, the three bodies... clarifies the benefits accorded accordingly. Regarding the phrase "the radiance of the Dharma-body has no boundaries":

because it is formless, it extends horizontally throughout the ten directions and vertically through the three periods of time. Regarding the phrase "the radiance of the Reward-body accords with true nature":
this refers to the self-enjoyment reward body, which accords with the nature of reality (dharmatā). As for the radiance of the Response-body...
Regarding the clarification of "inequality": it manifests according to the capacity [of beings], for it is unequal according to their capacities, locations, and times.
As for *yojana*, there is no standard translation; it refers to a lodging where a Wheel-Turning King halts during his tour of inspection, similar to the postal stations (*gongdi*) of this land.
"Only Amitābha’s universal illumination" means that Amitābha’s response-body universally illuminates the four lands (*catur-bhūmi*). These four lands are perfected...
Because they are fused; because the three bodies are one essence. Therefore, it is specifically named "Immeasurable Light" (Amitābha). This is precisely the Pure Land school of perfect fusion.

Second, clarifying the benefit according to [the capacity of] beings: as for the three bodies being neither identical nor different, the Buddha-body is inconceivable because it is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Since all three bodies are the Dharma-body, they act for the sake of sentient beings in accordance with the four *siddhārtha* (purposes).
This is merely a distinction made between "beneficial" and "otherwise. The first explanation of the Buddha’s immeasurable light is concluded.
△ Second, clarifying that the Buddha’s light is unobstructed.
[Commentary]: One should know that it is "unobstructed" with respect to sentient beings; because the affinity (*pratyaya*) between sentient beings and the Buddha is profound, the Buddha’s light...

Everywhere; there is no place in all the worlds where he is not seen perfectly. (As an example for what follows: since his lifespan is indeed infinite and the Buddha’s light illuminates the ten directions, why labor over verses of praise?)

[Commentary]: The Buddha’s light is originally neither obstructed nor unobstructed within the Buddha’s own sphere. What is termed "obstruction" or "non-obstruction" is discussed entirely from the perspective of sentient beings.
If sentient beings do not recite the Buddha’s name, their affinity with the Buddha is shallow;

because the affinity is shallow, it obstructs the profound [light], and thus there is obstruction. Now, because these sentient beings recite the Buddha’s name, their affinity with the Buddha is deep; because the affinity is deep...
Because the hindrances are shallow, wherever the Buddha’s light reaches, there is nothing in all the worlds that does not perfectly perceive the radiance of the three bodies (*trikāya*).
There are three kinds of worlds: first, the world of perfect enlightenment; second, the world of sentient beings of the nine realms;
and third, the world of the physical environment as a supporting retribution. The scriptural passage has already concluded its initial explanation based on this light.
△ Second, the explanation based on lifespan:
Furthermore, Śāriputra, the lifespan of that Buddha, as well as that of his people, is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) kalpas;
therefore, he is named Amitābha.
△ The commentary is divided into two parts. First, the direct explanation of the lifespan; second, the reiterated explanation of light and lifespan. The first part is further divided into two:

first, explaining that the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable; second, explaining that the lifespan of his birth is immeasurable. Within the first of these, there are three sections. The first explains it by way of realization.
Second, an explanation based on vows. Third, distinguishing the three bodies. △ Now, the first [section].
【Commentary】 The nature of the mind is luminous yet eternally quiescent; therefore, it constitutes "life-span. Now, one thoroughly realizes the immeasurable essence of the nature of the mind.
Therefore, his lifespan is immeasurable.
[Commentary] "The nature of the mind is luminous yet eternally quiescent" clarifies the essence of the realized principle (*dharmatā*).

The essence of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is neither quiescence nor luminosity, yet it is luminous while remaining eternally quiescent. This is precisely the true mark realized by Amitābha, which follows conditions.
It is eternally self-unchanging. Although it follows conditions of defilement or purity, its essence remains as-it-is (*tathatā*); therefore, it is called "life-span" (*āyus*).
To thoroughly realize the immeasurable essence of the mind-nature clarifies the virtue of severance (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) of the one who realizes.

"Thoroughly realizing" means that by means of the three types of cessation within the One Mind, one realizes the three types of liberation within the One Mind, proceeding from the realization at the stage of names (*nāma-mātra*) up to...
Ultimate realization: the essence of the immeasurable virtues of severance within the nature of mind is perfectly manifested; therefore, its lifespan is immeasurable.
△ Second, the explanation by way of vows. [Commentary]:
The lifespan of the Dharma-body is without beginning and without end. The lifespan of the Reward-body has a beginning but no end. This too is the Buddha’s...

The Buddha-way is the same; all may be named Amitāyus (Infinite Life). The response-body (nirmāṇakāya) accords with vows and adapts to capacities, such that its duration—whether extended or abbreviated—is not uniform.
Regarding the King of Vows, Dharmākara, he possessed the vow that both the Buddha and the people’s lifespans would be infinite.
Now that the fruition has been realized according to his vow, it is specifically named Amitāyus.

[Commentary] This also clarifies that distinct names are established according to the causes and conditions of one's vows. The Dharma-body is without beginning and without end because it is neither born nor extinguished.
The Reward-body has a beginning but no end: it has a beginning because there is "initial awakening" (shiqiao), and it has no end because it accords with the nature of reality (dharmatā).
These also share the same realization of the Way. The Response-body (Nirmāṇakāya) follows vows and adapts to capacities, extending or abbreviating [its manifestation] accordingly.
Regarding those who are unequal: if one wishes for longevity, life is extended; if one wishes for brevity, life is shortened. If the karmic capacity (*mātr̥kā*) is long, life is extended;

if the karmic capacity is short, life is shortened. Or, if one wishes for longevity while the karmic capacity is short, it shortens that which was long; or if one wishes for brevity while the karmic capacity is long.

Thus, they extend the short to make it long, each according to the four benefits. Sometimes they extend or shorten their lifespan; sometimes they extend or shorten their spiritual capacity (*indriya*).

Therefore, it is said that they are not equal. Because the Buddha possesses the wisdom of extending and shortening, the section on the Dharmakara [Bodhisattva] below clarifies the establishment of distinct names based on the causes and conditions of his vow-power.
△ Third, distinguishing the three bodies. [Commentary]:
*Asaṃkhyeya* (incalculable), *ananta* (boundless), and *apramāṇa* (immeasurable) are all names for calculation; they are the immeasurability of that which actually possesses measure.
Nevertheless, the three bodies are neither identical nor different. Thus, the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) may also be the immeasurability of the immeasurable.
[Commentary] Regarding "asaṃkhyeya" and so forth, which are all names for calculation: these are specific designations for calculation. There are ten such specific names, namely:

asaṃkhyeya (incalculable), aprameya (immeasurable), anantya (boundless), atulya (unequaled), agaṇeya (innumerable), asakṛta (incomparable), acintya (inconceivable), amāpya (unmeasurable), avaktavya (ineffable), and avaktavyāvaktavya (the ineffable of the ineffable). These are [the numbers] used by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Knowing calculation is something that even the followers of the Two Vehicles cannot fathom, let alone ordinary beings.

That which is "immeasurable" despite having a real measure refers to the immeasurability of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body), not the immeasurability of the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* (dharma and enjoyment bodies) which are without end.
This is because Amitābha attains *nirvāṇa*, and Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva will subsequently attain Buddhahood. However, this [view] is refuted from the perspective of the three bodies (*trikāya*).
This is a provisional calculation. This very response-body (nirmāṇakāya) is simultaneously the dharma-body and the reward-body; it is the immeasurable of the immeasurable.
The explanation of the Buddha’s immeasurable life-span is concluded.
△ Second, the explanation of the immeasurable lifespan of birth.
[Commentary] "And" (及) means "together with. "The people" refers to those from the stage of Equal Enlightenment (等覺) downwards.
This means that the Buddha’s lifespan, together with the lifespans of these people, are all equally immeasurable.
[Commentary]: "The people" refers to those from the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) downwards. In that land, only the Buddha is the King;

Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta are both among the people. Therefore, the preceding text states: "By taking the lowest of the low as an example, one may infer the highest of the high. If one were to take the high as an example for the low...

Generally, these refer to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). If one were to use the lower to exemplify the higher, they would generally refer to those on the level of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambuddha*).

Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Ordinary beings [are] exemplified as ascending to the stage of the Future Buddha (*upapatti-bhūmi*). This is an extraordinary proclamation and an ultimate discourse. Regarding the phrase "all immeasurable, etc.," the "etc. refers to the boundless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
This concludes the initial formal explanation of the lifespan.
△ Second, the double explanation of Light and Life has three parts: first, a general clarification; second, a specific clarification; third, a concluding exhortation. △ Now, the first [part].
【Commentary】 One should know that the names of Light and Life are all established based upon sentient beings. Because of the equality of sentient beings and Buddhas, they are able to...
For those who hold to the Name, their radiance and lifespan will be identical to the Buddha’s, without any difference.
[Commentary] Regarding the fact that the Name of Radiance and Lifespan is established based on sentient beings:

the Name, which vertically exhausts the past and horizontally pervades all, is fundamentally established upon the present single thought-moment of the sentient being's mind-nature. This is because the present single thought-moment of the mind-nature is, by its very nature...
From the vertical [axis] to the ultimate, and throughout the horizontal [expanse], it is therefore said that "sentient beings and Buddhas are equal.

That which enables those who hold the Name to be identical to the Buddha without distinction is the fruit of the manifestation of active practice (pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa) arising from the seeds inherently possessed (li-jū). This concludes the general explanation.

△ Second, the specific explanation, which is further divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the meaning of light; second, the explanation of the meaning of life-span. △ Now, the first part. [Commentary]:
Furthermore, by virtue of the meaning of immeasurable light, sentient beings are born in Sukhāvatī;

that is, they are born in the ten directions and behold Amitābha Buddha, which is equivalent to beholding all Buddhas of the ten directions. Being able to deliver themselves, they are thereby able to universally benefit all.
[Commentary] This clarifies the cause for upholding immeasurable light and the fruit of realizing immeasurable light.
"To be born in Sukhāvatī is to be born in the ten directions" means that Sukhāvatī is the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*).
To be born in the Flower Treasury World is to be born horizontally across the four lands. Amitābha Buddha is Vairocana; to see Vairocana Buddha is [to see the Dharmakāya].
One fully perceives the three bodies and is thus able to deliver oneself; that is, one suddenly shatters ignorance, whereby the five stages of dwelling are completely severed.

Therefore, the preceding text states: "Having offered a profusion of exquisite flowers as an offering to ten trillion Buddhas in other directions, he returns to his own land at mealtime to eat and practice walking meditation."
△ Second, the clarification of the meaning of "life-span" (āyus).
[Commentary]: Because of the meaning of immeasurable life-span, the people of Sukhāvatī are all those who will attain Buddhahood in one lifetime (ekajātipratibaddha);
they are all fixed as being destined for Buddhahood in one birth and shall not reach a second birth.
[Commentary] This clarifies the cause for upholding Infinite Life and the fruit of realizing Infinite Life.
This is precisely the perfect realization of the fruit of the three non-regressions. Part Two: The Specific Explanation is concluded.
△ Third, the exhortation to practice.
[Commentary: One should know that apart from the mind of immeasurable light and life within this very present thought-moment, where could there be the name of Amitābha Buddha?
And apart from the name of Amitābha Buddha, by what means could one thoroughly realize the present?
The mind of immeasurable light and longevity in a single thought—may you contemplate this deeply; may you contemplate this deeply.
[Commentary] This concludes by returning to the nature of the mind within the present single thought. That which is apart from the mind has no name or title:
it is like asking how ice can be formed without water. That one cannot realize the mind apart from names and titles: it is like asking what ice is apart from water.

This is to complete the section on Water. I pray that you reflect upon this deeply; it is especially intended as an exhortation for future worthies. The initial inquiry and explanation of the names and titles in the sutra text are now concluded.

II. A detailed explanation of the Principal and the Retinue, in two parts: A. A detailed explanation. B. A summary and indication. The first part [A] is further divided into two: 1. The Principal. [End of segment]
Second, the companions. △ Now, the first [section]. This also explains the phrase "now currently preaching the Dharma" from the separate introduction.
Śāriputra, since Amitābha Buddha attained Buddhahood, ten kalpas have passed until now.
The commentary is divided into two parts: first, the discussion on the formation of the three bodies (*trikāya*) over the kalpas; second, the clarification of the significance of the ten kalpas.
The first part is further divided into two: first, the general heading; second, the detailed discussion. Now, the first [part].
[Commentary] This clarifies the accomplishment of the Teacher of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
[Sub-commentary] There are six kinds of accomplishment: namely, faith, hearing, time, teacher, place, and assembly.
This refers to the accomplishment of the Teacher among the six accomplishments of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Since the Teacher is accomplished, when one is accomplished, all are accomplished.
△ Second, the detailed discussion is further divided into two parts: first, the discussion of *kalpas* (aeons); second, the discussion of "accomplishment" (*siddhi*). △ Now, the first part.

【Explanation】 However, the Dharma-body has neither accomplishment nor non-accomplishment; thus, one should not discuss *kalpas* regarding it. The Reward-body is called "accomplished" because its causes are perfected and its fruit is fulfilled.

The Response-body is called "accomplished" because it manifests birth for the sake of sentient beings; both of these may be discussed in terms of *kalpas*. Furthermore, the Dharma-body is accomplished through the cultivation of virtues.
The Manifestation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) may be discussed in terms of its formation and kalpas; however, the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) has nothing newly acquired.
The Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), like the moon reflected in a river, neither comes into being nor ceases to be, and thus should not be discussed in terms of kalpas.

[Commentary] The text is divided into two sections. All three bodies (trikāya) possess both phenomena and principle. The first section discusses them in terms of phenomena; the second section discusses them in terms of principle.
Regarding the fact that the Dharma-body has neither attainment nor non-attainment: it is inconceivable, and therefore one should not discuss it in terms of kalpas.

Regarding the Reward-body (sambhogakāya), its causes are perfected and its fruits are fulfilled: this means the causes of the ten thousand practices are perfected and the fruits of the ten thousand virtues are fulfilled; this is called "attaining Bodhi."

Therefore, the treatise is established. As for the statement that he manifested birth for the sake of sentient beings: it was for the sake of all beings that he manifested the eight phases of attaining enlightenment;
thus, the treatise is established. Because the treatise is established, one may discuss the number of kalpas. In the Sanskrit language, this is *kalpa*.

This is called "time-period" (*kalpa*). There are three types: small, medium, and great. One period of increase and one period of decrease constitute a small *kalpa* (*antarakalpa*). Twenty small *kalpas* constitute a medium *kalpa*.
The four periods of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness constitute a great *kalpa* (*mahākalpa*).

This is a discussion of the number of *kalpas* based on the formation and destruction of the world-system. Furthermore, from the perspective of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) downward, it is a discussion based on principle. [The term] "Dharma-body" refers to...

That which is manifested through the cultivation of merit is the stainless, supreme *dharmakāya*. Although the principle of the *dharmakāya* is inherently possessed, it must rely upon cultivation to be manifested.

It is like gold within ore: it requires the application of fire for the essence of the gold to be revealed. There are two aspects to the cultivation of merit, namely *prajñā* (wisdom) and *vimukti* (liberation).
Through *prajñā*, one illuminates the principle and severs delusions; when the illumination of the principle reaches its ultimate consummation, it is called [the perfection of wisdom].

The virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*). The ultimate severance of delusions is termed the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*). Adorned with these two virtues, the Dharma-body is called the "Stainless, Sublime, and Ultimate Dharma-body.
From the perspective of the virtue of cultivation (*bhāvanā-guṇa*), one may also discuss its formation and its kalpas; it is not that its formation-kalpa is definitively not discussed.
As for the Reward-body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*), there is nothing newly acquired therein; it is inherently present by principle. Since it belongs to the fundamental [nature],...

There is. Furthermore, there is neither accomplishment nor non-accomplishment. That the *saṃbhogakāya* is like the moon reflected in a river is because it is a manifestation of the shadows of the *dharmakāya* and *sambhogakāya*;
since it has no separate intrinsic substance of its own, there is likewise neither accomplishment nor non-accomplishment.

In all cases, one should not discuss *kalpas*. It is not something that can definitely be discussed in terms of accomplishment or *kalpas*. By realizing this union of principle and phenomenon (*dharma*), one is just barely freed from emotional calculations and pervasive attachments. Spontaneously...
Once one has transcended retribution, if one encounters the conditions for the *siddhānta* (the established tenet), one may then act on behalf of others to break their attachments.
△ Second, the discussion on accomplishment. [Commentary]:
However, when the Buddhas attain the Way, each has both a "trace" and a "ground. The original ground (*honji*) is entirely unfathomable; for now, we shall rely upon the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Speaking in terms of the traces manifested in his attainment [of Buddhahood], this refers to the three bodies (trikāya) wherein the attainment of one is the attainment of all;
it is also a discussion of attainment that is neither attained nor unattained.

[Commentary]: There are two aspects to the attainment of the Way: the general and the particular. The general aspect applies universally across the four teachings; the particular aspect specifically points to the manifestation of birth.

Regarding the provisional and the real (honji-suijaku), there are both general and specific aspects. Generally, there are six levels of the provisional and the real; specifically, they refer to the two gates of the Dharma Flower Sūtra:
the past and the present. As for the six levels of the provisional and the real: first, principle and phenomena. Here, the principle of ultimate truth is the real.

The matters of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) constitute the trace. Second, there are principle (*li*) and teaching (*jiao*). Principle encompasses both the phenomenal and the noumenal, taking the noumenal as its foundation;

the teaching that explains these phenomenal and noumenal principles constitutes the trace. Third, there are teaching and practice (*xing*). The teaching that manifests phenomenal matters is the foundation; receiving the teaching and cultivating practice constitutes the trace.
Fourth is essence and function: realizing the essence through causal practice is the fundamental; arising function from the essence is the trace. Fifth is the provisional and the real:

the initial attainment of the real is the fundamental; the intermediate application of the provisional is the trace. Sixth is the past and the present: what was already taught in the Trace Gate is the trace;
what is now being taught in the Fundamental Gate is the fundamental. That which is entirely unfathomable in its original ground is the Dharma.
Now, in this Flower [Sutra], the Teacher speaks of the Original Gate, which is entirely unfathomable. Take, for instance, Śākyamuni:

according to the "Life Span" chapter, he attained Buddhahood many aeons ago, as numerous as the atoms in a dust mote. Even the Compassionate Honored One in his final birth-stage cannot fathom it; who else could?
Regarding Amitābha Buddha’s attainment of Buddhahood, this is spoken merely in terms of the traces manifested in the Land of Ultimate Bliss;

it does not refer to the Original Gate (honmon). That is to say, although it is described as a manifested transformation body (nirmāṇakāya), it is simultaneously the Dharma-body and the Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya).
Although it is said that they are accomplished, this refers to the aforementioned principle that when the three bodies are accomplished, all are accomplished;

furthermore, it is discussed in terms of the three bodies being neither accomplished nor unaccomplished. This is not a partial discussion. The initial discourse on the accomplishment of the kalpa of the three bodies is concluded.
△ Second, explaining the intent behind the ten kalpas.

[Commentary]: Furthermore, the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable; yet now it is but ten kalpas. Thus, while the time for preaching the Dharma in the present is far from exhausted, he universally exhorts sentient beings of the two periods to swiftly seek rebirth so that they may share the Buddha’s lifespan and accomplish their goal in a single lifetime. Moreover—
The following passage mentions innumerable śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and those in their final birth (*caramabhavika*), all of whom have achieved [this state] over ten kalpas.
This clearly demonstrates that for those who attain rebirth in the ten directions and three periods of time without falling back, such attainment is both numerous and easy.

[Commentary] Regarding the statement "in these present ten kalpas," the Buddha has two intentions. The first intention is to show that the time for preaching the Dharma in the preceding passage has not yet ended.
"Not yet ended" means that the lifespan of Amitāyus has not reached its midpoint;
it is currently at its peak, and thus he universally exhorts [beings] to swiftly seek rebirth, as there must be no delay. The second intention is, furthermore, to reveal the Dharma-gate.
It is supreme; it encompasses the widest range of capacities and is the easiest to practice. Therefore, among those who have achieved success over ten kalpas, they are exceedingly numerous.
This concludes the initial section on the primary [teaching] of the sutra.
△ Second, the retinue.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, that Buddha has immeasurable and boundless śrāvaka disciples, all of whom are arhats;
they cannot be known by means of calculation. The assembly of bodhisattvas is likewise.

[Commentary]: Those of the two vehicles with fixed natures in other lands cannot be born there. However, if those who previously practiced the Lesser Vehicle, at the time of death, turn their merit toward Bodhi and make great vows, they will be born in that land.
Once born there, the Buddha teaches the Dharma according to their capacities, enabling them to sever the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*).

Therefore, they are called Arhats. They are like those in the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*) who sever the afflictions of views and thought at the seventh stage; they are not actual Śrāvakas.
This is because those who abide in the two vehicles of the Shared and Distinct Teachings do not hear the names of Buddhas in other directions;
whereas now, hearing the name of Amitābha and aspiring with faith to be reborn there, they belong entirely to the capacities encompassed by the Distinct and Perfect Teachings.
[Commentary] The text has two parts: first, it clarifies that they are not actual śrāvakas; second, it clarifies that they are in fact bodhisattvas.
"The Two Vehicles" refers to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. "Other directions" refers to worlds other than Sukhāvatī, such as Sahā and other distant realms.

"Fixed nature" means that having already severed the afflictions of views and thought (dṛṣṭi- and bhāva-kleśa), they are determined to proceed toward nirvana without remainder (anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa); therefore, [they cannot attain Buddhahood].

One is born [there]. If one has previously practiced the factors of the path of the Hīnayāna but has not yet severed the afflictions of views and thought, and at the point of death merely hears the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land and its supreme merits, one immediately turns from the Small Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle and makes a vow to seek birth there.

To make this vow to seek birth is itself the Great Vow. Once born in that land, the Buddha, in accordance with the practitioner's prior inclination for the Small Vehicle, teaches the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and *Pratyekabuddha* (Shared) teachings.

Regarding the *Mārgavarga* (Chapter on the Path): it causes one to sever the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*saṃjñā*), making one equal in rank to an Arhat; thus, they are "provisionally named" (*prajñapti-nāman*) Arhats.
This is like those in the Separate Teaching (*bhedavyākaraṇa-dharma*) who sever views and thoughts; in reality, they are Bodhisattvas, not actual Śrāvakas.

As for the statement that those below the *Saṃdhinirmocana* (Treatise) and *Sūtra* (Shared) Teachings do not hear the names of Buddhas from other directions: this is because the Buddha did not speak of them within the two teachings of the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and the *Sūtra*.
On the other hand, as for the matter of not hearing [the name], it is because it was not preached to them.

As for those who now hear the name of Amitābha and so forth—meaning those who hear the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land at the time of death—they were already of the Mahāyāna disposition in previous lives;
their current practice of the Lesser Vehicle is merely a temporary detour, and they will not remain bound by it for long. This applies equally to us today who hear the name of Amitābha.
Regarding the Name: those who, with faith and aspiration, seek birth [in the Pure Land] belong generally to the Bodhisattvas of both the Separate (Pratyekabuddha) and Perfect (Mahāyāna) teachings.
The initial detailed explanation of the text is concluded.
△ Second, the summary and demonstration.
Śāriputra, that buddha-land is adorned with such accomplished merits. [Commentary:
The Buddha, as well as the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, are all produced by the vows and practices of Amitābha during his causal stage.
Furthermore, they represent the "attainment of all through the attainment of one" in the state of fruition. Thus, the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and śrāvakas are each neither self nor other.

Self and others are non-dual; therefore, it is said that one "achieves such adornment of merit. This enables those who hold the Name with faith and aspiration to achieve [this adornment] in every thought-moment as well.

(The preceding section on the infinite, layered profundity ultimately culminates in the single sound of the Name. Thus concludes the initial extensive exposition of the wondrous fruits of the environment and inhabitants of that land, intended to inspire faith.

[Commentary] The text has two parts. The first clarifies that which is already accomplished. The phrase "able to cause" and below refers to what is currently being accomplished and what will be accomplished.

That the Buddhas, śrāvakas, and others are all accomplished through the vows and practices of Amitābha during his causal stage means that the Buddhas and so forth are the fruit, while the vows and practices are the cause.

The cause is that which is able to accomplish, and the fruit—the Buddhas and so forth—is that which is accomplished. Within the vows and practices of the causal stage, each is distinguished as the agent of accomplishment.

Regarding the object: with respect to the vow, the vow is that which initiates; the arising of the Truth of Suffering is that which is to be transcended; and the Buddha of the Truth of Cessation is that which is sought. Regarding the practice:
with respect to the practice, the practice is that which is enacted; the seven categories of the Truth of the Path are that which is practiced;

and the delusions of the Truth of Origination are that which is severed. These include the vows and practices of the Bhikṣu Dharmakara, the vows and practices for gathering sentient beings, and sentient beings themselves.
The vows and practices further encompass the Dharma-treasury; these vows and practices mutually interpenetrate one another, forming the cause for the non-obstruction of all phenomena.
This is also the case where the attainment of one thing entails the attainment of all things:

the unimpeded cause of the Dharma-treasury within the causal stage brings about the unimpeded fruit of Amitābha. Within the fruit, when the wisdom of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) manifests once, everything is fully realized.
Manifestation. This manifests the images of self and other, which are the cause for sentient beings' non-obstruction;

it accomplishes the fruit of the non-obstruction of śrāvakas and others. Within this fruit, consciousness-only transforms such that everything is transformed, transforming these images of self and other.

This is the fruit of the non-obstruction of phenomena (dharmadharmāpratigha), wherein they mutually accomplish one another. Thus, regarding Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas, each is neither self nor other:
the self is the self within the mind of the other, and the other is the other within the mind of the self.
That which is the other within the self’s own mind is not truly other; likewise, that which is the self within the other’s own mind is not truly self.
The Buddha is the Amitābha within the hearts of sentient beings; śrāvakas and others are the sentient beings within the Buddha’s heart.
Within the Buddha’s heart, all sentient beings are the Buddha; within the hearts of sentient beings, the Buddha is entirely the sentient beings.
As for the non-duality of self and other: self and other are nothing but this present, single mind of wondrous purity.
The luminous essence. How could there be "is" or "is not" within this? It enables the following:

that which is currently accomplished or will be accomplished serves as the substantial object (*ālambana*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), enabling us to believe in it moment by moment with such faith, to seek it moment by moment with such aspiration, and to maintain it moment by moment with such upholding. From oneself...
Nevertheless, it is certain that such accomplishment occurs within every moment of thought. This concludes the second section of the sutra text, on the excellence of the primary retribution.
This concludes the first major division of the treatise, which extensively describes the excellence of the environment and the primary retribution of that land to inspire faith.

Compiled by the Bhikṣu Hongluo, Dama.
Compiled by the Sramana Dalin of Zifu Temple. △ Section Two:
Special Exhortation for Sentient Beings to Seek Rebirth in Order to Make Vows. Part One: Revealing the Unsurpassed Causes and Conditions (this section is of great significance).
Part Two: Special Exhortation. Regarding the excellence of the Pure Land: it is called "rebirth with residual karma," whereby one transcends the Triple Realm horizontally.
Dwelling together, he universally possesses the four lands and reveals the Dharma wheel of the four teachings.
Sentient beings perfectly purify the four lands, perfectly perceive the three bodies, and perfectly realize the three non-regressions. All people attain Buddhahood in a single lifetime.
Such supreme distinctions and transcendence are entirely indicated within these two sections; one must investigate them with careful attention.
[Commentary]: These two sections constitute the great power and function of this single sutra. Therefore, the preceding text regarding power and function states:

"Superior goodness in one place" refers to birth in the Shared Residence (Sahā) Land; this already implies horizontal birth in the [other] three superior lands. "One life to attain Buddhahood" refers to non-retrogression in rank;
this already implies the perfect realization of the three types of non-retrogression. Fearing that people might overlook this, I have provisionally indicated it for our sake.
It is known.
△ Now, first, the unsurpassed causes and conditions are revealed:
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, all sentient beings who are born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss are [of the three kinds of] *avaivartika*."
Among those [in the three stages of non-retrogression], there are many who are in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*);
their number is so vast that it cannot be known by calculation, but can only be described as immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*).

The commentary is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive); second, the explanation of the *upapatti-paryantika* (one destined for the final birth). The first part is further divided into three sections: first, the formal exposition;
second, the pointing-out; third, the conclusion. Now, the first [section].

[Commentary]: *Avivartika* (阿鞞跋致) is translated here as "non-retrogression. First is non-retrogression in stage: having entered the stream of the sages, one does not fall back to the level of ordinary beings.

Second is non-retrogression in practice: constantly delivering sentient beings, one does not fall to the level of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Third is non-retrogression in thought: moment by moment, the mind flows into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).

[Commentary]: "Entering the stream of the sages and not falling into the stage of ordinary beings" means that the grasping at a self (*ātman*) has already been shattered and the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) have already been emptied;
thus, one enters the class of the sages and does not fall into the stages of the inner or outer ordinary beings.

"Constantly delivering sentient beings and not falling into the stage of the two vehicles" means that the grasping at the dharmas of the two vehicles is empty. *Sarvajñā*—this is translated as "all-aspect wisdom" (*sarvākārajñatā*). [It is like] the ocean.
This refers to the ocean of fruition (*phala-sāgara*).
△ Second, the pointing out, which is divided into two parts: first, pointing out the superiority; second, pointing out the transcendence. The first part is further divided into two:
first, showing the inferiority of the difficulty of realization in this land; second, showing the excellence of the perfect realization in that land. △ Now:
First. [Commentary:

If categorized according to this land, the first fruit of the *āgama* (Śrāvaka) stage is called "non-retrogression in rank and position," encompassing the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*) generally, and the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*) specifically; for the Perfect [Teaching], it refers to the first level of faith (*prathama-śraddhā*).

"Non-retrogression in practice" encompasses Bodhisattvas generally, and the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) specifically; for the Perfect [Teaching], it refers to the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). Specifically, it refers to the first ground (*prathama-bhūmi*); for the Perfect [Teaching], it is the first...
"Abiding" is called "non-retrogression through mindfulness.
[Commentary] This clarifies the sequence of the three stages of non-retrogression within this land. This is discussed entirely from a vertical perspective.

Although the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) is horizontal in terms of principle (*li*), it remains vertical in terms of phenomena (*shi*). Therefore, the stages of non-retrogression are definitively immovable. [The *Zang* (Treasury) states:]...

The first fruit is the *srotāpanna* fruit, here translated as "entry into the stream," meaning entry into the stream of the noble ones (*ārya*). It is also called "going against the stream," meaning going against the stream of ordinary beings.
This corresponds generally to the fourth stage of the Shared Teaching (*pāṭha-sādhāraṇa-yāna*), wherein one perceives the principle of the True Truth (*satyadharma*).

Specifically, it corresponds to the first dwelling of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-bhūmi*), namely the Dwelling of the Initial Resolve (*cittotpāda-vihāra*). In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), it corresponds to the first level of Faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), the stage of the positions of faith. This is...
This refers to the stages of non-retrogression regarding the level of realization (*adhigama*) within this land.

As for non-retrogression regarding practice (*caryā*), it does not exist in the *Hīnayāna* (Tripitaka) teachings, because those of the Two Vehicles do not cultivate the bodhisattva path, and even if they were bodhisattvas, they would still be subject to retrogression.

In the *Prajñāpāramitā* (Shared) teachings, it occurs at the ninth bodhisattva stage; prior to the ninth stage, there is still the possibility of retrogression. In the Distinct Teaching, it begins from the tenth stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
This refers to the distinct stage of the ten *pariṇāmanā* (dedications). In the preceding ten stages of practice (*caryā*), one has not yet attained complete non-retrogression.
In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), the ten faiths correspond to the eighth through the tenth faiths; prior to the eighth faith, there is still the possibility of retrogression.

This, then, is the position of non-retrogression in practice within this land. In the *Hīnayāna* (Tripitaka) teaching, this is entirely absent. In the *Shared* (Prajñāpāramitā) teaching, one must reach the ninth stage (*bhūmi*) to attain it. In the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), one must reach the tenth [stage].
In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), one must reach the stage of the Ten Faiths before attaining non-retrogression in practice; thus, its difficulty is evident.
As for non-retrogression in mindfulness (nian-bu-tui), even the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) lacks it, because it does not shatter ignorance (avidyā) nor realize the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).

Although it exists in the Distinct and Perfect Teachings, in the Distinct Teaching one must reach the first Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi), while in the Perfect Teaching one must reach the first Abiding of the Initial Resolve (prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra) before it begins.

Having shattered ignorance, one first beholds the Dharmakāya and first attains the continuous flow into the ocean of fruition at every thought-moment; thus, it can be seen that this realization is exceedingly difficult to attain.
△ Second, showing the excellence of the perfect realization in that land. The commentary states: "The significance of this section is extremely great, because..."
It is because we have brought our karma with us to be reborn [in the Pure Land], attaining Buddhahood in a single lifetime; there is nothing that is not a great causal condition for this matter.
Furthermore, it is said that such supreme excellence and transcendence are entirely indicated by these two headings.
This is the first indication of the power and function of this sutra.

[Commentary: Now, even those in the Pure Land who have committed the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds, yet achieve rebirth through ten recitations while still carrying their karmic burdens and dwell in the lowest of the lower grades, all attain the three non-regressions.
[Commentary]: Regarding the "five heinous crimes and ten evil deeds," the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra in Sixteen Contemplations*, in the chapter on rebirth in the lowest grade, states:
"There may be sentient beings who commit unwholesome karma—the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds—possessing all manner of unwholesome acts.
Such foolish people, by reason of their evil karma, ought to fall into the evil realms and undergo suffering without end for many kalpas. Such foolish people..."
At the time of death, one encounters a virtuous friend who exhorts one to recite the Buddha’s name. Thus, with a sincere mind, one maintains the sound without interruption for ten full recitations.
Within each of these recitations, the karmic offenses of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death are eliminated.
At the moment of death, one sees a golden lotus flower, like a sun-disk, appearing before that person in the space of a single thought-moment.
One immediately attains rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. As for the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*):

shedding the blood of a Buddha, killing an Arhat, killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, and causing a schism in the Saṃgha. The ten evil deeds (*daśākuśala*) may be understood accordingly. The five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds are of the utmost gravity;
yet the accomplishment of ten recitations is of the utmost lightness. That one immediately attains rebirth precisely refers to "rebirth while carrying one's karma."
They dwell in the lowest of the lower grades, yet all are together with those in the stage of "one more birth" (ekajātipratibaddha). This precisely refers to the non-retrogression of rank;

that is, they have already fully realized the three types of non-retrogression. To explain this in detail: those who attain rebirth while still carrying their karmic burdens and so forth can be known to have fully realized the non-retrogression of mindfulness (*smṛty-apratipatti*).

This means they have fully perceived the Dharma-body, fully purified the Land of Quiescent Radiance (*śāntaprabhāsa-kṣetra*), fully severed fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), and fully cultivated [the path].

The *bodhipākṣika-dharmas* (factors conducive to enlightenment) of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) involve the perfect realization of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) and the perfect transformation of the five turbidities of this Sahā world.

One may understand by analogy that these entail non-retrogression in practice and non-retrogression in rank. Thus, the Sūtra says: "As soon as sentient beings are born in that land, they all possess the three kinds of non-retrogression.

Among them, many are those who will attain Buddhahood in one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*). Those who will attain Buddhahood in one more birth will, in a single lifetime, [complete their cultivation]."
He is the Buddha. One who attains Buddhahood in a single lifetime does so because for one who practices mindfulness of the Buddha, every thought-moment is itself the Buddha.
△ Second, pointing out the transcendence [of the Pure Land], which has two parts: first, showing that it is difficult to transcend this land; second, showing the transcendence of that land.

△ First. [Commentary] However, according to the path of teaching: if one is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), then one is not among those who have attained the first fruit and so forth; if one is of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), then one is not among the bodhisattvas and so forth;
if one is a worldling (*bāla*), then one does not possess the nature of equal birth (*sabhāgatā*). Furthermore, "non-retrogression through mindfulness" is not...

Ordinary beings practice without regression; it is not merely that they do not regress during the stage of the Path of Seeing. It would be a great falsehood to claim that ordinary people can leap over stages [to attain realization].
Rather, "progress" refers to the relinquishing of what has been previously attained.
[Commentary] This one advance and one retreat clarifies that the path of teaching is not disordered.

An ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who is fully possessed of afflictions is, by their very nature, not the same as the noble ones (*ārya*) of the first fruit who have realized the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Furthermore, those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*) who do not resolve for enlightenment are likewise not of the same class as Bodhisattvas who constantly deliver sentient beings. "Ordinary beings" (*isattva*) refers to those at the stage of the Three Virtuous Stages (*trividha-śukla-bhūmi*), who are still characterized by ignorance (*avidyā*).

The [obstructions] have not yet been shattered; the Dharma-body has not yet been realized; one does not share the same essence as the Tathāgata. Therefore, one is called an "ordinary being" (*pṛthagjana*).
Furthermore, this is not the same nature as the Bodhisattvas of the First Ground who have realized the Dharma-body.

This constitutes one step forward, clarifying that those below cannot falsely leap over to the higher stages. Moreover, the "same-nature" of non-retrogression through mindfulness is no longer that of an ordinary being.
The three types of worthies are Bodhisattvas who have not yet regressed from their practice; they are certainly not merely those at the initial fruit of seeing the Way.
Sages who have not regressed from their stage are certainly not ordinary people who still possess afflictions.

This is one instance of "regression," clarifying that one cannot falsely assume the name of a lower rank. To "leap over ranks" means to bypass the proper sequence; thus, it constitutes a great falsehood and becomes an unwholesome act.
To claim one has attained what one has not attained, or to claim one has realized what one has not realized, is a great falsehood. Regarding the statement that "one abandons the old upon advancing":
when an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) advances, they acquire the new title of "sage" and thus abandon the former name of "ordinary person.

This extends even to an ordinary being who, upon advancing, acquires the new designation of the "First Ground" (prathamabhūmi) and thereby abandons the former names of the "Three Degrees of Worthiness" (trikalyāṇapudgala).
...and so forth.
△ Second, showing the transcendence of that land.
[Commentary: Only in the Shared Realm of Ultimate Bliss are all things neither-nor and all things both-yes-and-no.
[Commentary] "Both are neither" means to transcend perfectly. "Both are" means to be perfectly severed. "Severed" refers to being free from dependence;
it is non-conceptualization. Because it is non-conceptual, both are. That all things are "both neither and both" is stated with reference to the primary retribution (*vipāka*).
Thus, they are not ordinary people, not those of the two vehicles, not bodhisattvas, and yet they are also not Buddhas.

This is because they share the same essence as the Buddha, yet they are fully possessed of afflictions. Furthermore, they are all simultaneously everything: they are Buddhas because they share the same essence as the Buddha.

Because they are fully possessed of afflictions, they are also ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). From the perspective of their *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive environment), they are not of the *sahā-lokadhātu* (Shared World), for all are Bodhisattvas in their final birth (*ekajāti-pratibaddha*).
Yet, because they are all common people, they are also not of the *śānta-prabhāsvara-lokadhātu* (World of Tranquil Light).

Furthermore, because they are all common people, they are indeed of the *sahā-lokadhātu*. And because they are all Bodhisattvas in their final birth, they are also of the *śānta-prabhāsvara-lokadhātu*. Below...
The text states: If one claims this is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), yet they have not passed through the stage of a common worldling;

if one claims this is one bound for Buddhahood in a single lifetime (*ekajātipratibaddha*), yet they can still be called an ordinary person—remaining non-retrogressive in this Sahā world, such a state is difficult to realize and difficult to transcend. Yet, such is the rank and order of Sukhāvatī.
Such supreme excellence and transcendence may be called the wondrous gate of the inconceivable and the unsurpassed causal condition.
This concludes the second point.
△ Third, the conclusion and dedication.
[Commentary: Throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is no such name or designation, no such stage or rank, and no such Dharma-gate.

This is not the ultimate limit of the nature of mind, nor is it the marvelous merit of upholding the Name, nor the Great Vow of Amitābha. How could such things (as these various aspects of the Pure Land School of Ultimate Bliss) exist?
[Commentary] This concludes by returning to the three inconceivable causes. These three inconceivables are the three essentials.
Regarding the phrase "in the ten directions there are no such names or marks," it means that there are no such stages or levels of names and marks characterized by being neither both nor either.

Only in the Land of Ultimate Bliss do these designations of "neither both nor either" and "both being and not being" exist; only in the Land of Ultimate Bliss do these stages of "neither both nor either" and "both being and not being" exist.
That the Land of Ultimate Bliss possesses these is because it contains this dharma-gate of "neither both nor either" and "both being and not being.

"Neither both nor either" refers to Immeasurable Life (*Amitāyus*); "both being and not being" refers to Immeasurable Light (*Amitābha*). Therefore, it is said that upholding the name is the ultimate consummation of the non-mind-nature.

Regarding these extraordinary merits and the great vows of Amitābha: how do they come to be? Because the ultimate state of the mind-nature (cittatā) is luminous and eternal, there arise the names and characteristics of "luminous eternity.
Because of these extraordinary merits of luminous eternity—wherein "merit" refers to *guṇa* or spiritual achievement—the stages of luminous eternity first come into being.
Because of the great vows of luminous eternity, the Dharma-gates of luminous eternity arise. As for this ultimate state of the mind-nature:
The essential point of the mind; the marvelous merit of upholding the name; the essential point of the objective realm; the great vow of Amitābha;
and the essential point of the Dharma gate—these three essentials are precisely the three inconceivables. The initial explanation of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression) is hereby concluded.
△ Second, the explanation of those in their final birth (ekajātipratibaddha) has three parts: first, the formal explanation; second, the pointing out; third, the eulogy. △ Now, the first:
【Commentary】 "One who is in their final birth" refers to one who will attain the rank of Buddhahood in only one more lifetime, such as Maitreya, Avalokiteśvara, and others.
The inhabitants of Sukhāvatī all universally attain Buddhahood in a single lifetime; since every individual must truly realize the state of being in their final birth, there are many among them.
There are such supreme virtues as these, which cannot be fully enumerated.

[Commentary] "One who is in their final birth before Buddhahood" (ekajātipratibaddha) is another name for the threefold non-retrogression mentioned in the preceding text; it refers specifically to one who will attain the rank of Buddha in a single lifetime.

This corresponds to what is stated in the following passage: "Together exhausting ignorance and together ascending to wondrous enlightenment. This occurs within the stage of non-retrogression at every thought-moment (*kṣaṇāvinivartana*).
Having transcended the forty-one stages of causal practice, their rank is equal to that of Maitreya in this land and Avalokiteśvara in that land.
