This applies not only to a single individual, but to all the people of Sukhāvatī as well; even the parrots and starlings of this land who are reborn there are likewise so.
Because every thought-moment is itself the Buddha, they do not fall into the ranks of the ordinary or the sage.

Regarding the successive stages: one must truly realize the state of the "one more birth" (ekajātipratibaddha). Therefore, there are many such superior virtues among them that cannot be known by calculation.
Having fully realized the three non-regressions, one then perfectly transforms the five turbidities and perfectly perceives the three bodies;
all such powers and functions are contained therein.
△ Second, the pointing out. [Commentary:
Furthermore, throughout the entire period of Śākyamuni’s temporal teachings, it is only in the *Avataṃsaka* that the perfection of a single lifetime is clarified.

As for the cause of this perfection of a single lifetime, it is the ten great kings of vows within the "Universal Worthy’s Vows and Practices" chapter at the very end, which guide one back to the source.
"Peaceful Sustenance. Furthermore, this is used to exhort the assembly of the Flower Treasury Ocean.

[Commentary] This indicates its supreme excellence and transcendence. Regarding the "Dharma taught during the single lifetime": this refers to the teachings spoken by Śākyamuni throughout his forty-nine years.
Tiantai categorized these as the Eight Teachings of the Correct Period and the Five Periods; that is to say, the Flower...
The periods of the *Śīla* (Precepts), the *Āgama*, the Vaipulya, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Nirvāṇa*.

The eight teachings consist of the four teachings of the ritual format (*kai-i*) and the four teachings of the doctrinal content (*kai-hō*). A detailed study of the *Gangzong* (Outline of the Teachings) is not the objective here; therefore, it is not recorded.
As for the *Avataṃsaka* clarifying the perfection of a single lifetime, this refers to how, among the various sutras within the temporal teachings of a single dispensation, the *Avataṃsaka* alone...
This meaning does not exist elsewhere; it is found only in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which clarifies the causes for attaining perfect Buddhahood in a single lifetime.

Specifically, this refers to how the youth Sudhana first encountered Mañjuśrī and attained fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), and subsequently visited fifty-two spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and attained discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇa-jñāna*).
Regarding the causes for perfection in a single lifetime, it means that—within one...

This constitutes the cause for generating Buddhahood. Later, he encounters Samantabhadra, who guides him back to the fulfillment of the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss through the ten great kings of vows, beginning with "First, prostrating to all Buddhas.
This fulfillment is not achieved within this Sahā world. It was not only Sudhana alone; the entire assembly of the Flower Treasury Ocean heard and received this together.
Therefore, it is said that this is the Dharma-gate for seeking birth in the Pure Land, intended to encourage the assembly of beings in the Flower Treasury Ocean.
The *Chapter on Vows and Practices* states: "May I, when my life is about to end, be completely cleared of all obstacles;
may I behold that Buddha Amitābha face-to-face and immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss. Once I have been reborn in that land..."
Manifesting before me, this great vow was accomplished; all things were perfectly fulfilled without exception.

For the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to the entire realm of sentient beings, that Buddha’s assembly was entirely pure. At that time, I was born from an excellent lotus and personally beheld the Tathāgata Amitābha.
He manifested before me and bestowed upon me the prophecy of Bodhi. Having received that prophecy from the Tathāgata, I transformed...
With countless hundreds of koṭis of bodies, his power of wisdom is vast and pervades the ten directions, universally benefiting the entire realm of sentient beings.
If this sutra were to appear sequentially during the five periods [of the Dharma], it would arise in the third; if one discusses attaining Buddhahood within a single lifetime, [it is as follows].

This sutra alone is uniquely peerless. Thus, while in the *Avataṃsaka* it is only Sudhana who attains Buddhahood in a single lifetime, in this sutra one returns to the Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) in a single lifetime;
such attainment of Buddhahood in one lifetime is beyond the reach of calculation and may be called truly supreme, extraordinary, and transcendent.
△ III. Eulogy. [Commentary] Alas!
That ordinary beings should, as a rule, ascend to the stage of the Bodhisattva of the Final Birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*) is a marvelous proclamation and an ultimate discourse that cannot be fathomed.

What was received in the *Avataṃsaka* is, in fact, contained within this sutra; yet, throughout the world, from ancient times to the present, those who believe are few while those who doubt are many. The words are prolix and the meaning has been eroded. I—[the author]—...
It is nothing other than cutting open one's heart and draining one's blood.

[Commentary] "Ordinary beings are exemplified by those in the stage of the 'near-attainment' (sāmantaka)" means that the lowest of the low is used as an analogy for the highest of the high. "Exemplified" (re) means "generally" (kai).
This refers to treating the lowest of the low among people as identical to the highest of the high in the stage of near-attainment, without distinguishing between superior and inferior. This...
This is the inconceivable Pure Land school wherein every thought-moment is itself the Buddha.

This extraordinary proclamation and ultimate discourse—the principle that ordinary beings may, as a rule, ascend to the stage of the Bodhisattva who is next to Buddhahood—is found only in this sutra and is absent from other sutras. Therefore, this sutra is an unparalleled proclamation and a most wondrous discourse;

it may truly be called a sutra beyond measure. *Avataṃsaka*... Great [Sutra]... (Note: The text fragment provided ends with "華嚴大" (Huáyán Dà), which refers to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. As the source text was incomplete, the translation reflects the available portion.)

The meaning of attaining Buddhahood in a single lifetime as taught in the sutras, which ultimately leads one back to the Pure Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*), is found precisely in this very scripture.
Who can believe in this principle? And who, again, does not doubt it? Not only in the present day;

even the ancient *Huayan Helun* (Comprehensive Treatise on the Avataṃsaka) still claimed that the Western Paradise is provisional while the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*) is real. Therefore, it is said that throughout all time and across the world, those who believe in this are few.
There is much doubt regarding this. Although there are two or three commentaries, their language is excessively verbose.

The principle that ordinary beings generally ascend to the stage of the Bodhisattva of the Tenth Ground (Bhūmi), and the tenet that every thought-moment is itself Buddha—these meanings of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* upon which this scripture relies—are completely eclipsed.
"Eclipsed" (*shik*) means deficient. I, an old man, simply state below that I have no other dharma; I have only sliced open my heart and shed my blood.
And that is all. Therefore, this commentary—every single character—is the very heart-blood of an old man. The preceding text clarified the great causal conditions for our attainment of Buddhahood;
this, moreover, clarifies the great causal conditions for the Dharma-gate itself. Hence it is said that their significance is paramount.
Thus concludes the initial revelation of the unsurpassed causal conditions in the sutra text.
△ Second, the special exhortation:

Śāriputra, those sentient beings who have the good fortune to hear [of] this unsurpassed great matter and causal condition (mahā-kāraṇa-nidāna) as described above, should make a vow to be born in that land.
Why is this? Because one has been able to assemble in one place together with such superior and virtuous persons (who are incalculable in number and are in their final birth before Buddhahood).
[Commentary] Regarding "specific exhortation": it specifically exhorts sentient beings that they should seek rebirth by making a vow.
The aforementioned state of the supreme great cause and condition of attaining Buddhahood in one lifetime is now individually presented and shown; we have fortunately encountered it.
To hear [this teaching] is a blessing; it is to hear what one ought not to hear. Having already heard it, one should make a vow to seek rebirth there.
Once born in that land, one will immediately attain the rank of a candidate for Buddhahood (anujāta). If one does not make a vow to seek rebirth there, [the opportunity is lost].
It is a pity that [this person] has heard this sutra in vain.
△ The commentary is divided into four parts: first, explaining "excellent" (shàn); second, explaining "one place" (yīchù); third, identifying the Pure Land school;
fourth, emphasizing faith and aspiration. △ Now, the first part.

[Commentary]: The aforementioned Arhats and Bodhisattvas may simply be called "virtuous persons" (*satpuruṣa*). Only those in the final stage of rebirth (*caramabhavika*) occupy the ultimate limit of the causal stage;
therefore, they are called "superior. Since their number is extremely vast, they are referred to as "all" (*sarva*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement in the preceding text that Arhats and Bodhisattvas may simply be called "good people," those from the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) downward in that land are generally considered its "people.
Nevertheless, although they are people, they are people who possess untainted, inconceivable goodness.
Among good people, it is not improper to distinguish between superior, middling, and inferior. Arhats are the inferior among the good; Bodhisattvas are the middling among the good;
and those in the position of the successor (the final stage of the causal path) may be called the superior among the good.

Since there are many such superior ones, it is likewise not improper to further divide them into superior, middling, and inferior; thus, there is the distinction of three ranks and nine grades, continuing up to the Sublime [State].
Awakening. When ignorance is completely purified, then no categories can be obtained.

△ Second, the explanation of the "one place" is divided into three parts: first, a detailed demonstration of the coarseness and inferiority of this land; second, a pointed demonstration of the excellence and transcendence of that land;
third, a conclusion regarding the three inconceivables. The first part [of the first section] is further divided into two: first, showing the ordinary state; second, showing...
The Buddha’s World. △ Now, the first [section].
【Commentary】 "Gathering together in one place" means that ordinary beings and sages dwell together.

This is usually due to the past *sāsrava* (outflowing) karma of true sages, and the great compassionate vows of provisional sages; thus, ordinary beings are able to dwell together with sages until they reach the stage of true sainthood.

When the physical body is reduced to ashes, the provisional and sagely capacities are exhausted; thus, one’s ascent or descent varies greatly, and suffering and joy differ vastly. This is a temporary identity (like a spark from stone or a flash of lightning), not an ultimate identity.

Furthermore, within the space between heaven and earth, those who see and hear [of this] are few; even among those who have fortunately seen and heard it, those who can draw near and follow in its footsteps are few indeed.

[Commentary] The text has two parts: first, the general; second, the specific. "General" refers to a general explanation of the Land of Common Dwelling (*sahā-loka*). "Specific" refers to the distinct clarification of the heavens and the human realm.
"All meeting in one place" is like saying that ordinary beings and sages dwell together.

"Ordinary times" refers to before and after the Buddha’s appearance, distinguishing this from the era when the Buddha is in the world. Regarding "actual sages," within the Land of Common Dwelling, ordinary beings are exclusively of one kind.

There are two types of noble ones (*ārya*): one is the ultimate, and one is the provisional. The ultimate refers to those who have realized the state of a noble one through actual realization—namely, those who have directly realized the first, second, or third fruits of the path.
Although their past tainted karma (*sāsrava-karma*) and their afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*) have been severed, their afflictions of conduct (*bhāvanā-āsrava*) are not yet exhausted.

Conventional sages (*prajñā-satya*) consist of those from the three aforementioned lands as well as those who manifest from other directions. Real sages arise through karma, whereas conventional sages arise through vows;
thus, ordinary beings are able to dwell together with sages. As for real sages, when their karma is exhausted and their afflictions are emptied, [they transcend].
With the body reduced to ashes and wisdom extinguished, the provisional capacities of the sages are exhausted and their vows fulfilled;

as the path of resonance and response ceases, there is a vast difference between ascending and sinking, and suffering and joy are worlds apart. This is merely a temporary cohabitation, not the ultimate cohabitation of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Furthermore, beneath the heavens and earth, one separately distinguishes between the celestial and the human realms. "Heaven" refers to the five heavens of non-returners (*pañcānāgāmin*); "earth" refers to...
In the human realm, there are sacred sites of the Path, such as Mount Tiantai and Mount Wutai. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"The various heavenly kings of this Heaven of Non-returning have only heard of these with reverence, yet they cannot perceive or see them.

This is because places in the world such as vast wildernesses and deep mountains that serve as sites for the sacred Path are all sustained by Arhats; thus, they are beyond the reach of coarse worldly people."
It cannot be seen; though it is fortunate that one may see it, those who remain in close proximity for a long time are few—such as Han Shan, Shi De, and others.
It is fortunate that one may hear it, yet those who follow it from afar, stepping forward with diligence, are likewise not many.
△ Second, showing the Buddha’s era.

[Commentary: Furthermore, although there were many sages during the Buddha’s lifetime—rare and auspicious as they were—they could not fill the entire land, being like the stars or motes of dust in the air.
Moreover, though they dwelt together, their deeds and accomplishments were utterly distinct.
[Commentary] The preceding section was ordinary, clarifying their coarseness. This section cites the era of the Buddha to further reveal their inferiority.
While Bodhisattvas and others also appeared in the world during the Buddha’s lifetime, they were nonetheless as rare as precious jewels and as transient as auspicious omens;
they could not fill the land as extensively as in Sukhāvatī, remaining there constantly like the myriad stars.
Throughout the heavens, there are as many [beings] as there are motes of dust covering the earth. Furthermore, although they dwell together, their activities and accomplishments differ;
moreover, this is not like the Land of Ultimate Bliss, where all activities and accomplishments are identical.
Thus, there is only the provisional name of "co-residence," but no actual reality of co-residence. Therefore, it is called "crude and inferior."
△ Second, indicating that that land is superior and transcendent, in two parts: first, showing its excellence; second, showing its transcendence. △ Now, the first. [Commentary]:

Now, by means of identical outflow-free and inconceivable karma (through the causes and conditions of many roots of goodness and merit), they are born together in one place (attaining birth in that land) to serve as teachers and friends, as follows:
The *xun* is like the *chi*. Together they exhaust ignorance and together ascend to wondrous enlightenment.
[Commentary] Together, by means of untainted and inconceivable karma, they manifest birth and gather in one place; this demonstrates that their ultimate cause is identical.
This is superior and distinct from the aforementioned "what is done" and "what is accomplished," which are entirely different. Acting as teacher and friend, they are like the *xun* and the *chi*.
The *chí* (flute). This excellence and distinction, as marvelous as a rare treasure or an auspicious omen, occurs neither frequently nor constantly.
When [beings] together exhaust ignorance and together ascend to wondrous enlightenment, it reveals that their ultimate fruits are identical; thus, this is called "ultimate co-residence" (*jùtóng*).

The preceding text spoke of "birth co-residence," which already implies being born horizontally across the three higher lands. Regarding "outflow-free, inconceivable karma," every thought-moment is...

The practice of the Buddha completely transcends the outflows (*āsrava*) of the nine realms; therefore, it is called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*). It completely transcends the discrimination of the nine realms;

therefore, it is called "inconceivable karma. That which causes beings to be born together in one place refers to the fact that all phenomena produced by causes and conditions are, in their entirety, the non-arising ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Thus, they act as teachers and friends to one another, like the *xun* and *chi* flutes sounding in harmony.
They may become teachers and friends, or brothers; they do not abandon or separate from one another. *Xun* and *chi* are names for musical instruments.
In antiquity, there were two brothers, one playing the *xun* and the other playing the *chi*, who never parted. The *Book of Poetry* contains the lines:
"The elder brother blows the *xun*; the younger brother blows the *chi*. Together they exhaust ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the perfect severance of the five [hindrances].
Abiding in the four lands of perfect purity and so forth, they together ascend to wondrous enlightenment, thereby perfectly realizing the three bodies and perfectly realizing the three wisdoms;
all powers and functions are sovereignly contained therein.
△ Second, showing transcendence.
[Commentary]: This means that ordinary sentient beings, within the state of non-retrogression in thought-moment (*cittakṣaṇa*), transcend and exhaust the forty-one causal stages.

If one considers them to be ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), they do not yet pass through the stage of a commoner; they will certainly fulfill the office of a Buddha, being equal to Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta.

They are distinct. If one were to claim that being in the stage of "one birth remaining" (ekajātipratibaddha) can only be called an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and cannot be called an Equal-Enlightened Bodhisattva (*samyaksambuddha-bodhisattva*), these views are all beyond the reach of the net of the teachings and cannot be categorized by the net of the lands; [only this] is the Pure Land School of Ultimate Bliss.
[Commentary]: "This then" refers to the two meanings of "perfect transcendence" and "perfect severance" pointed out within the preceding discussion of superior distinctions;

these are precisely the two meanings of "unconditioned perfect fusion. "Ordinary beings below" refers to those who attain rebirth while still carrying their karmic burdens, such as Zhang Zhongqiu and Zhang Shanhe.
"Transcending all forty-one stages of causal progression" refers to these very same evil [beings].

A person, by means of the practice of "every thought-moment is itself Buddha," is reborn in that land in a single lifetime and directly attains the fruit of Buddhahood, without passing through the causal stages of a Bodhisattva;

hence it is called "perfectly transcending" (*yuanchao*). Since it is called "perfectly transcending," this refers to the perfect purity of the four lands, the perfect realization of the three bodies, and the perfect realization of the three non-regressions, and so forth.
As for the phrase "if one says... and below, it clarifies that [the practitioner] is neither ordinary nor sage. Furthermore—

To be both ordinary and holy at once: those whom the net of the teachings cannot ensnare—this is because the Tathāgata’s eightfold teaching is like a net, intended to scoop up and gather sentient beings;
yet those who cannot be gathered possess neither such names nor characteristics, nor such stages or positions.
Those whom the net of lands cannot encompass—Buddha-fields are also like a net, with worlds as the meshes and the mountain ranges of the Cakravāḍas as the cords, layer upon layer.
Their mutual inclusion is inexhaustible. As for those who cannot be categorized [by analogy], they likewise lack such names and characteristics, such stages and positions, and such co-residence;
therefore, it is impossible to draw comparisons. (2) This concludes the demonstration that the other land is superior and transcendent.
△ Three Bonds and Three Inconceivables.
[Commentary: One should know that the great matter of human beings shares a single gate; it is truly difficult to penetrate and escape (a plain truth).
Only the shared realm of the Utmost Bliss transcends all other shared realms throughout the ten directions. Only by understanding this can one develop deep faith in the Vow of Amitābha.
Through power—specifically, faith in the Buddha’s power—one can then deeply believe in the merit of the Name.
Through faith in upholding the Name, one can then deeply believe that the nature of our own minds is inherently inconceivable.
[Commentary]: The "great matter of cause and condition" for us humans refers to the great matter of cause and condition for attaining Buddhahood.

Regarding the most difficult things to escape from within the Shared [Land], it is the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) that are most difficult to sever, and the birth-and-death of limited segments (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*) that is most difficult to transcend.
Only the Shared [Land] of the Utmost Bliss World transcends all other Shared Lands in the ten directions; only the Shared Land of Utmost Bliss can completely sever [these obstacles].
Perfectly pure, perfectly realized, and perfectly liberated, one will certainly attain Buddhahood in a single lifetime, without reaching a second birth.
One who understands this realizes that it is most difficult to attain Buddhahood in this Land of Shared Dwelling, whereas it is most easy to attain Buddhahood in that Land of Shared Dwelling.
Only then will one truly believe in the power of Amitābha’s vows, for that Land of Shared Dwelling is established through the vows and practices of Amitābha. Thus, one believes in the Buddha.
Regarding the power of faith in the merit of the Name: it is because this is what is evoked by the pure karma of sentient beings who uphold the Name;
thus, one must first believe in the Name before one can believe that the nature of our own minds is fundamentally inconceivable.

This is because that [nature] is manifested by the Tathāgata’s Wisdom of the Species (jāti-jñāna) within the Land of Common Residence, and because it is a transformation of the consciousness-only (vijñapti-mātra) of sentient beings. [The nature of the mind is] the Wisdom of the Species, which is consciousness-only.
This is precisely the self-nature of the single thought-moment of my present mind.
Because the nature of the mind that manifests is inconceivable, that which is manifested—the shared dwelling—is also inconceivable.
Now, by understanding this inconceivability of what is manifested, one gains faith that the nature of the mind is fundamentally inconceivable. The explanation of the "one place" is complete.
△ The Three Points Reveal the Pure Land School.
[Commentary] Only when one possesses this profound faith can one give rise to the Great Vow. When faith and vow are united, they serve as the definitive guide to the Pure Land.
To then uphold the Name based upon this constitutes the primary practice.
[Commentary] When one possesses these three kinds of profound faith, that faith is necessarily genuine, for the three faiths are identical to the six faiths.

When genuine faith gives rise to a vow, that vow is necessarily earnest, for the innate goodness of the mind manifests. The union of this faith and vow constitutes the definitive practice of wisdom for the Pure Land;
it is a guide, specifically a compass, because the practice of wisdom serves as the vanguard. Holding fast to this is called [the Name].
This is called "practice within practice. When both the eyes and the feet move together, and these two practices support one another, it constitutes "correct practice.
4. Sole Emphasis on Faith and Vow. [Commentary]:
If faith and vow are firm and steadfast, then at the time of death, even ten recitations or a single recitation will certainly result in birth [in the Pure Land]. If there is no faith and vow...

Even if one were to maintain the Name until it becomes like a silver wall or an iron fortress, impenetrable by wind and undampened by rain, there would still be no principle by which birth [in the Pure Land] could be attained.

Those who practice the path of purity must not fail to understand this. (In this world, there is a class of people who attempt to suppress delusive thoughts by reciting the Name, yet do not know to seek birth; thus, this is a most forceful refutation.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (the Larger Version) likewise takes the arousal of the bodhicitta vow as its essential point, which is exactly the same as this.
[Commentary]: If one lacks faith and aspiration, one does not believe that the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is the mind-only and that Amitābha is one's own self-nature (svabhāva).
Instead, one merely believes that the deluded thoughts of conditioned reflections constitute the mind-only and self-nature; therefore, one does not give rise to the aspiration to seek birth there.
Although they do recite the Buddha’s name, it serves merely to suppress deluded thoughts. This practice not only fails to bring merit, but actually entails transgression;
because they lack faith and aspiration, they will inevitably incur the fault of slandering the Dharma.
Therefore, this is stated in advance as a warning for those who cultivate the Pure Land. Those who have correctly resolved upon the Bodhicitta vow and seek rebirth in the Pure Land—
Because of the vow for Bodhi, one must cultivate weary detachment toward seeking rebirth;

this weary detachment is precisely the vow to deliver boundless sentient beings, the vow to sever inexhaustible afflictions, the vow to study immeasurable Dharma-gates, and the vow to accomplish the unsurpassed path of the Buddha.
The text specifically exhorts sentient beings in two ways that they should seek rebirth therein.
The making of the vow is concluded.
△ Third, the formal demonstration of how the practitioner upholds the Name to establish their practice, in two parts: first, the formal demonstration of the unsurpassed cause and effect;
second, the concluding exhortation. △ Now, the first part.
Śāriputra, one cannot be born in that land by means of few roots of goodness, merit, or causal conditions. Śāriputra,
if there are good men or good women who hear the name of Amitābha Buddha and hold it fast—
whether for one day, two days, three days, four days, five days, six days, or seven days— [they shall be born there].
Their minds will not be distracted. When that person approaches the end of life, Amitābha Buddha, together with a multitude of holy beings, will appear before them.
At the time of death, this person’s mind will not be inverted, and they will immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.
△ The commentary is divided into three parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the refutation of doubts; third, the admonition and exhortation. Within the first part, there are five sections:
first, a general explanation of the unsurpassed cause and fruit; second, a specific clarification of the holder and that which is held; third, a specific clarification of the three types of wisdom.
Fourth, the two marks of rebirth; fifth, concluding the preceding and initiating the subsequent. The first [section] also has two parts: first, clarifying the cause;
second, clarifying the fruit. △ Now, the first.
【Commentary】 The correct path to Bodhi is called the "wholesome root" (kuśalamūla), which is the direct cause. Various aids to the path, such as giving, precepts, and meditation, are called...

Those with little merit—meaning those with few roots of goodness conducive to the enlightenment of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas as auxiliary conditions, or those with little tainted meritorious karma and merit pertaining to humans and devas—cannot all be born in the Pure Land.

Only by upholding the Name through faith and aspiration does every single utterance of its sound come to possess manifold roots of goodness and merit. Even if one recites the Name with a distracted mind, the resulting merit and goodness remain inexhaustible.
How much more so for those whose minds are not distracted! [Commentary] The text has two parts:
first, the direct explanation of roots of goodness and merit; second, the specific clarification of those who attain birth and those who do not.
From "Bodhi" (*bodhi*) downward explains the roots of goodness; from "various" (*vividha*) downward clarifies merit. As for "roots of goodness," this refers to the right path of Bodhi.

Bodhi is the wisdom that is able to cultivate the factors of enlightenment; therefore, it is called the "Right Path. As for the "direct cause," it is also termed the "cultivation cause" (*abhyāsa-hetu*).
The cultivation cause brings about the "cultivation fruit," which is the body of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as the sovereign of the collective retribution.

"Merit" refers to the various auxiliary paths, namely the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). As for the "auxiliary condition," it is also termed the "retribution cause" (*vipāka-hetu*). The retribution cause brings about the "retribution fruit."
The "fruit" refers specifically to the merit of individual retribution and so forth. Second, regarding the specific clarification of those who attain birth and those who do not:

first, the explanation of those who do not attain birth. Those with meager roots of goodness among *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*: for *śrāvakas*, this indicates the roots of goodness of Bodhi according to the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) teachings;

for *pratyekabuddhas*, it indicates the roots of goodness of Bodhi according to the *Vaipulya* (Shared) teachings. These two teachings, the *Āgama* and the *Vaipulya*, are not the causes for attaining Buddhahood.
Therefore, it is said that they are "few. Those among humans and devas who perform meritorious karma with outflows cannot escape the suffering of birth and death;

hence it is called "karma with outflows. Consequently, their merit and virtue are also slight. Because their wholesome roots of merit are not numerous, none of them can be born in the Pure Land or attain Buddhahood in a single lifetime.
The phrase "Only those below" clarifies that they are able to be born [in the Pure Land]. Within faith, all matters are fully contained.
Unimpeded faith; and within that vow, vows that are themselves unimpeded in every respect—these two are the direct causes for manifold roots of goodness and are called the "practice of wisdom.
Guided by wisdom, practice itself becomes unimpeded in every respect;
this is the auxiliary condition for manifold merit and is called the "practice of practice. Therefore, each and every sound is endowed with manifold roots of goodness.

One possesses great merit. Even if one recites the Name with a distracted mind, the resulting virtue and goodness are still beyond measure; how much more so for one whose mind is single-minded and undisturbed.
How could such a person not attain rebirth?
△ Second, clarifying the fruit.

[Commentary]: Thus, the Way of resonance and response intermingles. When the inscription is completed and the seal is broken, the holy assembly of Amitābha comes without coming, personally extending their hands to receive and guide them;
the practitioner’s consciousness goes without going, entrusting its substance to a precious lotus.
[Commentary] Therefore, it is said: "Because each and every matter is without obstruction, the Way of mutual resonance between the response and the stimulus is first attained.
The manifestation of the text and the destruction of the seal occur simultaneously; as soon as the Buddha is able to receive [the response], the sentient being is able to be born."
Regarding the mutual resonance of the Way: my own roots of goodness and merit serve as the "inducer," which may be either a hidden induction or a manifest induction;
the holy assembly of Amitābha serves as the "induced," whose compassionate response serves as the "responder," which may be either a hidden response or a manifest response.
The roots of goodness and merit of sentient beings serve as the necessary conditions.

If these roots of goodness and merit reach the stage of contemplative practice where the mind is single-minded and undisturbed, then there is a mutual resonance between the practitioner and the holy assembly of Amitābha in his transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) who dwells with us.

If they reach the stage of the "single-mindedness of the phenomenal" or the "resemblance to single-mindedness," then there is a mutual resonance with the holy assembly of Amitābha in his response body (saṃbhogakāya).

When the way of resonance and response intermingles—if one has reached the ultimate principle of single-mindedness without distraction—this is also called partial realization of single-mindedness without distraction;
thus, one resonates with the holy assembly of the Dharma-body and Reward-body within the True Reward Land and the Land of Quiescent Light.
If one has not yet reached single-mindedness without distraction, then one merely resonates with the holy assembly of the Dharma-body; this is simply a silent resonance with the unmanifest.
It responds. Response and induction are but a single mind; therefore, there is no obstruction. Regarding the phrase "the pattern forms and the seal is destroyed," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"For example, it is like a wax seal being pressed into clay. As the seal and the clay meet, the seal dissolves and the pattern forms.

This refers to casting an image from copper: once the pattern of the image is formed, the wax mold is destroyed. This serves as a metaphor for when the manifest aggregates (*skandhas*) of sentient beings perish, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arises.
The formation of the [Pure Land] realms occurs simultaneously. To borrow an analogy for this: when the text describing the Pure Land is established, the seal of the Sahā world is destroyed;

this occurs within a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*). Whether it be the text establishing the Realm of Common Dwelling, or even the texts establishing the Real Reward Land and the Land of Quiescent Light—their formation and destruction depend solely upon the one mind.
Therefore, it is said to be "unimpeded. The holy assembly of Amitābha does not come.

As for "coming here and personally extending a hand of guidance," this refers to the holy assembly of Amitābha; yet this Amitābha is the Amitābha within the minds of sentient beings, and therefore he does not come.
This phrase pertains to principle (*li*), which is the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*). The subsequent phrase pertains to phenomena (*shi*);

thus, he comes and personally extends a hand of guidance, which is the gate of birth-and-death (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*). These two gates are nothing other than the one mind (*ekacitta*); thus, when there is guidance...
It is definitively a meeting. That which comes does not truly come. The mind-consciousness of sentient beings goes where it does not go.

As for "reposing one's substance upon a precious lotus," Pure Land is the pure land within the minds of sentient beings; therefore, there is no going. While the Gate of True Suchness (Tathatā-mukha) involves no going, reposing one's substance upon a precious lotus belongs to the Gate of Birth-and-Death (Utpāda-nirodha-mukha).

These two gates are but a single mind; thus, birth— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the philosophical context of the T'ien-t'ai/Tendai school regarding the relationship between the two gates and the nature of rebirth.*
Thus, birth is determinate; yet, in departing, there is truly no departure. Coming and going are but this single mind; therefore, there is no obstruction.
This concludes the general explanation of the unsurpassed cause and effect.
△ Second, a specific explanation of that which sustains and that which is sustained.

[Commentary: Regarding "good men and women," this refers to those without distinction of whether they are monastics or laypeople, noble or lowly, old or young, or belonging to the six destinies or four modes of birth.
Merely hearing the name of the Buddha causes the roots of goodness from many kalpas to ripen; even the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds are then termed "good."
Amitābha Buddha is the great name of myriad virtues. By invoking virtue through this name, it is fully and exhaustively realized;

therefore, the practice of upholding the name is established as the primary practice. There is no need to further engage in practices such as visualization or investigative inquiry (the words of Perfect Ultimateity).
It is most simple and most direct.
[Commentary]: "Good men and women" refers to those who are able to uphold [the name]; "the great name" (Hongming) refers to that which is upheld.

That the five heinous crimes and the ten evil acts are all called "good" refers to "goodness by name" (*mingzi-shan*), "goodness of contemplative practice" (*guanheng-shan*), and so forth. Merely hearing the name constitutes "goodness by name";

initiating practice and cultivation constitutes "goodness of contemplative practice," and so on. As for the "great name of myriad virtues," each of the hundred realms possesses the functions of the hundred realms.

Virtue; thus, it is said briefly as "ten thousand virtues. "Name" is used to summon virtue. "Exhaustively without anything left out" means that "name" refers to a provisional name (*prajñapti*), while "summoning" means to call out.
"Virtue" refers to actual, substantial virtue. Now, by using a provisional name to call out its actual virtue, the actual virtue is fully realized within the provisional name.
Outside of the provisional name, there is no actual virtue. It is like water being entirely transformed into ice; the ice [is nothing other than the water].
There is no water outside; it is unnecessary to further engage in practices such as visualization or investigation.
One need not seek water apart from the ice. This is the ultimate in simplicity and ease, the ultimate in being direct, swift, and proximate, because every thought-moment is itself Buddha.
Thus concludes the second section: the specific explanation of the grasper and the grasped.

△ Third, the specific explanation of the three types of wisdom is further divided into three parts: first, the explanation of the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); second, the explanation of the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); and third, the explanation of the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
△ Now, the first [part]. 【Commentary】 One hears and then believes;
believing, one makes a vow; only then does one willingly take up and uphold [the teaching]. If one does not believe and does not vow, it is equivalent to not having heard it at all. Although...
It serves as a remote cause, but it is not called "wisdom derived from hearing" (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
[Commentary]: This distinguishes it from wisdom derived from hearing. Only when all three provisions are complete is it designated as wisdom derived from hearing;
if even one is lacking, it is no different from not having heard at all.
△ Second, explaining the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), which is further divided into two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation. △ Now, the first part.

【Commentary】 To "maintain" means to recollect the Buddha’s name in every thought-moment; therefore, this is the wisdom of reflection. However, there are two types: maintaining through phenomena (*dharmata*) and maintaining through principle (*tattva*) (the long-standing error may be corrected here).

[Commentary] Regarding those long-standing errors that may be rectified: other commentators explain this "holding the name" and "single-mindedness without confusion" without relying on the teachings and contemplations;
therefore, their explanations are erroneous. I now provide a revised version. To "revise" means to establish the correct interpretation based upon the teachings and contemplations.
△ Second, the explanation has two parts. First, the maintenance through phenomena (*dharma*). Second, the maintenance through principle (*tattva*). △ Now, the first. [Commentary]:

Regarding "maintenance through phenomena," this refers to believing that there is Amitābha Buddha in the Western Quarter, yet not yet realizing that "this mind creates the Buddha" and "this mind is the Buddha.
It is merely a matter of resolutely vowing to seek birth [in that land], like a child longing for its mother, never forgetting it for even a moment.

[Commentary]: This clarifies that the practice of ritual observance (*sajji-hō*) consists solely of genuine faith, earnest aspiration, and actual practice; it does not yet clarify the principle of the self-nature of the mind-only.
Regarding the statements "this mind creates the Buddha" and "this mind is the Buddha," it means that all other Buddhas are entirely one's own mind.
One’s own mind is entirely the Buddha of others.
△ Second, the maintenance through principle.
[Commentary] As for "maintenance through principle," it means believing that Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land is fully possessed within one's own mind and is created by one's own mind.

One takes the great name, which is produced by and inherent within one's own mind, as the object for binding the mind, ensuring it is not momentarily forgotten (yet without abandoning worldly affairs).

[Commentary] This clarifies that because one has realized its principle, maintaining it through phenomena is itself maintaining it through principle. This concludes the section on the wisdom of reflection.
△ Section Two: The Cultivation of Wisdom through the Three Clarities. First, clarifying the fixed period of seven days; second, clarifying "one-pointed mind without distraction.
△ Now, the first [section].

【Commentary】 "From one day to seven days" refers to accomplishing the task within a fixed period. Those of sharp faculties achieve non-distraction in a single day, while those of dull faculties require up to seven.

For those of medium faculties, the period of non-distraction lasts two, three, four, five, or six days, as it is not fixed; this is the method for beginners who set a specific term (whereas for those of inferior faculties, there are various seven-day periods, which are likewise methods for setting a term according to one's inclination). Furthermore, those of sharp faculties can remain undistracted for seven days, while those of dull faculties remain undistracted for only a single day.
For those of medium faculties, the duration of non-distraction—six, five, four, three, or two days—is not fixed;
this is the method for those who have practiced for a long time (and for those of medium and inferior faculties, there are likewise various seven-day periods).
[Commentary] The text has two parts: first, those who are beginners; second, those who have long been refined. Regarding "one of sharp faculties attains non-distraction in a single day":

although such a person is a beginner in this life, their past causes were already matured long ago; thus, in this life, they attain it for the first time through the effort of a single day, whereby they immediately achieve the state of "single-minded non-distraction.
Here, "a single day" is the means by which it is attained (*nengde*), and "non-distraction" is that which is attained (*suode*).
Among those who have attained this, there are some who remain undisturbed for one day, two days, or even several days;
some attain non-distraction regarding phenomena (*dharma*), while others attain non-distraction regarding principles (*naya*). This is not fixed.

As for those of dull faculties who only become undisturbed after seven days, it is because their prior causes lacked sufficient cultivation; therefore, in this present life, they only just manage to become undisturbed after seven days. Regarding this...

Within this state of non-distraction, one may attain either the phenomenal (dharma) or the principle (artha); it is not fixed. Compared to those of superior faculties mentioned above, these are called dull;
yet compared to those of inferior faculties, they are still called sharp. This is because those of inferior faculties must pass through a certain number of seven-day periods.

As for those of middling faculties who [attain realization] in two, three, or four [periods], it is because their prior causes of cultivation were unequal, such that they are able to give rise [to realization] in this life.
It is not uniform. Within this state of non-confusion, there are also instances where for one day or two days it is not equal;

this is also because matters and principles are not fixed. The following clarifies the "long-term refinement": this refers to after one has already attained the stage of *kung-fu*, continuing to refine and practice for a long time.

If we speak in terms of matters and principles being non-confused, this refers to after one has already destroyed the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*), further destroying the two kinds of delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-āsrava*).

As for those of sharp faculties who can remain undisturbed for seven days: this may refer to a single seven-day period, or, if they have been refined to maturity, it may be for an indefinite number of seven-day periods.
Those of dull faculties who can remain undisturbed for only a single day do so because their root-nature is dull;
though they practice and refine for a long time, they achieve only one day of non-distraction and cannot exceed that. As for those of middling faculties:
Alternatively, it may be attained in six days, five days, or an indefinite period; even among those of middling and inferior faculties, there are various durations.

This means that those of middling faculties attain it within this lifetime after more than seven days have passed, while those of inferior faculties may attain it after one or two periods of seven days.
"Various" refers to an indefinite number. This concludes the clarification regarding the fixed period of seven days.
△ Second, explaining "single-mindedness without distraction.

[Commentary]: Single-mindedness is also of two kinds. Whether it be upholding through practice (*śīla*) or upholding through principle (*dharma*), until the afflictions (*kleśa*) are suppressed and eliminated, and even until the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are first exhausted, these are all "single-mindedness of practice" (*sāmayika-ekacitta*).
Whether it be upholding through practice or upholding through principle, until the mind opens and one perceives...
The Buddha of Original Nature: both the principle single-mind (*li yixin*) and the phenomena single-mind (*shi yixin*) are not disturbed by the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).

The principle single-mind is not disturbed by the two extremes. (Each character is drawn out like the *shang* and *yao* notes in music). This is precisely the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*).

[Commentary] The text has two parts: first, the clarification of the single mind; second, the clarification of non-distraction. Regarding the distinction between maintaining by means of phenomena (*dharma*) and maintaining by means of principle (*li*):

here, because one does not yet penetrate the principle, it is judged as "maintaining by means of phenomena. Now, because one penetrates that principle, what was previously "maintaining by means of phenomena" is judged to be "maintaining by means of principle.
Nevertheless, this does not abolish the phenomenon; thus, phenomenon and principle are a single unified upholding, and therefore [the former distinction] is not discussed.
"Maintaining [the name] until the afflictions are subdued and eliminated" means that by upholding the name, one reaches the stage of the five ranks of contemplative practice (*guanxing wu pinwei*).

To subdue the delusions of views (*jianhuo*) is called "subduing" (*fu*). If one reaches the first level of faith (*xin*), the delusions of views are realized as empty; this is called "eliminating" (*chu*). If one reaches the seventh level of faith, the delusions of thought (*sihuo*) perish;

this is called "the prior exhaustion of views and thoughts. When the phenomenal delusions within the realm of desire (*jie-nei shihuo*) are severed, it is called "single-mindedness regarding phenomena" (*shi yixin*). This is maintaining [the name] until the mind...

Regarding the opening of vision to see the Buddha of one's original nature: from the stage of the eight levels of faith through to the first dwelling of the initial resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*), ignorance is shattered and one directly realizes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Because delusions regarding principle are shattered, it is called "single-mindedness of principle" (*li-yixin*); because the ego-clinging of phenomena has perished, it is called "single-mindedness of phenomena" (*shi-yixin*).

Therefore, one is not disturbed by views or afflictions (*kleśa*). Since the attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*) has been exhausted through the principle of single-mindedness, one is not disturbed by the two extremes.
This constitutes cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). The detailed explanation of the three types of wisdom is hereby concluded.
△ Fourth, the two signs of rebirth. [Commentary:
Because one is not disturbed by the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), one perceives the manifestation of the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha and the various assemblies of sages before oneself.

One’s mind no longer gives rise to the inverted perceptions of the three realms of existence within the Sahā world. This constitutes the two types of rebirth: the Shared Land (*sahāloka*) and the Land of Expedient Means (*upāyabhūmi*).
Because they do not allow the world of bliss to be disturbed by the two extremes, the Sambhogakāya Buddha and the assembly of sages appear before them.

Their minds no longer give rise to the inverted dualistic views of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; they are reborn in the two kinds of ultimate Sukhāvatī worlds: the Realm of True Reward and the Land of Quiescent Light.

[Commentary] This explains the passage in the sutra stating that when such a person approaches the end of life, Amitābha Buddha, together with the assembly of holy beings, appears before them, and so forth.
The preceding two sections specifically clarify the unsurpassed cause; this section specifically clarifies the unsurpassed fruit.
Regarding the phrase "because one is not disturbed by the afflictions of views and thoughts," this follows from the previous discussion on the single-mindedness of practice (shishu ichinen).

He said: "If one's ordinary practice reaches the stage of 'one-pointedness of mind regarding phenomena,' because the grasping at a self is empty, at the time of death one will not be disturbed by the afflictions of views and thoughts.

One will enter as if into meditative concentration, and through the mutual resonance of the Way, the Transformation Body Buddha and the various holy assemblies will appear before one. At the moment of this person's passing, the mind will no longer give rise [to delusions]."
Within the Sahā world, there are the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, as well as the perversions of self-clinging.
If self-clinging is subdued, one will be reborn in the Shared Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss; if self-clinging is exhausted, one will be reborn in the Expedient Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
"Not being disturbed by the two extremes" refers to single-mindedness (ekāgratā) as established by the preceding textual principles.

Ordinarily, if one attains single-mindedness through the ultimate principle, attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) will perish. At the time of death, one will not be disturbed by the two extremes of emptiness and existence;

rather, like entering meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), there will be a mutual resonance between the practitioner and the Sambhogakāya Buddha and the assembly of holy ones, who will appear before them.
At the time of this person's death, the mind no longer gives rise to the two inverted views of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
If the portion of ignorance is shattered, one is born into the Ultimate Bliss of True Reward; if ignorance is completely destroyed, one is born into the Ultimate Bliss World of Tranquil Light.
This concludes the two aspects of rebirth.
△ Fifth, concluding the preceding and initiating the subsequent.
[Commentary]: It should be understood that upholding the Name is both simple and direct, yet it leads to the sudden and the perfect.

Because every thought-moment is itself the Buddha, there is no need for visualization and no necessity for investigation. It is perfectly luminous from the very beginning, without remainder and without deficiency.

Those of the highest of high faculties cannot transcend its threshold (because every thought-moment is itself Buddha); yet those of the lowest of low faculties can also reach its domain (because every thought-moment is itself Buddha).
The lands of Buddhas manifested through such resonance often surpass [other realms] (as this is precisely the Pure Land school), nor are they uniform.

It may be said that horizontally it encompasses the eight teachings and vertically penetrates the five periods (thus achieving a perfect inclusion that is perfectly transcendent). Therefore, out of a heart of ultimate compassion, he spoke spontaneously without being asked, and deeply lamented that it is difficult to believe.
[Commentary] This concludes the preceding formal explanation and introduces the subsequent refutation of doubts.

"Immediately perfect and luminous, without remainder and without deficiency" means that contemplation, visualization, and investigation are all contained within this single phrase of the Name; there is nothing superfluous and no lack whatsoever.
Since both Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra sought rebirth there, those of the highest faculties cannot surpass its threshold;
since even parrots and mynah birds attained rebirth there, those of the lowest faculties likewise reach its domain. That they often achieve further progress is not uniform across all cases.
The Buddha’s division into three bodies and the lands’ division into four realms are merely general and provisional explanations. If one considers both...

If one were to discuss this in detail, it would not be uniform. Because the superiority or inferiority of merit and practice, as well as progress and regression, are unequal, and because the Buddha’s bodies and lands are inconceivable, the four lands are each divided into three grades and nine ranks.

That which encompasses horizontally and penetrates vertically—the five periods and eight teachings—is not outside the four teachings; these four teachings are themselves the single phrase of the Buddha-name. This is the cause.

That which is dependently originated is itself emptiness, itself the provisional, and itself the Middle Way. Because this Dharma-gate is profound and far-reaching, it is spoken ex cathedra without being questioned.
Furthermore, it is praised as a teaching difficult to believe. This concludes the summary of what preceded and the introduction of what follows; the initial formal explanation is finished.

△ Second, the Dispelling of Doubts. There are twelve questions and answers in total, which comprise seven sections: first, the doubt that visualization is unnecessary; second, the doubt that investigation is unnecessary;
third, the doubt as to how one can be certain it is not a demonic manifestation; fourth, the discernment between the seven-day period and the single thought-moment;
fifth, the doubt regarding the attainment of the distant goal; sixth, the doubt concerning the distinction between the two practices; seventh, the capacity to eliminate transgressions.
Dispelling Doubts. △ Now, the first [section]. 【Commentary】 Question:

The *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra* specifically clarifies the practice of visualization (*dhyāna*). Why, then, is it said that "one need not laboriously practice visualization"? Answer: This meaning is derived from the *Sūtra* itself.
That sūtra states that because the *vīra-darśana* (superior vision) is beyond the mental capacity of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it is treated separately as the thirteenth [chapter].

The visualization of the inferior image (serving simultaneously as an introduction for beginners of the *Contemplation Sūtra*) was taught; yet those with heavy karmic obstructions were still unable to perform the recollection of that Buddha (this term "recollection" refers to the visualization described in the *Contemplation Sūtra*).

Therefore, at the sixteenth contemplation, the gateway of invoking the Name was extensively opened. Since this present sūtra addresses an age when those with heavy obstructions are numerous, it focuses primarily on the sixteenth contemplation.
One should know that although human faculties may be dull, the physical body of the Buddha—whether sixteen feet or eight feet in height—is not lacking.
The name of Amitāyus Buddha has never failed to be taken as the mind itself by those who contemplate it. Thus, for those of inferior capacity, there is no need for the superior contemplation;
even those who merely recite the name do not require the labor of visualization.
[Commentary] Regarding that sutra’s statement that the excellence of the contemplation cannot be reached by the mental power of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*):
that sutra refers to the marks of the *saṃbhogakāya*. "The white ūrṇā-hair curls like five Mount Sumerus; the deep blue eyes are as clear as the four great oceans.

How could such things be observed by an ordinary being? Therefore, regarding the separate opening of the contemplation of the inferior image among the thirteen [contemplations], the sutra says: "If one wishes..."

Those who aspire with a sincere mind to be born in the Western Quarter should first contemplate an image one zhang and six chi in height, situated upon the waters of the pond, as previously described.

Although the body of Amitāyus Buddha is immeasurable in size and beyond the reach of the mental power of ordinary beings, by virtue of that Tathāgata’s power of past vows, those who maintain mindful recollection will certainly achieve success. Amitābha Buddha’s spiritual...
He possesses supernormal powers that extend throughout the lands of the ten directions, manifesting with sovereign mastery.
He may manifest a vast body that fills the void of space, or he may manifest a small body of one zhang and six chi or eight chi. All manifested bodies are of a true golden color (and so forth).
Yet, those whose karmic obstructions are heavy still cannot bring that Buddha to mind; therefore, at the sixteenth [stage], the invocation of his name is extensively opened.

Regarding the "Gate," the Chapter on Rebirth in the Lower Grade states: "When such a foolish person approaches the end of life, they encounter a virtuous friend who exhorts them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
Thus, with a sincere mind, they maintain the sound of recitation without interruption, fulfilling ten recitations (*daśa-smṛti*).
Within each thought-moment, the sins of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death are eliminated. At the moment of death, they see a golden lotus flower, as if..."
Like the orb of the sun appearing before that person, in a single moment of thought, one immediately attains rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss.
One should know that regarding the image of sixteen or eight feet and the name of Amitāyus Buddha, there has never been a case where the mind does not take them as being "the mind" or "is this.
This means: "This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. This mind creates the Name; this mind [is the Name]."
This is the name. The Sūtra says: "The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are the body of the Dharma-realm; they enter into the thoughts and minds of all sentient beings.
Therefore, when you contemplate the Buddha in your mind, this very mind is the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. The ocean of the Buddhas' right and universal knowledge arises from the mind."
The perception arises. Therefore, one who contemplates the inferior does not need to exert effort in the previous superior contemplations.
Now, when it is said that one cultivates the sixteenth contemplation by reciting its name, it implies that the preceding thirteen contemplations also do not require effort.
△ Second, the argument that it is unnecessary to investigate the doubt; this has two parts. First, the direct refutation of the claim that investigation is unnecessary.
Second, the simultaneous refutation of the refusal to apply one’s heart with total resolve. △ Now, the first part.
[Commentary] Question: The various patriarchs, such as Tianqi and Dufeng, all took "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name? as their primary koan for investigation.
Why do you say that investigation is not necessary? Answer: This point is precisely what emerged from the various patriarchs, including Tianqi.

Because those who recite the Buddha’s name did not accord with Śākyamuni’s thorough compassion, the former patriarchs could not bear it and directly interrogated them, providing a sudden, forceful awakening.
To cease this long night and return to the dawn—this is what we have been striving for until this very day. Yet we still refuse to die our hearts and practice nianfo;
instead, we bitterly cling to the "tile for knocking," wishing to strike our own biological parents from within the house.
This makes us evil rebels against the Patriarchs, rather than virtuous and compliant disciples (the True Sect’s liberation from the old ruts of the veteran masters).

[Commentary]: Regarding the patriarchs Tianqi and Dufeng—namely, Chan Master Tianqi Benrui and Chan Master Dufeng Benshan—the former patriarch [Tianqi] felt that practitioners of nianfo did not accord with his compassionate heart because they were unwilling to "die their hearts" in the practice of nianfo.
Since their hearts did not die, they were unable to realize and attain the samādhi of nianfo; failing to attain this samādhi, they could not achieve accord.

Therefore, the mind cannot be opened. Because the mind is not opened, one cannot shatter ignorance, nor can one realize that this very mind creates the Buddha and that this very mind is the Buddha—this is the essential meaning.
Consequently, one does not accord with the ultimate heart of compassion. Regarding "those who were dissatisfied on the sidelines":
the ancients were those who were dissatisfied with the conventional approach; they would directly interrogate and suddenly provide a sharp reminder.

The "awakened one" is precisely one who has been uplifted by the instruction to open their mind and shatter the delusive thoughts of objective conditions, thereby realizing the principle that this very mind creates the Buddha and that this very mind is the Buddha.
Thus, Tianqi addressed the assembly, saying: "Throughout the day you recite the Buddha’s name, yet you do not know that your entire being is the Buddha.
If you do not know this, simply look at the one who is reciting the Buddha’s name—who is it? This is how one realizes that single point.
The Buddha Amitābha is, in his entirety, the nature of the mind; therefore it is said, "This mind creates the Buddha;

this mind is the Buddha. Since the Buddha who is the object of mindfulness is, in his entirety, the mind that performs the mindfulness, then all that is seen, heard, and perceived—how could these not be the mind that sees, hears, and perceives? Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*...
He said: "This seeing and its objects are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi. How could there be 'is' or 'is not' within them?
Since you have realized that this mind creates Buddhas and that this mind is the Buddha, you must also realize that this mind creates lands and that this mind is the land.
Once you have realized that this mind is the land, then the delusive thoughts of objective shadows will naturally [dissolve]."
Suddenly, one comes to rest; one spontaneously resolves to die the heart’s death in the recitation of the Buddha’s name and seeks birth in the Pure Land.

"Not merely returning to dawn from the long night" means it is not merely that. It signifies that it does not stop there. The deluded thoughts of conditioned reflections are the ignorance of the long night;

since beginningless time, one has taken these conditioned reflections to be the nature of the mind. If one realizes that these conditioned reflections are not the mind, then [the true nature] is revealed.

"Mind, awaken yourself! To 'awaken' means to be enlightened. The metaphor of 'bitterly clinging to the broken tile for knocking at the door' refers to being unwilling to die the death of the mind while reciting the Buddha’s name.
It means one bitterly refuses to set aside the golden brick for knocking at the door and instead picks up the broken tile, regarding it as a supreme treasure.
This is like beating one's own biological parents inside the house; the 'house' is a metaphor for one's own body, and the 'parents' are a metaphor for one's own mind."

The body is the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) directly produced by one's own mind; therefore, it is likened to one's biological parents who gave birth to one. "Striking" is a metaphor for asking oneself, "Who am I?
As for the phrase "regarding all the patriarchs," the patriarchs were originally of a single, wholesome and compliant mind;
yet, because one does not understand this for oneself, it conversely becomes rebellious and perverse. To truly break through this, there is no need to seek ultimate realization elsewhere.
△ Second, simultaneously refuting those who are unwilling to resolve their minds [upon the truth].
[Commentary: He asks further: "This may be acceptable for one whose mind is already resolved, but how can it be appropriate for one who is not yet resolved? He replies: "Alas!
It is precisely because you are not yet resolved that I require your mind to be in accord with resolution. Your true faith has not yet opened; it is as if you were still living."
One cannot bend or fold leather; one should know that for those with eyes, there is certainly no principle of lighting a lamp beneath the sun.

Yet why must those without eyes laboriously seek out lamps and torches in the daylight? (This is the extreme of ordinary folly, failing to realize its solitary loftiness—what is called a "difficult-to-believe" teaching.
The Dharma Prince Mahāsthāmaprāpta said: "Without relying on expedient means, one spontaneously attains the opening of the mind. This is the great mass of fire within the *ekavyūha-samādhi*.
This is a statement. Should anyone dare to provoke it, would they not surely be burned?
[Commentary] As for the "further inquiry," this advances one level beyond the previous question. It means that what has just been said is applicable only to those who are willing to die their hearts;
yet our own natures and minds have not yet opened, nor are we yet willing to die our hearts. Why?
"One who attains this is endowed with thorough compassion. The response, "Ai," is a sound of regret. It means: what I have spoken is not for those who already possess a willing mind;
it is solely for you who have not yet developed such a mind, so that you may give rise to a mind of willingness.
Therefore it is said: "If you simply prepare a willing mind, I shall certainly not deceive you. This refers to when right faith has not yet...
"Opening" refers to the fact that the principle of "Mind-Only" has not yet been correctly believed. It is like raw hide:
if the principle of Mind-Only is not understood, one will certainly be unable to abandon the two attachments to self and phenomena; therefore, it cannot be bent or folded.
One should know that "having eyes" is a metaphor for having already opened correct faith, clearly realizing that all phenomena are nothing but one's own mind, and thus being willing [to let go].

When one dies the mind to recite the Buddha’s name, there is no further principle for investigation or inquiry. The metaphor of "one who lacks eyes" illustrates that when right faith has not yet opened, it is precisely the time to die the mind and recite the Buddha’s name;
once the mind opens of itself, why must one laboriously seek the mind within the mind?
Therefore, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Chapter on Mahāsthāmaprāpta) says: "If sentient beings, with their minds, remember the Buddha and recite his name... [the Buddha appears before them].
In the future, you will certainly behold the Buddha; you will not be far from him. Without relying on expedient means, you will spontaneously attain the opening of the mind.

These two phrases, "without relying on expedient means" and "spontaneously attaining the opening of the mind," are like a great mass of fire within the single-practice samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Who would dare to touch this great fire without being burned? This metaphor clearly illustrates that mindfulness has reached the state of one-pointedness of mind.
If there is no confusion, how could the mind not open? Therefore it is said: "Without relying on expedient means, one spontaneously attains the opening of the mind.
Second, there is no need to investigate the ultimate limit of doubt.
△ Third, the doubt as to whether this might be the work of a demon.

[Commentary] Question: When a Buddha appears at the moment of death, how can one be certain it is not a māra? Answer: For a practitioner who does not cultivate the visualization of the Buddha, for a Buddha to appear suddenly when it was not their original intention is termed a "māra-activity.
However, for one who recites the Buddha's name to see the Buddha is already a sign of resonance;
how much more so when this occurs at the time of death—why should there be any doubt that it is not a manifestation of the Buddha?
[Commentary]: For a practitioner of Zen who has not habitually cultivated the visualization of the Buddha, the sudden appearance of the Buddha is not what their original mind anticipated;
therefore, it is a demonic realm. For a practitioner of Nianfo who hopes to see the Buddha, the manifestation of the Buddha before them already accords with their mind.
At this time, they should give rise to a sense of shame and remorse, rather than boasting or being self-conceited.
△ A Fourfold Analysis of the Seven Days and a Single Thought-Moment.
[Commentary] Question: Does "not being distracted for seven days" refer to one's ordinary life or to the moment of death? Answer: It refers to one's ordinary life. Question:

After not being distracted for seven days, if one again gives rise to delusions and creates karma, can one still attain birth [in the Pure Land]? Answer: Provided that one truly attains single-mindedness without distraction, one will.

Such a person has no further occasion to give rise to delusions or create karma (The Precious Mirror Illuminates Demons). Question: Regarding the ten recitations of the Great Sūtra and the single thought-moment of the Treasure King [Sūtra].
"Is this during one's ordinary life, or at the time of death? Answer: "The ten recitations apply to both times. The 'ten recitations at dawn' belong to the period of ordinary life;
the 'attaining birth through ten recitations' is identical to the ten recitations of the name in the *Amitābha Sūtra* and belongs to the time of death.

As for the 'single recitation,' it refers exclusively to the time of death. Question: "If both ten recitations and a single recitation can lead to birth, why is a seven-day period required? Answer: "If..."
If one lacks seven days of practice during one's leisure time, how can there be ten firm recitations at the moment of death?

Even if a single thought arises in a person of the lowest grade who has committed grave evils, it is because their past causes have matured, such that they encounter a virtuous friend at the end of life and, upon hearing [the teaching], immediately develop faith and aspiration.
Such an occurrence happens but once in ten thousand cases; how can one rely on mere luck? This point is most severely criticized in the *Wenji* (Questions and Answers on the Pure Land).
Detailed Explanation: People today must read this.
[Commentary] The text has two parts. First, examining whether one attains "uninterrupted single-mindedness" (ekacittāsampramoṣa) during the seven days;

if one truly attains the state of uninterrupted single-mindedness in affairs, then the grasping at a self (ātman-grāha) is already empty, and there is no further arising of delusions or the creation of karma. This is because...

This gives rise to the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhava-kleśa*), leading to the performance of outflowing (*sāsrava*) karma; how much more so, then, regarding the principle of single-mindedness without distraction.
Second, the distinction between ten recitations and a single recitation: "The Great Sūtra" refers to the *Mahā-ārya-mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* (here, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*).

"Jewel King" refers to the *Nianfo Sanmei Baowang Lun* (Treatise on the Jewel King Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation). "Ten Recitations at Dawn" refers to the *Chenzhao Shiniàn Fǎ* (Dharma of Ten Recitations at Dawn) by Master Ciyun.

Those of the lowest-of-the-low grade who commit rebellious and evil acts—such as those who hang up *zhōngqiú* (spiritual guardians against demons)—are all individuals for whom prior causes have already reached full maturity;
they are merely triggered in this life by the single invocation of the ten names and titles.

Otherwise, why would one encounter a virtuous friend at the moment of death, hear their guidance, and immediately develop faith and aspiration? How could this be considered mere luck? How could it be that such things happen only during times of crisis?

Without being diligent in authentic cultivation, they vainly hope for rebirth through the ten recitations at the moment of death. This concludes the examination of the seven-day period versus the single thought-moment.
△ Fifth, the doubt regarding whether one arrives from afar or immediately.
[Commentary] Question: The Western Land is one hundred trillion lands away from here; how can one be reborn there so immediately? Answer:
One hundred trillion lands do not lie outside the nature of mind within my present single thought-moment, for the nature of mind has no exterior.

Furthermore, by relying on the Buddha-power of one’s own mind to provide guidance, how could it be difficult to be reborn immediately? It is like seeing dozens of layers of mountains reflected in a mirror.

The water pavilions appear with their stories perfectly distinct; there is truly no distance between them, yet they are all perceived simultaneously upon a single reflection, seen without any sequence of before or after.
Thus, passing from here through a hundred trillion Buddha-lands to the west, there is a world named Sukhāvatī (Ultimate Bliss), which is also like this.
In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha, who is currently preaching the Dharma, and he is also like this. Such is the person.
At the time of death, Amitābha Buddha, together with the assembly of holy beings, will appear before that person.
At the moment of their passing, their mind will not be inverted, and they will immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.
It should be known that every single character is the spiritual text of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, the Sea-Seal Samādhi.
[Commentary] The intent of the question is clear. The answer is divided into four parts: first, the direct response; second, an illustration by analogy;

third, the application to the Dharma; and fourth, the concluding summary. Regarding the first, the direct response, it says: "Not departing from the mind-nature of a single thought-moment. A single thought-moment possesses four divisions:

the "single thought-moment" is the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*); the "mind" is the self-verifying division (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*); and the "nature" is the division that verifies the self-verifying division (*svasaṃvittisaṃvedana-bhāga*). As for the "one hundred trillion lands":

This refers to the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect). Since the four parts are not separate from the single mind, it is said that they do not go outside. This is because the nature of the mind is fundamentally without exterior;
since the *tathatā* (suchness) nature of the mind is vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive, it is fundamentally without interior or exterior.
Furthermore, by relying on the power of the Buddha within one's own mind to guide sentient beings who are within the Buddha's mind, how could it be difficult to attain immediate arrival?

Regarding "arising," it is illustrated by the analogy of a mirror as follows: the mirror represents the four divisions of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). The mirror itself represents the self-verifying division (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*);

the copper of the mirror represents the verifying-the-self-verifying division (*svasaṃvitti-saṃvitti-bhāga*); the illumination represents the seeing division (*darśana-bhāga*); and the mountains, waters, pavilions, and towers represent the image division (*nimitta-bhāga*).

The distinct layers are clearly present; this is a metaphor for the distinct layers of the Buddha-land being clearly present. It further illustrates that when the Buddha receives one, he certainly receives one;

when one is born there, one certainly is born there. Thus, coming and going are clearly manifest. In reality, however, there is no distance or proximity; this is a metaphor for the Buddha-land having no inherent nature.
It further illustrates that when the Buddha comes, in truth he does not come; when one departs to be born there, in truth one does not go. Thus, coming and going [are ultimately non-existent].
