There is no substantial nature [to these]. A single illumination brings all to understanding; there is no sequence of before and after in seeing. This is illustrated by the metaphor of the four parts not departing from a single mirror.
The mutual resonance between the capacity to respond and the stimulus occurs simultaneously. From this point downward, the following three sections apply the Dharma to the metaphors.

It is called "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī) in this way; the preaching of the Dharma in the present is likewise in this way. This clarifies that the two types of retribution—the primary environment (*niśraya*) and the secondary body (*sambhoga*)—are not...
The four parts of the preceding thought appear; the layers within the mirror are perfectly distinct. These layers have no inherent nature;
they are all understood simultaneously upon a single illumination. There is no sequence in their perception. Amitābha and his holy assembly appear before one, and the mind is free from delusion.
Attaining rebirth is likewise so. It is clear that coming and going does not transcend the four phases of the present single thought-moment.
Just as coming and going appear vividly within a mirror, they lack inherent nature; both are fully understood within a single thought-moment, and no sequence of before or after is perceived.

"One should know" and so forth is the fourth section, the conclusion. "Every single character is the Ocean-Seal [Samādhi]" means that every character and every phrase of this sutra is a manifestation of the Ocean-Seal Samādhi, the mystical text of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).

Both samādhi and mirror-wisdom are alternative names for the nature of the mind within the present single thought-moment. Because all phenomena are inherently contained within its principle, it is called the "Ocean."
The seal of samādhi: phenomena are produced through actualization; this is named the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.

Principle and phenomenon, inherent and actualized—the two layers of the three thousand realms—reside together within a single moment of the mind-nature. This concludes the section on the fifth [point], "Reaching the Distant" and "Resolving Doubts."
△ Doubt regarding the distinction between the two types of practice. [Commentary] Question:
If the "holding of the name" is judged to be the practice of practice, then it is an auxiliary practice (*upāya-caryā*). Why is it called the primary practice (*samyak-caryā*)? Answer:

Faith, vow, and practice are taught based on the one mind; they are not sequential, nor are they fixed as three. Indeed, without the vow there is no true faith, and without practice there is none at all.
Faith alone is not called the true vow; without faith and the vow, it is not called true practice.

Now, because the recitation of the Name is sustained entirely by faith and the vow, these three—faith, vow, and practice—are perfectly complete in every sound. This is why it is called "the causal condition of many roots of goodness and merit."
This refers to what is stated in the *Amitābha Sūtra*: "By reciting the Buddha's name, one eliminates the sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas in every thought-moment.
If one’s merit and goodness were not abundant, how could such great sins be eliminated?

[Commentary] Regarding the question concerning the classification of "holding the name" as the practice of conduct (*caryā-caryā*): the preceding text states that faith and aspiration constitute the practice of wisdom (*prajñā-caryā*), while holding the name constitutes the practice of conduct.
Just as eyes and feet function in tandem, since holding the name is classified as the practice of conduct, it is therefore an auxiliary practice (*upāya-caryā*).
What constitutes correct practice? The answer is: it is taught that faith, aspiration, and practice are based upon the one mind. Faith, aspiration, and practice are nothing other than the one mind.
Because they are solely the one mind, they do not exist sequentially, nor are they fixed as three distinct entities. This is according to the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

As for the passage "entirely through faith and aspiration [one] holds the name" and so forth, this is discussed from the standpoint of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*). "Holding the name by means of faith and aspiration" refers to faith and aspiration.
The three—practice, faith, and vow—are mutually dependent. Through true faith, one gives rise to earnest vows; through earnest vows, one establishes actual practice;
and through actual practice, one is finally able to manifest true faith and earnest vows. Therefore, within each sound of these three—faith, vow, and practice—they are perfectly complete.
Because they are perfectly complete, this is called the cause and condition for many roots of goodness and much merit.
Thus ends the section on doubts regarding the distinctions in the practice of the second hexagram-line.
△ Seventh, doubts concerning whether one can eliminate transgressions, which is further divided into two parts: first, doubts about eliminating transgressions through daily practice;
second, doubts about eliminating transgressions through distracted mind. △ Now, the first part.

[Commentary] Question: At the moment of death, such intense and urgent resolve can eliminate much sin. If one invokes the Name with a sincere mind during one's daily life, will that also eliminate sin?
Answer: Just as the rising sun dispels all darkness, so too does invoking the Great Name extinguish ten thousand sins.
[Commentary] This analogy explains that the nature of sin is fundamentally empty, being created by the mind. When the mind ceases, the sin has already perished.
This means that when the mind creates sin, it is entirely the Buddha that becomes the sentient being; outside of the sentient being, there is no other Buddha.
It is like the setting of the sun: when it sets, all light becomes darkness, and outside of that darkness there is no further light.
When the mind invokes the Great Name, all sentient beings become Buddhas, and outside of those Buddhas there are no further sentient beings. It is like the rising of the sun.
When total darkness becomes light, there is no longer any darkness outside of that light. Therefore, when one thought-moment corresponds [to the Buddha], it is the Buddha of one thought-moment;
when every thought-moment corresponds, it is the Buddha of every thought-moment.
△ 2. Dispelling Doubts Regarding the Removal of Sin through a Distracted Mind. This section has two parts: first, the question; second, the answer.
△ First, the question. 【Commentary】 Question: If one recites the name with a distracted mind, will the sin also be removed?
△ Second, the response, which is further divided into two parts: first, the direct answer; second, the citation of scriptural evidence. △ Now, the first part. 【Commentary】 Answer:

The merit of the Name is inconceivable; how could it not eliminate transgressions? However, one does not necessarily attain birth [in the Pure Land], because the indeterminate, scattered good roots of ordinary practice find it difficult to counteract the accumulated transgressions of beginningless time.
One should know that even if these accumulated transgressions were to possess a substantial body, [the Name would still overcome them].
As for its characteristics: even the entirety of the realm of empty space could not contain it.

Although Amitābha’s name is recited one hundred thousand times throughout a hundred years of day and night, and each single utterance extinguishes eighty billion kalpas of birth and death, the sins thus extinguished are like soil on a fingernail, while the sins not yet extinguished are like the soil of the great earth.
Only when mindfulness reaches the state of "single-mindedness without distraction" is one like a strong man breaking through a siege.
And he departed. It was no longer possible for the three armies to restrain him.
[Commentary] "Yōuyō" (the indeterminate) means not being focused. "Like the soil on a fingernail" refers to the soil on one's hand.
When the Buddha was beneath a tree, he plucked a leaf and asked Ānanda, "Are there more leaves on the tree, or are there more leaves on my fingernail? Ānanda—

[The interlocutor] said: "There are many leaves on the tree. The Buddha said: "I have already taught the Dharma like the leaves upon my fingernails; the Dharma not yet taught is like the leaves upon the tree.

[In India,] they call the hand *hasta*, but they mostly call it *nakhā* (fingernail). Only those who reach the state of single-mindedness without distraction—there are two kinds of single-mindedness without distraction.
Regarding the "valiant person who breaks through the encirclement": "breaking through" (*tū*) means to shatter. One shatters the Saha world.

He emerges from the enclosure of the four kinds of defiled lands; he can no longer be restrained by the three armies—the army of views and afflictions, the army of dust-like [delusions], or the army of ignorance.
△ Second, citing scriptural evidence.
[Commentary: Thus, reciting the Name immediately becomes the seed for attaining Buddhahood; it is like a diamond that can never be destroyed.

Śāriputra, just as I now praise the inconceivable benefits of the meritorious virtues of Amitābha Buddha,
so too in the eastern direction there are Buddhas such as Akṣobhya Buddha, Sumerukūṭa Buddha, Mahāsumeru Buddha, Sumeruprabhāsa Buddha, and Gadgadasvara Buddha—
Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, each of whom, in their respective lands, extends a broad and long [tongue].
His tongue-marks extend to cover the entire trichiliocosm. He speaks words of truth:
"You sentient beings, you should believe this Sutra on the Praise of Inconceivable Merit, which is protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas."
[Commentary] *Akṣobhya* means "Immovable. This refers to being unmoved by the three obstacles within the nine realms.

The Buddhas of the *Tripiṭaka* and *Pratyekabuddha* vehicles are not moved by the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *saṃyojana-kleśa*), nor by out-flowing karma (*āsrava-karma*), nor by the bitter fruits of suffering of the six classes of ordinary beings.

The Buddha of the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-kṣetra*) is not moved by the delusions as numerous as dust motes, nor by the movement of untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*), nor by the movement of the fruit of suffering resulting from transformation (*pariṇāma-dukha-phala*).

The Buddha of the Land of True Reward (*samyak-vipāka-kṣetra*) is not moved by ignorance (*avidyā*), nor by the movement of karma belonging to the two extremes, nor by the movement of the Bodhisattva’s fruit of suffering resulting from transformation.

The Buddha of the Land of Peaceful Light (*śānta-prabhāsa-kṣetra*) is, in principle, immovable; there is no movement in name, and no movement in the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*).
Movement... up to ultimate non-movement. Regarding the "form of Mount Sumeru": this is called the form of the Wondrous High (*Miaogao*). "Wondrous" means inconceivable.
A Buddha of the Land of Common Residence is "wondrous" because he cannot be conceived by the six classes of ordinary beings; he is "high" because he is above these six classes.

A Buddha of the Land of Expedient Means cannot be conceived by those of the three vehicles; he is [superior] to the nine types of persons (the two vehicles of the *Zang* [Hīnayāna] and the three vehicles of the *Tong* [Mahāyāna]).

It stands apart from the three stages of the worthy (śaikṣa) and above the ten stages of faith (śraddhā) of the Perfect Teaching; hence it is called "Sublime High" (*Sumeru*). The Buddha of the Land of Real Reward is beyond the conceptualization of bodhisattvas and dwells above the nine realms.
Within the Land of Quiescent Light, there exists the aspect of the "sublime high" corresponding to the stage of principle (*li-ji*), up to the ultimate aspect of the sublime high.
As for the "Great Sumeru," there are small and large Sumeru mountains; the Brahma King is thus the father of all sentient beings.
It is like a small Mount Sumeru. The Buddha of the *sahā-lokadhātu* (Shared Land) is the compassionate father of the four modes of birth and the teacher of devas and humans;

therefore, he is called Great Sumeru. The Buddha of the land of skillful means (*upāya-bhūmi*) is the father of the three vehicles. The Buddha of the land of true recompense (*samyak-vipāka-bhūmi*) is the father of the bodhisattvas.

In the land of tranquil light (*śāntaprabhā-bhūmi*), there is the father at the level of "identity-in-principle" (*li-ji*), the father at the level of "names and words" (*ming-tzu*), and even the ultimate father.
Furthermore, regarding "Sumeru Light": Mount Sumeru is composed of four treasures, and these four treasures all possess radiance.
This is a metaphor for the Buddha, who is composed of four virtues, and these four virtues all emit radiance; therefore, it is called "Sumeru Light.
As for the Buddha of the Shared Residence, he is composed of the four "withered" virtues—namely, impurity, suffering, impermanence, and non-self—and thus emits the [four]...
The light of the "withered" is produced by the four virtues of prosperity through skillful means—namely, permanence, bliss, self, and purity—and thus it emits the four lights of prosperity.
The light of the "true reward" is produced by the virtues that are neither withered nor prosperous—the four virtues of the Middle Way—and thus it emits the light of the Middle Way.
Within the Light of Quiescence, there are the four lights of the principle-aspect, up to and including the four lights of the ultimate aspect; these are the wondrous [lights].
Regarding "sound": the Buddha possesses sixty-four kinds of Brahma-sounds; therefore, it is called "wondrous sound. The Buddha of the Shared Residence has the wondrous sounds of the four teachings.
The Buddha of Expedient Means employs the wondrous sounds of the Distinct and Complete Teachings. The Buddha of True Reward possesses only the wondrous sound of the Complete Teaching.
The Buddha of the Peaceful Light possesses the wondrous sounds of the six stages of identity.
The commentary is divided into five sections: first, the explanation of the merits; second, the explanation of the Buddha’s name; third, the explanation of the eastern direction;

fourth, the explanation of the tongue-mark; and fifth, the explanation of the title. The first section [the explanation of the merits] is further divided into two: first, the explanation of the Buddha’s merits;
second, the clarification of his own merits. Now, the first [of these].
[Commentary] There are briefly five meanings to the term "inconceivable" (*acintya*): 1. Transcending the three realms horizontally, without waiting for the severance of afflictions (*kleśa*).

2. The Western Land horizontally possesses the four lands; this is not attained through gradual realization (meanings such as "non-retrogression in a single lifetime" are all subsumed within this second meaning).

3. Merely holding the name, without relying on meditative contemplation or other skillful means (this is of great merit for the Pure Land). 4. Taking seven days as the limit, without depending on many kalpas, many lifetimes, or many years and months. 5. Holding... [text ends]
To recite the name of one Buddha is to be protected and remembered by all Buddhas; this is no different from upholding the names of all Buddhas.
All of this is accomplished through the great vows and practices of the Teacher; therefore, it is called "the benefit of the inconceivable merit of Amitābha Buddha."

[Commentary] "Transcending the three realms horizontally without waiting for the severance of delusions" means transcending the three realms of the Shared Residence (tongju), the three realms of Expedient Means (fangbian), and the three realms of True Reward (shibao) horizontally.
Because the single thought-moment of the practitioner’s mind-nature is itself the Land of Constant Quiescent Light (changjiguangtu), when it accords with the Buddha-name, no delusions can be found;
thus it is said that one does not wait for their severance. The remaining text...
This can be understood.
△ Second, clarifying one's own merit. [Commentary]:

Furthermore, when a practitioner maintains the Name with faith and aspiration, they fully incorporate the Buddha’s merit to form their own merit (those who are clever in this are few). Therefore, it is also said:
The benefits of the inconceivable merit of Amitābha Buddha.

[Commentary]: Regarding "fully encompassing the Buddha’s merits to form one's own merits": because the vast name of ten thousand virtues invokes those virtues by its very name, there is nothing that is not completely exhausted. This concludes the explanation of "merit."
△ Second, the explanation of the Buddha’s name.
[Commentary: Akṣobhya means "Immovable. A Buddha possesses immeasurable virtues and should therefore have immeasurable names; these are established according to the capacities of sentient beings.
One may take the cause, the fruit, the nature, the marks, or the vows and practices, and so forth. Although only one is mentioned here...
Each name possesses the four *siddhāntas*. Each individual name reveals the virtues it signifies; even if one were to speak of them for an eon, they could not be fully exhausted.

[Commentary] "Name" refers to a provisional designation (*prajñapti*). "Virtue" refers to actual qualities. Since these virtues are immeasurable, names are established according to those virtues; thus, the names are likewise [immeasurable].
The term "Immeasurable" (Amitābha), which is universally acclaimed by the world, is established in accordance with the capacities of the four *siddhāntas*.

Some take it as referring to causal practice, such as "Immeasurable Diligence" (*Amitābhyutsāha*) and so forth; others take it as referring to the merit of the fruit, such as "Immovable" (*Acalā*) and so forth;
or it may refer to the nature (*dhātu*) or the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Nevertheless, while citing one corner [of this example], it nonetheless possesses all four *siddhāntas*.
"Corners" refers to the cardinal directions; it is a metaphor for how by mentioning a single direction, one still encompasses all four directions.

Regarding "each and every single name," this means that factors such as cause, effect, nature, characteristics, practice, and vows are universally applicable and fully present in each and every phenomenon (*dharma*).
Therefore, they cannot be fully described.
△ Third, the explanation of the eastern direction. [Commentary]:

The space of the eastern direction is inexhaustible; the worlds therein are also inexhaustible. Since the worlds are inexhaustible, the Buddhas dwelling within those worlds are likewise inexhaustible.
This is merely a brief mention of as many as the sands of the Ganges.
[Commentary] The Ganges is the Gaṅgā River. "Gaṅgā" is the name of a river deity; it is named after this deity.
This [name] means "Come from Heaven," as it is seen to come from a high place. The old rendering "Sandy River" (Shāhé) is an error.
Zhang’an said: “The reason many sutras take the Ganges as a standard of measure is that it possesses the four *siddhāntas*:

first, because most people are familiar with it; second, because those who enter [the teaching] thereby obtain merit; third, because the Ganges is vast among rivers; and fourth, because it is the place where the Buddha was born.
This river is forty *li* wide, and its sand is as fine as flour; therefore, the sands of the river are used as a metaphor for their great number.”
△ Fourth, the explanation of the mark of the broad and long tongue.

[Commentary: These various Buddhas each extend their broad and long tongues to exhort sentient beings to believe in this sutra; yet, that sentient beings still do not produce faith shows how utterly stubborn and deluded they are.
An ordinary person who does not speak falsely for three lifetimes has a tongue that can reach the nose and conceal the crown of the head.
Throughout three great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, the Buddha has never uttered a falsehood. His tongue is thin, broad, and long, capable of covering his face;

now, having realized the wondrous gateway of the Mahāyāna Pure Land, it extends to cover the trichiliocosm. This signifies that his principle is truly in accord with reality, and his facts are indeed without error.

[Commentary] "The Buddha of the fruition of the Tripitaka" refers to the Buddha of fruition according to the Tripitaka teachings. "Three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas" refers to the cultivation of the practices of the six *pāramitās*.
This is, for example, as with Śākyamuni Buddha: in a previous life, he was a potter named Mahāprabha.
At that time, there was a Buddha named Śākyamuni, whose disciples were named Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and Ānanda. The Buddha and his [disciples]...
The son went together with her to the potter’s house. At that time, the potter spread grass and lit lamps as an offering to the Buddha, and he made this vow:
"In the future, may I become a Buddha just like this Buddha, and may the names of my disciples also be the same. This was the first moment he generated the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).
From that point until the appearance of Ratnaśikhin Buddha, the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* was completed; during this time, she was forever freed from the female body. From the time of Ratnaśikhin...
Upon reaching the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, two *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* were completed.

At that time, the Bodhisattva made an offering of seven blue lotuses to the Buddha, spread his hair to cover the mud, and the Buddha bestowed upon him the prophecy that he would become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.

From the time of Dīpaṃkara until Vipaśyin Buddha, three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* were completed; thereafter, for another one hundred *kalpas*, he cultivated the causes for the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. Upon reaching [Vipaśyin],...
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he resided in the stage of the "Successor" (Upapadya) as the Bodhisattva Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
This demonstrates the manifestation of Śākyamuni Buddha’s practice throughout three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas; it is precisely this that constitutes the fruition-Buddha of the Tripiṭaka teachings.
As for "pervading the trichiliocosm," this refers to one Brahmakāyika Heaven of the First Dhyāna, one of the Six Heavens of Desire, and one Mount Sumeru.
One solar system, comprising one sun and moon, one set of four continents, and one Cakravāḍa mountain range, constitutes a single set of four continents.
One thousand such sets of the first dhyāna heavens are governed by one second dhyāna heaven; this is a small chiliocosm.
One thousand such second dhyāna heavens are governed by one third dhyāna heaven; this is a medium chiliocosm. As...
These one thousand heavens of the third dhyāna are governed by a single heaven of the fourth dhyāna, constituting a great trichiliocosm.
Because "thousand" is stated three times—small, medium, and great—it is called a "trichiliocosm of three thousandfold worlds.
It contains ten billion sets of four continents, up to ten billion heavens of the first dhyāna. Now, his speech for the three periods of time is not false; the mark of his tongue extends to—
His speech is always trustworthy; how much more so his truthfulness throughout three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. His tongue covers his face.
Now, having realized the wondrous gateway of the Mahāyāna Pure Land, his tongue’s appearance universally covers the trichiliocosm.
This signifies the sincerity of his principle and the reality of his facts. Sincerity of principle accords with true nature; reality of fact means it is definitively not otherwise.
This is erroneous. If sentient beings no longer give rise to faith, they may be called great icchantikas devoid of faith;
therefore, he speaks words of truth, which is termed "exhorting faith for the sake of circulation."
△ Fifth, the explanation of the title. [Commentary]:
This sets forth the title of the sutra, which is the foundation for its dissemination. Master Kumārajīva, following the preference of this region for brevity, translated the current title;
it happens to coincide with the wondrous practice of holding the name. Master Xuanzang translated it as *The Sutra on Praising the Pure Land and Being Received by the Buddha*. The text contains...
Whether detailed or concise, the meaning neither increases nor decreases.
[Commentary] Regarding the "brief citation of titles," this refers to Śākyamuni Buddha’s brief citation of the names of the sutras designated by the Buddhas of the ten directions;
it is a praise of the inconceivable merit of Amitābha Buddha, which all Buddhas [extol].

This is the *Sūtra on the Protection and Mindfulness*. Regarding the presentation of the sūtra’s title as the basis for its circulation: the title designated within the sūtra itself is precisely the original name of this scripture.

Master Kumārajīva, conforming to the preference of the people of this land for brevity, translated it as the *Buddha-sprokene Amitābha Sūtra* (*Fo-shuo Amituo jing*), so that it would harmonize with the wondrous practice of holding the name. Dharma Master Xuanzang translated it as follows:
The *Sūtra on Praising the Pure Land Buddha’s Acceptance* and the [preceding] three titles differ in wording, yet their meaning is non-dual.
The text of the sūtra concludes with the section on the eastern direction.
△ Second, the southern direction. Śāriputra,
in the world-systems of the southern direction there are Buddhas such as Candrasūryapradīpa Buddha, Yaśaḥprabha Buddha, Mahārciskandha Buddha,
Merupradīpa Buddha, and Anantavīrya Buddha— Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, each of whom, at their respective...
In that land, he extends his broad and long tongue, completely covering the trichiliocosm, and speaks these truthful words:
"You sentient beings, you should believe this Sutra on the Praise of Inconceivable Merit, which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas."

[Commentary]: Regarding the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa (Moon-Sun-Lamp Buddha): the sun illuminates the day, which is a metaphor for the Buddha’s knowledge of the aspects of all paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), which illuminates the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

The moon illuminates the night, which is a metaphor for the Buddha’s omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), which illuminates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). A lamp illuminates equally both day and night, which is a metaphor for the Buddha’s knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), which illuminates both truths simultaneously.
This refers to the Buddhas of the *sahā* (homogeneous) lands, who possess two types [of manifestation]: those subject to birth and death, and those free from birth and death.

There are three kinds of wisdom. In the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-bhūmi*), there are two kinds of the three wisdoms: the immeasurable and the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*). In the Land of True Reward (*vipāka-bhūmi*), there is only one kind of the three wisdoms: the unconditioned.
In the Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhā-bhūmi*), the six [levels] are identical to the three wisdoms. Regarding "fame-light" (*kīrti-prabhā*): "name" (*nāman*) refers to renown;

"hearing" (*śravaṇa*) refers to being heard everywhere; "light" (*prabhā*) refers to the light of sound. This means that one's fame and reputation are universally heard throughout the four lands. *Zang* (Treasury).

The Buddha of the Shared Teaching is universally heard in both the *sahā* (tolerant) and *sahabhū* (co-resident) lands; the Buddha of the Distinct Teaching is universally heard in the lands of Expediency (*upāya*) and True Reward (*satyavipāka*);

and the Buddha of the Perfect Teaching is perfectly heard throughout all four lands. Regarding the term "Great Flame Shoulder" (*Mahājvālāṃsa*): "shoulder" carries the meaning of bearing a burden, while "flame" carries the meaning of burning.
This refers to the two shoulders bearing the flames of the two wisdoms—expedient and real—which burn away the defilements of the three truths within sentient beings.

Furthermore, the Buddhas of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and *Pratyekabuddha* (Shared) teachings burn the six ordinary realms; the Buddha of the *Vaipulya* (Distinct) teaching burns the nine realms; and the Buddha of the *Vaipulya* (Perfect) teaching burns the ten realms in their entirety.
Moreover, this is divided into the burning of the six stages of realization (*liuji*). Furthermore, regarding the term "Great" (*da*):

it refers to the Greatness of the six ordinary realms in the *Āgama* teaching, the Greatness of the *Āgama* within the *Pratyekabuddha* teaching, the Greatness of the *Pratyekabuddha* within the *Vaipulya* teaching, and the Greatness of the *Vaipulya* within the *Vaipulya* teaching. As for the "Lamp of Mount Sumeru," the lamp takes the sense of illumination; that is to say, the Wondrous High [Mount Sumeru].

The Lamp Buddha refers to the Buddhas of the *Tripiṭaka* (Zang) and *Shared* (Tong) vehicles. They illuminate the Four Truths for the six classes of ordinary beings and transcend the "false lamps" of ordinary people and externalists;
therefore, they are called "Sublime High. The Buddhas of the *Distinct* (Bie) and *Complete* (Yuan) vehicles illuminate the Four Truths beyond the realms and transcend the ten realms;
therefore, they are called the "Sublime High Lamp Buddha. As for "Immeasurable Diligence," it refers to the six...

The perfection of all practices is diligence; the diligence of the four lands and four teachings; and the diligence of the six stages of realization. This concludes the section on the Southern Quarter.
△ Third, the Western Quarter:
Śāriputra, in the world-system of the West, there is the Buddha Amitāyus, the Buddha Amitābha, and the Buddha Amitadhvaja.
The Buddha Great Radiance, the Buddha Great Clarity, the Buddha Jewel Mark, the Buddha Pure Light—
these and other Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each within their own land, extend their broad and long tongues until they completely cover the trichiliocosm,
and speak these words of truth: "You sentient beings, you must believe in this praise of inconceivable merit and all..."
*The Sutra on the Buddha’s Protective Recollection*.
[Commentary]: Regarding the "Infinite Life" (Amitāyus) Buddha: in the Tripitaka Teaching, it is the life of arising and ceasing;

in the Shared Teaching, it is the illusory life; in the Distinct Teaching, it is the life of infinite succession; and in the Perfect Teaching, it is the life of non-action (*anabhisamskāra*). These all reside in the Land of Common Abode.
There are two kinds of lifespan: the provisional lifespan and the actual retribution lifespan. Furthermore, these six are themselves immeasurable lifespans. Regarding the aspect of immeasurability:
in the *Zang* (Tripitaka) teaching, it consists of the immeasurable arising and ceasing of the thirty-two marks; in the *Tong* (Shared) teaching, it consists of eighty-four thousand marks;
in the *Bie* (Distinct) teaching, it consists of marks as immeasurable as the atoms of all lands; and in the *Yuan* (Perfect) teaching, it consists of the inconceivable true reality (*dharmatā*).

The "immeasurable marks" (apramāṇa-lakṣaṇa) reside together in four types [of teachings], while the two types of "expedient means" (upāya) pertain to the Shared and Distinct Teachings; the "True Reward" (sambhoga) and "Peaceful Light" (nirvāṇa-prabhāsa) lands belong exclusively to the Perfect Teaching.

Furthermore, the six stages of "identity" (liù jí) constitute the immeasurable marks. Regarding the "Immeasurable Banner" (apramāṇa-dhvaja): "banner" refers to the banner of the Dharma. Since the Dharma-gates are immeasurable, the establishment of the Dharma-banner is likewise immeasurable.
This means that the banner of the Dharma of arising and ceasing is immeasurable, extending even to the banner of the Dharma of non-arising.

Regarding the measures (*pramāṇa*): from the stage of "Dwelling Together" (*sahabhu*), which possesses all four [measures], up to the "Sixfold Identity" (*ṣat-tathatā*) of the *Śāntaprabhāsa* (Peaceful Light) realm. As for "Great Light" (*mahā-prabhā*):

"light" (*prabhā*) signifies the sense of illumination. It illuminates the Four Noble Truths, illuminates the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, illuminates the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), and extends even to the Four Teachings.
Regarding the four lands, the six stages of realization (*liù jí*), and the "Great Illumination" (*dà míng*): "illumination" (*míng*) means clear understanding;

it refers to clearly understanding the three truths—namely, the partial truth, the ultimate truth, the sequential [truth], and the truth of the single mind. Regarding the four lands, the six stages of realization, and the "Precious Marks" (*bǎo xiàng*): "precious" (*bǎo*) takes the sense of being highly valued.
The thirty-two marks of treasure are esteemed by ordinary people and non-Buddhists. The eighty-four thousand marks of treasure are esteemed within the heavenly realms.

The marks of treasure as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field are esteemed by those of the Three Vehicles. The marks of the treasure of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) are esteemed by all ten realms.

Regarding the four lands and the six stages of realization, "pure light" refers to the purity of analytical emptiness, the purity of essential emptiness, sequential purity, and the purity of the single mind.
"Purity.
[Commentary: Amitāyus Buddha shares the same name as Amitābha. There are immeasurable Buddhas throughout the ten directions who share these names.
Nevertheless, he is indeed the Guide; yet, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, it is not contradictory for him to turn and praise Śākyamuni.
Thus spoke the Tathāgata.
△ Fourth, the northern direction:
Śāriputra, in the world-system of the north, there are the Buddhas Jvālāṃsa, Varasvara, Durjayanta, and Sūryodaya.
The Buddha, Net-Luminosity Buddha, and all such Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each within their own lands, extend their broad and long tongues,
completely covering the trichiliocosm, and speak these words of truth: "You sentient beings,
you should believe this Sutra on the Praise of Inconceivable Merit, which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas."
[Commentary] The Buddha Jvālāṃsa (Flame-Shoulder) is as described previously. Furthermore, he possesses the meaning of "warmth" (*uṣman*):
that is to say, the Buddha bears the fire of the two wisdoms upon his two shoulders to warm the roots of goodness of the three wisdoms of sentient beings, causing the sprout of existence to grow.

As for "Supreme Sound," this refers to the sound of the Four Truths, the sound of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, the sound of the Six Perfections, the sound of arising and ceasing, and the sound of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). "Supreme" means—

It surpasses the six ordinary realms; it surpasses the Tripitaka teachings; and even the Perfect [Teaching] surpasses the Separate [Teaching]. Regarding the four lands and the six stages of realization (*ṣaḍ-yukti*), these are most supreme and difficult to obstruct.
"Obstruct" (*ju*) means to stop or to block. It is not obstructed by the six ordinary realms, nor by the three vehicles, nor by Bodhisattvas, nor by partial realization.
Regarding "born of the sun": if the Tathāgata does not appear in the world, the ten directions are eternally in darkness.
Darkness. When the Tathāgata appears in the world, the ten directions are all clearly illuminated. The four teachings arise with the sun; the four lands arise with the sun;
the six stages of realization arise with the sun. Regarding "Jālinīprabha," there are two kinds of nets: the net of worlds and the net of the Dharma-teachings.
In the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, it is said that when the Buddha was in the palace of the fourth dhyāna heaven, he observed the banner of the net and said: "The worlds of the ten directions are like..."
The mesh of the net: my teaching is also like this. The world-net consists of the two truths of suffering and its origin;

the teaching consists of the two truths of the path and its cessation. There is the illumination of the four truths of birth and death, up to the illumination of the four truths of non-action, and even the four lands and the six stages of identity.
△ Fifth, the direction below.
Śāriputra, in the world-systems of the direction below, there are Buddhas named Siṃha, Yaśas, Prabhāsa, and Dharma.

The Buddha Dharmadhvaja, the Buddha Dharmadhara, and other Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each in their respective lands, extend their broad and long tongues, completely covering the trichiliocosm, and speak these words of truth: "O sentient beings!..."
One should believe in this *Sūtra on the Praise of the Inconceivable Merit and the Protection and Mindfulness of All Buddhas*. [Commentary:

The lion is the king among beasts; it serves as a metaphor for the Buddha being the king within a single realm. This refers to the two types of Buddhas belonging to the *Pitaka* (Tripiṭaka) and *Agnostic* (Śrāvaka) vehicles.
The King among the six ordinary beings; the King among the distinct Buddhas and the three vehicles; the King among the ten realms for the Perfect Buddha.

Regarding the four lands and the six stages of realization (*ṣat-bhūmi*), the "Fame" Buddha is as previously described. As for "Light," this refers to the name itself, which is the light of the *dharmakāya*.

There is also the light of the name that involves birth and death, up to the unconditioned (*anabhisamskāra*). *Dharma* here is translated as "Dharma. It comprises the Four Noble Truths and Dependent Origination.
The six perfections, up to the four teachings, the four lands, and the six stages of identity—this applies equally to Dharmadhvaja Buddha and Dharmadhara Buddha. [Commentary:

Beneath the water-wheel, gold-wheel, and wind-wheel of this realm, there further exists a lower realm consisting of the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and so forth.
...up to the point of being infinitely layered and inexhaustible. *Dharma*—this is translated as "Dharma.
[Commentary] Regarding this realm’s water-wheel and so forth: the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that the three-thousandfold world system is formed through immeasurable causes and conditions.
The great earth rests upon the water-wheel, the gold-wheel, the wind-wheel, and the space-wheel; space has nothing upon which it depends. The multitude...
The world is established through the retribution of karmic actions. Furthermore, regarding those in the lower realms and so forth:

beneath the wheel of space, there are again the worlds of the lower direction, including the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), the heavens of the fourth dhyāna, the six heavens of the desire realm, Mount Sumeru, and the four continents.
The great ocean, the Iron Ring Mountains, and the great earth are layered and inexhaustible;
because the space below is inexhaustible, the worlds are likewise layered and inexhaustible.
△ Sixth, the upper direction.
Śāriputra, in the world-system above, there are the Buddhas Brahmaghoṣa, Nakṣatrarāja, Gandhottama, and Gandhaprabha.
The Buddha Mahārciskandha, the Buddha Citraratnapuṣpavicitritaśarīra, the Buddha Sālarājendra, the Buddha Ratnakusumaguṇa,
the Buddha Sarvārthadarśin, the Buddha Merukalpa— these and other Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
each in their own land, extended their broad and long tongues, completely covering the trichiliocosm, and spoke words of truth.
"You sentient beings, you should believe in this Sutra on the Praise of the Inconceivable Merit and the Protection and Mindfulness of All Buddhas.

[Commentary] Regarding the Sanskrit term *buddha*: "Buddha" (*buddha*) means purity. It refers to the purity of both the sound of arising-and-ceasing and the sound of non-arising. It is that which can purify.

The six classes of ordinary beings and the five turbidities (*pañcakaṣāya*). The distinct and perfect [teachings] are the Sanskrit term for "purity. They are able to purify the five turbidities outside the realm [of saṃsāra]. Regarding "the king of the constellations": "constellation" refers to the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*);

the moon is the king among the constellations, and the Buddha is the king among sentient beings. Regarding "superior fragrance": this is the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcadharmakāya*), namely:

precepts (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśana*). Only the Buddha is supreme regarding this fragrance.
"Light" refers to the light of the Tathāgata’s body, from which all sublime fragrances emanate. "Great Flame Shoulders" is as described previously.
"Adorned with Bodies of Variegated Jewel-Flowers" means that the flowers of the causes of the ten thousand practices adorn the wondrous fruit of the One Vehicle.

"King of the Śāla Trees" is translated here as "Firm and Solid Tree. There are four types of withered trees, four types of flourishing trees, and four types of trees that are neither withered nor flourishing.

The four "withered" [states] are the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). The four "flourishing" [states] are the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*). That which is neither withered nor flourishing is the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad-vipaśyanā*).

It is firm among the six classes of ordinary beings, firm among the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), and firm among bodhisattvas. As for "the virtue of precious flowers," it refers to birth-and-death, non-arising, and so forth.
"Seeing all meanings" refers to the meaning of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the meaning of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and the meaning of middle truth (*madhya-satya*). Thus it is.
As for Mount Sumeru: it is like Sumeru, the king of all mountains; it is like Sumeru, composed of the four precious substances;
it is like Sumeru, which dwells in the great ocean without moving; it is like Sumeru, the abode of devas and humans.

△ The commentary consists of three parts: first, a brief clarification of the higher realms; second, questions and answers to dispel doubts; third, an exhortation to later worthies. △ Now, the first part.

【Explanation】 This realm is not above the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana). Furthermore, there are wind-wheels and gold-wheels of the higher realms, as well as the [other] three realms.
...and so forth. These are layered and inexhaustible.

△ Second, the refutation of doubts through question and answer, in two parts: first, the doubt regarding the partial praise of the Western [Pure Land]; second, the doubt regarding the universal contemplation of the Dharma-realm.
△ First. [Commentary] Question:
Since there must be pure lands in all directions, why do you single out the West for praise? Answer: This, too, is not a good question.
Even if one were to praise the land of Akṣobhya Buddha, you would again suspect a partiality toward the East. Such shifting conceptual proliferation (a skillful answer).
△ Second, the doubt regarding the universal cognition of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). This has two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. △ Now, the first: [Commentary] Question:
Why does it not universally cognize the dharma-realm? (A close examination of the following answer shows that this is also not a good question.)

[Commentary] "Object-condition" (ālambana) means to take as an object. This refers to "universal object-conditioning" (paryantālambana), which means recollecting the Buddhas of the eastern direction, then the southern, and so on, up to the lower direction, and then the upper direction—taking as one's object every place reached is what constitutes universal object-conditioning.
To fail to understand that the single thought-moment of the present is the very backbone of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is a fundamental error.
△ Second, the response consists of two parts: first, the response in terms of phenomena; second, the response in terms of principle.
△ Now, the first. [Commentary]: There are three reasons for this response: to enable those of initial capacity to easily set their minds upon it; because the Original Vow of Amitābha is supreme;

and because the Buddha has a particular affinity with the sentient beings of this land. Generally, as the Buddha saves sentient beings, they receive his transformation through various degrees of difficulty and ease.

Shallow and deep alike depend entirely upon conditions. Wherever these conditions reside, their benevolent merit is vast and profound (*en-de hóng-shēn*). Through the various teachings they initiate (*biāo-xīn*), they can cause one to joyfully believe and enter [the path] (*huān-xǐ*);
they can cause one’s latent seeds to be stirred and awakened (*shēng-shàn*); they can cause demonic obstacles to be rendered impossible to obstruct (*pò-è*);
and they can cause the fundamental nature to unfold and manifest (*rù-lǐ*). For this reason, the myriad virtues are reverently received, and all spirits bow toward the Pole Star.

[Commentary] The text has two parts: first, the presentation of the three meanings; second, the explanation of the reasons for these three meanings. Regarding "to enable those of initial capacity to easily manifest their mind":

this means to cause those of initial capacity to focus single-mindedly on the realm of Immeasurable Light and Life, so that they may easily attain the clear manifestation of the mind-nature that is horizontally pervasive and vertically exhaustive.
The section beginning with "For the Buddha’s deliverance of those born in the lower realms" explains the causes and conditions for the three meanings.
Regarding the statement that "the Buddha’s saving of sentient beings and their receiving of transformation all depend upon conditions," this means they depend entirely upon prior conditions.

If prior conditions are shallow, then sentient beings find it difficult to receive transformation and the Buddha finds it difficult to save them. If prior conditions are deep, then sentient beings easily receive transformation and the Buddha easily saves them.
We see clearly that Amitābha is easy for sentient beings to transform and easy for them to be saved by; is this not because of Amitābha?
Amitābha possesses a unique affinity compared to all other Buddhas. Wherever this affinity resides, its benevolent merit is vast and profound.
The locus of this affinity in the present life is the benevolent merit bestowed in previous lives. If the benevolent merit is shallow, the affinity is shallow;
if the benevolent merit is deep, the affinity is weighty. We see clearly that Amitābha’s affinity is weighty; is this not due to the benevolent merit of his Forty-eight Vows?

It surpasses all other Buddhas. Furthermore, we currently see the various teachings initiated by Amitābha, namely this very sutra, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Sixteen Contemplations), and others, which enable sentient beings to attain the four *siddhāntas*.
Is this not indeed making it easy to set one's mind [on enlightenment]?

The "development of the essential nature" refers to the development of the essential nature of the *dharmatā* (true reality), which is the attainment of rebirth in the Pure Land. Therefore, throughout the ten directions...

Tens of thousands of virtues, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are reverently received and praised; immeasurable and boundless beings in their final birth before Buddhahood (bodhisattvas in the stage of *upapadya-parinirvāṇa*) stand with palms joined like the stars surrounding the North Star.
Because he possesses these three superior qualities that surpass those of all other Buddhas, he alone is singled out for praise and mindfulness.
△ Second, the answer according to principle. [Commentary:
One should know that the Buddha-seed arises from conditions. Conditions are precisely the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). A single thought-moment is all thought-moments; a single birth is all births.

Whether it be a single fragrance, a single flower, a single sound, or a single form—even down to the reception of repentance, the bestowal of prophecy, and the placing of hands upon the crown of the head—[it all arises from conditions].

The hands [of the Buddhas] pervade and harmonize all throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time; therefore, this superior causal condition is called the "Dharmadhātu-dependent Origination.
This is precisely what is meant by "universally conditioning the Dharmadhātu."

[Commentary] This is an answer based on principle (*li*). It clarifies that what was previously described as partial objectification and partial mindfulness is, in its entirety, the universal objectification of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Regarding the phrase "the Buddha-seed arises from conditions": "Buddha-seed" refers to the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), which is the single true Dharma-realm.

"Arising from conditions" means it arises through the conforming cause (*anuvartana-hetu*) and the understanding cause (*parijñāna-hetu*). These "conditions" are themselves the Dharma-realm; they constitute both the conforming cause and the understanding cause.
This is precisely the entirety of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Regarding "one thought-moment is all thought-moments": Amitābha is the body that is the treasury of the Dharma-realm;
thus, to recollect Amitābha, the One Buddha, is to recollect all Buddhas.
Regarding "one birth is all births": Sukhāvatī is the land that is the treasury of the Dharma-realm; therefore, to be born in Sukhāvatī, the one land, is to be born in all Buddha-lands.
Regarding "a single incense, a single flower," and so forth: a single incense is the incense of the Dharma-realm treasury (*dharmadhātu-garbha*).
To offer incense in one place is to offer incense in all places. The same applies to a single flower and the like; even to perform repentance in one place is to perform repentance in all places.

Whether receiving repentance, receiving a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), having one’s head rubbed, or having one’s hand grasped—whichever dharma one takes up is entirely the Dharma-realm. Therefore...
It is said that horizontally it pervades the ten directions, and vertically it exhausts the three periods of time; there is nothing that is not universally pervasive and interfused.

Therefore, this partial mindfulness gives rise to partial birth; as the dominant condition, the causal condition, and the completing condition, it is precisely the true cause—the dharma-realm dependent origination.
This is exactly what is meant by "universally conditioning the dharma-realm. Your so-called mindfulness of the West is, moreover, also mindfulness of the East.
He contemplates the lower direction, and again contemplates the upper direction. He is merely one who correctly claims to offer partial praise and partial contemplation.
The section on "Questioning and Answering to Dispel Doubts" concludes.
△ Third, the exhortation and admonition for later worthies.

[Commentary]: Those at the shallow stage may simply resolve their will to seek exclusively [the Pure Land], for it does not lie outside the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Those at the profound stage need not abandon the Western Land to separately seek the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*), for what could exceed the Dharma-realm?

To claim that the Western Land is provisional while the Flower Treasury World is real, or that the Western Land is small while the Flower Treasury World is great, is to fall entirely into the pervasive conceptual attachments of sentient beings;
this arises from failing to realize that the provisional and the real are of one essence, and that the small and the great are non-dual.
"It is because they lack intrinsic nature" (this resolves the delusions of over a thousand years). [Commentary]:
If one were to claim that the Western Regions are provisional and so forth, these are the words of Master Li [Tongxuan] from his *Huayan He lun* (Compendium on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra).
He judges that the *Huazang* (Flower Treasury) is the ultimate reality (*satya*), while the Western [Pure Land] is provisional (*upāya*). Thus, the preceding text states:

"It is not heterodox" (*na mithyā*)—this refutes the habitual delusions accumulated in the末代 (final age); "it is not provisional"—this refutes the errors of the *Huayan helun* (Treatise on the Synthesis of the Avataṃsaka).

Those who fall entirely into the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) of sentient beings—if one judges this according to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*)—it remains nothing other than the *parikalpita-agraha* (imagined grasping) of dharma-attachment. Regarding the three natures: [The text continues: ...Regarding the three natures...

There are three natures: first, the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); second, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); and third, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Regarding the "thoroughly imagined":
this refers to the self and phenomena that foolish people universally imagine and cling to as being truly existent;
it is precisely the dual grasping at self and phenomena. Regarding the "dependent nature": it exists based on the combination of various conditions; therefore, it is like an illusion.

Phenomena are not existent, yet they appear to be existent; being existent, they are immediately non-existent. This refers herein to the illusory manifestations of the provisional and the real, and the Great and the Small Vehicles.
Perfectly accomplished reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the dharma-nature that is perfectly fulfilled and realized.

This refers herein to the true nature of the single essence and absence of self-nature. Failing to realize that the provisional and the real are of one essence, and that the Great and the Small Vehicles lack self-nature—

The provisional is also the Dharma-realm; the real is also the Dharma-realm; both the provisional and the real are the Dharma-realm. Therefore, in the Western [Pure Land], the four lands are horizontally possessed simultaneously.

That is to say, the land of common residence (*sahā-loka*) is itself the land of serene light (*śānta-prabhāsa*) and the land of retributive fruition (*vipāka-phala*). Regarding the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) in the great and the small:

although the Flower Treasury World (*padma-garbha-loka*) is vast, it likewise lacks a self-essence, for it exists through the harmonious combination of all worlds. Thus, even the "great" lacks intrinsic nature. In the West...

Although it is small, it horizontally encompasses the four lands and likewise lacks the nature of smallness. Because they do not realize that the Western Land horizontally encompasses the four lands, they reckon it to be small.
Furthermore, they fail to understand that the provisional and the real, the great and the small, all arise dependently, are like illusions and transformations, and possess no substantial reality;
there is only the single nature of perfect, consummate reality. Therefore, this constitutes the pervasive attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*).
This is the calculation of the underlying principle. The initial brief citation of the title from the scripture is concluded.
△ Second, the interrogation and explanation of the scriptural title:
"Śāriputra, what do you think? (The name that extols its merits has already been explained in detail above. For what reason is it called 'All'"?
*The Sūtra on Being Protected and Mindfully Kept by All Buddhas*: "Śāriputra, if there are good sons or good daughters who hear this sūtra and receive and uphold it,
or who hear the names of the various Buddhas, all these good sons and good daughters shall be protected and mindfully kept by all Buddhas,
and they shall all attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
[The three types of] enlightenment. Therefore, Śāriputra, you and all others should believe and accept my words, as well as what has been spoken by all the Buddhas.
[Commentary: "What do you think?"—this is a self-posed inquiry. "Śāriputra," and so forth, is the self-explanation. This is a praise.

Regarding the phrase "the names of merits and so forth": this is the full title of the sutra, namely, *The Sutra Praising the Inconceivable Merits and Being Protected by the Recollection of All Buddhas*. Why, then, is only the latter half of the title explained?

Therefore, it is said that the preceding half-scroll of the sutra text has already provided a detailed explanation of the former half of the title; thus, this sutra uniquely reveals the Dharma of Names.
The realms are inconceivable. △ The commentary divides this into three parts:
first, the explanation of protection and mindfulness; second, the explanation of the awakening to fruition; third, the concluding exhortation to believe.
The first part [of the first section] further has two sub-sections: first, the direct explanation; second, the analytical discussion. △ Now, the first [sub-section].
[Commentary]: This sutra uniquely elucidates the unsurpassed essence of the mind. The names of all Buddhas likewise elucidate the unsurpassed, perfect, and ultimate myriad virtues.
Therefore, those who hear it are all protected and remembered by all Buddhas. Furthermore, hearing this sutra and upholding it is equivalent to grasping and holding the Name;
for the Name of Amitābha is that which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas.

[Commentary] The text has two parts of explanation: first, explaining "protection and mindfulness" (*ārakṣaṇa-smaraṇa*) in relation to hearing the sutra; second, explaining "protection and mindfulness" in relation to upholding the name.
"To express" (*qian*) means to reveal. Therein are the expressive (*vācaka*) and the expressed (*vācya*).

The expressive is this very sutra. The expressed has three aspects: first, the essential core of the unsurpassed mind; second, the names of all Buddhas; third, that which collectively expresses the myriad unsurpassed virtues. This constitutes the three.
The secret treasury of virtue and the essential core of the mind are the very nature of the recollecting mind.
The names of the Buddhas are the titles of the Buddhas who are recollected. Since the subject and object are non-dual, this is the unsurpassed, perfect, and ultimate perfection of all virtues.
Because the Buddha is the Honored One of the ten realms, his wisdom and virtue are perfected, and his merit of cessation is ultimate;

thus, the Dharma-body is manifest. Therefore, he is called the Compassionate Honored One of Myriad Virtues. This secret treasury of the three virtues is that which all Buddhas have collectively realized;

hence, he is protected and cherished by all Buddhas. Furthermore, regarding the passage "hears the sutra" and below, it is explained in terms of upholding the name. Having heard the sutra and received [it]...
"Holding" refers to grasping and maintaining the name. This concludes the formal explanation.
II. Distinguishing the Two [Aspects]. A. The Question. B. The Answer. Now, the first [part]: the question.
[Commentary] Question: If one merely hears the names of the various Buddhas but has not yet upheld the sutra, will one still receive their protective mindfulness and attain non-retrogression?
Part Two: The Answer, which is further divided into two sections. First, clarifying the two meanings of "restricted" and "universal. Second, clarifying the two powers of "self" and "other.

The first section [clarifying restricted and universal] is further divided into two parts. First, clarifying the restricted meaning. Second, clarifying the universal meaning. The first part [clarifying the restricted meaning] is further divided into two sections. First, clarifying other sutras. Second, clarifying... [text continues]
This sutra. △ Now, first: [Commentary] Answer:

This meaning has both a restricted and a universal application. Regarding "observing with a confused and defiled mind," although one recites my name, it does not constitute hearing it, because one cannot give rise to decisive faith and understanding;
one merely obtains worldly rewards of merit and does not [attain the ultimate fruit].

This brings about vast, profound, and wondrous benefit. If one attains the Samādhi of One Practice, one then achieves a mind of vast and subtle practice, which is called "attaining a semblance of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas" (anuloma-akṣānti). This constitutes being able to hear the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions.

[Commentary]: "Occupancy and Investigation" (Zhan-cha) refers to the *Sūtra on the Investigation of the Retribution of Good and Evil Karma*. "Restricted" (ju) means confined; it does not apply universally. It is discussed in terms of the vertical progression [of the stages].
"A mind muddled by confusion and defilement" refers to being disordered by the defilements of the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*).

Although one may recite [the teachings] orally, it does not constitute "hearing" [the Dharma], because one is unable to give rise to definitive faith and understanding. This is because the water of concentration...

Pure, yet the moon of wisdom does not shine brightly; thus, one receives only the wholesome retributions of humans and devas. Since the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) are not destroyed, one cannot attain the benefit of entering into principle through the *paramārtha-siddhānta*.
"Extensive" refers to the inherent nature (*prakṛti-parigraha*). "Great" refers to the measure of the nature (*prakṛti-pramāṇa*).

"Profound and wondrous" refers to the essence of the nature (*prakṛti-svabhāva*). The *ekavyūha-samādhi* is precisely "one mind without distraction. When the delusions of view and thought are emptied, one enters [into this].

The stage of resemblance is called the "resemblance to the patience of non-arising" (*anuloma-anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). It is the resemblance to the essence, nature, measure, and endowment of reality;
it is the resemblance to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). This occurs upon hearing the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
△ Second, explaining this sutra. [Commentary:

This case should also be understood in the same way. Therefore, one must hear it and uphold it until reaching the state of "one-pointed mind without distraction" before it can truly be called hearing the names of the Buddhas and receiving the protection and mindfulness of the Buddhas; this is the restricted meaning.

[Commentary] If one maintains the practice until reaching the state of single-mindedness without distraction regarding phenomena (*shishi*), the grasping at a self (*ātman*) is shattered, views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are emptied, and ordinary sentiments are shed;

thus, one accords with all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*). "All-encompassing wisdom" is a name for the Response Body Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya-buddha*); consequently, one receives the protective mindfulness of the Response Body Buddha.

If one reaches the state of single-mindedness without distraction regarding principle (*lishi*), the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) is shattered, ignorance (*avidyā*) is emptied, and sagely understanding vanishes.
This is then to be in correspondence with the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā). The "knowledge of all modes" is a name for the Dharma-body Buddha (dharmakāya-buddha).
Thus, one receives the protective mindfulness of the Dharma-body Buddha. This concludes the clarification of the restricted meaning.
△ Second, the explanation of the general principle.
[Commentary] As for the general principle: the compassion of all Buddhas is inconceivable, and their names and merits are likewise inconceivable.
Therefore, upon hearing the name of a Buddha even once—regardless of whether one possesses a focused mind or not, or whether one has faith or not—it all becomes a causal condition (*pratyaya*).

How much more so for the Buddha’s deliverance of sentient beings, which makes no distinction between enemies and kin and is ever free from weariness? If one merely hears the Buddha’s name, the Buddha will surely protect and mind them;
why, then, should there be any doubt?
[Commentary] The text is clear. This concludes the explanation of the two meanings of "universal" and "restricted.
△ Second, the explanation of the two powers of self and other, which is further divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the difficulty of self-power;
second, the explanation of the ease of other-power. △ Now, the first part.

[Commentary]: However, according to the *Vajrasamādhi* and the *Three Treatises*, a Bodhisattva whose faculties are mature is protected by the Buddha’s mindfulness, residing in the distinct stages (*bhūmi*) and the stage of perfect abiding (*pariniṣṭhita-vihāra*).
This is based on their own power; it is only when they necessarily enter the nature of co-arising (*sahaja-gotra*) that they can receive such protective mindfulness.
[Commentary]: The *Vajra-tri-śāstra* refers to the three treatises that explain the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. They were composed by the two Bodhisattvas Asaṅga and Vasubandhu.

Regarding "the nature of being born together" (*sahaja-gotra*): the stage of the three sages is the "nature of being an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjana-gotra*), because their contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) differs.

Once they enter the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*), their contemplative wisdom becomes identical; therefore, it is called the "nature of being born together. This is because they directly realize the *dharmakāya*.
This is because one receives the Buddha’s protective mindfulness.
△ Second, clarifying the ease of relying on other-power.
[Commentary]: Now, by relying on other-power, one receives protective mindfulness even at the stage of semblance; this applies from that stage all the way back down to the stages prior to it.

All of these also possess the meaning of universal protection and mindfulness. Even down to the single instance of hearing a Buddha’s name, there is a power that inspires and nurtures one within the dharmatā of the same essence;
thus, one obtains a remote cause through which one shall ultimately never fall back.
[Commentary]: The preceding passage concerned self-power, wherein one recollects one's own Buddha; here, we rely on other-power, wherein one recollects another Buddha.

To recollect one's own Buddha requires reaching the stage of partial realization (*pradeśa-prativedha*) before one can receive protection and mindfulness. Now, because one recollects another Buddha, one receives protection and mindfulness even at the stage of semblance (*pratirūpaka*).
This, moreover, relies on the power of actual practice; it is when one reaches "one-pointedness of mind without distraction" (*shì-yī-xīn-bù-luàn*) that [this occurs].

This is what is meant. However, those who achieve "single-mindedness without distraction" have already exhausted the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) and will be reborn in the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-bhūmi*).
As for those reborn in the Land of Common Dwelling (*sahā-loka*), they do not necessarily reach the stage of "semblance" (*sādṛśya*).

Therefore, it is said: "down to the stage of semblance and below. The stage of semblance and below refers to the stage of contemplative practice (*kuan-hsing-wei*). Upon merely hearing the Buddha’s name, one is so designated.

This refers to the position of the characters. Regarding the power of mutual stimulation within the single-substance *dharmatā*: since Buddhas and sentient beings share the same *dharmatā*, they are said to be "of one substance.
Precisely at the moment of hearing the name, this is the power of *dharmatā* which nurtures the seeds and causes them to manifest as active functioning (*pravṛtti*).
Since one has not yet attained their immediate fruit, it is called the "non-retrogression of the remote cause. First.
The explanation of *Nur-smṛti* (Anurakṣaṇā) is complete.
△ Second, the explanation of the awakening to the fruit (*phala-bodhi*).
[Commentary: *Anuttara* means "unsurpassed" (*an-uttara*). *Samyak-saṃbodhi* means "perfectly equal and perfect awakening" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
This refers to the fruit-enlightenment of the Mahāyāna.
[Commentary] "The fruit-enlightenment of the Mahāyāna" refers to the fruit-enlightenment of the Great White Ox Vehicle. Regarding the two teachings of the *Āgama* (Zang) and *Vaipulya* (Tong):

There is no principle of attaining Buddhahood that is not truly real; it is distinct from the wondrous enlightenment [of the provisional teachings]. It remains the Bodhisattva of the two practices within the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
Therefore, the fruition-enlightenment of the first three teachings possesses only its name; only the single, perfect, wondrous enlightenment is designated as fruition-enlightenment.
The five abodes are completely exhausted and the two deaths are forever extinguished; therefore, it is called "unsurpassed.
Returning to that which is unattainable and perfecting bodhi, it is therefore called "samyaksambuddha" (perfectly and fully awakened).
△ Third, the exhortation to believe.

[Commentary]: "Perfecting the three non-regressions" is an alternative name for attaining Buddhahood in a single lifetime; therefore, he exhorts Śāriputra and others that they should all believe and accept this.
Such are the merits of hearing the Name, as proclaimed by Śākyamuni and all the Buddhas of the ten directions. It may be trusted.
Do you not believe? Having finished exhorting you to believe and circulate [this sutra], the *Chao* (Commentary) states:
This sutra is the scripture for attaining Buddhahood in a single lifetime; therefore, the Buddha entrusted it to Śāriputra, exhorting him:
"You bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings—everyone should believe, understand, receive, and uphold it. Even the merit of merely hearing its name is [immeasurable]."
If this is so, how much more so for those who uphold, recite, and chant [this sutra], which is proclaimed by the mark of the broad and long tongue— how could they not believe it? △ Second,
the exhortation to aspire to its circulation.
Śāriputra, if there are those who have already made a vow, are now making a vow, or will make a vow,
desiring to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, all such persons shall attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Whether they have already been born, are being born now, or will be born in that land— therefore, Śāriputra, [it is so].
All sons and daughters of good family who possess faith should make a vow to be born in that land.

△ The commentary divides this into three parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the dispelling of doubts; third, the concluding praise. The first part [the direct explanation] further has two sections:
first, clarifying the intent behind the three exhortations; second, clarifying that the vow relies upon the Four Great Vows. △ Now, the first section.
[Commentary] "Vows already made for past lives," "vows now made for this life," and "vows to be made for future lives" clearly demonstrate that the vows inspired by faith are never in vain.
Without faith, one cannot form a vow; without a vow, faith likewise does not arise. Therefore, it is said: "If there is faith, one should make a vow.
Furthermore, a vow is the warrant for faith and the pivot of practice; it is of paramount importance.
Diligence: To raise the vow is to have faithful practice contained within it; this is why there are three earnest exhortations.
[Commentary] The text has three parts. First, it reveals that the vow is never in vain; it specifically reveals that with one thought-moment of resonance, one thought-moment is produced.
Second, it clarifies that faith and the vow assist one another; for without faith, one cannot generate the vow and so forth.

These are the faith and vow of names and words, which assist in accomplishing the faith and vow of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). Therefore, it says: "If there is faith, one should generate a vow.

If there is no vow, then the faith of contemplative practice cannot arise. Third, it clarifies the essentials among the three provisions. "Voucher" (*quan*) refers to concise wording. "Pivot" (*shu*)...
This refers to the pivot of the gate. It is illustrated by the fact that if faith possesses aspiration, then the text is held in one's hand and there will never be cause for regret or reversal.
If practice possesses aspiration, then practice has a point of return and is definitively free from error; therefore, it is a matter of vital importance.
This is why faith and practice are each encouraged once, whereas aspiration is earnestly encouraged three times.
△ Second, explaining that the vow relies upon the Four Great Vows.

[Commentary] Furthermore, the aspiration to be born in that land involves both the gate of delight and the gate of aversion. Aversion toward Saṃsāra corresponds to the two kinds of great vows generated based on the two truths of Suffering and its Origin.
Delight in seeking the Land of Ultimate Bliss corresponds to the [vows] based on the two truths of the Path and its Cessation.

Because it is conjoined with the two kinds of great vows (mahāpraṇidhāna) issued from the truths, one attains non-retrogression on the path to Great Bodhi. (These are all the essential instructions of the Pure School; most people in the world are muddled and do not understand them, so although they practice, they achieve no merit.)

[Commentary]: The Bodhisattva’s Four Great Vows are generated based upon the Four Noble Truths. Based on the Truth of Suffering, he generates the vow: "Sentient beings are boundless; I vow to deliver them all.
Based on the Truth of the Origin [of Suffering], he generates the vow: "Afflictions are inexhaustible; I vow to sever them all. Based on the Truth of the Path, he generates the vow:
"Dharma-gates are immeasurable; I vow to study them all. Based on the Truth of Cessation, he generates the vow: "The Buddha-way is unsurpassed; I vow to perfect it. Now...

Seeking birth in the Pure Land subsumes all four great vows. Specifically, the gate of weary detachment corresponds to the two great vows associated with the two truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*);
the gate of joyful seeking corresponds to the two great vows associated with the two truths of the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*).
Since one has already conformed with the causes of bodhi, one shall not regress from the fruit of bodhi. The initial formal explanation is concluded.
△ Second, the refutation of doubts. [Commentary] Question:
If one now makes a vow, one may only say "I shall be born [in the future]"; why is it called "being born now"? Answer: This also has two meanings. First, ...

1. "The present" refers to a single lifetime (only with this meaning can the essential commitment of one life be rendered free from error). One makes a vow and holds the Name in the present life; at the time of death, one will certainly be born in the Pure Land. 2.

"The present" refers to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) (only with this meaning can one enter deeply into the Samādhi of Single Practice). When a single thought corresponds [to the Name], one is born in that very thought; when every thought corresponds, one is born in every thought. Wondrous cause and wondrous fruit are not separate from the one mind.
Just as the rise and fall of the two ends of a scale are simultaneous, what need is there to wait for the *sāha* world?
Only when one's retribution is exhausted will one be raised in the precious pond;

yet now, by means of faith, aspiration, and the holding of the Name, the lotus bud is radiant and glorious, and the golden terrace appears—thus, one is no longer a person within the realm of Saṃsāra (this is the principle within the phenomenon, not a mere discourse on principle).

[Commentary]: Regarding "a thought-moment of correspondence, a lotus is born in a thought-moment": at the very moment one is practicing *nien-fo* with faith and aspiration, a lotus bud has already been produced within the pool of the seven treasures.
If one is diligent and courageous, the lotus bud will flourish with radiant glory; if one is indolent or regresses through regret, it will not.
Day by day they grow increasingly withered. If it is so for a single thought-moment, it is so for every successive thought-moment.

In this land, mindfulness is the wondrous cause; in that land, birth is the wondrous fruit. Although these two are distinguished as "this" and "that," they do not exist outside the self-nature of the present thought-moment before us.
This is illustrated by the two ends of a scale: they are not separate from the single scale itself; though their rising and falling are distinct, they occur simultaneously.
Why must one wait until the moment of death for rebirth to occur? This is a matter that accords with principle; it is not merely a theoretical discussion.

In ancient times, there was Great Master Kejū, who constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and was thus called "Kejū Hoke" (Kejū of the Lotus). In the eighth year of the Yuanyou era, he passed away while sitting in meditation. Three days later, he returned and said to people, "I traveled to the Pure Land."

He beheld various sublime realms, which accorded perfectly with the scriptures. Among those who had practiced the Pure Land path here, the names of those destined for the Flower-Petal Terrace were already inscribed: first, Master Xun of the Guangjiao Monastery in Chengdu; second, Mr. Sun Shierlang of Mingzhou; and third, Kejiu.

Those destined for the Silver Terrace were inscribed as follows: the Daoist Nun Xu of Mingzhou. Having finished speaking, he transformed away again. When Nun Xu passed away, a wondrous fragrance filled her chamber; when Mr. Sun Shierlang passed away, celestial music resounded in the sky.

(○ Lady Wang of Yueguo was the wife of Prince Jing, the paternal uncle of Emperor Zhezong of the Song dynasty. She led her maids and handmaidens to practice the Pure Land path exclusively. Later, one maid died without illness. That night, the lady dreamed that the maid came to express her gratitude, saying: "I am fortunate to have been exhorted and corrected by you, and thus I have attained birth in the Pure Land.")

The lady asked, "Can the Western Paradise be reached? The maidservant replied, "It can. She then led the lady forward. After a short while, they saw a great pond, within which lotus flowers were interspersed in various sizes—some flourishing, others withered. The lady asked for the reason behind this.

The maidservant said, "For those in the world who cultivate the Western Paradise, as soon as a single thought arises, a lotus flower is produced here. Depending on whether their diligence or indolence differs, the state of the flowers—whether flourishing or withered—also varies accordingly.
