Among them was one person sitting in court robes, his body adorned with a precious crown and necklaces. The lady asked, "Who is this? The maidservant replied, "This is Yang Jie. There was another person sitting in court robes; she asked again, "Who is this? and was told, "This is Ma Yu. Both men cultivated the practices of the Pure Land; the details of their lives are recorded in their respective biographies. The lady...

The woman asked, "Where shall I be reborn? The maidservant led her along for several li until they saw a flower pedestal, resplendent with gold and emerald, its radiance brilliantly penetrating. She said, "This is the place where the lady will be reborn; it is the highest grade of the 'Birth upon the Golden Pedestal'."

When he awoke, sorrow and joy welled up within him simultaneously. That year, on his birthday, he rose at dawn, took up the incense burner, and stood gazing toward the Hall of Guanyin. Just as his relatives were approaching to offer him congratulations on his longevity, they looked upon him and saw that he had already passed away while standing.
△ Third, the praise of the conclusion.
[Commentary] It is utterly perfect and utterly sudden; it is difficult to discuss and difficult to conceive. Only those with great wisdom can truly believe in it.
[Sub-commentary] These wondrous causes and wondrous fruits do not depart from the one mind. This principle of the Perfect and Sudden is not like that of Śāriputra.
Wisdom. One cannot simply cut through to a state of non-doubt. The section on the two exhortations for the circulation of the scripture is concluded.
△ Third, the exhortation to practice the circulation has two parts: first, the praise by all Buddhas; second, the concluding eulogy by the Master of the Teaching.
△ Now, the first part.
Śāriputra, just as I now praise the inconceivable merit of all Buddhas, so too do those Buddhas praise my own inconceivable merit, saying: "The Buddha Śākyamuni..."

They are able to perform a most difficult and rare feat: to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi within the Sahā world-system, amidst the five turbidities of this evil age—the turbidity of the kalpa, the turbidity of views, the turbidity of afflictions, the turbidity of sentient beings, and the turbidity of life—and to preach for all sentient beings this Dharma that is difficult for all the world to believe.
(This sentence emphasizes the power of upholding the Name; therefore, it is an exhortation to practice.)
△ The commentary is divided into three parts: first, the Buddhas’ successive praise; second, the performance of rare and marvelous deeds;
third, the world of sentient beings. △ Now, the first part.
[Commentary] Although the merit and wisdom of all Buddhas are equal, there are differences in the ease or difficulty of their transformative activity.
It is easy to attain enlightenment in a Pure Land, but difficult in a turbid world. It is easy to preach the Dharma for sentient beings in a Pure Land, but difficult for those in a turbid world.

Even preaching the gradual teaching (*anupūrva-dharma*) for sentient beings in a turbid world is relatively easy, whereas preaching the sudden teaching (*tada-dharma*) is difficult. For a turbid world...
To speak of other sudden teachings for sentient beings is still relatively easy; however, to speak of the Pure Land method of horizontal transcendence—a sudden teaching—is even more difficult.

To explain to the sentient beings of this turbid age the wondrous contemplation of the Pure Land’s sudden cultivation and sudden realization through horizontal transcendence is already no small matter.

To further explain this method—which requires no arduous labor of cultivation or realization, but merely the holding of the Name, leading one directly to the stage of non-retrogression—is truly extraordinary, supreme, and wondrous.
Transcending all thought, this foremost skillful means is the most difficult among the difficult;
therefore, there is not a single Buddha throughout the ten directions who does not extol me, Śākyamuni, as being preeminently courageous and valiant.
[Commentary] This passage reveals Śākyamuni’s heroic prowess by contrasting the ease and difficulty of the two lands; therefore, all Buddhas offer their praise.
Regarding the merits of the Buddhas, from "ease" to "difficulty": if considered in terms of self-realization, the path of every Buddha is identical;
if considered in terms of transforming others, the path of every Buddha differs. That it is easy to attain *bodhi* in a Pure Land and difficult in a turbid world is explained briefly as follows.

There are ten kinds [of differences]. It is easy in the Pure Land because one constantly sees the Buddha; it is difficult in the turbid world because one does not constantly see the Buddha. It is easy in the Pure Land because one constantly hears the Dharma;
it is difficult in the turbid world because one does not constantly hear the Dharma. It is easy in the Pure Land because those of superior goodness assemble together;

it is difficult in the turbid world because one is entangled by evil friends. It is easy in the Pure Land because there are no demonic activities; [it is difficult in the turbid world because of them].
It is easy. It is difficult because the various demons of the defiled world cause turmoil and confusion. It is easy because in the Pure Land one does not undergo the cycle of rebirth.
It is difficult because in the defiled world the cycle of rebirth never ceases. It is easy because in the Pure Land there are no three evil realms.

It is difficult because in the defiled world it is hard to escape the miserable destinies. It is easy because in the Pure Land superior conditions assist the path. It is difficult because in the defiled world worldly conditions obstruct the path.
It is easy [to teach] because the lifespan in the Pure Land is immeasurable; it is difficult because the lifespan in the defiled world is short.

It is easy because one attains non-retrogression through perfect realization in the Pure Land; it is difficult because there is much retrogression in practice in the defiled world. It is easy because one becomes a Buddha in a single lifetime in the Pure Land;
it is difficult because it is hard to achieve Buddhahood in the defiled world even over many kalpas. Thus, it is easy to preach the Dharma for sentient beings in the Pure Land.
Regarding the difficulty for those in the defiled age: it is because the faculties in the Pure Land are sharp, whereas the faculties in the defiled age are dull.

The gradual teachings refer to the previous three teachings; as they are spoken according to the intentions of others, they are easy. The sudden teaching refers to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*); as it is spoken according to one's own intention, it is difficult.
Other sudden teachings refer to all other aspects within the Perfect Teaching, excluding the horizontal transcendence of the Pure Land, which involves contemplating one’s own [mind].

The Dharma-gate of the Buddha is relatively easy; those with sharp faculties may enter it. However, the Pure Land method of horizontal transcendence and sudden realization—the Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha—is even more difficult, indeed exceedingly difficult.
This is because one need not wait to sever afflictions in order to be reborn while still carrying one's karmic burdens;
hence it is called "exceedingly difficult. Since the sudden cultivation and sudden realization of wondrous contemplation are already difficult in themselves, [this method is even more so].
It is said: "It is not difficult. This teaching requires no toil, labor, or arduous cultivation and realization;
one need only hold the Name, and in seven days the merit will be perfected, leading directly to the stage of non-retrogression. This may truly be called the most difficult among difficulties.

In this defiled world, I am now able to accomplish what is hard to accomplish and preach what is hard to preach; therefore, there are none among the Buddhas of the ten directions who do not recommend it.
Let me, Śākyamuni, be preeminently courageous.
△ Second, explaining the ability to perform rare deeds, which has four parts: first, explaining that wondrous conduct can transform;
second, explaining that wondrous conduct can attain; third, explaining what Śākyamuni has attained; fourth, explaining what Śākyamuni has taught. △ Now...
First. [Commentary:

Regarding the "impurity of the kalpa" (kalpa-kaṣāya): it is a time when impure phenomena congregate. Within this impurity of the kalpa, one who has not practiced the path of escaping by means of karma cannot possibly cross over [to liberation] (it is impossible to break through the encirclement).

[Commentary] These five turbidities (pañca-kaṣāya) exist substantially within the realm of shared residence (sahabhū-lokadhātu), though their principle extends throughout the three higher realms. For now, we shall consider them in relation to the shared residence.
Regarding the "convergence of the turbid dharmas": this refers to the convergence of the five turbidities during the final dharma period at the end of a kalpa of decrease.

It is not possible for those who possess karmic obstructions to escape horizontally [to the Pure Land] by means of a single recitation of the name of Amitābha Buddha unless they can transcend this turbidity of the kalpa (kalpa-kaṣāya).

[Commentary] Regarding the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*): the five types of sharp-facultied afflictions (*tīkṣṇa-kleśa*)—namely, the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and various false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)—are so dense, obscure, and submerged that they are called "turbidity.
Within this turbidity of views, it is not that skillful means (*upāya*) are unnecessary; yet one can certainly not cross over [the stream of existence] (for opinions are not permitted).
[Commentary] "Defilement of views" refers to the afflictions of view. Regarding the "five sharp-faculties" (pañca-kleśa): "sharp" means keen; "faculty" (kleśa) means to drive or impel.

This means that sentient beings are driven by these five kinds of delusive afflictions to wander through the cycle of rebirth. "Increasing and flourishing" means growing and becoming intense. 1. The view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*):
This refers to falsely identifying the four great elements as a self. 2. The view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*): This refers to [the view held] regarding the above...

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*): either grasping [the aggregates] as annihilated or grasping them as eternal; these are called the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism. Third, wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*):

this refers to apprehending principles with a distorted mind and repudiating cause and effect. Fourth, the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*): this refers to not repudiating cause and effect, yet regarding what is not a fruit as being a fruit.
Fifth, the adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*): this refers to regarding what is not a cause as being a cause. Furthermore, there are the sixty-two types of wrong views.
Various delusions of view, such as those beginning with "seeing," are dark, turbid, and submerged; they confuse and obscure the true nature, and are therefore called a "defilement.

While dwelling amidst this defilement of views, if one merely recites the name of Amitābha Buddha without relying on expedient practices, one will certainly be unable to cross over this defilement of views.

[Commentary]: Regarding the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*): it refers to the intensification of the five dull latent afflictions (*anuśaya*), namely greed, anger, ignorance, pride, and doubt.
Because they cause agitation and disturbance, they are called "turbidity. Within this turbidity of afflictions, the ordinary mind is not itself the practice of the Buddha-mind.
One will certainly be unable to cross over [it] (there being neither grasping nor abandoning).
[Commentary]: "The turbidity of afflictions" refers to the delusions of thought (*suhuo*). Regarding the "five dull messengers": "dull" means sluggish;

they are called "dull" in contrast to the aforementioned "sharp messengers. First is greed (*rāga*), which means insatiable attraction and grasping. Second is anger (*pratigha*), which means wrathful resentment.

First is anger; second is hatred; third is delusion, meaning a lack of understanding due to ignorance; fourth is pride, meaning relying on oneself and looking down upon others; fifth is doubt, meaning indecisive hesitation.
While situated within this turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kāṣāya*), merely reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha is not the practice of "mind-as-Buddha" in the present moment;
one will certainly be unable to cross over this turbidity of afflictions through such means alone.

[Commentary]: Regarding the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*): it refers to the coarse and inferior five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) produced by views and afflictions, which are conventionally designated as "sentient beings.
Since both their physical form and mind are uniformly base and deficient, it is called "turbidity. Within this turbidity of sentient beings, there is no practice of either aspiration or revulsion.
One will certainly be unable to cross over [as the grasping and rejecting blaze].

[The Sub-commentary] states, "That which is produced by the afflictions of views," etc. "Views" refers to the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). "Afflictions" refers to the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
With these two turbidities as the cause and the performance of tainted karma (*sāsrava-karman*) as the condition, one brings about the coarse, wretched, and evil five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

The combination [of these elements] is conventionally designated as a "person. (The six realms are all contained within. Regarding those whose form and mind are base and inferior: "form" refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*);
"mind" refers to the four aggregates of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā*, *saṃjñā*, *saṃskāra*, and *vijñāna*-skandhas).

All of these are impure, all are suffering, all are impermanent, and all are without self; therefore, they are called "base and inferior. Dwelling amidst this turbidity of sentient beings, one must not only recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, but also cultivate weariness [with this state].
To leave behind turbid evil and joyfully seek pure conduct, one will certainly be unable to cross over this *sattva-kaṣāya* (degeneration of sentient beings).

[Commentary] As for the *āyuḥ-kaṣāya* (degeneration of lifespan), both cause and effect are inferior; lifespans are short and brief, not even reaching a full hundred years. Therefore, it is called "turbidity.
Within this *āyuḥ-kaṣāya*, even if one does not waste kalpas of time and does not exert oneself in arduous practices, one will certainly be unable [to attain liberation].
[To eat] to satiety [in accordance with the proper measure]. [Commentary]:

Regarding those whose causes and effects are both inferior: as for the cause, the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*) and the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*) constitute the inferiority of the cause; the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*) [constitutes the inferiority of the effect].

This is because the fruit would be inferior. To dwell amidst this defilement of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*), one cannot transcend it merely by the practice of reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha for seven days.
The first section, clarifying that wondrous practice can transform [the defilements], is concluded.
△ Second, explaining that sublime practice can attain [the goal].
[Commentary]: Furthermore, it is precisely this single recitation of "Namu Amida Butsu," adorned with faith and aspiration, that transforms the turbidity of the kalpa into a pure sea assembly;
transforms the turbidity of views into immeasurable light; transforms the turbidity of afflictions into the light of eternal quiescence; and transforms...
The defilement of sentient beings is transformed into birth by transformation within a lotus; the defilement of lifespan is transformed into Immeasurable Life.
[Commentary] This clarifies that a single phrase of "Amitābha Buddha" perfectly transforms the five defilements and perfectly accomplishes the five purities.
This very "Amitābha Buddha" recited once, adorned with faith and aspiration, is precisely the power of faith, aspiration, concentration, and wisdom. Adorned...

Yan Guang’s life is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). To speak of "a single sound" is to take the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) as the basis for clarifying the meaning of vertical exhaustion and horizontal pervasiveness.

If one follows the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, all six faculties and six sense objects are vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive. However, here we follow the perspective of sentient beings;
since the ear-faculty is the easiest to enter, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "If drums are struck simultaneously in the ten directions, [the sound reaches] the ten locations..."

At one time it was heard: "This horizontal pervasion throughout the ten directions is 'Immeasurable Light' (*Amitābha*). Birth and cessation are both perfectly transcended; this is the eternal reality.
This vertical exhaustion of the three periods of time is 'Immeasurable Life' (*Amitāyus*). Now, by the power of faith and aspiration, one adorns this Dharma-body Amitābha Buddha.
To transform the turbidity of the kalpa into a pure sea-assembly—this 'turbidity of the kalpa' refers to..."

The assembly of turbid dharmas now becomes an assembly of pure dharmas through rebirth in the Pure Land. If the contemplative practice transforms, it becomes the assembly of purity in the land of shared residence;

if it transforms at the level of semblance, it becomes the assembly of purity in the land of skillful means; if it transforms through partial realization, it becomes the assembly of purity in the land of retribution for true reward;

and if it transforms to the ultimate degree, it becomes the assembly of purity in the land of tranquil light. When the turbidity of views is transformed into immeasurable light, the delusions of view become wisdom.
Because its nature is luminous, it is called "light. Now, by being reborn in the Pure Land, it is transformed into the immeasurable light of wisdom-virtue;

or it becomes the immeasurable light of the Land of Common Residence, the immeasurable light of the Land of Expedient Means, and so on, up to the immeasurable light of the Land of True Reward and the Land of Quiescent Light.

Regarding the transformation of the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*) into the light of eternal quiescence (*nitya-prabhāsvara*): afflictions are the delusions of thought (*sahaja-kleśa*). By being reborn in the Pure Land, these are transformed into the virtue of severance (*prahāṇa-guṇa*);

hence it is called the light of eternal quiescence. Alternatively, this refers to the virtue of severance within the Land of Common Residence (*sahā-loka*), up to the virtue of severance within the Land of Quiescent Light.

The defilement of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*) is transformed into birth by transformation within a lotus; that is, one attains birth by transformation in the Land of Common Abode, and so forth, up to birth by transformation in the Land of Quiescent Light (*śāntābhāsvara*).

The defilement of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*) is transformed into Infinite Life; that is, one attains Infinite Life in the Land of Common Abode, and so forth, up to Infinite Life in the Land of Quiescent Light.
This concludes the second section clarifying how sublime practice can attain these results.
△ The Three Clarifications on What Śākyamuni Attained.
[Commentary: Therefore, a single utterance of "Namo Amitābha Buddha" is the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* dharma attained by our original teacher Śākyamuni in this world of five turbidities.
(The profound essence of the Pure Land school, spanning a thousand ages, has suddenly manifested its spiritual power—how rare and marvelous!)
[Commentary] "Therefore" refers to the preceding statement that Amitābha Buddha’s wondrous practice is able to perfectly revolve and perfectly realize;
thus, it is the very essence of the causal practice performed by Śākyamuni and the fruit of enlightenment he realized. This concludes the third section:
the explanation of what Śākyamuni attained.
△ Fourth, the explanation of what Śākyamuni taught.
[Commentary: Now, this entire body of the fruit-enlightenment is bestowed upon sentient beings in this turbid and evil world;
it is the sphere of practice of all Buddhas, which only Buddhas and Buddhas can fully exhaust. It is not something that the nine realms can believe or understand through their own power.
[Commentary] These four sections all explain how the sutra text is able to perform an exceedingly difficult and rare feat.

The preceding section explained that Śākyamuni was able to attain Bodhi amidst the five turbidities; this section clarifies that he was further able to preach this dharma so difficult to believe for sentient beings living in an age of turbid evil.
Therefore, it says "bestowing. This single thought-moment of the nature of mind is [only known by] the Buddha...
The realization is ultimate; therefore, only a Buddha can exhaustively fathom it, for it cannot be believed or understood through the self-power of the nine realms.
This concludes the second section, clarifying that [the Buddha] can perform rare and marvelous deeds.
△ Third, the world of sentient beings. [Commentary]:

"All sentient beings" specifically refers to those of the five turbidities and evil persons. "The entire world" generally refers to the receptacle worlds of the four lands and the worlds of sentient beings within the nine realms.
[Commentary] There are three kinds of worlds: first, the world of perfect enlightenment, which is the Buddha-realm;
second, the world of sentient beings, so called because all nine realms possess the thought of sentient beings; third, the receptacle world, which refers to the land of dependent retribution;
because this dependent retribution is insentient, it is like a vessel. In the sutra text, [the Buddha] preached this for the sake of all sentient beings.
"The Dharma difficult for all the world to believe" refers specifically to the six classes of ordinary beings within the sentient world;
therefore, they are called "the wicked people of the five turbidities.
Regarding "all the world," among the three worlds—excluding the world of the perfectly awakened ones—it includes both the receptacle world and the sentient world; thus it is so stated.
This is a general reference. The initial section of the sutra text concludes with the various Buddhas offering mutual praise.

△ Second, the Principal Teacher’s concluding eulogy. Previously, the exhortation to believe and circulate [the teaching] was the entrustment of the various Buddhas; here, it is the entrustment of the Original Teacher.
Although the wording of the entrustment is slightly distinct, it follows the general pattern, simply stating "all worlds," just as the previous Buddhas did.
As it is said: "You sentient beings should know that Mañjuśrī, Kāśyapa, and the others are all included in this entrustment.
[Commentary] This clarifies the intent of the section. This section is titled "The Teacher’s Concluding Praise," and is also known as "Entrustment and Circulation.
While the preceding text exhorted faith for circulation, this refers to the Buddhas’ entrustment of their respective lands to all the worlds; this is the original [text].
The Master entrusted all the worlds of this Sahā world-system. Regarding the brief distinction between the specific and the general in these instructions:

in the preceding passage, there were two meanings—the specifically indicated and the generally indicated. Now, in the text of this sutra, it does not say "for the sake of all sentient beings," but rather says "for the sake of all worlds.
This is an abbreviation of the specific meaning, following the general meaning; for by means of the general, the specific is subsumed.

It is just as previously stated in the section on encouraging faith and circulation: "O sentient beings, you should believe in these meanings such as 'praise' and so forth," which are identical in intent.
Regarding the phrase "Mañjuśrī and others," since it refers to "all the world," one should know that Mañjuśrī, Kāśyapa, and all others are included among those to whom this is entrusted.
Śāriputra, you should know that in this world of five turbidities, I have performed this difficult task:
having attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I preach this dharma so difficult to believe for the sake of all the worlds. This is truly most difficult.
△ The commentary is divided into four sections: first, the rarity of encountering this Dharma-gate; second, the elucidation of the five certainties;
third, the errors of ignorance; fourth, the correctness of knowing the difficulty. △ Now, the first section.

[Commentary: This single practice of faith, aspiration, and the recitation of the Name does not involve worldly activities; it revolves perfectly through the five turbidities. Only through faith can one enter it;

it is not a realm accessible to discursive thought. Had it not been for the Original Teacher coming into this evil world to manifest the attainment of Bodhi, and seeing, teaching, and speaking of this practice out of his great wisdom and great compassion, by what means could sentient beings have received it?
[Commentary] The text is clear.
△ Second, the explanation of the five certainties.

[Explanation] (These five sections should be read in conjunction with the instruction on the five things that necessarily prevent crossing over. However, we who dwell within the *kalpa-kaṣāya* (the age of defilement) are certainly confined by time and pressed by suffering; we dwell amidst views.
Amidst the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), they are inevitably entangled by false wisdom and deluded by evil teachers.

Amidst the turbidity of defilements, they are inevitably trapped by craving and stung by evil karma. Amidst the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), they are inevitably settled in foulness and impurity, unable to awaken to clarity;
they relish weakness and are unable to exert themselves toward flight. Amidst the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*)...
In the midst [of this], one is inevitably swallowed by impermanence; like sparks from a flint or a flash of lightning, there is no time to prepare.
[Commentary]: This clarifies that those dwelling in the Sahā world cannot avoid the five turbidities (pañca-kaṣāya).
It means that when we dwell amidst the assembly of turbid dharmas, we are inevitably confined by time. "Confined" (yòu) refers to being enclosed, like a prisoner in a garden enclosure.
In the age of the *kalpa*-defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*), one’s own correct vision remains unopened;
being thus inevitably ensnared by false wisdom, how could one possibly escape, given that false teachers expound the Dharma as numerous as the sands of the Ganges?
Within the age of the *kalpa*-defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-kāṣāya*), one is inevitably mired in lustful desire; such a pitfall is like a basin filled with scorpions—how dire!

Karma is like the five poisons; it is difficult to escape its sting. Amidst the turbidity of sentient beings, one remains settled within this stinking sack, unable to clearly awaken to its impurity, suffering, and emptiness.
One takes pleasure in being among inferior and weak beings, unable to accept that one’s own nature is originally that of a Buddha.
Amidst the turbidity of lifespan, one is certainly [destined for] non-existence...
One is constantly swallowed by the Great Ghost. This very body and mind, arising and ceasing from moment to moment, are themselves the Great Ghost of Impermanence;
they are not ghosts existing outside the body. This ghost has never been separated from us since time immemorial, and therefore we are certainly being swallowed by it.
As soon as one resolves to cultivate the path, one finds oneself already overwhelmed and unable to cope.
△ The Error of Threefold Ignorance.

[Commentary]: If one does not deeply understand that this is extremely difficult (one should know that the meaning of "extremely difficult" has never been explicitly revealed), one will assume there exists some other dharma by which one may escape the five turbidities from within this house of blazing flames—a place where frivolous proliferation is rampant (certainly, certainly).

[Commentary]: If one does not deeply realize that it is extremely difficult to escape from the five turbidities, nor deeply realize that the practice of nianfo will certainly enable one to cross over, one will think to oneself:
"I possess another esoteric and wondrous teaching that can deliver me from the five turbidities."
Such people are certainly brought about by the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). Enveloped by false wisdom and deluded by false teachers,

they remain within this great burning house of stinking smoke and flames, greedily attached to frivolous play, their false wisdom and false views giving rise to a chaotic proliferation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
△ Four: Knowing that it is difficult.

[Commentary] Only by deeply realizing its extreme difficulty will one be willing to exhaust all traces of the thieving mind and treasure this single practice (the merit of which shall endure for ten thousand ages).
This is why our Original Teacher spoke with his utmost voice of its extreme difficulty and earnestly exhorted us to know it. First: Universal Exhortation.
[End. [Commentary:

Only those who deeply realize that it is extremely difficult to escape the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) and who are certain that mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) can surely deliver them will be willing to exhaust themselves in practice.
Those who harbor a "thieving mind" hoping for some other secret transmission of the wondrous Dharma—even if they recite a single phrase of Amitābha—will not succeed.

The Buddha is the supreme treasure; therefore, it is said that this single practice is "treasured. Our Original Teacher spoke of this as being extremely difficult to accomplish, deeply entrusting us with the knowledge that it is very hard to escape the five turbidities, yet that by recollecting the Buddha, one will certainly be delivered.
This concludes the second section of the sutra text, the joint praise of the two teachers. This concludes the first major section, the general exhortation.
△ Second, the conclusion and exhortation:

After the Buddha had spoken this sutra, Śāriputra, the bhikṣus, and all those in the world—gods, humans, asuras, and others—hearing what the Buddha had taught, rejoiced, believed, and accepted it; they paid homage and departed.
[Commentary] This Dharma-gate is inconceivable, difficult to believe, and difficult to understand; there was not a single person capable of posing a question.

The Buddha’s wisdom discerns the capacities [of beings], and knowing that the conditions for the assembly to attain Buddhahood have ripened, he speaks spontaneously without being asked, enabling them to obtain the four benefits.
Like a seasonal rain that brings transformation, they joyfully believe and accept it. To have one's body and mind filled with serenity is called "joyful"; it means to be entirely free from doubt.

To recognize [the teaching] is called "faith" (*śraddhā*). To receive it and not forget it is called "reception" (*pratigraha*). To feel profound gratitude for its great benevolence and cast oneself down in submission is called "prostration" (*namaskāra*).
To practice according to the instructions without ever retreating for a moment is called "departing" (*gata*).
[Commentary] The text has two parts: first, a general presentation of the four benefits; second, a specific identification of the four benefits. The first part is easily understood.
Regarding the second part, from "body and mind" (*śarīra-citta*) onwards, the four benefits are specifically identified. The serenity and joy of body and mind is called "joy" (*prāmodya*);

this is the benefit of joy according to the *loka-siddhānta*. The absence of any doubt is called "faith" (*śraddhā*). The receptive retention without forgetting is called "receiving" (*udgraha*); this is [the benefit] according to the *pudgala-siddhānta*.

The *dāna-siddhānta* (the standpoint of giving) is the benefit of generating goodness; it is the benefit of being moved by great kindness and virtue, casting oneself down to take refuge and prostrate.
The *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of counteracting) is the benefit of destroying evil; this means that by taking refuge in the Buddha, one immediately destroys the evils of the nine realms.

To practice according to the teachings without retreating for even a single step is called "going forth" (*yāna*); this is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the standpoint of ultimate truth), which is the benefit of entering into principle.

This means that once one attains rebirth there, one immediately ascends to the stage of non-retrogression. This refers to the four benefits of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), not those of the three preceding teachings.
The section on the Propagation of the Dharma concludes. The exegesis of the sutra is complete.
△ Third: The Epilogue, in two parts. First, the author’s own epilogue; second, the epilogue by another. △ Now, the first: [Epilogue to the Commentary]. The Sūtra says:
"In the age of the Final Dharma, among billions upon billions of people who practice, scarcely one attains the Way. Only by relying on the recitation of the Buddha's name can one attain deliverance.
Alas! Now is precisely that time (revealing my heart and soul). If one abandons this inconceivable Dharma-gate, how could one possibly achieve excellence?"

When Xu left the household life, he relied on his own realization of the *zong* (the essence of the teaching) to preach the Dharma in his present body. He held himself in high esteem and looked down upon the scriptural teachings (*jiao*), recklessly claiming that the practice of reciting the name was intended only for those of middling or inferior capacity.

Later, due to a severe illness, he resolved to return to the West [to seek the Dharma]. Thereupon, he again studied the *Miaozong chao*, the *Yuanzhong chao*, as well as the commentaries by Yunqi and others.
Only then did he realize that the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation is truly the unsurpassed King of Jewels; it was only then that he was willing to die.
When the mind upholds the Name, even ten thousand oxen cannot pull it back. My friend Qubing has long devoted himself to the practice of pure karma (*śukla-karman*).
Desiring that the essential purport of this sutra be made brilliant and clear without verbose rhetoric, he requested that I compose a concise commentary.

I, wishing to bring all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm together to be born in Sukhāvatī, could not in principle refuse his request (though I spoke of being compelled by necessity). I took up my pen in the year Dinghai.
On the twenty-seventh day of the ninth month, the draft was presented; by the fifth day of the tenth month, after nine days, it was completed.

It is my wish that every phrase and every word shall serve as a provision for the path, and that all who see or hear it may together attain the stage of non-retrogression (every character is a manifestation of reality; indeed, indeed!).

May both those with faith and those with doubt plant the seeds of the Way, and may those who praise or revile alike find liberation. I look up and pray that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will graciously accept and bear witness to this.

Recorded by the fellow student and friend [Name], who rejoices in and adds his supportive empowerment. At the western end, the practitioner Ouyi Zhixu set down his brush and thus wrote this postscript.

[Commentary] The text is divided into four parts. First, from the beginning up to "the Dharma-gate should be made to flourish," it is the introduction to the Dharma-gate.

Second, from "when [Xu] left home" down to "the principle cannot be set aside," it introduces the causes and conditions for this commentary. Third, from "raising the pen myself" down to "completed on the ninth day," it records the date and year of composition.
Fourth, it consists of the vow and dedication. Regarding the term *bāyǔ* (跋語): *bā* means "foot. It serves as a supplement to the introduction.

this is the meaning of circulation, and it is also called the "Postscript.

Regarding the "Dharma of the Final Age," of the three periods of the Śākya’s Dharma remaining in the world, the first millennium after the parinirvāṇa of the Śākya is the period of the True Dharma (Saddharma). After that millennium, furthermore—
One thousand years constitute the Semblance Dharma (Saddharma-pratirūpaka), and the subsequent ten thousand years constitute the Final Dharma (Saddharma-vipralopa).
At this time, we are currently in the Final Dharma, having already reached two thousand years. Therefore, it is said that "this is precisely that time. "Shu" means "good.
The subsequent passages may be understood accordingly.

△ Now, the first: [Commentary Postscript]. The Sūtra says: "The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. An ancient said: "Recite the name of Amitābha of the Self-nature, and you shall be born [in the Pure Land]."

"The Land of Purity is Mind-Only. When one contemplates this in its entirety, the meaning becomes clear: "This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. Outside of the mind there is no Buddha; outside of the Buddha there is no mind.

Yet later generations failed to understand this. They abandoned the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss to speak separately of a "Mind-Only Pure Land," and they abandoned the World-Honored One of Ten Thousand Virtues and Compassion to speak separately of a "Self-Nature Amitābha. Is this not, in effect, to seek [the Buddha] outside of the mind?

There is a Buddha. Is there a mind outside of the Buddha? Master Lingfeng deeply awakened to the essence of the mind-nature which has no exterior, and specifically extracted this essential commentary for this sutra.
Upon opening it for the first time and reading it, one may personally grasp the ticket of faith, aspiration, and the holding of the Name.
Not only are its words concise and its meaning comprehensive, but it also causes this rare and most difficult school to be as [accessible as...].
The sounding of drums and gongs has opened the entirety of the scriptural treasury, leaving nothing hidden away; this is truly unprecedented in the history of past and present.
It is entitled *Yaojie* (Essential Explanations). Is this not indeed the supreme essence of the mind? This is respectfully recorded by the disciple of Pure Practice from Ancient Wu, Zhengzhi Qubing.

[Commentary] The text has two parts: first, clarifying the errors of later generations; second, praising the merits of this interpretation. Within the first part, there is first the citation of scriptural evidence, followed by the formal explanation.
The scripture states: "The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. This is a citation of the Buddha’s teaching.
This clarifies that all phenomena within the three realms of the Sahā world are solely mind.

When the ancients said, "Contemplate Amitābha of self-nature and be born in the Pure Land of the sole mind," they were citing the words of the Patriarchs to clarify that all phenomena within the three realms of Sukhāvatī are likewise solely mind.
Viewing these together, it means that both lands are manifestations of the sole mind and the sole consciousness.
Transformation. Since all things are manifested solely by the mind and transformed solely by consciousness, it is the mind that creates the Buddha, and the mind itself is the Buddha.
Outside the mind there is no Buddha; outside the Buddha there is no mind. It is like a vessel fashioned entirely from gold: the entire vessel is nothing but gold.
Outside of gold there is no vessel; outside of the vessel there is no gold. Thus, the principle that "the myriad dharmas are mind-only" is made clear. Second, the correct elucidation:
later generations fail to comprehend the intent that "it is this mind that creates the Buddha" and "this mind is the Buddha.

They abandon the Buddha-land of the Western [Pure Land], which is mind-only, and instead falsely grasp at the deluded thoughts of objective reflections as being the mind-only Buddha-land. Is this not a great pity?

To claim that there is a Buddha outside the mind or a mind outside the Buddha is like seeking gold apart from the vessel it is contained in; this would contradict the consensus of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Second, praising the attainment of this understanding: "Lingfeng" refers to Lingfeng on Mount Baimu in the north, which was the place where the Great Master left the household life.
"Deeply awakening that the nature of the mind has nothing external" means deeply awakening that the Sahā world [is not separate from the mind].
The Land of Ultimate Bliss does not exist outside the single thought-moment of the mind-nature, for the mind-nature fundamentally has no exterior.
To specifically extract the essential interpretation for this sutra is precisely to extract the essential interpretation of the mind that has no exterior.
Regarding faith, aspiration, and the holding of the Name—matters upon which a person can personally hold their own ticket—once one has believed that all phenomena are but mind, then...
The Land of Ultimate Bliss is the pure substance inherently present within one's own mind; the Sahā world is the defiled substance inherently present within one's own mind.
It is only right that the defilement of one's own mind be abandoned and the purity of one's own mind be embraced.

If this is so, then faith, aspiration, and the recitation of the name need not be earnestly and laboriously exhorted; every person can grasp their own ticket for themselves, as if holding a written contract in the palm of their hand.
Thus, it is logical that this defiled land of Sahā should be abandoned, and it is logical that the pure land of Sukhāvatī should be established.
Just as when a drum or gong is struck, it is rare and difficult to hear [the sound];

yet the principle of Mind-Only (Cittamātra) is like striking a drum or gong—the profound resonance fully manifests, completely opening the treasury of the *Cittamātra Sūtras* so that nothing remains hidden. This is truly unprecedented in the history of past and present.
This is a book. That which is titled *Yaojie* (Essential Explanations) refers to the explanations of the essential points of the unsurpassed mind. Zhengzhi is his given name;
Qubing is his style name; Shi is pronounced "Zhi" and means "to record."
